Two weeks before presentation she applied an over-the-counter medium-potency topical corticosteroid cream for presumed seborrhoea after the lesion appeared. She has no recent travel, no recent systemic antibiotics, and no known household members with a similar scalp problem.

Scalp scrapings and plucked hairs sent for direct microscopy with potassium hydroxide preparation show abundant arthroconidia coating the hair shafts and fragmented hairs, consistent with an ectothrix pattern. Full blood count is 7.9 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein is 16 mg/L. Routine bacterial culture of crusted material is negative.
Examination with a Wood's lamp in a darkened room produces bright green fluorescence of multiple affected hairs and adjacent scale within the lesion.

On further questioning she reports that she adopted a 3-month-old stray kitten from a local shelter 10 days before the scalp lesion began. The kitten has patchy alopecia and crusted lesions on the face. The shelter noted recent clusters of dermatologic disease among young cats.

explanation: The presentation is an inflammatory tinea capitis with broken hairs and crusting. Direct microscopy showing ectothrix arthroconidia and bright green Wood's lamp fluorescence point to a zoophilic dermatophyte that invades the hair shaft from outside. Recent close contact with an infected kitten identifies the most likely pathogen as Microsporum canis. Confirmation is by culture.

hints.text: A 29-year-old woman presents to a sexual health clinic with a 10-day history of vaginal irritation, intermittent malodorous discharge, and discomfort with intercourse. She describes a yellow-green discharge and mild dysuria; on speculum exam there is copious yellow-green discharge and diffuse vulvovaginal erythema, and she is afebrile.

She is otherwise healthy, not pregnant, and started a new male sexual partner about six weeks before symptom onset with inconsistent condom use. She had one prior episode of vaginitis treated empirically two years ago and reports no recent antibiotic use or overseas travel.

High vaginal pH is 5.2. Microscopy of vaginal fluid shows numerous polymorphonuclear leukocytes, no budding yeast on KOH, and no clue cells on wet prep. NAATs for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae are negative, and peripheral white cell count is 7.8 × 10^9/L.

Transvaginal ultrasound shows a normal-sized uterus and ovaries with no adnexal masses or tubo-ovarian abscess. There is no pelvic free fluid and the cervix appears structurally normal apart from superficial mucosal erythema.

Her male partner developed urethral discharge and was examined; microscopy of his urethral swab revealed motile, pear-shaped flagellated protozoa. He received partner treatment and his urethral symptoms resolved promptly.

explanation: Vaginal discharge with raised vaginal pH and abundant neutrophils with negative tests for yeast and common bacterial STIs points toward a non-bacterial, protozoan cause. Identification of motile, flagellated protozoa on the partner's urethral microscopy and the sexual exposure history confirm a sexually transmitted protozoan infection as the diagnosis for this patient.

hints.text: A 24-year-old man presents to an urban sexual health clinic with a 10-day history of a painless ulcer on the distal shaft of the penis. He reports no fever or dysuria, and examination shows a single well-demarcated clean-based ulcer about 1.2 cm in diameter and a firm, non-tender 2 cm left inguinal lymph node.

He is otherwise healthy, not on HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis, and had unprotected vaginal intercourse with a new partner three weeks before symptom onset. He denies prior sexually transmitted infection diagnoses and has not taken antibiotics since the exposure.

Dark-field microscopy of lesion exudate showed motile helical organisms with corkscrew motility. A non-specific antibody screening test returned reactive at a titre of 1:32, and a specific confirmatory serologic assay for the suspected pathogen was positive. Peripheral blood count WBC 6.8 × 10^9/L.
Ultrasound of the groin demonstrated multiple enlarged oval left inguinal lymph nodes, largest 2.1 cm, with preserved fatty hilum and increased vascularity but no fluid collection or abscess.
He later learned that the new partner developed a painless genital sore a few days after their encounter and was treated at another clinic with a single intramuscular dose of long-acting penicillin.

explanation: A painless genital chancre with non-tender regional lymphadenopathy, motile corkscrew organisms on dark-field microscopy, a reactive non-treponemal titre and a positive confirmatory serologic assay indicate infection with Treponema pallidum. The partner history and response to single-dose long-acting penicillin support this diagnosis.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 36 hours of fever, progressive confusion, and lightheadedness. He is febrile to 39.2°C, blood pressure 86/52 mmHg, pulse 118 min−1, and has a diffuse petechial rash on both lower limbs and a small area of erythema on the right forearm without obvious purulence.

Medical history is notable for splenectomy after motor vehicle trauma 12 years earlier and daily heavy alcohol use. He lives alone, works part time doing maintenance, and reports no chronic immunosuppressive medications.

Laboratory studies show leukocytes 2.3 × 10^9/L, platelets 42 × 10^9/L, lactate 5.8 mmol/L, creatinine 210 μmol/L, C-reactive protein 320 mg/L, and INR 2.1. Two sets of blood cultures flagged positive at 48 hours and Gram stain from broth reveals thin, fusiform Gram-negative rods.

Contrast CT of the head shows several small cortical and subcortical haemorrhagic lesions consistent with septic embolic infarcts. Ultrasound of the right forearm shows soft tissue oedema but no drainable fluid collection.
On further questioning the family reports he was bitten on the right forearm by a neighbour's dog three days before symptom onset; the puncture was small and he rinsed it at home.

explanation: Severe sepsis with petechiae, DIC, and septic emboli in an asplenic patient suggests a fulminant bacteremia. Growth of thin fusiform Gram-negative rods from blood cultures together with a recent dog bite points to a fastidious zoonotic organism transmitted by dog bites or saliva. These features make a dog-associated Gram-negative fusiform rod the most likely cause in this case.

hints.text: A 57-year-old man presented with two weeks of low-grade fevers, malaise, and progressive exertional dyspnoea. On arrival his temperature was 38.1°C and cardiac examination revealed a new grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla.

He has known mitral valve prolapse with chronic mild regurgitation diagnosed five years earlier and takes no regular cardiovascular medications. He denied intravenous drug use, recent indwelling lines, or recent respiratory infections.

Blood tests showed haemoglobin 102 g/L, white cell count 9.8 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 46 mg/L. Two of three sets of blood cultures became positive at 48 hours for gram-positive cocci in chains; colony growth on blood agar showed greenish alpha-haemolysis and the isolates were optochin-resistant.

Transoesophageal echocardiography demonstrated an 8 mm mobile vegetation attached to the atrial surface of the posterior mitral leaflet with new moderate mitral regurgitation and no periannular abscess.
The patient underwent a dental extraction for an abscessed molar 10 days before symptom onset and reported poor dentition without any antibiotic prophylaxis.

explanation: Subacute presentation with a new mitral regurgitant murmur, mobile mitral vegetation on TOE, and blood cultures growing alpha-haemolytic, optochin-resistant gram-positive cocci in chains after a recent dental procedure points to viridans streptococci endocarditis.

hints.text: A 54-year-old woman presents to the regional hospital with 3 weeks of persistent fevers, night sweats, increasing fatigue and a dry cough. On arrival she is febrile 38.4°C, heart rate 106/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, oxygen saturation 95% on room air, and examination shows a mechanical valve click with a new soft systolic murmur at the apex and mild right upper quadrant tenderness with palpable hepatomegaly.

She underwent mitral valve replacement with a mechanical prosthesis 18 months earlier and takes long-term anticoagulation. She has no history of intravenous drug use, recent dental procedures, or indwelling lines. Symptoms began while she was at home after a short stay away from the city two to five weeks earlier.

Laboratory testing shows white blood cell count 7.4 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 118 g/L, platelets 160 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 96 mg/L, ALT 156 U/L and AST 132 U/L. Three sets of aerobic and anaerobic blood cultures remained sterile after 7 days. Routine respiratory PCR panels and serology for common atypical respiratory pathogens were negative.

Transthoracic then transoesophageal echocardiography demonstrates a small, poorly mobile echodensity on the sewing ring of the mitral prosthesis with mild paravalvular regurgitation, findings judged suspicious for prosthetic valve infection. Chest radiograph shows a small right lower zone airspace opacity without cavitation.

On further questioning she reports assisting with lambing on a small mixed farm four weeks before symptom onset and handled placentas and bedding in an enclosed barn without respiratory protection; the household also consumed unpasteurised goat milk during that visit. This exposure raised suspicion for a zoonotic cause of culture-negative prosthetic valve endocarditis.

explanation: Culture-negative prosthetic valve endocarditis with concurrent atypical respiratory symptoms and transaminitis after close contact with parturient small ruminants strongly points to a zoonotic intracellular bacterial cause. The combination of sterile blood cultures, prosthetic valve involvement, and the specific farm exposures supports the diagnosis in this patient.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presented to a district hospital with three weeks of intermittent high fevers, worsening frontal headache, and increasing daytime sleepiness with nocturnal insomnia. He returned four weeks ago from a six-week agricultural project in rural central Africa; on exam temperature 38.6 C, a tender 3 cm posterior cervical lymph node, slowed speech, and a mildly broad-based gait were noted.

During the trip he slept in simple riverside huts and spent long days clearing brush along riverbanks. He had numerous insect bites, received routine vaccinations before travel, has no chronic illness, and tested HIV negative on screening performed on admission.

Full blood count showed haemoglobin 105 g/L, white cell count 13.2 × 10^9/L, platelets 210 × 10^9/L. Giemsa-stained peripheral blood film revealed motile extracellular flagellated protozoa with an undulating membrane and a single anterior flagellum, about 15–25 µm in length. Lumbar puncture produced CSF with 120 × 10^6/L nucleated cells (lymphocyte predominant), protein 1.2 g/L and glucose 2.2 mmol/L.

Brain MRI demonstrated diffuse T2 hyperintensity in periventricular white matter and basal ganglia with mild leptomeningeal enhancement, without focal abscess or restricted diffusion. Radiologic impression was meningoencephalitic involvement consistent with an infectious inflammatory process.

The patient recalled a painful daytime bite from a large horsefly-like insect while clearing brush, and a small tender ulcer formed at the site and healed over two weeks. Local health workers reported other villagers with progressive sleep disturbance and neurologic decline after identical exposures to that apparent tsetse fly habitat.

explanation: The combination of relapsing fevers, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, neurocognitive decline, motile extracellular flagellated protozoa on blood film, CSF pleocytosis, and a history of daytime bites in rural central Africa supports infection with Trypanosoma brucei.

hints.text: A 29-year-old man presents to a rural clinic with 3 months of progressive fatigue and exertional dyspnoea. He also reports intermittent crampy lower abdominal discomfort and two episodes of dark, loose stools; on exam he is pale, heart rate 108/min, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg with a 12 mmHg orthostatic systolic drop, and a tender erythematous papule on the plantar surface of his right foot.

He is a subsistence rice farmer who emigrated from northern India six months earlier and describes daily work barefoot in irrigated paddies. He denies menorrhagia or overt bleeding, took a 4-week course of oral iron prescribed by a primary clinician without symptomatic improvement, and has no chronic medical conditions or regular medications.

Full blood count shows haemoglobin 82 g/L, MCV 68 fL, platelet count 420 × 10^9/L, white cell count 12.1 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.6 × 10^9/L. Serum ferritin 8 µg/L and transferrin saturation is low. Two separate stool tests are positive for fecal occult blood.

A chest radiograph obtained for an intermittent dry cough shows a patchy right lower zone air‑space opacity; the finding resolved on a follow-up radiograph two weeks later. Abdominal ultrasound shows no structural cause for blood loss.

He reports handling fresh human night soil used as fertiliser at the fields and sometimes eating uncooked greens from those plots. He brought a 1 cm pale threadlike object he noticed in his stool; duodenal aspirate and stool concentration recovered adult worms whose buccal capsules contained a pair of prominent oral teeth and numerous thin-shelled ovoid eggs on microscopy.

explanation: Progressive microcytic anaemia with low ferritin, eosinophilia, transient pulmonary infiltrates and barefoot exposure in an endemic region point to an intestinal blood‑feeding nematode. Visualization of adults with prominent oral teeth in duodenal aspirate confirms Ancylostoma duodenale as the cause of the chronic blood loss and anaemia.

hints.text: A 48-year-old woman presents to the transplant clinic 13 months after a deceased-donor kidney transplant with 3 weeks of progressive oliguria, fatigue and new peripheral oedema. Her blood pressure is 155/95 mmHg and temperature 37.8°C; the transplanted kidney is mildly tender on palpation. Her baseline serum creatinine since discharge was 90 µmol/L, now 320 µmol/L.

She takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil and prednisone for maintenance immunosuppression. Five months ago she had an acute cellular rejection treated with high-dose corticosteroids. She reports no recent urinary tract instrumentation, no current dysuria or obstructive symptoms, and no recent aminoglycosides or radiographic contrast exposure.

Serum WBC 6.5 × 10^9/L, CRP 14 mg/L. Urinalysis shows 1+ protein, microscopic haematuria and pyuria. Urine culture is sterile at 48 hours. Serum creatinine is 320 µmol/L and tacrolimus trough is within the previously targeted range.

Doppler ultrasound of the allograft demonstrates preserved arterial flow and no hydronephrosis. The cortex is diffusely echogenic and the resistive index is 0.82, findings more suggestive of an intrinsic parenchymal process than obstructive uropathy.

Routine transplant surveillance urine nucleic-acid test returns 7.4 × 10^6 copies/mL of viral DNA and plasma viral DNA is 3.8 × 10^4 copies/mL. Urine cytology shows epithelial cells with markedly enlarged hyperchromatic intranuclear inclusions consistent with reactivation of a latent urinary tract virus after immunosuppression.

explanation: A renal allograft recipient with rising creatinine, sterile pyuria, high-level viruria and viraemia and viral cytopathic changes is most consistent with BK virus nephropathy from reactivation under immunosuppression.

hints.text: A 34-year-old right-handed man presented to the emergency department 48 hours after progressive pain and swelling of the dorsum of his right hand. He was febrile to 38.3°C, had a 1-cm puncture wound over the second metacarpophalangeal joint, marked tenderness with tense soft-tissue swelling, and reduced active extension of the index finger.

He was previously healthy, worked as a bartender, smoked about 10 cigarettes per day and drank alcohol socially. He denied diabetes, HIV risk factors, recent dental procedures, immunosuppressive therapy, or prior antibiotics for this problem; he waited two days before seeking care because symptoms seemed minor at first.

White blood cell count 13.8 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 110 mg/L. Purulent fluid aspirated from the wound showed numerous polymorphonuclear leukocytes and a small number of thin gram-negative bacilli on Gram stain; aerobic cultures produced pinpoint, slow-growing colonies after 48 hours.

Plain radiographs demonstrated soft-tissue swelling without gas. MRI of the hand revealed fluid tracking in the extensor tendon sheath of the index finger and cortical irregularity at the second metacarpal consistent with early osteomyelitis.

On repeat history he admitted to a bar altercation three days earlier during which his knuckle contacted another person’s mouth. The isolate from the wound was a fastidious, slow-growing gram-negative bacillus that was resistant to clindamycin and metronidazole yet susceptible to ampicillin and third-generation cephalosporins.

explanation: A clenched-fist (human bite) injury with progressive hand cellulitis, tenosynovitis and early osteomyelitis plus a fastidious gram-negative bacillus from the wound that is resistant to clindamycin points to an oral-flora pathogen commonly implicated in human bite infections. The growth pattern and susceptibility profile make that organism the most likely cause in this clinical context.

hints.text: A 54-year-old woman presents to clinic with six months of progressive fatigue, intermittent right upper quadrant discomfort, and new numbness and burning in the soles of both feet. On examination she has scattered palpable purpura over the lower legs and mild, non-tender hepatomegaly; blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, no fever, gait preserved.

She reports a history of an emergency blood transfusion after a road traffic collision in 1991 and denies intravenous drug use or heavy alcohol consumption. She has had years of intermittent joint pains and noted darkening of urine several times in the past year, but never required hospital admission for liver disease.

Blood tests show ALT 120 U/L and AST 95 U/L, platelet count 120 × 10^9/L, creatinine 130 μmol/L. Complement C4 is low at 0.06 g/L, rheumatoid factor elevated, and serum cryoglobulins are detected; urinalysis shows proteinuria of 1.4 g/day with microscopic haematuria.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates a heterogenous, slightly nodular liver contour with a 15 cm spleen and mild portal hypertension. Transient elastography measures liver stiffness 16.5 kPa, consistent with advanced fibrosis.

Serology returned reactive for antibody against a blood-borne hepatotropic single-stranded RNA virus and nucleic acid amplification detected viral RNA at 2.3 × 10^6 IU/mL. The combination of the remote transfusion exposure and positive serology with detectable viraemia provides the specific infectious link to her chronic liver disease and systemic immune-complex manifestations.

explanation: The picture is chronic infection with a blood-borne hepatotropic single-stranded RNA virus acquired by transfusion decades earlier. Ongoing viraemia with elevated transaminases and elastography-proven fibrosis explains the hepatomegaly and portal hypertension. Low C4, positive cryoglobulins, palpable purpura, neuropathy and proteinuric renal involvement reflect immune-complex mediated disease from chronic infection.

hints.text: A 28-year-old woman presents to the sexual health clinic with 5 days of increased vaginal discharge and a noticeable malodour that she first noticed after her last period. She has mild vulvar pruritus but no fever or dysuria, is afebrile and hemodynamically stable. On pelvic examination there is a thin, homogenous greyish discharge coating the vaginal walls, the cervix is non-tender and there is no adnexal tenderness.

She completed a 7-day course of oral amoxicillin for sinusitis 2 weeks ago and reports intermittent vaginal douching. She has a new male sexual partner this month and uses condoms inconsistently. No history of recent sexually transmitted infection, not pregnant, no intrauterine device in place.

Vaginal pH measured 5.2. A KOH whiff test produced a fishy odour. Wet mount microscopy shows numerous epithelial cells with small bacteria obscuring cell borders, only sparse polymorphonuclear leukocytes and no motile protozoa. Gram stain of the secretion demonstrates many small gram-variable coccobacillary organisms adherent to epithelial cells with reduced lactobacillary morphotypes.
Transvaginal ultrasound was obtained to exclude pelvic inflammatory disease and shows a normal-sized uterus and ovaries, no free pelvic fluid and no tubo-ovarian complex.
She was prescribed oral metronidazole and reported marked reduction of malodour and discharge within 48 hours, with near complete resolution at one week follow-up.

explanation: Rapid improvement with oral nitroimidazole supports that diagnosis and the absence of motile protozoa on wet mount argues against trichomoniasis.

hints.text: A 56-year-old man presented to hospital with 5 days of fever, progressive dyspnoea and a dry cough. He became increasingly breathless and arrived hypoxic, SpO2 88% on room air and respiratory rate 28/min, with bilateral inspiratory crackles on chest auscultation.

He has type 2 diabetes and well controlled hypertension. He reported an initial influenza-like illness with myalgias and fever, was given oral antibiotics in primary care three days before admission and deteriorated despite treatment; he had no known immunosuppressive therapy.

Full blood count showed leukocytes 6.2 × 10^9/L with lymphocytes 0.7 × 10^9/L and platelets 120 × 10^9/L. Serum creatinine rose from a baseline of 95 μmol/L to 220 μmol/L, CRP 150 mg/L, and ALT 95 U/L. Blood cultures remained sterile and an upper respiratory PCR panel was negative for influenza and RSV.

Portable chest radiograph showed bilateral patchy airspace consolidation. Contrast CT chest demonstrated multilobar peripheral ground-glass opacities with areas of consolidation and small bilateral pleural effusions, changes that progressed over 48 hours toward acute respiratory distress.

When asked further, he recalled a 10-day work trip to the Arabian Peninsula two weeks before admission during which he visited a live animal market and handled dromedary camels. Lower respiratory tract PCR returned positive for the same virus linked to severe pneumonia clusters in that region following camel exposure.

explanation: Severe febrile pneumonia with hypoxaemia, lymphopenia and acute kidney injury in a patient who recently travelled to the Arabian Peninsula with dromedary exposure points to Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus infection. The negative influenza/RSV tests, progression to ARDS on imaging and a positive lower respiratory PCR for the regionally linked virus support this diagnosis.

hints.text: A 47-year-old man presented to the outpatient clinic with ten weeks of profuse watery diarrhoea and an 8 kg weight loss. He reports up to eight watery stools per day with nocturnal urgency and progressive fatigue, and on examination he was afebrile with dry mucous membranes and mild temporal muscle wasting.

He received a deceased-donor kidney transplant nine months earlier and remains on tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil and prednisone. He had treatment for acute rejection three months ago with high-dose corticosteroids and denies recent antibiotic use or foreign travel.

Stool bacterial culture and Clostridioides difficile toxin were negative. Standard ova and parasite microscopy on three separate specimens did not show helminths or protozoa. Twenty-four hour faecal fat was increased at 18 g/day, haemoglobin 110 g/L, white cell count 4.2 × 10^9/L and lymphocytes 0.6 × 10^9/L, CRP 12 mg/L.

CT enterography demonstrated diffuse mild thickening of jejunal and proximal ileal folds with increased luminal fluid and mucosal enhancement. The colon and terminal ileum appeared normal and there was no obstructing lesion.

Empiric oral ciprofloxacin and metronidazole for two weeks produced no clinical change. A 14-day course of oral albendazole resulted in marked reduction in stool frequency within ten days and weight stabilisation by two weeks.

explanation: An immunosuppressed solid-organ transplant recipient with chronic watery diarrhoea, negative routine stool tests, small-bowel mucosal disease and fat malabsorption who improves rapidly with albendazole most consistent with infection by microsporidian parasites. The combination of the clinical context, negative standard diagnostics, and specific antiparasitic response supports microsporidia as the likely pathogen.

hints.text: A 47-year-old man presents to dermatology with a three-month history of slowly progressive skin lesions on both lower legs and increasing swelling of the left foot that limits his ability to walk. He is afebrile, pulse 82/min, and exam shows multiple discrete purple-red macules and raised nodules 0.5–2.5 cm clustered around the ankles and dorsum of the left foot with non-pitting oedema of the left foot.

He has seropositive rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate and low-dose prednisone for four years. He reports 5 kg weight loss over three months, intermittent night sweats, and no recent new medications or skin trauma.

Blood tests show haemoglobin 110 g/L, white blood cells 6.3 × 10^9/L, platelets 210 × 10^9/L. CRP 12 mg/L. Hepatitis B and C serology negative. HIV antibody test negative. A punch biopsy of a leg lesion was sent to pathology.

CT thorax performed for cough shows multiple ill-defined peribronchovascular nodules in both lungs and small bilateral pleural effusions. Flexible bronchoscopy notes several friable, vascular-appearing plaques on the bronchial mucosa.

He emigrated from East Africa 16 years ago and reports no recent travel. Skin biopsy demonstrates a spindle cell vascular proliferation with slit-like vascular spaces and red cell extravasation, and immunohistochemistry reveals strong nuclear staining of lesional cells for a viral latent nuclear antigen.

explanation: The cutaneous purple nodules, unilateral lymphoedema, pulmonary mucosal plaques, and spindle cell vascular lesion with nuclear staining for a viral latent antigen point to Kaposi sarcoma driven by human herpesvirus 8 infection, facilitated here by chronic immunosuppression.

hints.text: A 68-year-old man presented to urgent clinic with four days of progressively purulent cough, increased dyspnoea on exertion, and low-grade fever. On examination he was afebrile at recheck, respiratory rate 22/min, oxygen saturation 91% on room air, with diffuse expiratory wheeze and coarse crackles at the bases; he reported inability to complete his usual walk at home because of breathlessness.

He has known COPD treated with tiotropium and a long-acting β2-agonist, and a 40 pack-year smoking history; no prior bronchiectasis or recent hospital admissions. Three weeks earlier his preschool-aged granddaughter had a prolonged upper respiratory illness and several household contacts developed purulent conjunctivitis; the patient completed a five-day course of oral amoxicillin for presumed sinusitis two weeks before this presentation.

Peripheral blood showed white cell count 12.8 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance and C-reactive protein 68 mg/L. Sputum microscopy revealed many neutrophils and mixed bacterial flora; an aerobic culture grew a moderate amount of a non-fastidious gram-negative organism, identification pending. Blood cultures were negative after 48 hours.

Chest radiograph demonstrated peribronchial cuffing and patchy, bilateral perihilar air-space opacities without a dense lobar consolidation. Non-contrast CT showed bronchitic changes with centrilobular nodules and small peribronchial infiltrates, no cavitation and no focal abscess.

He was started empirically on oral amoxicillin with minimal clinical improvement after 48 hours. Final microbiology reported oxidase-positive gram-negative diplococci from the sputum that produced a beta-lactamase, were resistant to penicillin, and were susceptible to amoxicillin with clavulanate and doxycycline; after switching to amoxicillin with clavulanate the patient defervesced and sputum production and dyspnoea improved over 72 hours.

explanation: An older patient with COPD presenting with increased purulent sputum and bronchitic imaging suggests a bacterial COPD exacerbation or bronchopneumonia. The sputum isolate described as oxidase-positive gram-negative diplococci that produce beta-lactamase and. Recent household exposure to children with mucosal infections and recent amoxicillin use support selection of a beta-lactamase producing respiratory coloniser.

hints.text: A 38-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 10 days of progressive fatigue, dark urine and jaundice. He reports right upper quadrant discomfort and one episode of vomiting. On examination he is afebrile, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, heart rate 96/min, scleral icterus is present and the liver is palpable 4 cm below the right costal margin and tender to palpation.

He was diagnosed with chronic hepatitis B infection six years ago and has not received antiviral therapy. He drinks alcohol only occasionally and has no recent travel history. He reports intermittent injection drug use and has had multiple sexual partners in the past year.

Laboratory tests show ALT 1 450 U/L, AST 1 300 U/L, total bilirubin 220 µmol/L and INR 2.1. White cell count is 6.2 × 10^9/L and platelets 130 × 10^9/L. Serology is HBsAg positive with anti-HBc IgG positive and HBV DNA 350 IU/mL. Tests for acute hepatitis A IgM and hepatitis C RNA are negative.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates an enlarged liver without focal lesion, normal-appearing biliary tree and patent portal and hepatic veins. There is small-volume ascites and no biliary dilation to suggest obstructive jaundice.

He acknowledges recent needle sharing and unprotected sexual contact with a male partner known to be HBsAg positive. The partner developed abrupt severe hepatitis a few weeks earlier after acquiring an additional blood-borne agent that can only assemble an envelope in the presence of hepatitis B surface antigen.

explanation: A patient with established HBsAg positivity who develops acute severe transaminitis and coagulopathy with relatively low HBV DNA suggests superimposed injury from another agent. The exposure history of parenteral and sexual contact with an HBsAg-positive partner and the note that the agent needs hepatitis B surface antigen to form its envelope point to a satellite RNA virus that causes severe acute hepatitis in HBV-infected hosts.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man presented to the emergency department with three weeks of productive cough, intermittent low-grade fevers and a 6 kg weight loss, and with new progressive headache and confusion for 48 hours. On arrival he was febrile to 38.3°C, RR 22/min, oxygen saturation 93% on room air. Chest auscultation revealed reduced breath sounds and coarse crackles over the left upper zone. Neurological exam showed mild expressive aphasia and 4/5 power in the right upper limb.

Medical history notable for polymyalgia rheumatica treated with oral prednisolone 20 mg daily for four months. He had received two courses of oral amoxicillin in the community without clinical improvement. He has no known HIV infection and no diabetes. He is otherwise independent in activities of daily living.

Admission blood tests showed WBC 14.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance and CRP 92 mg/L. Blood cultures remained sterile at 72 hours. Sputum Gram stain demonstrated branching filamentous gram-positive organisms. A modified acid-fast stain of the same specimen showed faint, variable retention of carbol fuchsin within the filaments.

Contrast CT thorax revealed a 5 cm left upper lobe consolidation with central cavitation and several adjacent nodules. Contrast MRI brain identified a 2.5 cm ring-enhancing lesion in the left frontal lobe with surrounding oedema and mild mass effect, radiologically most consistent with an abscess.

On further questioning he described regular work in his garden, turning compost and clearing damp beds in the months before illness. He recalled a thorn puncture to his left index finger about eight weeks earlier that produced a small slowly draining papule before healing.

explanation: Corticosteroid-treated patient with cavitating pulmonary disease and a solitary ring-enhancing cerebral abscess raises disseminated infection from an environmental filamentous bacterium. The sputum shows branching gram-positive filaments with weak, variable retention on a modified acid-fast stain and there is a history of soil exposure with a puncture wound, findings most consistent with Nocardia asteroides.

hints.text: A 29-year-old man presented to the sexual health clinic with a 6-day history of fever, myalgias and a painful papulopustular eruption on his hands and forearms. He noted 12 discrete lesions, several involving the palms. Examination revealed a tender 3 cm left inguinal lymph node and temperature 38.2°C.

He is living with HIV and has been on antiretroviral therapy for 5 years, with an undetectable viral load and a CD4 count of 0.58 × 10^9/L recorded two months earlier. He reports two new male sexual partners at a crowded outdoor event 10 days before symptom onset. He denies recent travel, rodent or pet contact, and does not recall prior smallpox vaccination.

PCR assays from a lesion were negative for herpes simplex virus and varicella zoster virus. Bacterial culture of lesion material showed no growth after 48 hours. Complete blood count showed leukocytes 5.2 × 10^9/L with lymphocytes 0.9 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein was 32 mg/L.

Close clinical photographs show multiple firm, deep-seated pustules with central crusting and surrounding erythema. Lesions at several sites are at similar stages of evolution and a few show a subtle central depression on careful inspection. No oropharyngeal mucosal lesions were photographed.

Contact tracing identified several other attendees of the same event who developed similar febrile illness with cutaneous lesions after intimate skin-to-skin contact. Electron microscopy of a lesion crust demonstrated large brick-shaped viral particles and PCR of lesion material was positive for a large double-stranded DNA virus consistent with poxvirus morphology.

explanation: The combination of a febrile prodrome, painful deep-seated pustular lesions including palms, prominent regional lymphadenopathy, recent intimate skin contact at a mass gathering, and detection of large brick-shaped virions on electron microscopy points to infection with Mpox virus. Negative HSV and VZV PCR and sterile bacterial cultures make those alternatives less likely.

hints.text: A 56-year-old woman presented to clinic with a 6-month history of daily productive cough, intermittent low-grade fevers and a 7 kg unintentional weight loss. She reports increasing exertional dyspnoea and reduced exercise tolerance; on exam she had inspiratory crackles at the right midlung field and oxygen saturation 96% on room air.

She is a lifelong non-smoker with no known tuberculosis contact and no systemic immunosuppression. She has a prior diagnosis of non-cystic bronchiectasis made 4 years earlier after recurrent chest infections and has had several partial responses to repeated oral antibiotic courses.

Three separate expectorated sputum specimens showed acid-fast bacilli on Ziehl-Neelsen staining. A rapid nucleic acid amplification test for the tuberculosis complex was negative. Haemoglobin 110 g/L, white cell count 8.6 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 22 mg/L.

High-resolution CT chest demonstrates multifocal cylindrical bronchiectasis with numerous small centrilobular nodules and tree-in-bud change most pronounced in the right middle lobe and lingula, without large cavitary lesions.

The patient lives in a rural house, refills backyard bird feeders weekly and showers using untreated well water. After four weeks of incubation on specialised solid medium multiple sputum cultures grew a slow-growing, non-pigmented acid-fast organism; molecular sequencing matched environmental species commonly recovered from household water and bird-associated samples and the isolate was clarithromycin-susceptible.

explanation: Chronic nodular bronchiectatic disease focused in the middle lobe and lingula, repeated AFB-positive but tuberculosis PCR-negative sputum, culture of a slow-growing environmental acid-fast organism, and bird/water exposure point to pulmonary infection with Mycobacterium avium complex. The clinical pattern, imaging distribution and clarithromycin susceptibility support this diagnosis rather than tuberculosis or rapidly growing environmental species.

hints.text: A 10-month-old previously well infant is brought to the emergency department after a first-time generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. Parents report 18 hours of high fever with measured Tmax 40.2°C; on arrival the child is febrile 39.0°C, alert and consolable, with a soft anterior fontanelle and no focal neurological deficit. The seizure lasted about 90 seconds and the child returned to baseline within 15 minutes.

The infant attends a busy daycare and has two older siblings at home. Both siblings had brief febrile illnesses in the preceding month; there was no recent travel, no known toxin exposure, and no chronic medical conditions or immunodeficiency in the infant. Routine immunisations are up to date.

Blood tests show WBC 8.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 3.8 × 10^9/L and lymphocytes 3.2 × 10^9/L, CRP 5 mg/L. Serum electrolytes and glucose are normal. Lumbar puncture produced clear cerebrospinal fluid with 2 leukocytes × 10^6/L, protein 0.18 g/L and glucose 3.8 mmol/L.

Non-contrast head CT performed because of the prolonged seizure shows no acute intracranial abnormality. Subsequent bedside EEG demonstrates no epileptiform focus, only transient diffuse slowing that resolves as the child is observed and remains clinically well.

On hospital day 2, as the fever resolved, a blanching pink maculopapular rash appeared over the trunk and neck and spared the face; the rash faded over 48 hours. Parents report that one older sibling had an almost identical brief febrile illness two weeks earlier with a similar rash that appeared as the fever broke.

explanation: A previously healthy infant under 2 with several days of high fever provoking a febrile seizure, normal inflammatory markers and CSF, and the characteristic defervescence-associated trunk-centred rash with household spread point to primary infection with Human herpesvirus 6. The clinical course and contact history make invasive bacterial meningitis or other exanthematous viral infections less likely.

hints.text: A 57-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with 48 hours of rapidly worsening pain and swelling of her right hand. She reported progressive redness and inability to straighten her fingers, had temperature 38.6°C and pulse 105/min, and exam showed a tense, erythematous dorsal hand with a 1 cm puncture wound over the second metacarpal and marked tenderness along the flexor tendons.

Her medical history included type 2 diabetes treated with metformin with recent home blood glucose readings around 14–16 mmol/L. She cares for an indoor cat and initially denied any bite or scratch but described routine close contact while cleaning the animal's carrier.

Blood tests showed white cell count 14.2 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 186 mg/L. A wound Gram stain demonstrated numerous neutrophils and small pleomorphic Gram-negative coccobacilli; aerobic cultures were pending.

Ultrasound of the hand revealed a 2.5 cm complex fluid collection in the deep palmar space tracking along the flexor tendon sheath without radiographic evidence of foreign body or gas on plain film. The surgical team proceeded to incision and drainage.

On reinterview the patient recalled that two days before symptom onset the cat bit her dorsal hand while she was separating it from a trapped mouse. The surgical wound culture grew small, rapidly appearing colonies on blood agar within 24 hours that were identified by MALDI-TOF as the likely isolate and showed susceptibility to penicillin and ampicillin.

explanation: Rapid cellulitis and an abscess after a cat bite, recovery of small pleomorphic Gram-negative coccobacilli from the wound, and penicillin susceptibility make Pasteurella multocida the most likely pathogen.

hints.text: A 29-year-old previously healthy man presents with 6 days of intermittent fevers, drenching night sweats, progressive fatigue, headache and myalgia. He reports dark urine and mild jaundice. On examination temperature is 38.9°C, heart rate 110/min, conjunctival pallor is present and the spleen is palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin.

He has no chronic medical conditions and takes no regular medications. He describes a brief, self-limited febrile illness while living overseas about eight months ago that was not fully investigated and resolved without a documented diagnosis.

Blood tests show haemoglobin 88 g/L, leukocytes 4.0 × 10^9/L, platelets 110 × 10^9/L, total bilirubin 45 µmol/L and lactate dehydrogenase 420 U/L. Peripheral blood film demonstrates low parasitaemia at approximately 0.3% with ring-stage parasites and infected erythrocytes that are mildly enlarged with fine stippling and occasional oval-shaped infected cells with slightly irregular margins.
Abdominal ultrasound shows moderate splenomegaly with a maximal bipolar length of 14 cm and no focal hepatic lesions or collections.

He spent three months working in rural western sub-Saharan Africa starting ten months ago, sleeping without bed nets and without taking malaria chemoprophylaxis. He recalls the earlier febrile episode occurred while living there and the current illness began months after that event.

explanation: The combination of travel to western sub-Saharan Africa, a prior unexplained febrile illness followed months later by recurrent fevers, low-density parasitaemia with enlarged oval erythrocytes and fine stippling, and splenomegaly points to relapsing malaria due to a species that forms dormant hepatic stages. These features most consistently support infection with Plasmodium ovale in this clinical context.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man presented to a community clinic with a 3-week history of intense pruritus and a new papular rash on his trunk and shoulders. He reports worse itching at night and poor sleep; on examination there are numerous excoriated erythematous papules concentrated beneath clothing edges and a temperature of 37.8°C.

He is unemployed and has been sleeping intermittently in a crowded overnight shelter for the past two months after losing his flat, with limited access to laundry facilities and wearing the same heavy coat most days. He denies recent travel, sexual contacts with similar symptoms, or use of new topical products.

Full blood count shows haemoglobin 102 g/L, MCV 76 fL, WBC 8.9 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 6.0 × 10^9/L, platelets 320 × 10^9/L. C reactive protein 6 mg/L. Iron studies show low ferritin 9 μg/L. Bacterial swab from an excoriation grew mixed skin flora.

Clinical photographs taken in clinic show grouped and linear excoriated papules concentrated along the waistline, axillary folds and beneath shoulder straps, with no mucosal involvement or generalized urticarial eruption.

Inspection of the patient’s coat revealed multiple small flattened wingless insects about 2–3 mm long clinging to fabric seams and numerous oval translucent eggs firmly attached to the threads; removal and high-heat laundering of the coat led to rapid cessation of new bites.

explanation: The combination of pruritic papules clustered at points of clothing contact, recent prolonged use of the same outer garment in a crowded shelter, iron deficiency consistent with chronic blood feeding, and direct observation of small wingless insects and eggs on clothing indicate infestation with the human body louse, Pediculus humanus corporis.

hints.text: A 34-year-old farmer with 9 months of severe pruritus and progressive hypopigmented, lichenified patches on both lower legs. He sleeps poorly and reports 2 months of blurred vision in the left eye. Exam shows multiple excoriations and a 2 cm mobile subcutaneous nodule on the right thigh.
No chronic disease or immunosuppression. Treated with topical corticosteroids and oral antihistamines without improvement. Family members in village had similar skin problems.
Eosinophils 0.9 × 10^9/L. Skin snip microscopy demonstrates motile microfilariae in superficial dermal tissue.
Ultrasound of the thigh nodule shows a 2.1 cm tubular hypoechoic structure with internal movement suggestive of a living nematode within a subcutaneous mass.
Patient lived beside a fast-flowing river in West Africa until 1 year ago and reported frequent bites from small riverine flies while farming. Several neighbours had nodules and visual problems.

explanation: Dermal microfilariae on skin snip, a subcutaneous nodular adult worm, chronic pruritic dermatosis and progressive ocular involvement after riverine fly exposure point to infection with Onchocerca volvulus.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man presents to clinic with a 3-week history of intermittent, pruritic swellings of his forearms and two recent episodes of right eyelid swelling with foreign body sensation and blurred vision. The swellings appear suddenly, migrate over several hours, and then partly resolve; on examination temperature is 37.3°C, there is a 3 cm tender, mobile subcutaneous swelling on the flexor surface of the right forearm and mild conjunctival injection of the right eye.

He is otherwise fit, takes no regular medications and is HIV negative. Symptoms began about 6 months ago, recur every few weeks and last 24 to 48 hours, and have not responded to short courses of oral antihistamine or cephalexin taken for presumed cellulitis.

Full blood count shows leukocytes 13.0 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 3.6 × 10^9/L. A midday peripheral blood film and fresh wet mount demonstrate numerous motile, sheathed microfilariae, density approximately 9.2 × 10^3 per mL.

Slit-lamp examination and high-resolution ultrasound of the right orbit performed while symptomatic show a 4 cm linear, motile, tubular echogenic structure in the subconjunctival space that moved inferiorly into the upper eyelid between images.

On detailed travel history he reports a 10-month period working at river-side logging camps in the rainforest of central West Africa, with frequent painful daytime horsefly bites while clearing vegetation near streams.

explanation: Migratory subcutaneous swellings and transient eyelid involvement with marked eosinophilia and high-density, daytime microfilaremia after repeated painful daytime horsefly bites in central African rainforest point to infection with the filarial parasite Loa loa. Visualization of a motile adult worm in the subconjunctival space confirms an adult filarial migration and explains the episodic clinical flares.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man who lives in a long-term care facility presented with 48 hours of progressive left flank pain and fever. He reported cloudy urine from his indwelling urinary catheter and had reduced urine output; on examination T 38.6°C, heart rate 102/min, and left costovertebral angle tenderness.

He has a cervical spinal cord injury and has had an indwelling urethral catheter for 6 months. He has had several treated urinary tract infections over the past year and completed multiple courses of oral antibiotics, most recently cefalexin 3 weeks ago.

Urinalysis showed leukocyte esterase positive, 60 to 80 white cells per high-power field, and urine pH 8.6. Peripheral blood count demonstrated a white blood cell count 14.2 × 10^9/L and serum creatinine 160 μmol/L. Urine culture grew >10^5 CFU/mL of a gram-negative bacillus; final identification pending.

Non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder showed a large branching calculus occupying the left renal pelvis and calyces with obstructive hydronephrosis and surrounding inflammatory change consistent with an infected obstructing stone.

During percutaneous nephrolithotomy the removed stone and catheter tip were cultured. The laboratory reported a strongly urease-positive, non-lactose-fermenting, highly motile gram-negative bacillus with a characteristic swarming pattern on solid media and intrinsic resistance to nitrofurantoin.

explanation: This patient with long-term catheter use, alkaline urine, and a staghorn/branching infected stone, together with isolation of a urease-positive, swarming non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative bacillus that is nitrofurantoin-resistant, is most consistent with Proteus mirabilis. Urease activity explains the high urine pH and formation of infection-related renal calculi in this setting.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 6 days of fever, frontal headache, diffuse myalgias and progressive malaise. He is an informal market vendor in a coastal city and developed a faint erythematous maculopapular rash over his trunk on day 4, temperature 39.0°C, heart rate 104/min, and he reported difficulty working because of fatigue.

He has no chronic medical conditions, takes no regular medications, and is not immunosuppressed. He denied recent antibiotic use, had not travelled outside the region in the preceding month, and denied tick bites or new sexual contacts; several neighbours and co‑workers had nonspecific febrile illnesses recently.

Blood tests showed white cell count 3.8 × 10^9/L, platelet count 95 × 10^9/L, sodium 129 mmol/L, AST 142 U/L, ALT 110 U/L and C-reactive protein 48 mg/L. Blood cultures remained sterile at 48 hours and a malaria smear was negative.
Chest radiograph was unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated mild hepatomegaly with a spleen measuring 13.5 cm and no focal fluid collection.

On further questioning he said he had been feeding a stray cat near the market two weeks before illness and had removed numerous fleas from the animal; he also noted an increased number of rats around his boarding house during the same interval.

explanation: The combination of subacute febrile illness with a trunk-predominant maculopapular rash, thrombocytopenia, mild transaminitis, hyponatraemia and splenomegaly points to a flea-borne rickettsial infection. Recent contact with a flea-infested stray cat and rodent activity makes Rickettsia typhi the most likely pathogen in this patient. Confirmation is by specific PCR or paired serology, and empiric doxycycline should be started without delay.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presents with three months of progressive fatigue, intermittent crampy lower abdominal pain, and episodes of bloody diarrhoea. He returned home two weeks ago after seasonal work abroad. Temperature 37.6°C, heart rate 92/min. On examination he is pale with mild scleral icterus, a liver edge palpable 4 cm below the right costal margin and a spleen palpable 6 cm below the left costal margin.

He spent the prior year doing agricultural work in East Asia and had several outpatient courses of antibiotics for presumed bacterial gastroenteritis without sustained benefit. He has no known chronic liver disease and tested HIV negative three months earlier. He recalls intermittent pruritic papular rashes after outdoor work but denies intravenous drug use or recent blood transfusion.

Full blood count shows haemoglobin 90 g/L, platelets 95 × 10^9/L, white cell count 8.5 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.6 × 10^9/L. Liver tests reveal ALT 82 U/L, AST 76 U/L, albumin 32 g/L and INR 1.3. Stool bacterial cultures and Clostridioides difficile toxin are negative, faecal occult blood is positive.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates hepatomegaly with prominent hyperechoic bands tracking along the portal tracts consistent with periportal fibrosis. The portal vein is dilated to 15 mm and there are multiple splenic and perigastric collateral veins. No biliary dilatation or focal hepatic mass is seen.

On detailed history he describes frequent wading and bathing in slow-moving irrigation canals and flooded rice paddies in rural eastern China during the wet season. Concentration stool microscopy performed at the regional reference laboratory recovered numerous small ovoid trematode eggs.

explanation: Chronic intestinal bleeding with portal hypertension and splenomegaly, peripheral eosinophilia, periportal fibrosis on imaging, and a history of freshwater exposure in endemic East Asia point to an intestinal trematode acquired from contaminated water. Recovery of numerous small ovoid fluke eggs in stool confirms an egg-producing schistosome infection as the unifying diagnosis for this presentation.

hints.text: A 68-year-old woman presents to clinic with a 3-week history of low-grade fevers, night sweats and worsening fatigue. She reports new exertional dyspnoea and unintentional 4 kg weight loss over two months, and on examination has temperature 38.2°C, heart rate 94/min and a new grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur at the apex; there is no skin rash or peripheral stigmata of chronic liver disease.

Her past medical history includes long-standing iron deficiency anaemia managed with oral iron and hypertension. She has had several months of constipation and occasional dark stools that she did not previously seek care for. She is not diabetic, takes no immunosuppressants, and had a dental scaling two months prior.

Laboratory tests show haemoglobin 95 g/L, white cell count 11.8 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 45 mg/L. Two sets of blood cultures drawn on separate occasions flagged positive after about 30 hours, yielding small catalase-negative Gram-positive cocci in chains that produced alpha-haemolysis on blood agar and were penicillin-susceptible.

Transoesophageal echocardiography demonstrates a 10 mm mobile vegetation on the posterior mitral leaflet with mild regurgitation. MRI of the lumbar spine obtained for persistent lower back pain shows L3–L4 vertebral osteomyelitis with a small adjacent paravertebral phlegmon.

Because of iron deficiency and occult bleeding the patient underwent colonoscopy which found a fungating lesion in the sigmoid colon; biopsy confirmed moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma. Cultures from the resected colonic tissue grew the same alpha-haemolytic Gram-positive cocci as the blood cultures.

explanation: Subacute bacteremia with catalase-negative, alpha-haemolytic Gram-positive cocci in chains causing mitral valve vegetation and vertebral osteomyelitis in an older patient with iron-deficiency anaemia and a sigmoid adenocarcinoma is most consistent with Streptococcus gallolyticus. Isolation of the same organism from blood and tumour tissue supports a colonic source of the endovascular infection.

hints.text: A 7-year-old boy from a suburban neighbourhood presents with three weeks of intermittent dry cough and right upper quadrant abdominal discomfort. He has low-grade fevers to 38.0°C and progressive fatigue, and his parents report a 1.5 kg weight loss. On examination he is pale with hepatomegaly 3 cm below the costal margin and normal cardiorespiratory auscultation.

He was previously well, up to date with routine immunisations, and has no history of recent travel. The family adopted a young puppy three months ago, and the child spends long periods playing in a backyard sandbox where the dog defecates; the parents note occasional pica behaviour.

Full blood count shows WBC 16.8 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 4.8 × 10^9/L. C reactive protein 18 mg/L, alanine aminotransferase 65 U/L. Stool microscopy for ova and parasites is repeatedly negative. An ELISA returns positive for IgG to tissue-migrating nematode antigens.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates multiple small, well defined hypoechoic lesions in the liver measuring 6–12 mm. Chest radiograph shows fleeting, patchy peripheral airspace opacities that were not present on a radiograph taken six weeks earlier.

Detailed exposure history confirms the puppy has not received recent anthelmintic treatment and the sandbox is frequently contaminated with dog faeces. The child is known to put sand in his mouth while playing.

explanation: Marked peripheral eosinophilia with hepatic nodules, transient pulmonary infiltrates, positive serology for tissue-migrating nematodes, and close contact with an untreated puppy plus pica point to infection with a dog-associated larval nematode. Negative stool studies fit a migrating larval infection rather than an adult intestinal helminth. The constellation is most consistent with Toxocara canis visceral larva migrans in a child.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man presents to the internal medicine clinic with two weeks of intermittent fevers, drenching night sweats, fatigue and headaches. He reports the fevers come in attacks separated by symptom-free intervals; at presentation temperature is 38.3°C, pulse 96/min, he has conjunctival pallor and the spleen is palpable 4 cm below the costal margin.

He describes similar milder febrile episodes over the preceding 10 months that he treated at home with analgesics and that resolved spontaneously. He has no chronic medical conditions, takes no regular medications, is HIV negative by prior testing, and has never undergone splenectomy.

CBC shows haemoglobin 95 g/L, MCV 85 fL, leukocytes 6.8 × 10^9/L and platelets 110 × 10^9/L. Markers of haemolysis are present with bilirubin 35 µmol/L, haptoglobin low and LDH 420 U/L. A thin blood film reveals intraerythrocytic parasites at low density, parasitaemia estimated at 0.3%.
Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates homogeneous splenomegaly with spleen length 14.5 cm and no focal hepatic or renal lesions. Chest radiograph is unremarkable.

On detailed review he reports a three-month work assignment in rural West Africa 18 months earlier during which he inconsistently used bed nets and did not complete chemoprophylaxis. His current febrile attacks have become more stereotyped, with rigors and high temperature followed by an afebrile interval so that peak fevers recur at approximately 72-hour intervals.

explanation: The combination of chronic intermittent febrile attacks recurring on a roughly 72-hour cycle, low-density intraerythrocytic parasitaemia, splenomegaly and haemolytic anaemia after remote travel points to Plasmodium malariae. The long low-level parasitaemia and quartan periodicity distinguish it from other human malaria species. Confirm with species-specific PCR or repeat thin films and treat directed at blood-stage infection.

hints.text: A 38-year-old man presented to the emergency department after 7 days of progressive illness with high fever, severe frontal headache, and diffuse myalgia. He developed a new maculopapular rash on his trunk on day 5 and over the last 24 hours became increasingly confused and unsteady on his feet. On arrival temperature was 39.8°C, blood pressure 95/60 mmHg, heart rate 110 beats per minute, and he was disoriented to time with a diffuse, blanching rash over the chest and abdomen.

He is a recently arrived refugee who spent two weeks in an overcrowded reception centre before transfer to the city shelter three days ago. He has no known chronic illnesses and takes no regular medications. Several other residents had febrile illnesses while he was at the centre, and he received five days of oral amoxicillin for presumed bronchitis without clinical improvement.

Initial blood tests showed leukocytes 3.2 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 123 g/L, platelets 78 × 10^9/L, sodium 128 mmol/L, creatinine 150 μmol/L, ALT 185 U/L, and CRP 120 mg/L. Two sets of blood cultures remained sterile at 48 hours and malaria microscopy and rapid antigen testing were negative.

Chest radiograph demonstrated patchy bilateral interstitial air‑space changes without focal lobar consolidation. Non-contrast CT brain performed for altered mental state showed no acute intracranial lesion.

On directed questioning he reported heavy lice infestations at the reception centre with frequent sharing of clothing and bedding, and there had been no organised delousing. Several neighbours there had similar febrile rash illnesses and one elderly resident recently died after a brief febrile encephalopathy.

explanation: Prolonged high fever with severe headache followed by maculopapular rash, new encephalopathy, thrombocytopenia, transaminitis and hyponatraemia in the setting of crowded housing and documented body lice exposure is most consistent with epidemic typhus due to Rickettsia prowazekii.

hints.text: A 29-year-old male maintenance technician presents with 4 days of high fever, profound myalgia and a rapidly progressing skin eruption that began on the face. On arrival temperature is 39.3°C and pulse 112/min, and exam shows dozens of firm, deep-seated papulopustular lesions concentrated on the face and dorsal hands, several of which are painful and limit his ability to grasp objects.

He is previously healthy, takes no regular medication and reports no immunosuppression. He denies recent travel, has no known household contact with chickenpox or shingles, and was born after routine childhood vaccination against an eradicated human virus was discontinued; he cannot recall receiving that vaccine.

Blood tests show leukocytosis 14.2 × 10^9/L and CRP 120 mg/L. Bacterial blood cultures are pending, and lesion swabs are negative by PCR for varicella zoster and herpes simplex; direct cytology of lesion fluid demonstrates prominent eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies.

Chest radiograph shows new bilateral patchy airspace consolidation most pronounced in the perihilar regions, compatible with viral pneumonitis. Photographs of several cutaneous lesions were taken and archived in the record for infectious disease review.

Twelve days before rash onset he assisted in unsealing and moving a freeze-dried, labelled historical vial from a national archive that stores the only remaining sealed stocks of an eradicated, strictly human virus held under international control; he recalls a small skin prick while handling the vial and no recent occupational vaccination.

explanation: The prodrome of high fever followed by deep, firm papulopustular lesions on face and distal extremities, intracytoplasmic inclusions on lesion cytology, negative varicella testing, absence of routine childhood vaccination and a documented percutaneous breach while opening a sealed archival vial of an eradicated human-only virus together point to infection with that historical eradicated agent retained in reference repositories.

hints.text: A 62-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 36 hours of rapidly increasing right calf pain, swelling, and fever. He reported severe pain that prevented weight bearing, temperature 38.9°C, heart rate 112/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, and exam showed tense erythema of the posterior calf with a 3 cm central dusky patch and marked tenderness out of proportion to visible findings.

He has alcohol-related cirrhosis with known portal hypertension and compensated synthetic dysfunction, and well controlled type 2 diabetes. He was ambulatory and independent before this illness, denied recent hospitalisation or intravenous drug use, and had no prior chronic leg wounds.

Laboratory tests on arrival showed WBC 22.4 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 19.1 × 10^9/L, platelets 95 × 10^9/L, creatinine 210 µmol/L, and lactate 4.6 mmol/L. Two sets of blood cultures flagged positive and Gram stain from blood showed gram-negative curved bacilli.

Contrast CT of the lower leg demonstrated diffuse subcutaneous oedema, marked fascial thickening and enhancement with small linear fluid collections tracking along the fascial plane, findings felt most consistent with an early necrotising soft tissue infection rather than a simple cellulitis. No large discrete abscess or gas was identified.

On detailed questioning the patient said he had been shucking and eaten raw oysters harvested from a local estuary 48 hours before symptom onset, and sustained a small skin abrasion on his hand while preparing them.

explanation: Rapidly progressive necrotising soft-tissue infection with sepsis and bacteremia by curved gram-negative rods in a patient with chronic liver disease who consumed raw oysters strongly points to a virulent marine gram-negative bacillus acquired from shellfish. The combination of host susceptibility, exposure, and the organism morphology on Gram stain supports this specific diagnosis.

hints.text: A 58-year-old retired schoolteacher presents in mid-August with 4 days of fever, headache and progressive confusion. Family reports a new coarse resting tremor and difficulty rising from a chair; temperature 38.9°C, pulse 96/min, he is disoriented to time and has proximal lower‑limb weakness graded 4/5 on bedside testing.

His past medical history includes type 2 diabetes and hypertension, both well controlled on oral therapy. Symptoms began with systemic malaise and headache, then evolved over 48 hours to confusion and new motor impairment without prior focal stroke or recent hospitalisations, and he has no history of recent travel outside the region.

Blood tests show leukocytes 12.4 × 10^9/L and CRP 18 mg/L. Lumbar puncture yielded clear CSF with WBC 120 × 10^6/L (70% lymphocytes), protein 1.2 g/L and glucose 3.8 mmol/L with serum glucose 5.2 mmol/L. CSF bacterial culture and PCR for herpes simplex and enterovirus are negative.

MRI brain shows bilateral T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in the thalami and posterior basal ganglia with mild leptomeningeal enhancement. Cervical spine MRI demonstrates T2 hyperintensity localized to the anterior horn cells from C3 to C6 without compressive lesion.

He lives on the edge of a small river valley and reports spending most evenings at his cottage since late July, often outside after dusk. He had many mosquito bites, and neighbours noted several dead corvids in the area over the same period.

explanation: Late-summer onset in an older adult with fever, encephalopathy, new tremor and asymmetric motor weakness plus CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis points to a viral neuroinvasive process. MRI involvement of the thalami and anterior horn cells together with heavy mosquito exposure and local dead corvids supports neuroinvasive infection due to West Nile virus.

hints.text: A 28-year-old male agricultural worker presents to the clinic with three months of progressive swelling of the right lower leg and intermittent low-grade fevers that are worse at night. He reports increasing difficulty walking, and examination shows non-pitting edema from the mid-calf to the ankle with mild overlying skin thickening and tenderness, temperature 37.8°C, and an antalgic gait.

He was born and raised in a coastal West African region and moved to the city three years ago but returns yearly to help on the family rice farms. He recalls prior brief episodes of fever and transient swelling in the same leg during childhood. He is otherwise well, HIV test last year was negative, and he is not taking immunosuppressive medications.
Complete blood count shows WBC 12.4 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 2.6 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein 18 mg/L. A peripheral blood film obtained in daytime hours did not demonstrate circulating larvae.

Scrotal and inguinal ultrasonography reveals multiple dilated lymphatic channels and mobile, tubular echogenic structures within lymphatic channels and the scrotal sac consistent with live intralymphatic organisms producing focal movement on real-time imaging.

On detailed questioning he describes frequent nocturnal mosquito bites while planting rice. A thick blood sample drawn at 02:15 showed sheathed, motile microfilariae; the posterior nuclei terminate before the tail tip on microscopy.

explanation: Chronic unilateral lower‑limb lymphedema with intermittent nocturnal fever, marked eosinophilia, ultrasound evidence of motile intralymphatic structures, night-biting mosquito exposure, and nocturnally periodic sheathed microfilariae whose nuclei do not extend to the tail are diagnostic of infection with Wuchereria bancrofti. The combination of imaging, nocturnal periodicity, and tail‑nuclei morphology distinguishes this parasite from other lymphatic filarial species.

hints.text: A 34-year-old previously healthy man presents with five days of high fevers, severe myalgias and progressive dark urine. He is febrile at 39.2°C, visibly jaundiced, reports nausea and one episode of coffee-ground vomiting, and has a tender palpable liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin.

He returned ten days before presentation from a two-week trip in rural West Africa where he worked on a small road project. He did not seek pre-travel care and reports numerous mosquito bites; he has no history of chronic liver disease and takes no hepatotoxic medication.

Laboratory tests show AST 3 200 U/L, ALT 1 150 U/L, total bilirubin 86 µmol/L, platelet count 48 × 10^9/L, white blood cell count 2.1 × 10^9/L, creatinine 248 µmol/L and INR 2.1. Rapid tests for malaria were negative and routine hepatitis serologies were non-reactive.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates hepatomegaly without biliary dilatation or focal hepatic lesion and no ascites. There is no sonographic evidence of obstructive biliary disease to explain the jaundice.

Local public health reported an outbreak of a mosquito-transmitted febrile illness causing severe jaundice and gastrointestinal bleeding in the same region during his visit. Acute serum obtained on day six of illness returned positive by RT-PCR for the outbreak virus while dengue PCR and routine bacterial cultures were negative.

explanation: Severe acute hepatitis with jaundice, marked AST-predominant transaminitis, thrombocytopenia and haemorrhage after travel to an endemic West African area without vaccination, plus outbreak-linked RT-PCR positivity, points to a viscerotropic mosquito-borne viral infection. The pattern and epidemiology strongly support the diagnosis in this clinical context.

hints.text: A 47-year-old man presented to the regional hospital with 72 hours of fever, rigors and worsening right groin pain. He had marked malaise and was difficult to stand, temperature 39.4 °C, heart rate 112 min−1 and blood pressure 100/64 mmHg. Examination showed a single, exquisitely tender 5 cm firm inguinal lymph node with surrounding erythema and limited hip flexion because of pain.

He is a smallholder who keeps sheep and stores grain in an outbuilding, normally well apart from type 2 diabetes controlled with metformin. He reported no urethral discharge, no recent new sexual partners in the past month, and no skin lesions on the lower limb. Symptoms began suddenly after working for several days in a derelict barn, but he did not seek care until the pain and fever intensified.

Blood tests showed white cell count 18.6 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance, C-reactive protein 182 mg/L and creatinine 142 μmol/L. Aspiration of the gland produced purulent fluid; Gram stain reported small Gram-negative coccobacillary organisms and routine blood cultures later grew non-lactose-fermenting colonies after 48 hours.

Chest radiograph obtained because of new cough on day 2 showed patchy bilateral airspace opacities, greater at the right lower zone, with a small right pleural effusion. There was no radiographic evidence of osteomyelitis on pelvis radiographs performed for persistent groin pain.

On re-interview the patient described finding multiple dead wild rodents in the grain store the week before illness and recalled numerous small insect bites afterwards. Local public health notified clinicians that a recent die-off of small mammals had been reported in neighbouring farms.

explanation: The acute febrile illness with painful regional lymphadenopathy and purulent aspirate yielding small Gram-negative coccobacilli plus growth of non-lactose-fermenting colonies points to an invasive zoonotic Gram-negative rod. The history of rodent die-off and flea exposures provides the epidemiologic link. These features together are most consistent with infection by Yersinia pestis, with secondary pulmonary involvement evident on chest radiograph.

hints.text: A 29-year-old woman presents to the antenatal clinic with 4 days of low-grade fever, a diffuse nonpruritic maculopapular rash, and aching of the wrists and ankles that makes dressing uncomfortable. She also reports mild redness of both eyes without discharge. On examination temperature 38.1°C, pulse 86/min, rash concentrated on trunk and proximal limbs, small joint point tenderness without synovitis, otherwise well appearing.

She is primigravida; a home pregnancy test was positive 5 weeks ago and her last menstrual period puts estimated gestation at 8 weeks at the time of initial presentation. No chronic medical problems, no known immunodeficiency, no recent live vaccinations, and no household contacts with a diagnosed exanthem.

Full blood count shows leukocytes 3.2 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 1.8 × 10^9/L, platelets 120 × 10^9/L. C reactive protein 4 mg/L. Point-of-care dengue NS1 antigen negative and chikungunya RT-PCR on serum negative; rubella serology requested.

On follow-up at 18 weeks gestation a targeted obstetric ultrasound demonstrates fetal head circumference at the 3rd centile for gestation with periventricular calcifications and mild ventriculomegaly. The placenta appears unremarkable and no other major extracranial anomalies are identified.

She reports a 10-day trip to northeastern Brazil three weeks before symptom onset during which she sustained multiple daytime mosquito bites. Her partner returned from the same trip one week earlier and had a brief febrile rash; they had unprotected sexual intercourse after his return.

explanation: A pregnant woman with acute febrile maculopapular rash, conjunctival injection and arthralgia, leukopenia with mild thrombocytopenia, negative dengue NS1 and chikungunya testing, subsequent fetal intracranial calcifications, and recent travel plus sexual exposure to an endemic area points to Zika virus infection causing congenital infection. The combination of maternal arboviral illness in early pregnancy with fetal neuroimaging abnormalities and possible sexual transmission supports this diagnosis.

hints.text: A 58-year-old woman presented to the emergency department 48 hours after discharge with a 24-hour history of fever, rigors, dysuria and left flank pain. She reported marked urinary urgency and could not tolerate oral fluids, on examination temperature was 38.9 °C, heart rate 110 min−1, blood pressure 110/65 mmHg, and there was left costovertebral angle tenderness with suprapubic discomfort.

She has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and was hospitalised 10 days earlier for a small bowel obstruction; a urinary catheter had been in place for four days during that admission. She received a five-day course of a third-generation cephalosporin while an inpatient and was discharged on day 7 after an uncomplicated recovery.

Urinalysis demonstrated marked pyuria (>100 × 10^6/L leucocytes) and nitrite positive. Peripheral white cell count was 15.6 × 10^9/L. Urine culture grew a Gram-negative bacillus that was non-lactose fermenting on MacConkey agar and showed resistance to ampicillin and cefazolin with preserved susceptibility to ciprofloxacin and meropenem.
Contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed left-sided acute pyelonephritis with striated nephrogram and perinephric fat stranding but no drainable abscess or ureteric obstruction.

Infection control review found other urinary isolates from the ward over the prior two weeks and persistent bright red biofilm noted in the ward sink drains and a no-rinse soap dispenser. Environmental swabs from those sites yielded the same non-lactose fermenting organism with a red pigmented colony on culture that matched the patient isolate by susceptibility profile.

explanation: The presentation is a post-hospital catheter-associated complicated urinary tract infection in a patient with diabetes. The organism is a nosocomial non-lactose fermenting Gram-negative bacillus with an AmpC-like resistance pattern, and the epidemiologic link to red pigmented environmental colonies points to Serratia marcescens. Findings fit a urinary source producing pyelonephritis without abscess.

hints.text: A 54-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 36 hours of rapidly worsening pain, swelling and erythema of his right lower leg. He was febrile to 38.9°C and borderline hypotensive with blood pressure 95/58 mmHg, the anterior shin was tense with bullae and severe pain out of proportion to touch.

His past medical history included alcohol-related cirrhosis and type 2 diabetes mellitus with peripheral neuropathy. He reported a superficial abrasion over the same shin five days earlier after a fall while doing outdoor recreational activities; he cleaned the wound at home and continued to work, noticing progressive local worsening over the subsequent two days.

Initial blood tests showed white cell count 22.1 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 310 mg/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L and creatinine 165 µmol/L. Two sets of blood cultures flagged positive within 14 hours for a motile Gram-negative bacillus; wound swab grew a similar organism.

Contrast CT of the lower leg demonstrated diffuse subcutaneous oedema with gas tracking along multiple fascial planes of the anterior compartment and thin fluid collections consistent with necrotizing soft tissue infection. There was no periosteal reaction or deep foreign body identified.

On repeat questioning the patient recalled falling into a shallow inland river while hiking several days before the abrasion. Culture work-up from blood and wound specimens identified a facultatively anaerobic, oxidase-positive, motile Gram-negative bacillus commonly recovered from freshwater environments and aquatic animals; the isolate was resistant to ampicillin but susceptible to ciprofloxacin and cefotaxime, and the patient improved after debridement plus targeted fluoroquinolone therapy.

explanation: Rapidly progressive necrotizing soft tissue infection in a patient with cirrhosis and recent freshwater contamination of a skin abrasion, with blood and wound cultures growing an oxidase-positive motile Gram-negative bacillus resistant to ampicillin and responding to ciprofloxacin, points to a freshwater-associated Gram-negative bacillus known to cause wound infections and sepsis in this context. The combination of exposure, clinical course, culture characteristics and.

hints.text: A 29-year-old woman presented with 10 days of progressive severe occipital headache, photophobia, and neck stiffness. She also described intermittent paresthesia of both hands and a feeling of unsteadiness on walking. Temperature 37.8°C and pulse 92/min, there was nuchal rigidity and mild bilateral hip flexor weakness on examination.

She had returned three weeks earlier from two weeks of volunteer work in rural Southeast Asia, spending time in rice paddies and community gardens. She recalled eating salads and sampling local street dishes of lightly dressed freshwater greens while there. She had no chronic medical conditions and was not taking immunosuppressive medication.
