Initial blood tests showed WBC 11.8 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.4 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 132 g/L, platelets 260 × 10^9/L, CRP 6 mg/L. HIV and syphilis serology were negative. Lumbar puncture opening pressure was 240 mmH2O, CSF was clear with WBC 320 × 10^6/L predominantly lymphocytes, protein 1.1 g/L and glucose 3.2 mmol/L. CSF Gram stain and routine bacterial culture were negative.

Contrast MRI of brain and spine showed patchy leptomeningeal enhancement over the posterior fossa and small scattered T2 hyperintense lesions in the cervical cord and conus medullaris. No focal intracerebral abscess or large infarct was identified.

On re-interview she recalled tasting a small raw snail offered by a host in the village. Parasitology examination of a repeat CSF sample identified a single thin motile larva about 2 mm in length. Repeat CSF WBC was 580 × 10^6/L with 42% eosinophils.

explanation: Progressive meningitic symptoms after travel, new peripheral eosinophilia, leptomeningeal and spinal cord imaging abnormalities, and a repeat CSF showing eosinophilic pleocytosis with a recovered motile larva point to infection with Angiostrongylus cantonensis. Recovery of a larva from CSF provides the diagnostic confirmation in this clinical context.

hints.text: A 57-year-old man presented to the regional hospital with 10 days of progressive fever, productive cough, and a painful swelling of the left thigh. He was febrile to 38.6°C, heart rate 110/min, oxygen saturation 92% on room air; chest auscultation disclosed coarse crackles in the right lower zone and there was a 5 cm tender, fluctuant mass on the anterolateral left thigh with surrounding erythema.

He has a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes treated with insulin, most recent HbA1c 10.2%, and chronic alcohol use. He had completed a short course of oral amoxicillin-clavulanate as an outpatient with no clinical improvement and denied recent hospital admission, indwelling lines, or intravenous drug use.

Laboratory tests showed WBC 15.8 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 13.2 × 10^9/L, CRP 210 mg/L and creatinine 110 μmol/L. Two sets of blood cultures became positive at 48 hours for an aerobic gram-negative bacillus; preliminary biochemical panels did not produce a match with common enteric fermenters.

Contrast CT chest demonstrated multiple bilateral nodular consolidations with variable cavitation, the largest 3.5 cm in the right upper lobe. Contrast CT abdomen showed several 0.5–1.5 cm low-attenuation lesions in the liver and spleen compatible with microabscesses.

On further questioning he recalled a puncture abrasion to the left thigh while wading in flooded crop fields during the recent rainy season three weeks before symptom onset. Microbiology from blood and aspirate cultures identified an oxidase-positive, motile, non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative bacillus that was resistant to gentamicin and colistin and susceptible to ceftazidime and meropenem.

explanation: A diabetic patient with pneumonia, multiorgan microabscesses and a soft-tissue abscess after wading in flooded agricultural fields, together with growth of an oxidase-positive non-fermenting gram-negative bacillus showing resistance to gentamicin/colistin and susceptibility to ceftazidime/meropenem, points to Burkholderia pseudomallei. The combination of environmental exposure, imaging pattern, and the characteristic antimicrobial profile supports this diagnosis.

hints.text: A 48-year-old man presented to a community clinic with a 9-month history of progressive thickening and crumbling of the right great toenail. He reports mild pain when wearing closed shoes and intermittent itching between the toes. On examination the right hallux nail plate is markedly thickened, approximately 4 mm, with distal onycholysis and yellow-brown discolouration. There is no erythema of the surrounding skin and he is afebrile.

He has well controlled type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and works as an office administrator. He swims at a municipal pool once weekly and had a cosmetic pedicure about 10 months before symptoms began. He has intermittently applied over-the-counter topical antifungal cream without sustained improvement.

Nail clippings were sent for microscopy and culture. Direct KOH preparation of clippings showed numerous branching septate fungal hyphae within nail keratin. Routine bacterial cultures were negative and samples for fungal culture were incubated.

Plain radiograph of the right forefoot showed no bony erosion or periosteal reaction. High-frequency ultrasound of the nail unit demonstrated a thickened nail plate with hypoechoic subungual material consistent with hyperkeratosis and no cortical disruption of the distal phalanx.

After 2 weeks fungal growth produced slow-growing, woolly white colonies on Sabouraud agar with a pronounced deep red to brown pigment on the underside. Microscopy of the colony mount showed numerous narrow septate hyphae bearing abundant small pyriform microconidia along the hyphae.

explanation: Chronic distal subungual nail dystrophy with visible septate hyphae on KOH indicates dermatophyte onychomycosis. The combination of slow-growing white colonies with a deep red reverse pigment and pyriform microconidia is characteristic of Trichophyton rubrum. His intermittent communal water exposure and diabetes increased susceptibility and explain the chronic course.

hints.text: A 56-year-old man presented to an urban emergency clinic with 6 weeks of low-grade fevers, drenching night sweats, progressive exertional dyspnea and a 6 kg weight loss. He reported intermittent chills and new breathlessness on minimal exertion. On examination he was febrile at 38.3°C, pulse 110/min, and had a new grade 3/6 systolic murmur best heard at the cardiac apex. He appeared pale and had a spleen tip palpated 3 cm below the left costal margin.

He has been sleeping rough in city shelters for the past 2 years with frequent short-term stays in overcrowded hostels. He drinks alcohol daily and has poor dentition. He denies injecting drug use and had a dental extraction for an abscess 4 months earlier. He describes several prior clinic visits for similar intermittent fevers that partially eased after short courses of oral amoxicillin.

Blood tests showed hemoglobin 92 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 84 fL, leucocyte count 7.4 × 10^9/L, CRP 112 mg/L and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 70 mm/h. Three separate pairs of routine aerobic and anaerobic blood cultures drawn over 48 hours remained sterile after 7 days. Serologic testing for Coxiella burnetii and Brucella spp. returned negative.

Transthoracic then transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated a 12 mm mobile vegetation on the posterior mitral leaflet with moderate regurgitation and focal leaflet perforation. Contrast CT of the abdomen identified two small splenic infarcts consistent with septic emboli. Because of progressive heart failure and persistent fever the patient underwent mitral valve replacement and the excised tissue was sent for extended microbiology and molecular testing.

Routine culture of the valve remained negative, but broad-range 16S rRNA PCR from valve tissue yielded a sequence matching a louse-transmitted, fastidious small Gram-negative bacillus known to cause relapsing febrile illness and culture-negative endocarditis among people with chronic homelessness. The patient acknowledged a months-long problem with body lice while sleeping in crowded shelters. Subsequent indirect immunofluorescence showed high IgG titres against the same organism.

explanation: This is culture-negative endocarditis in a person with chronic homelessness and documented body lice exposure, with valve tissue 16S rRNA sequence and high serologic titres identifying a louse-borne, fastidious gram-negative bacillus. Those clinical and microbiologic features are consistent with Bartonella quintana infection causing subacute endocarditis.

hints.text: A 47-year-old male presented from home with 10 days of progressive crampy abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea. He reports up to eight loose bowel motions daily with tenesmus and lightheadedness when standing; on arrival pulse 108 bpm, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, temperature 37.9°C, and focal tenderness in the right lower quadrant without peritonism.

He is a non-smoker with well controlled type 2 diabetes by metformin and no chronic immunosuppression. He had a brief course of oral amoxicillin for sinusitis three weeks earlier, has not left the region recently, and says his work involves animal husbandry on a small rural property but gives no further details initially.

Bloods show white cell count 14.2 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 115 g/L, CRP 96 mg/L, sodium 133 mmol/L. Stool testing returned negative bacterial culture and negative nucleic acid test for Clostridioides difficile, while direct stool microscopy reported numerous faecal leucocytes and visible red cells.

Contrast CT abdomen and pelvis shows circumferential mucosal thickening and submucosal oedema of the cecum and ascending colon with adjacent fat stranding, no free air, and no abscess. Radiology favours an infectious or inflammatory colitis localized to the right colon.

On further questioning the patient admits to regular handling of piglets and cleaning pens; wet-mount examination of fresh stool reveals large ovoid motile protozoan trophozoites about 80–150 μm long with rapid directional movement driven by surface cilia and a prominent internal macronuclear body, plus round thick-walled cysts on concentration technique.

explanation: Right-sided colitis with faecal leukocytes, pig exposure, and a very large ciliated trophozoite on wet mount identify the cause as Balantidium coli. The imaging and dysentery help distinguish this from toxin-mediated or small-bowel diarrhoeas. Identification depends on the characteristic large ciliate trophozoite and cysts in stool.

hints.text: A 36-year-old man employed at a municipal meat market presented on day 4 of fever with severe myalgia, headache and progressive confusion. He was febrile to 39.6°C, pulse 118/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, and examination showed scattered petechial macules on the chest and active bleeding from the gums.

He had been well previously with no chronic illnesses and took no regular medications. Ten days before symptom onset he travelled to a nearby farming village for a family event and continued routine work at the market handling carcasses and cleaning animal stalls during the week before becoming unwell, reporting several small insect bites that he dismissed as benign.

Admission bloods showed white cell count 2.1 × 10^9/L, platelet count 28 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 112 g/L, AST 1 150 U/L, ALT 420 U/L, creatinine 160 µmol/L and INR 2.1. Blood cultures were negative at 48 hours and a thick film for malaria was negative.

Contrast CT of the abdomen showed new retroperitoneal haemorrhage with small-volume free intraperitoneal fluid and no vascular aneurysm. Chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral patchy airspace opacities without focal consolidation.

Public health later informed the team that two coworkers from the same market had developed similar febrile illnesses with bleeding and that plasma PCR at the national reference laboratory from those coworkers and from ticks collected near the market was positive for the regional high-consequence tick-borne haemorrhagic fever virus; his own plasma PCR returned positive for the same virus.

explanation: A previously healthy abattoir worker with acute febrile illness, marked thrombocytopenia, raised transaminases, coagulopathy and spontaneous internal bleeding raises concern for a viral haemorrhagic febrile syndrome. Occupational exposure to livestock and positive PCR from patients and local ticks point to Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever virus as the most likely cause in this epidemiological context.

hints.text: A 28-year-old woman admitted with two weeks of worsening cough, copious purulent sputum and progressive exertional dyspnea. She has baseline exercise limitation from chronic bronchiectasis diagnosed in childhood. Temperature 38.3°C, respiratory rate 22/min, oxygen saturation 92% on room air. Chest auscultation reveals coarse crackles and scattered wheeze and she has digital clubbing.

She performs twice daily treatments with a home jet nebulizer for bronchodilator therapy and has had frequent antibiotic courses over the past year. Three months ago she was hospitalised for a pulmonary exacerbation and received an aminoglycoside together with a third generation cephalosporin for ten days. She does not carry a current diagnosis of cystic fibrosis and is otherwise HIV negative.

White cell count 14.2 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 86 mg/L. Sputum Gram stain shows numerous neutrophils and gram-negative bacilli. Preliminary sputum culture grew a non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod that is resistant to gentamicin and colistin and retains susceptibility to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

Chest CT compared with a scan three months earlier shows new multifocal airspace consolidation and worsening bronchiectasis with mucus plugging. A small cavitating focus is present in the right lower lobe. Findings correlate with the clinical decline despite recent inpatient antibiotics.

Infection-control investigation recovered the same non-fermenting gram-negative rod from the patient sputum, the jet nebulizer reservoir and a diluted antiseptic used to clean the device. The isolates had identical antibiograms and matched by molecular typing. The organism was motile, oxidase positive, produced yellowish colonies at 30°C and showed intrinsic resistance to many aminoglycosides and polymyxins while remaining susceptible to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

explanation: A young patient with chronic bronchiectasis who uses a home nebulizer, a non-fermenting oxidase-positive gram-negative rod resistant to aminoglycosides and polymyxins, and identical isolates from sputum and nebulizer point to an equipment-associated pulmonary infection with Burkholderia cepacia complex. TMP-SMX susceptibility and growth in diluted antiseptic support that diagnosis and explain the outbreak-like recovery from the cleaning solution.

hints.text: A 19-year-old university student presents to the emergency department with eight days of sore throat and fever now complicated by two days of pleuritic chest pain and new right-sided neck pain. He is febrile at 38.8°C, pulse 112/min, oxygen saturation 94% on room air, throat erythematous without obvious exudate, and there is a 3 cm tender, firm swelling along the right anterior neck that limits rotation.

He was seen at a campus clinic on illness day five and started on oral amoxicillin for presumed bacterial pharyngitis. He took the antibiotic for three days but stopped because of nausea, then developed progressive neck pain, shortness of breath, and haemoptysis over 48 hours. He has no chronic illness, no intravenous drug use, and no recent dental extraction.

Blood tests show WBC 17.8 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 15.0 × 10^9/L and CRP 219 mg/L. Two sets of blood cultures flagged positive at 48 hours, yielding obligate anaerobic Gram-negative bacilli on direct smear.

Contrast CT of chest shows multiple bilateral peripheral nodules, several with central cavitation and surrounding ground-glass change, most consistent with septic emboli. Neck ultrasound demonstrates a non-compressible right internal jugular vein with intraluminal echogenic material extending inferiorly.

After 48 hours of intravenous benzylpenicillin the patient remained febrile and breathless. Metronidazole was added, therapeutic anticoagulation started for the jugular thrombus, and a small peritonsillar collection was drained. The patient defervesced within 48 hours and oxygenation improved, and later microbiology speciated the blood isolate as a non-spore-forming pleomorphic obligate anaerobe susceptible to metronidazole.

explanation: A previously healthy young adult with recent pharyngitis who developed unilateral internal jugular vein thrombosis, septic pulmonary emboli, anaerobic Gram-negative bacilli in blood cultures, and rapid clinical response after adding metronidazole supports infection with Fusobacterium necrophorum.

hints.text: A 29-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 6 days of fever, diffuse myalgias and a progressive, severe frontal headache. Over the preceding 48 hours he developed photophobia and neck stiffness; examination showed temperature 38.7°C, pulse 96/min, and marked nuchal rigidity with slowed responses but no focal limb weakness.

He was previously healthy, took no regular medication and had not travelled outside the region in the prior month. The illness began with a brief febrile viral syndrome that partially improved after 48 hours, then evolved into worsening headache and meningitic symptoms, and he had no known immunosuppression, recent surgery, or transplant.

Blood count showed leukopenia with white cells 3.2 × 10^9/L and platelets 150 × 10^9/L. Lumbar puncture yielded CSF with 220 × 10^6/L leucocytes (85% lymphocytes), protein 1.2 g/L, glucose 3.0 mmol/L; CSF bacterial culture was sterile and PCRs for herpes simplex and enterovirus were negative. Serum ALT was 132 U/L.

Brain MRI with contrast demonstrated diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement most pronounced over the cerebral convexities and mild T2 hyperintensity in the mesial temporal lobes without restricted diffusion or mass lesion. No intracranial haemorrhage or abscess was identified.

On further questioning the patient reported buying a young pet Syrian hamster three weeks before symptom onset; the animal died within days of arrival. Regional public health testing detected the same short-segment ambisense RNA sequence in swabs from the pet and in the patient’s CSF by PCR, consistent with a rodent-borne viral source.

explanation: The biphasic febrile illness progressing to lymphocytic meningitis, mild transaminitis, leptomeningeal MRI enhancement, and a recent pet hamster exposure that yielded identical viral RNA indicate infection with lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus. The CSF pattern and negative common viral PCRs support an uncommon rodent-borne viral cause confirmed by sequence concordance between human and rodent samples.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man presents to a regional hospital with 4 days of high fever, severe myalgia, headache, diffuse abdominal pain and repeated vomiting. He is febrile at 39.5°C, hypotensive with blood pressure 86/52 mmHg and tachycardic at 120/min, and he is mildly confused on arrival. On examination he has conjunctival injection, scattered petechiae on the trunk, small areas of mucosal bleeding at the gums, dry mucous membranes and oliguria.

He returned 12 days ago from a two-week work assignment at an informal mining camp in East Africa where he slept in communal quarters and helped with clearing debris at several abandoned shafts. He has no chronic medical conditions, takes no regular medications and recalls that several co-workers developed febrile illnesses during the same trip; two of those co-workers died rapidly after becoming ill. He reports no recent hospital procedures or transfusions.

Initial blood tests show leukopenia 1.8 × 10^9/L, thrombocytopenia 34 × 10^9/L and haemoglobin 120 g/L. Chemistry shows creatinine 210 μmol/L, AST 840 U/L and ALT 460 U/L. Coagulation studies reveal PT 21 s, aPTT 62 s, fibrinogen 0.7 g/L and D-dimer 6.2 mg/L FEU. Blood film and rapid malaria antigen are negative and blood cultures are pending.

Focused abdominal ultrasound demonstrates moderate hepatosplenomegaly and layering free fluid in the pelvis with internal echoes consistent with haemorrhagic ascites. Chest radiograph shows small bilateral pleural effusions without focal consolidation. Bedside cardiac ultrasound shows a small pericardial effusion and a hyperdynamic left ventricle.

On further questioning he admits spending several nights inside an abandoned underground mine clearing bat guano three weeks before admission and describes large colonies of fruit bats seen in the shafts. Several miners who entered the same mine developed similar febrile illnesses and two died; public health teams investigating the cluster identified the same haemorrhagic fever virus in acute samples from affected co-workers and linked the outbreak to the bat‑infested mine.

explanation: The timeline, rapid progression to high fever with gastrointestinal symptoms, mucosal bleeding, profound thrombocytopenia, marked transaminase elevation and hypofibrinogenaemia indicate a viral haemorrhagic fever with capillary leak and coagulopathy. The occupational exposure in an abandoned mine with large fruit bat colonies and a cluster among co-workers points to Marburg virus infection.

hints.text: A 38-year-old woman presented with six weeks of dull right upper quadrant pain, intermittent low-grade fevers, and progressive anorexia. On examination temperature was 38.2°C, the liver was palpable 3 cm below the right costal margin and tender to deep palpation, and she had lost 5 kg since symptoms began.

She had no chronic medical conditions and took no regular medications. Three months earlier she spent two weeks with relatives in a river valley where the family keep sheep; she swam in a local stream and ate salads prepared with home-grown aquatic herbs without routine boiling.

Full blood count showed leukocytosis 14.2 × 10^9/L with marked eosinophilia 3.8 × 10^9/L. Liver tests were cholestatic with alkaline phosphatase 420 U/L and total bilirubin 38 µmol/L, ALT 62 U/L; three separate stool ova and parasite examinations were negative.

Abdominal ultrasound followed by contrast CT demonstrated multiple branching subcapsular low-attenuation tracts in the right hepatic lobe with mild intrahepatic biliary dilatation. There were no discrete solid masses, no gallstones, and no well formed fluid collection to suggest a typical pyogenic abscess.

At ERCP a bile aspirate contained large operculated eggs measuring about 130–150 µm, and the patient acknowledged frequent ingestion of raw watercress and other stream-grown aquatic herbs while at the family farm.

explanation: Marked eosinophilia with subcapsular branching hepatic tracts and biliary dilatation after freshwater plant exposure, together with large operculated eggs in bile, indicate infection with Fasciola hepatica. Negative stool exams early in disease and the migratory hepatic pattern help distinguish fascioliasis from bacterial abscess or gallstone disease.

hints.text: A 48-year-old man presents to a regional clinic with five months of progressive productive cough, night sweats, an 8 kg weight loss, and painful shallow ulcers on the buccal mucosa. He reports intermittent hoarseness and reduced exercise tolerance; on exam oxygen saturation is 95% on room air, there are multiple friable oral ulcers and non-tender cervical lymphadenopathy, and bilateral coarse crackles on chest auscultation.

He is a lifelong agricultural worker who handles soil and harvests crops, with a 20 pack-year smoking history and daily alcohol intake. He has no known diabetes or prior immunosuppressive therapy and reports no close contact with anyone treated for tuberculosis.

Bloods show haemoglobin 95 g/L, leukocytes 8.6 × 10^9/L, ESR 80 mm/h and CRP 58 mg/L. Three sputum samples were negative for acid-fast bacilli by smear, HIV antigen/antibody testing was negative, and fine needle aspiration of a cervical node showed granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells; fungal stains were requested and cultures remain pending.

Chest CT demonstrates bilateral perihilar and upper-lobe reticulonodular opacities with scattered nodules and two small cavitary lesions in the right upper lobe, plus mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy. Flexible laryngoscopy performed for persistent hoarseness shows ulcerative mucosal lesions of the supraglottic larynx.

On further questioning he confirms decades living in rural South America working in disturbed soil on small plantations. Histopathology of an oral ulcer tissue sample with silver stain shows multiple narrow-based buds radiating from a larger central yeast cell, producing a characteristic 'pilot-wheel' arrangement.

explanation: Chronic pulmonary disease with mucocutaneous ulcers, granulomatous lymphadenitis, rural agricultural exposure in South America and the pilot-wheel multiple-budding yeast on silver stain point to Paracoccidioides brasiliensis infection. The clinical course and negative AFB smears make tuberculosis less likely. Culture or specific serology would confirm the diagnosis.

hints.text: A 34-year-old male subsistence farmer presented to a district clinic with a 3-day history of severe burning pain and a tense blister on the anterior aspect of his right lower leg that spontaneously ruptured. He had low-grade fever, could not bear full weight on the right leg, and examination showed a 3 cm shallow ulcer with serous drainage and a tender, cord-like structure palpable beneath the skin.

He is otherwise well, with no diabetes, no known immunosuppression and no recent antibiotic use. He reports working barefoot in irrigated fields and regular minor thorn injuries; he remembers a brief febrile illness about 10 months ago after heavy rains but no prolonged systemic symptoms since then.

Full blood count showed white blood cells 9.2 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.6 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein was 20 mg/L. Three stool ova and parasite examinations were negative and blood cultures showed no growth.

Point-of-care ultrasound of the lesion demonstrated a slender, tubular, hypoechoic structure about 2 mm in diameter running along the subcutaneous plane for at least 30 cm, with subtle undulating movement on real-time imaging and no arterial Doppler signal.

While irrigating the ulcer during clinic care the patient reported that a thin white structure protruded; under local analgesia staff gradually wound a living, white, threadlike female helminth approximately 60 cm long onto a stick over two days. He then recalled drinking untreated surface water from a seasonal pond about 10 months before symptoms began.

explanation: A long, live female nematode emerging from a subcutaneous ulcer after a prolonged interval following ingestion of surface water, with corresponding ultrasound and eosinophilia, points to Dracunculus medinensis. The gradual winding extraction of a 50–70 cm threadlike worm confirms the diagnosis in this clinical context.

hints.text: A 31-year-old man presented to the emergency department with five days of fever, daily rigors, headache, myalgia and progressive shortness of breath. He was febrile 39.4°C, tachycardic 118/min, blood pressure 94/58 mmHg and had jaundice, scleral icterus and a palpable spleen 3 cm below the left costal margin; he was mildly confused on arrival.

He returned 8 days before presentation from a two-week contract working on road repairs in a rural, forested area of Southeast Asia and reported many mosquito bites while sleeping in basic communal huts. He took some malaria chemoprophylaxis but interrupted the course after a few doses because of gastrointestinal side effects; he had no known chronic illnesses and no prior splenectomy.

Blood tests showed haemoglobin 85 g/L, platelets 42 × 10^9/L, total bilirubin 88 μmol/L, creatinine 220 μmol/L and lactate 4.0 mmol/L. Peripheral thin film demonstrated intraerythrocytic parasites with a parasitaemia of 6% of erythrocytes, a mix of delicate ring forms and later band-like trophozoites, and a rapid fall in platelet count over 12 hours.

Chest radiograph and CT showed bilateral patchy alveolar and interstitial opacities without cardiomegaly, consistent with non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. Abdominal ultrasound confirmed moderate splenomegaly and no free intraperitoneal fluid.

Local public health notified the hospital of several recent human febrile illnesses in the same district after village workers reported frequent long-tailed macaques near camps; reference PCR on this patient detected a simian-origin erythrocytic parasite known to produce daily febrile peaks and capable of high parasitaemia.

explanation: Severe acute febrile illness after recent forest travel, high parasitaemia with mixed ring and band-stage forms, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury and pulmonary oedema together with documented macaque-associated, daily-cycle infection on reference PCR indicate Plasmodium knowlesi. The rapid clinical course and exposure to macaque habitat distinguish it from other human malaria species.

hints.text: A 32-year-old woman presents to a district hospital on day 6 of fever with progressive weakness, sore throat and new onset oral bleeding. She is a nurse, febrile at 38.8 °C, tachycardic at 110/min, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, with injected conjunctivae and scattered petechiae on the buccal mucosa; she reports oliguria over the past 24 hours.

She is previously well and returned 12 days before presentation from a two-week visit to relatives in a rural area of Sierra Leone where she assisted with routine household tasks and attended a funeral. She reports close contact with several sick family members while away and occasional bites from small rodents in the compound, but no known sharps injury at work.

Admission bloods show leukopenia 2.6 × 10^9/L, thrombocytopenia 68 × 10^9/L and hemoglobin 102 g/L. Liver enzymes are elevated with AST 420 U/L and ALT 220 U/L, creatinine 140 µmol/L, INR 1.8, and dipstick urinalysis 2+ protein.
Chest radiograph demonstrates small bilateral pleural effusions without focal lobar consolidation. Focused abdominal ultrasound shows mild hepatomegaly and a small volume of free fluid in the pelvis.

Blood and throat swab PCR return positive for an enveloped single-stranded ambisense RNA virus known to cause endemic viral haemorrhagic fever in parts of West Africa; rising virus-specific IgM is detected on paired serology. Public health investigators note household exposure to rodents in the patient’s village and several locally clustered febrile illnesses over the prior month.

explanation: Recent rural travel to West Africa with household rodent exposure, a protracted febrile illness complicated by mucosal bleeding, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and marked transaminitis suggest a viral haemorrhagic fever. Imaging shows capillary leak with small effusions and mild hepatomegaly, and confirmatory PCR plus rising IgM for an enveloped ambisense RNA virus endemic to the region identifies the causative agent.

hints.text: A 7-year-old previously well girl presents with a 5-week history of a painless, progressively enlarging right lateral cervical mass and intermittent low-grade fevers. She now has limited neck rotation and a 3.5 cm firm, mobile supraclavicular node with overlying skin intact. Temperature 37.8°C, no cough or weight loss reported.

Parents report a 2-week course of oral amoxicillin before presentation with no change. She received childhood immunisations including BCG in infancy. There is no known household contact with active respiratory tuberculosis and no recent international travel.

Blood count shows WBC 7.8 × 10^9/L, CRP 24 mg/L, ESR 38 mm/h. Fine needle aspirate cytology demonstrates necrotising granulomatous inflammation. Routine bacterial and fungal cultures remain sterile and Ziehl-Neelsen smear from the aspirate is negative.

Neck ultrasound shows a 4.0 cm multiloculated, partly cystic mass replacing the involved lymph node with internal septations and peripheral vascularity. Chest radiograph is normal without hilar lymphadenopathy or parenchymal disease.

Excisional node culture and environmental sampling from the family's untreated garden well each yielded the same slow-growing colonie s on egg-based medium after 3–4 weeks, producing an orange pigment when grown in the dark. Molecular sequencing at reference laboratory provided a definitive match between patient and well isolates.

explanation: Isolation of a slow-growing scotochromogenic mycobacterium from both the node and the household water source with matching sequence data identifies Mycobacterium scrofulaceum as the pathogen in this case.

hints.text: A 34-year-old fisherman presents with 6 weeks of productive cough and intermittent haemoptysis. Afebrile, SpO2 96% on room air, reduced breath sounds at the right base.
Symptoms began during and after a 3-month coastal fishing season. Two courses of oral amoxicillin produced no improvement; HIV test negative, no known TB contact.
WBC 14.8 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 2.9 × 10^9/L. Sputum bacterial cultures sterile.
Chest CT shows a 3.5 cm thin-walled cavity in the right lower lobe with adjacent nodular consolidation, small pleural effusion, and subpleural linear tracks.
He ate undercooked freshwater crabs at a riverside festival three months before symptoms. Sputum microscopy recovered ovoid operculated eggs consistent with a lung fluke.

explanation: Chronic haemoptysis with marked eosinophilia, a cavitary right lower lobe lesion with pleural involvement, freshwater crustacean ingestion, and operculated eggs in sputum indicate infection by a lung fluke.

hints.text: A 32-year-old man presents to an urban infectious diseases clinic with three weeks of fever, drenching night sweats, progressive weight loss and a dry cough. He reports new flesh-coloured papular skin lesions on his face and trunk that have become crusted at the centre, and on exam he is febrile to 38.6°C with a palpable spleen 3 cm below the costal margin.

He was diagnosed with HIV infection three months ago but has not started antiretroviral therapy because of difficulty accessing care. Recent baseline testing showed a CD4 count of 0.04 × 10^9/L and a documented oral thrush episode treated with topical antifungal.

Initial blood tests show haemoglobin 85 g/L, white blood cell count 2.1 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 1.0 × 10^9/L, platelet count 72 × 10^9/L, CRP 120 mg/L, ALT 95 U/L and AST 110 U/L. Two sets of routine bacterial blood cultures are pending and a skin lesion punch biopsy was sent for microbiology and histology.

Chest computed tomography demonstrates bilateral nodular and patchy ground-glass opacities with several 5–10 mm nodules in both lungs and no large cavitary lesion. Abdominal ultrasound confirms moderate splenomegaly without focal abscess.

He returned to the city six weeks ago after a three-month stay visiting family in the Mekong Delta region where he helped clear a riverside plot and occasionally handled trapped rodents. Two weeks after presentation the laboratory informed the team that blood and bone marrow cultures grew a dimorphic fungus that produced a red diffusible pigment on mould media at 25°C and that tissue histology showed small intracellular yeast-like cells with transverse septation.

explanation: Advanced untreated HIV with profound CD4 lymphopenia, fever, disseminated papular skin lesions, cytopenias and splenomegaly point to an opportunistic systemic mycosis. The travel to the Mekong Delta combined with isolation of a thermally dimorphic fungus producing a red pigment and yeast-phase organisms with transverse septation identifies Talaromyces marneffei.

hints.text: A 68-year-old retired postal worker presents in late August with 3 days of worsening frontal headache, fever, confusion and new unsteady gait. On arrival temperature 38.9°C, he is disoriented to time, has intermittent left upper limb myoclonus, and requires assistance to stand because of truncal ataxia.

He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus controlled with oral agents. He lives in a riverside small town, spent most evenings on his porch this summer, and reports many mosquitoes around the property but no travel outside his state, no recent hospital admissions, and no immunosuppressive medications.

Blood white cell count 12.4 × 10^9/L. Lumbar puncture shows opening pressure 18 cm H2O, total nucleated cells 180 × 10^6/L with 80% lymphocytes, CSF protein 0.90 g/L, CSF glucose 3.6 mmol/L with serum glucose 6.4 mmol/L. CSF PCR for herpes simplex and enterovirus is negative. Routine bacterial cultures are sterile.

Brain MRI with contrast performed on day 2 demonstrates bilateral T2/FLAIR hyperintensity involving the thalami and caudate nuclei with mild leptomeningeal enhancement. No intracerebral haemorrhage or large territorial infarct is seen.

Local public health reports Culex mosquito pools positive by RT-PCR for a flavivirus this season and sentinel chicken seroconversions in the county. Convalescent serum from the patient shows IgM to a locally circulating flavivirus and a neutralizing antibody titre at least fourfold higher against the virus isolated from local mosquito pools than against West Nile virus.

explanation: The presentation is a neuroinvasive febrile illness with CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis and MRI involvement of deep grey nuclei, features consistent with a mosquito-borne flavivirus. Seasonal Culex activity and matched neutralization between the patient serum and local mosquito isolates point to the locally circulating flavivirus. These findings support a diagnosis of St. Louis encephalitis virus infection confirmed by neutralization testing and environmental surveillance.

hints.text: A 36-year-old previously well man presented to clinic with 6 weeks of productive cough, intermittent fevers, night sweats and an unintentional 7 kg weight loss. Over the past 2 weeks he developed a painless, slowly enlarging crusted plaque on the right forearm; exam shows a 3 cm verrucous lesion with central crust and coarse crackles in the right upper chest. Temperature 38.2°C, respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen saturation 95% on room air.

He works as a carpenter and does home renovation on weekends. He has no chronic illnesses, is not on systemic corticosteroids or other immunosuppressants, and a point-of-care HIV test in clinic was negative. He completed two courses of oral antibiotics prescribed by his primary physician without improvement.

Complete blood count shows WBC 12.8 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 112 g/L, platelets 320 × 10^9/L. Sputum bacterial cultures and Gram stain were non-diagnostic, acid fast bacilli smear and PCR for mycobacteria were negative, and serum procalcitonin was 0.08 µg/L.

Chest CT demonstrates a 4.5 cm irregular consolidation with central low attenuation and early cavitation in the right upper lobe, with several smaller peripheral nodules in the same lobe and no significant mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Radiology differential included necrotic pneumonia, fungal infection, or primary lung malignancy.

Punch biopsy of the forearm lesion stained with PAS and GMS showed large, thick-walled yeast forms 10–20 µm in diameter displaying broad-based budding. Tissue fungal culture incubated at 25°C converted to a mould phase with characteristic round conidia after 2 weeks. The patient recalled a canoe trip and clearing riverbank brush along an inland river about 8 weeks before symptom onset.

explanation: The biopsy demonstration of large, thick-walled yeast with broad-based budding and recovery of a mould phase on culture establishes the diagnosis. These features, together with recent freshwater/soil exposure, indicate infection with Blastomyces dermatitidis.

hints.text: A 34-year-old previously well man presented to primary care with three months of intermittent lower abdominal discomfort and bloating. He reported a 4 kg unintentional weight loss and intermittent notice of pale fragments in his stool. He denied fever, vomiting, or neurological symptoms. On examination he was afebrile, pulse 76/min, and his abdomen was soft with mild suprapubic tenderness but no palpable organomegaly.

He recalled living for six months in a rural agricultural community in Eastern Europe two years earlier, where he ate at family-run kitchens and open markets. He has no chronic medical problems, takes no immunosuppressive medications, and tested HIV negative last year. He works in finance and has no household contact with recent febrile or neurological illness.

Full blood count showed haemoglobin 142 g/L, white cell count 6.8 × 10^9/L and eosinophils 0.6 × 10^9/L. Routine chemistry was normal. Stool microscopy demonstrated spherical eggs about 30–40 µm in diameter with a thick, radially striated shell.

Abdominal ultrasound visualised a thin, linear echogenic intraluminal structure in the proximal jejunum extending over several centimetres that shifted position on repeat scanning. Because the team was concerned about potential neuroinvasive disease an MRI brain was performed and showed no cystic lesions or parenchymal abnormalities.

When asked specifically about food he confirmed frequent consumption of lightly cooked beef at community gatherings during his stay abroad. He brought a photograph of a long, flat, ribbon-like white segment recovered from stool and provided a small preserved segment. Light microscopy of the preserved proglottid demonstrated a single lateral genital pore and more than a dozen lateral uterine branches on each side of the central uterine canal.

explanation: The combination of adult tapeworm segments reported in stool, taeniid-type eggs on microscopy, history of ingesting undercooked beef, and proglottid morphology with many lateral uterine branches points to an adult beef tapeworm. Absence of brain cysts reduces the likelihood of the pork tapeworm that can cause neurocystic disease. These findings support a diagnosis of Taenia saginata infection.

hints.text: A 34-year-old woman presents to clinic with 10 days of an expanding rash on her right thigh, intermittent headache, and increasing fatigue. She is febrile at 38.0°C and on examination has an annular erythematous lesion about 12 cm in diameter with central clearing, and she reports mild migratory stiffness of her right knee that limits kneeling.

She is otherwise healthy with no regular medications and no immunosuppressive conditions. Symptoms began roughly one week after a weekend of outdoor gardening and camping in late spring; she initially attributed the skin change to a bite and waited to seek care.

Complete blood count is within reference range with WBC 7.2 × 10^9/L. C reactive protein is mildly elevated at 18 mg/L. Serum enzyme immunoassay for a suspected tick-borne infection is positive and a confirmatory immunoblot shows IgM band reactivity consistent with recent infection.
Point-of-care ultrasound of the right knee shows a small anechoic joint effusion without synovial hypertrophy. No osseous abnormality is seen on plain radiographs of the knee.

Two weeks before the rash she removed an engorged hard-bodied tick from the exact area of the thigh after camping in wooded coastal New England. Local public health has received several reports of similar post-tick rashes this season.

explanation: An expanding annular rash with central clearing after recent woodland exposure, low-grade fever, and migratory arthralgia suggests early cutaneous infection acquired from a feeding tick. Positive enzyme immunoassay with confirmatory immunoblot and a compatible joint effusion support recent dissemination. These combined findings point to the specific tick-borne bacterial cause responsible for this clinical syndrome.

hints.text: A 42-year-old previously well man presented to the emergency department 18 hours after a family meal with progressive diplopia, dry mouth and difficulty swallowing. He reported slurred speech and inability to lift his head; on exam he was afebrile, had bilateral ptosis and ophthalmoplegia, a weak gag reflex, symmetric proximal upper limb weakness with preserved sensation, and normal deep tendon reflexes.

He had no chronic medical conditions, was not taking any regular medications and had no history of neuromuscular disease. He denied recent travel, tick bites, new medications or illicit injection drug use; two other family members who attended the same meal experienced only transient nausea.

Routine bloods showed WBC 6.2 × 10^9/L and CRP 2 mg/L, electrolytes and arterial blood gas within reference ranges. Lumbar puncture produced clear cerebrospinal fluid with opening pressure normal, cell count 1 × 10^6/L and protein 0.35 g/L. Nerve conduction testing demonstrated low amplitude compound muscle action potentials with facilitation after brief voluntary exercise, indicating a presynaptic neuromuscular transmission disorder.
Non-contrast CT brain was normal with no acute intracranial abnormality. Chest radiograph showed low lung volumes without focal consolidation or overt aspiration.

He recalled eating green beans from a jar that his partner had home-canned and left unrefrigerated; public health testing of the remaining jar identified heat-resistant anaerobic spores and a neurotoxin that prevents presynaptic acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction.

explanation: Acute, symmetric descending cranial nerve palsies with bulbar weakness, preserved sensation, normal inflammatory markers and EMG evidence of a presynaptic block point to a neurotoxin-mediated neuromuscular junction disorder. Identification of a neurotoxin and anaerobic spores in home-canned food confirms foodborne botulism due to Clostridium botulinum.

hints.text: A 38-year-old man presents with eight weeks of progressive lower back pain and increasing difficulty rising from a chair. He reports intermittent low-grade fevers and a 6 kg weight loss over two months, and on examination he is febrile 37.9°C with focal lumbar paraspinal tenderness and reduced straight-leg raise on the right.

He has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and an HbA1c of 7.8% measured two months ago. Three months before presentation he had a brief nonproductive cough treated outpatient with two courses of oral antibiotics, no hospital admission, and no known tuberculosis contacts.

Blood tests show WBC 12.1 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 9.6 × 10^9/L and eosinophils 0.5 × 10^9/L, CRP 145 mg/L and ESR 78 mm/h. Percutaneous CT-guided biopsy of the L3 lesion demonstrated granulomatous inflammation with mixed inflammatory cells and periodic acid Schiff positive fungal elements; bacterial cultures and mycobacterial PCR were negative and fungal culture was pending.

Lumbar MRI reveals collapse and lytic destruction of the L3 vertebral body with a 4.5 cm paravertebral fluid collection extending into the epidural space and compressing the thecal sac. Contrast CT chest done the same week shows a 1.8 cm thin-walled cavitary nodule in the right upper lobe.

On further questioning he recalls a six-week contract three to four months ago doing earth-moving and trench work in the San Joaquin Valley, California, where he was repeatedly exposed to dust during several large wind events.

explanation: A subacute pulmonary illness followed by destructive vertebral osteomyelitis with paravertebral abscess in a patient with diabetes and granulomatous inflammation containing fungal elements points to a soil-borne dimorphic fungus endemic to arid regions. The history of heavy dust exposure in the San Joaquin Valley makes that diagnosis most likely in this clinical context.

hints.text: A 29-year-old woman presents to the clinic with three months of progressive exertional shortness of breath and fatigue. She reports lightheadedness when climbing stairs and has visible conjunctival pallor and a pulse of 110 bpm on examination.

She moved to the city from a rural farming region six months ago and says she had persistent poor appetite and 5 kg weight loss over the prior four months. Menstrual periods have been heavier than usual for the past year and she has not received deworming or iron supplementation since childhood.

Blood tests show hemoglobin 72 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 62 fL, ferritin 8 µg/L and transferrin saturation 6%. White cell count 8.7 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.8 × 10^9/L. Stool occult blood positive and ova and parasite exam shows ovoid thin-shelled eggs consistent with a blood-feeding soil-transmitted nematode.

Upper endoscopy performed for ongoing iron loss reveals multiple small, slender reddish organisms attached to the duodenal mucosa. One worm removed and photographed shows a curved anterior end bearing two small ventral rows of hook-like teeth.

On further questioning she recalls frequent barefoot work in irrigated wheat fields in northern India before relocating, and regular consumption of raw leafy greens washed with well water. She denies recent travel to the Americas.

explanation: Severe iron-deficiency anemia with eosinophilia, stool ova showing a soil-transmitted nematode, and duodenal adult worms with ventral hook-like teeth in a patient with barefoot agricultural exposure in northern India point to Ancylostoma duodenale. The ventral teeth on the adult distinguish this species from other hookworms and explain the chronic blood loss.

hints.text: A 28-year-old previously healthy man presents with 5 days of progressive exertional dyspnoea and intermittent central chest discomfort. He reports a fall in exercise tolerance from running 10 km to being breathless after climbing a flight of stairs; on arrival he is tachycardic at 112/min, blood pressure 106/68 mmHg, and has cool peripheries with faint bibasal crackles on lung auscultation.

Ten days earlier he had a brief febrile illness with sore throat, low-grade fever and small painful ulcers at the back of his mouth, which resolved over three days. He takes no regular medication, does not smoke, reports no recent travel or new sexual partners, and works full time caring for children in a community daycare centre.

High-sensitivity troponin I is 1 850 ng/L, B-type natriuretic peptide 980 ng/L, C-reactive protein 72 mg/L and white cell count 8.4 × 10^9/L. Blood cultures are sterile and PCR panels for common respiratory viruses from a nasopharyngeal swab are negative.

Transthoracic echocardiography shows left ventricular ejection fraction 30% with global hypokinesis. Cardiac MRI demonstrates patchy mid-wall late gadolinium enhancement and increased T2 signal consistent with acute myocarditis.

Staff at his daycare reported that several toddlers developed a febrile illness the week before his symptoms, with posterior oropharyngeal ulcers and vesicular lesions on palms and soles. Viral RNA sequencing performed on his blood matched the sequence obtained from a buccal swab of an affected child at the centre.

explanation: Acute myocarditis following a brief febrile oropharyngeal illness and a concurrent outbreak of vesicular hand and mouth disease in children points to Coxsackievirus. The elevated troponin, depressed LVEF, and cardiac MRI pattern support viral myocarditis caused by this agent, which is commonly transmitted in childcare settings.

hints.text: A 57-year-old man on day 9 of invasive mechanical ventilation for aspiration pneumonitis developed fever and increasing purulent tracheal secretions over 48 hours. He was febrile to 38.9°C, required 60% FiO2 to maintain SpO2 92%, and had coarse bilateral crackles with thick yellow material visible in the endotracheal tube.

His admission began 3 weeks earlier after emergency laparotomy for perforated diverticulitis, with a prolonged ICU stay. He received broad-spectrum therapy including 7 days of a carbapenem and 5 days of vancomycin, has a right internal jugular central venous catheter and enteral feeding, and has not been neutropenic.

White cell count was 16.8 × 10^9/L and CRP 180 mg/L. Endotracheal aspirate Gram stain showed many polymorphonuclear leukocytes and Gram-negative rods. Culture grew a non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative bacillus that was resistant to imipenem, meropenem, gentamicin and piperacillin-tazobactam, and remained susceptible to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and minocycline.

Chest CT demonstrated new bilateral patchy consolidations greatest in dependent lower lobes with peribronchial thickening, and no cavitation or pleural collection. The central line projects over the superior vena cava without focal pulmonary infarction.

Samples from the bedside nebulizer reservoir and the sink drain in the patient bay yielded an organism matching the endotracheal isolate by molecular typing, producing pale yellow colonies on culture and growing well at 30°C. The combination of an environmental ICU source, non-fermenting Gram-negative bacillus phenotype, intrinsic carbapenem resistance, and TMP-SMX susceptibility pointed to a single environmental hospital pathogen.

explanation: A ventilator-associated pneumonia after prolonged ICU care and prior carbapenem exposure, with recovery of the same non-fermenting Gram-negative bacillus from nebulizer and sink, indicates an environmental multidrug-resistant hospital pathogen. The phenotype of pale yellow colonies, intrinsic resistance to carbapenems and aminoglycosides, and retained susceptibility to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole supports Stenotrophomonas maltophilia. Treating with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole produced clinical improvement in this patient.

hints.text: A 6-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department after three weeks of progressively worsening cough. The cough occurs in violent paroxysms with brief apnoeic spells and occasional post-tussive vomiting, the child is feeding poorly, oxygen saturation is 92% on room air and temperature is 37.0°C on arrival.

Born at term, no significant medical history. The family reports the infant received the first routine combination infant immunisations at 2 months but missed subsequent scheduled doses, and the mother has had a persistent 'cold' cough for about three weeks while working in a local childcare centre.
Full blood count shows white blood cell count 32 × 10^9/L with absolute lymphocyte count 22 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein is 6 mg/L and blood gas shows mild hypercapnia with PaCO2 6.2 kPa.
Frontal chest radiograph shows peribronchial cuffing and hyperinflation without focal lobar consolidation or lobar collapse.

A nasopharyngeal aspirate sent for molecular testing returned positive for the organism's toxin gene. Contact testing identified an identical positive result in the symptomatic mother who cares for children at the same childcare centre.

explanation: Prolonged paroxysmal coughing with apnoea in a young infant who has incomplete infant immunisation, marked lymphocytosis, and peribronchial changes on chest radiograph points to infection with Bordetella pertussis. Confirmation by PCR detecting the organism's toxin gene in both the infant and the symptomatic household contact supports the diagnosis.

hints.text: A 38-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 3-week history of progressively worsening frontal headache, increasing confusion, and two episodes of vomiting. On arrival he was febrile at 38.1°C, mildly disoriented to time, had photophobia and neck stiffness on passive flexion, and was unable to return to work because of cognitive slowing.

He has treated HIV infection but reports poor adherence to antiretroviral therapy over the past year; outpatient labs two months earlier showed a CD4 count of 75 × 10^6/L. He denied recent travel, intravenous drug use, or recent corticosteroid therapy.

Lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 32 cm H2O. CSF was clear, WBC 12 × 10^6/L with lymphocyte predominance, protein 0.9 g/L, glucose 1.8 mmol/L (serum glucose 5.2 mmol/L). CSF Gram stain and routine bacterial cultures were negative.
MRI brain demonstrated bilateral T2 hyperintense, cystic-appearing dilated perivascular spaces in the basal ganglia and mild leptomeningeal enhancement without large focal abscesses or mass effect.
He recalled cleaning a heavy pigeon roost on his apartment balcony about two weeks before symptom onset and noted abundant droppings and nesting material at that time.

explanation: Subacute meningitis in a patient with advanced immunosuppression, markedly elevated CSF opening pressure with a relatively low CSF cell count, and MRI showing dilated perivascular spaces point to a meningoencephalitis from an inhaled encapsulated environmental yeast. The history of heavy pigeon droppings exposure strongly supports infection by Cryptococcus neoformans, which would be confirmed by CSF culture or antigen testing.

hints.text: A 29-year-old woman presents to primary care with a 3-month history of intermittent perianal itching and increasing sleep fragmentation. Symptoms are described as a burning itch that wakes her several nights per week, she is afebrile, pulse 84/min, and examination shows multiple small excoriations around the anal verge without visible rash or discharge.

She has no chronic medical problems and takes no regular medications beyond occasional ibuprofen. She underwent a gynaecology review and a negative STI screen two months earlier after being treated empirically for presumed vulvovaginitis, and topical antifungal and mild topical steroid courses produced no sustained benefit.

Full blood count and C reactive protein are within reference range with WBC 6.8 × 10^9/L and eosinophils 0.2 × 10^9/L. Two separate stool ova and parasite examinations were reported negative and a single perianal adhesive swab performed in clinic during daytime was unrevealing.

Pelvic MRI requested for intermittent lower abdominal cramping shows no pelvic inflammatory change and no appendiceal abnormality. Images note subtle superficial soft tissue thickening at the distal perianal skin but no mass or deep collection.

On further questioning she reports that her sister's 4-year-old attends childcare and stayed in the house last month; the child had recent nightly anal itching and the sister reported finding small white threadlike objects on the child’s underwear and on bed linen several mornings.

explanation: Persistent nocturnal perianal pruritus with perianal excoriation in an otherwise well adult, repeated negative stool ova exams, and a household contact who had visible short white threads in underwear point to an enteric nematode transmitted by close contact. The combination of nocturnal symptoms, perianal findings, and infected preschool contact is most consistent with Enterobius vermicularis infection in this patient.

hints.text: A 34-year-old woman presents to a regional hospital with three months of progressive right upper quadrant discomfort and early satiety. She reports a 4 kg weight loss and intermittent low-grade fevers, and on examination has a smooth liver edge palpable 3 cm below the costal margin without jaundice.

She grew up in a rural sheep-rearing region and now visits family there several times a year. She is otherwise healthy, takes no regular medication, has no history of immunosuppression or abdominal surgery, and recalls assisting with home slaughter as a child but has not had recent international travel.

Full blood count shows WBC 8.6 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.5 × 10^9/L. Liver tests show ALP 360 U/L, AST 78 U/L, ALT 62 U/L. A serum IgG antibody test targeting a parasitic cyst wall antigen returns strongly positive.

Abdominal ultrasound followed by contrast CT demonstrates a 9 cm well circumscribed multilocular cyst in the right hepatic lobe with multiple internal daughter cystic structures and peripheral curvilinear calcification, producing mass effect on the adjacent stomach.

On further questioning she admits that during childhood the household kept many dogs that were often fed raw offal after local sheep slaughtering. Family members still maintain that practice when she visits.

explanation: A large multilocular hepatic cyst with daughter cysts, peripheral calcification, eosinophilia and positive cyst wall antibody in a patient with a history of dogs and sheep exposure points to liver infection by a cestode transmitted in pastoral settings. The clinical and imaging pattern and exposure history are most consistent with infection by Echinococcus granulosus.

hints.text: A 72-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 10 days of low-grade fevers, fatigue, and progressive exertional dyspnoea. He was febrile to 38.1 °C, pulse 96/min, and examination revealed a new grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur at the cardiac apex with bibasilar crackles.

He has long-standing benign prostatic hyperplasia and underwent transurethral resection of the prostate three weeks earlier. He had a short period of urinary catheterisation after the procedure and received a single perioperative dose of a third-generation cephalosporin; he has no history of intravenous drug use or recent dental work.

Blood tests showed WBC 12.8 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 110 g/L and CRP 74 mg/L. Two of three peripheral blood culture sets flagged positive at about 20 hours with gram-positive cocci in short chains, catalase negative; the isolate hydrolysed esculin in bile, grew in 6.5% NaCl and was PYR positive.
Transoesophageal echocardiography demonstrated an 8 mm mobile vegetation on the posterior leaflet of the mitral valve with moderate mitral regurgitation and no perivalvular abscess.

A urine culture taken 10 days after the urologic procedure grew the same organism with an identical antibiogram to the blood isolate, showing resistance to ceftriaxone and susceptibility to ampicillin. The timeline suggests urogenital manipulation led to bacteremia and seeding of the mitral valve.

explanation: Blood cultures with gram-positive cocci in short chains that are PYR positive, bile-esculin hydrolysing and grow in 6.5% NaCl indicate Enterococcus faecalis. The recent transurethral procedure with an identical urinary isolate and a mitral valve vegetation confirms urogenital-source infective endocarditis.

hints.text: A 20-year-old woman university student presents with 10 days of progressive fatigue, fever to 38.7°C, sore throat and difficulty swallowing. On examination she has tender bilateral anterior cervical lymphadenopathy measuring about 2–3 cm, a palpable spleen 3 cm below the left costal margin, and low-volume erythematous oropharynx without frank purulent exudate.

She is previously healthy, lives in shared student housing, and reports a new sexual partner three weeks ago with unprotected oral contact. She denies recent travel, intravenous drug use, or known sick contacts and had no prior similar illnesses.

Full blood count shows WBC 12.8 × 10^9/L with lymphocytes 7.8 × 10^9/L and 16% atypical lymphocytes. ALT 215 U/L and AST 178 U/L. Rapid streptococcal test is negative and fourth-generation HIV antigen/antibody screen is non-reactive.

Abdominal ultrasound performed to evaluate the palpable spleen demonstrates splenomegaly with a maximal longitudinal diameter of 14.5 cm and otherwise normal liver echotexture. No focal splenic lesions are seen.

Her primary care clinician had prescribed amoxicillin for presumed bacterial pharyngitis before the lab results returned. Within 48 hours of starting the antibiotic she developed a widespread erythematous maculopapular rash over trunk and limbs that intensified despite stopping the drug and improved with topical emollients and oral antihistamine.

explanation: Young adult with fever, prolonged sore throat, tender cervical adenopathy, splenomegaly, atypical lymphocytosis and transaminitis points toward a viral lymphoproliferative syndrome. The development of a generalized maculopapular eruption after aminopenicillin exposure strongly supports the specific viral etiology most consistent with this clinical constellation.

hints.text: A 24-year-old woman presents to urgent care two days after returning from a week-long work trip to Dhaka. She reports sudden onset of profuse watery diarrhoea with crampy abdominal pain and nausea that began 12 hours before presentation, eight watery stools in the past 24 hours, light-headedness on standing, pulse 112/min, blood pressure 100/64 mmHg, and dry mucous membranes on exam.

She is previously well, not taking regular medications, and received routine travel vaccinations. While abroad she ate several types of street food including salads and mayonnaise-based sandwiches, and drank ice made from local tap water. No bloody stools, no high fever, and she did not take antibiotics before coming to clinic.

Peripheral blood count is WBC 8.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 5.1 × 10^9/L. Serum creatinine 115 µmol/L and sodium 133 mmol/L, consistent with mild volume depletion. Stool microscopy shows watery stool with no fecal leukocytes, fecal occult blood negative. Stool culture grew a lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod.
An abdominal radiograph obtained to exclude obstruction shows a non-obstructive gas pattern without dilated loops or free air. No focal bowel wall thickening was seen on bedside ultrasound.

Public health later notified of a small cluster of travellers from the same hotel with similar illness. Molecular testing of the cultured isolate identified plasmid-borne genes encoding both heat-stable and heat-labile enterotoxins, consistent with a toxin-mediated, noninvasive enteric infection acquired from contaminated food or water.

explanation: The patient has an acute, watery traveller's diarrhoea with signs of volume depletion, absence of fecal leukocytes, and growth of a lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod on stool culture. Detection of plasmid-encoded heat-stable and heat-labile enterotoxin genes confirms the diagnosis of enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli.

hints.text: A 24-year-old previously healthy woman presents to the emergency department with 48 hours of severe crampy abdominal pain and frequent bloody diarrhoea. She reports eight watery bowel movements in the past 24 hours followed by visible blood, temperature 37.8°C, pulse 110/min, abdominal examination notable for left lower quadrant tenderness without peritonism.

No chronic medical conditions, not taking immunosuppressants, and she is not pregnant. She has not taken antibiotics recently, and she gave herself a single dose of loperamide at home which she felt was followed by worsening abdominal cramping.

CBC shows WBC 13.2 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 136 g/L, platelets 230 × 10^9/L. Serum creatinine 70 μmol/L. Stool microscopy demonstrates numerous red blood cells and leukocytes. Routine stool culture to date has no Salmonella or Shigella identified.
Contrast CT of the abdomen shows segmental circumferential thickening and submucosal oedema of the sigmoid and descending colon, consistent with left-sided colitis, without free air or abscess.

Three days before symptoms she ate a rare hamburger at a large outdoor barbecue. Two other attendees who ate the same burger developed bloody diarrhoea and one 4-year-old subsequently required admission for acute kidney injury with microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia.

explanation: Bloody diarrhoea following ingestion of undercooked ground beef with a linked secondary case complicated by acute kidney injury and microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia points to a toxin-producing enteric bacterium transmitted in contaminated beef. Left-sided colitis on imaging and exclusion of Salmonella and Shigella support this diagnosis in the clinical context.

hints.text: A 24-year-old woman presents to the outpatient clinic with three months of burning epigastric pain and early satiety. She reports intermittent dark stools and a 3 kg weight loss, and on examination she is afebrile with epigastric tenderness and a pulse of 82/min.

She has no chronic medical conditions and takes no regular non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or aspirin. She previously received short courses of a proton pump inhibitor with partial symptom relief and her father had gastric cancer in his 60s.
Full blood count shows haemoglobin 100 g/L with MCV 72 fL. Ferritin is 8 µg/L and a faecal occult blood test is positive.

Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy reveals a 1.5 cm ulcer on the anterior wall of the gastric antrum with surrounding erythema. Multiple mucosal biopsies were obtained from the ulcer edge and adjacent antrum.

Two household members previously underwent endoscopy for chronic dyspepsia and had positive rapid urease tests on biopsy. Her own gastric biopsy produced a positive rapid urease result within minutes and a stool antigen assay returned positive.

explanation: Chronic epigastric pain with antral ulceration, iron deficiency anaemia and positive biopsy urease and stool antigen point to a gastric mucosal infection that causes peptic ulcer disease. Absence of NSAID use and partial PPI response support an infectious cause rather than NSAID-induced ulceration.

hints.text: A previously well 3-year-old boy was brought to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of high fever, severe sore throat and progressive difficulty breathing. He was sitting forward, drooling, had inspiratory stridor, respiratory rate 40/min and oxygen saturation 90% on room air.

Parents report the child attends a small home daycare and that routine childhood immunisations were declined. He had no chronic respiratory or neurologic disease and had been well until the acute onset tonight.

Blood results showed white blood cells 18.4 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 14.2 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 150 mg/L. A rapid streptococcal antigen test from the oropharynx was negative and blood cultures were sent.
Lateral neck radiograph obtained after stabilisation revealed a markedly enlarged, rounded epiglottic shadow with narrowing of the supraglottic air column consistent with acute epiglottic swelling.

One other child from the same daycare was hospitalised two days earlier with invasive upper airway infection. That contact's blood culture grew small pleomorphic gram-negative coccobacilli that failed to grow on standard blood agar but grew on heated blood agar and required both hemin and NAD; its capsule reacted with polyribosylribitol phosphate antiserum.

explanation: Acute epiglottitis in an incompletely immunised toddler together with neutrophilic leukocytosis and lateral neck radiograph showing an enlarged epiglottis points to an invasive capsulated respiratory bacterium. The culture and antigen data from a close contact identifying a small gram-negative coccobacillus that requires hemin and NAD for growth and has a polyribosylribitol phosphate capsule confirm Haemophilus influenzae as the cause.

hints.text: A 28-year-old woman presents to primary care with 48 hours of fever, right flank pain, nausea and burning on urination. Temperature 38.8°C, pulse 102/min, and there is marked tenderness to percussion at the right costovertebral angle.

She is otherwise healthy, not pregnant, and reports a new sexual partner two weeks ago with recent use of spermicide. She had an episode of uncomplicated cystitis six months earlier treated in the community, no recent antibiotics, no urinary catheterisation and no hospital admissions.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis performed because of persistent fever shows an enlarged right kidney with a wedge-shaped striated nephrogram and perinephric fat stranding. There is no obstructing stone or hydronephrosis.

The illness began in the community, she works in a daycare setting, and there was no recent travel, swimming in lakes, or exposure to hospital or long-term care facilities. Household contacts have no similar symptoms.

Urinalysis shows pyuria and nitrite positivity. Urine culture yields >10^5 CFU/mL of pink lactose-fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar that are oxidase negative and indole positive; the isolate is resistant to ampicillin and susceptible to nitrofurantoin and ciprofloxacin.

explanation: Presentation and CT findings are consistent with acute community-acquired pyelonephritis. The urine culture phenotype of lactose-fermenting, oxidase-negative, indole-positive colonies identifies Escherichia coli as the etiologic agent.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man presents with a 6-week history of intermittent fevers to 38.5°C, progressive exertional dyspnoea, non-productive cough, drenching night sweats and a 6 kg weight loss. On examination he is afebrile at the visit, oxygen saturation 95% on room air, has a palpable spleen tip 3 cm below the costal margin and scattered bibasilar crackles on chest auscultation.

He has seropositive rheumatoid arthritis treated with a tumour necrosis factor alpha inhibitor for the past 10 months after intolerance to methotrexate. He initially denied recent travel or animal bites and has no history of HIV infection. He stopped the biologic two weeks ago when fevers began.

Blood tests show haemoglobin 95 g/L, white cell count 2.1 × 10^9/L with lymphopenia, platelets 95 × 10^9/L. C reactive protein 68 mg/L, alkaline phosphatase 320 U/L, AST 78 U/L, ferritin 1500 µg/L. HIV antibody test is negative. Blood cultures remain sterile at 48 hours.

Contrast CT chest demonstrates innumerable 1–3 mm nodules in a diffuse miliary distribution with mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy. Abdominal ultrasound confirms splenomegaly to 16 cm and multiple small hypoechoic lesions in the liver.

On re-questioning he describes a weekend spent caving in a limestone cavern system in the Ohio River valley region three months earlier, repeatedly disturbing large deposits of bat guano and returning with heavily dusted clothing. Bone marrow aspirate performed for cytopenias showed numerous small intracellular budding yeasts within macrophages on silver stain.

explanation: The combination of prior heavy exposure to bat guano in caves and bone marrow showing small intracellular budding yeasts within macrophages points to a thermally dimorphic fungus that survives intracellularly and causes disseminated disease in immunomodulated hosts.

hints.text: A 29-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 10 days of progressive fatigue, nausea and anorexia and three days of dark urine and yellowing of his eyes. He reports a dull right upper quadrant discomfort; on exam he has scleral icterus and a tender, mildly enlarged liver, temperature 37.8°C and heart rate 92/min.

He was previously well and drinks alcohol only rarely. He reports a new sexual partner about ten weeks before symptom onset and admits to unprotected intercourse; he denies recent travel or intravenous drug use and does not recall receiving childhood vaccination against a preventable hepatic virus.

Serum alanine aminotransferase 2 400 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 1 150 U/L, total bilirubin 95 μmol/L, INR 1.6 and platelets 210 × 10^9/L. Routine serology for a common enterically transmitted hepatitis was negative.

Right upper quadrant ultrasound shows hepatomegaly with a normal-calibre biliary tree and no gallstones; portal and hepatic vein flow is patent on Doppler. There is mild periportal oedema without focal hepatic lesion.

Local public health later notified him that his recent sexual partner's antenatal screen returned positive for a blood-borne hepatotropic virus that is routinely screened for in pregnancy and she reported long-standing infection. He had not received postexposure prophylaxis and had never completed vaccination against that virus.

explanation: The patient has an acute icteric hepatitis with very high transaminases and coagulopathy after a plausible sexual exposure to a blood-borne hepatotropic virus identified on antenatal screening. The exposure history, lack of vaccination, and the pattern of symptomatic acute liver injury are most consistent with acute infection by Hepatitis B virus.

hints.text: A 58-year-old primary-school teacher presents to outpatient hepatology with 4 months of progressive fatigue, intermittent right upper quadrant discomfort, and increasing easy bruising. On examination she has scleral icterus, a liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin, temperature 37.2°C and no peripheral oedema or ascites.

She reports no recent travel and drinks alcohol only socially. Her past medical history includes type 2 diabetes and a motor vehicle collision in 1990 that required multiple red cell transfusions; she denies recent injecting drug use.

Blood tests show ALT 184 U/L, AST 152 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 112 U/L and total bilirubin 34 µmol/L. Platelets are 118 × 10^9/L, albumin 41 g/L and INR 1.0. Rheumatoid factor is elevated and complement C4 is low at 0.06 g/L, with circulating mixed cryoglobulins detected.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates a coarse, nodular hepatic surface and mild splenomegaly without focal lesions. Transient elastography measures liver stiffness 14.0 kPa, concordant with advanced fibrosis.

Review of records confirms the 1990 transfusions occurred before implementation of nucleic acid screening of the blood supply. Current plasma PCR detects viral RNA consistent with an enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded hepatotropic virus, viral load 1.8 × 10^6 IU/mL.

explanation: Chronic transaminitis with advanced fibrosis and hypocomplementemic mixed cryoglobulinaemia suggests a longstanding blood-borne hepatotropic infection. The history of transfusion before routine nucleic acid screening plus detection of plasma RNA from an enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded hepatotropic virus identifies the blood-borne hepatitis virus responsible for chronic infection in this patient.

hints.text: A 28-year-old woman presented to outpatient gynaecology with 4 months of intermittent post-coital spotting and increasing pelvic discomfort. On speculum examination there was a 2.0 cm friable, exophytic lesion on the ectocervix with mucopurulent discharge, blood loss estimated as small, and vital signs were within normal limits.

She had a deceased-donor kidney transplant five years ago and takes tacrolimus and mycophenolate. She smokes about 8 cigarettes per day, missed recommended cervical screening after transplantation, and reports no history of vaccination against the relevant virus.

Liquid-based cervical cytology returned a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion. Punch biopsy of the cervical lesion showed full-thickness epithelial dysplasia with marked nuclear atypia and perinuclear clearing suggestive of viral cytopathic change. Nucleic-acid amplification on the cervical swab detected DNA from high-risk oncogenic viral types.

Colposcopy demonstrated dense acetowhite epithelium with mosaicism and punctation confined to the ectocervix around the lesion. Pelvic MRI measured a 1.8 cm lesion limited to the cervix, with no parametrial invasion or abnormal pelvic lymphadenopathy.

She reports a new male sexual partner in the past year who had visible flesh-coloured papules on his external genitalia and received cryotherapy for them. She describes inconsistent condom use with this partner.

explanation: Persistent infection with a squamous epitheliotropic DNA virus explains the exophytic cervical lesion, HSIL on cytology, and biopsy showing perinuclear clearing. Immunosuppression and smoking increase risk of persistence and progression. Positive high-risk viral DNA testing and a partner treated for external genital papillomas point to human papillomavirus as the responsible pathogen causing high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia.

hints.text: A 38-year-old office manager presented to urgent care 48 hours after abrupt onset of fever, severe myalgias, headache and a dry cough. On arrival she was febrile to 39.2°C, pulse 112/min, respiratory rate 22/min, and said the fatigue was so profound she could not look after her two young children.

Two of her children developed fevers and rhinorrhoea over the past 72 hours and were kept home from nursery. She has no chronic cardiopulmonary disease, does not smoke, and received the current season's inactivated respiratory virus vaccine four months ago. She has not travelled recently and has no known immunodeficiency.

Full blood count showed WBC 3.4 × 10^9/L with lymphocytes 0.8 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein was 22 mg/L. A point-of-care nasopharyngeal antigen panel for common seasonal respiratory viruses was negative.
