Chest radiograph demonstrated mild bilateral peribronchial cuffing and increased perihilar markings without focal lobar consolidation or effusion.

Because of high clinical suspicion and early presentation she was started on oral oseltamivir within 36 hours of symptom onset. Her fever resolved within 24 hours and myalgias and functional status improved substantially over the next 48 hours.

explanation: Rapid onset systemic symptoms with cough during a household outbreak, lymphopenia and a viral-pattern chest radiograph suggest a seasonal respiratory viral infection.

hints.text: A 19-year-old male university student presents with 48 hours of progressive left-sided jaw swelling, pain that worsens with chewing, and malaise. Temperature is 38.4°C and exam shows a firm tender swelling over the angle of the left mandible extending to the preauricular region with mouth opening limited to 2 cm.

He lives in a crowded dormitory and is a first-year student. He denies recent dental procedures, trauma, dehydration, or chronic illness, and reports uncertain childhood immunisation records without any documented adolescent booster.
Serum amylase is 820 U/L (reference < 100 U/L). C-reactive protein is 18 mg/L and white blood cell count is 5.8 × 10^9/L with lymphocytes 1.8 × 10^9/L.

Ultrasound of the left salivary region shows diffuse enlargement of the parotid gland with hypoechoic areas and increased Doppler flow. There is no obstructing salivary stone and no discrete abscess collection.

Two dormitory contacts developed similar painful jaw swelling over the past week and one contact subsequently developed acute unilateral testicular pain and swelling five days after their salivary symptoms. Public health was notified and targeted buccal and throat swabs for viral testing were arranged.

explanation: Acute unilateral parotid-region swelling with painful chewing, markedly elevated serum amylase, ultrasound showing nonobstructive gland enlargement, and a dormitory cluster that includes delayed-onset orchitis point to mumps virus infection. The patient’s unclear immunisation status and close living quarters increase the likelihood of this viral salivary gland infection.

hints.text: A 78-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 48 hours of fever, progressive confusion, and unsteady gait. On arrival temperature 38.6 °C, heart rate 102/min, blood pressure 128/74 mmHg; examination showed drowsiness, nuchal rigidity, and a right-sided horizontal gaze palsy with truncal ataxia.

He has type 2 diabetes mellitus and has been taking oral prednisone 10 mg daily for the past month for polymyalgia rheumatica. He lives alone, is independent in activities of daily living, and denies recent travel, animal bites, or obvious skin infections.

Blood tests demonstrated leukocytosis 14.2 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 145 mg/L. Lumbar puncture yielded opening pressure 220 mmH2O, CSF leukocyte count 820 × 10^6/L with 82% neutrophils, protein 2.2 g/L, CSF glucose 1.8 mmol/L with concurrent plasma glucose 6.9 mmol/L; Gram stain of CSF showed small Gram-positive coccobacillary organisms.

MRI brain with diffusion-weighted and T2/FLAIR sequences showed hyperintense signal with restricted diffusion in the dorsal pons and medulla consistent with rhombencephalitis, without a large focal abscess.

On targeted review of recent diet he reported eating several servings of soft unpasteurised farmhouse cheese and refrigerated smoked salmon over the preceding week; he noted the household refrigerator had been intermittently above 8 °C.

explanation: An elderly patient with neutrophilic CSF pleocytosis, Gram-positive coccobacilli on CSF stain, brainstem rhombencephalitis on MRI, and recent consumption of unpasteurised refrigerated dairy points to Listeria monocytogenes. This diagnosis explains the predilection for older or mildly immunosuppressed hosts and requires targeted antimicrobial coverage beyond third-generation cephalosporins.

hints.text: A 67-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 36 hours of fever, rigors, pleuritic right-sided chest pain and a productive cough. He produced thick blood-tinged mucoid sputum and was hypoxic with oxygen saturation 88% on room air, temperature 39.2 °C, pulse 110/min and respiratory rate 28/min. Chest examination revealed bronchial breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the right upper lung.

He has a 30-year history of heavy alcohol use and poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus. Family say he had a heavy drinking episode two nights before presentation and was briefly unconscious at home. He lives alone and has no recent hospital admissions or antibiotic use.

Peripheral blood tests showed WBC 16.5 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 210 mg/L. Sputum Gram stain demonstrated numerous neutrophils and many large Gram-negative rods. Two sets of blood cultures were drawn and remained pending at the time of initial management.

Chest radiograph displayed dense lobar consolidation of the right upper and middle lobes with apparent bulging of the horizontal fissure. CT chest confirmed homogeneous lobar consolidation with early central necrosis but no diffuse interstitial pattern.

Family report that after the heavy drinking episode he vomited and had a witnessed period of depressed consciousness, suggesting an aspiration event immediately before the onset of respiratory symptoms.

explanation: Acute lobar consolidation with thick blood-tinged mucoid sputum, Gram-negative rods on sputum stain, radiographic bulging fissure and a clear aspiration risk from heavy alcohol use together point to Klebsiella pneumoniae. The organism is a frequent cause of necrotising lobar pneumonia in patients with alcohol use and aspiration events.

hints.text: A 28-year-old previously well man presents with 6 days of worsening fatigue, anorexia, nausea, dark urine and progressive yellowing of the eyes. He is a bar manager, afebrile, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, pulse 86/min; on exam he has marked scleral icterus, mild right upper-quadrant tenderness to palpation and a palpable liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin.

Five weeks earlier he spent eight days on a coastal vacation; he recalls eating raw oysters at a crowded street festival on day 3 of the trip and worked two shifts at a seaside food stall before returning home. He denies recent injection drug use, blood transfusion, surgical procedures, or chronic liver disease, and he reports he did not receive immunisation against enterically transmitted hepatitis viruses.

Serum tests show ALT 3 240 U/L, AST 1 120 U/L, total bilirubin 132 µmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 210 U/L, INR 1.4, WBC 6.4 × 10^9/L, platelets 245 × 10^9/L. Toxicology screen shows undetectable paracetamol level. Screening for chronic hepatotropic viral markers and autoimmune hepatitis panel are negative.

Right upper-quadrant ultrasound demonstrates a mildly enlarged liver without focal lesions, normal gallbladder, and a common bile duct measuring 5 mm with no intrahepatic or extrahepatic biliary dilatation. Doppler flow in the portal and hepatic veins is patent and unremarkable.

Public health notified after two other festival attendees report similar jaundice. Acute-phase serum IgM against the enterically transmitted hepatotropic virus was positive and stool reverse-transcription PCR detected viral RNA consistent with a recent single-serotype, non-chronic infection.

explanation: The patient has acute hepatitis with a cholestatic-concurrent transaminitis and recent exposure to raw shellfish in an area with clustered cases. Imaging excludes biliary obstruction and other common causes have been screened out. Positive acute-phase IgM and stool PCR for an enterically transmitted hepatotropic virus confirm recent infection, fitting an acute, self-limited viral hepatitis acquired by the fecal-oral route.

hints.text: A 34-year-old male agricultural worker presents with 6 months of slowly progressive numbness of the right hand and multiple skin lesions. He reports several pale, slightly raised patches on the forearms and cheeks that have lost normal sensation to light touch and pinprick. On examination the right ulnar nerve is palpably thickened at the elbow and there is early clawing of the fourth and fifth digits with preserved proximal muscle strength. He has no fever, weight loss, or systemic symptoms.

He grew up in a rural region of northeastern Brazil and moved to a city two years ago for work. He recalls that an uncle in the same household had a chronic skin and nerve problem treated years ago. He is HIV negative by last test 18 months ago and takes no immunosuppressive medications.

Slit-skin smear from a forearm lesion stained with Ziehl-Neelsen shows numerous acid-fast bacilli with a high bacillary index. Full blood count is within reference range with haemoglobin 145 g/L and white cell count 6.8 × 10^9/L.

High-resolution ultrasound of the right ulnar nerve shows fusiform enlargement and hypoechoic changes with increased intraneural vascularity consistent with active neuritis. There is no osteomyelitis or deep tissue abscess on regional ultrasound.
On further questioning he admits to regular childhood and adolescent contact with wild armadillos, including hunting and butchering the animals, and occasional consumption of their meat.

explanation: Chronic hypopigmented anaesthetic skin patches, palpable peripheral nerve thickening with neuritis on imaging, and a high bacillary load on slit-skin smear point to a chronic peripheral nerve–predominant mycobacterial infection. The history of prolonged household and zoonotic exposure to armadillos supports transmission risk. These features together are diagnostic for infection with Mycobacterium leprae.

hints.text: A 24-year-old previously healthy man presented to the emergency department with 48 hours of fever, crampy abdominal pain and profuse watery diarrhoea that progressed to several bloody stools. He was febrile 38.9°C, pulse 110/min, appeared mildly dehydrated with dry mucous membranes, and had diffuse abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs.

Symptoms began about 12 hours after a weekend family barbecue. He takes no regular medications, has no chronic illness, denied recent antibiotics or hospitalisation, and reported that three other family members who ate the same chicken dish developed similar symptoms.

Peripheral blood count showed leukocytosis 12.6 × 10^9/L with 86% neutrophils and CRP 58 mg/L. Stool microscopy showed numerous fecal leukocytes and occult blood. Routine blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours and stool culture was submitted.

Contrast CT abdomen performed for persistent pain demonstrated segmental circumferential thickening of the terminal ileum and proximal right colon with mild pericolonic fat stranding. Radiology report favoured focal infectious enterocolitis rather than new inflammatory bowel disease.

He remembers handling raw chicken while assembling a chicken salad and eating undercooked portions. Public health follow-up found that symptomatic contacts and a leftover chicken sample yielded motile, oxidase-negative, gram-negative bacilli producing hydrogen sulfide on triple sugar iron agar and forming non-lactose-fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar.

explanation: Acute febrile bloody diarrhoea beginning after a poultry exposure with fecal leukocytes and CT evidence of right-sided enterocolitis fits a foodborne enteric bacterial infection. The culture phenotype of a motile, oxidase-negative, non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative bacillus that produces hydrogen sulfide is diagnostic for a non-typhoidal enteric Salmonella species.

hints.text: A 19-year-old university student presented to the campus clinic with 12 hours of severe bifrontal headache, high fever and escalating neck pain. He was alert but lethargic, T 39.5°C, heart rate 110/min, had marked nuchal rigidity and several non-blanching petechial lesions over his trunk.

He lives in a crowded dormitory and attended a large house party 48 hours before symptom onset. He has no chronic illnesses, smokes socially, and reports he did not receive an adolescent booster of routine vaccinations.

Non-contrast CT of the head was done before lumbar puncture and showed no mass lesion. CSF obtained was cloudy with leukocyte count 2.8 × 10^9/L (95% neutrophils), glucose 1.0 mmol/L (serum glucose 6.0 mmol/L), protein 2.2 g/L. Gram stain of CSF demonstrated gram-negative diplococci.
Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain showed diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement consistent with meningitis and no focal abscess or significant cerebral oedema.

Nasopharyngeal swabs from two close contacts grew an oxidase-positive, gram-negative diplococcus that fermented glucose and maltose. Contact tracing confirmed multiple close contacts at the party including kissing and shared drinks.

explanation: Acute febrile meningitis with a petechial rash in a young adult from communal housing, together with neutrophil-predominant CSF, low CSF glucose and gram-negative diplococci on Gram stain, points to meningococcal infection. The isolate's oxidase positivity and fermentation of both glucose and maltose support identification as Neisseria meningitidis. Rapid transmission among close contacts explains the outbreak pattern and mandates urgent public-health action.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presents with six weeks of intermittent fevers, progressive fatigue, and increasing abdominal fullness. He reports a 6 kg weight loss and daily low-grade fevers. On examination he is febrile at 38.2°C, pale, and has a palpable spleen approximately 8 cm below the left costal margin.

He has no chronic medical conditions and is not immunosuppressed, HIV test on admission was negative. He returned four months ago from a three-month construction job in a rural part of the Indian subcontinent where he frequently slept outdoors and noted many nocturnal insect bites; stray dogs were common around the work site.

Laboratory results show haemoglobin 78 g/L, white blood cell count 2.1 × 10^9/L, platelets 72 × 10^9/L. Total protein is 98 g/L with albumin 27 g/L and C-reactive protein 48 mg/L. Thick and thin blood films for malaria are negative.
Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates marked splenomegaly with craniocaudal length 20 cm and mild hepatomegaly. No focal hepatic lesions or intra-abdominal abscesses are seen.

Because of persistent cytopenias a bone marrow aspirate was performed. Giemsa stain shows macrophages packed with small ovoid intracellular bodies 2–4 µm in diameter, each containing a rod-shaped kinetoplast, and the patient recalls heavy exposure to biting insects at night while in the rural region.

explanation: Prolonged fever, substantial splenomegaly, pancytopenia, and hypergammaglobulinaemia after travel to an endemic rural area raise concern for a visceral parasitic infection. Visualization of small intracellular bodies with a rod-shaped kinetoplast in marrow macrophages confirms infection by Leishmania species.

hints.text: A 34-year-old woman presents to clinic with 10 days of progressive symmetric pain and swelling of the wrists and proximal interphalangeal joints, with morning stiffness lasting about one hour. She reports fatigue and intermittent low-grade fevers to 38.0°C and noticed a faint erythematous macular flush across both cheeks five days earlier. On examination the PIPs are tender with mild synovitis and her grip strength is reduced, other joints are uninvolved and vital signs are otherwise normal.

She is previously well, not pregnant, takes no regular medications and has no personal or family history of autoimmune rheumatologic disease. Two weeks before joint symptoms she had a brief upper respiratory prodrome that resolved. She works full time as a kindergarten teacher and has no recent travel or animal exposures.

Complete blood count shows haemoglobin 78 g/L, white blood cells 6.7 × 10^9/L and platelets 250 × 10^9/L. Reticulocyte count is low at 0.5% and C-reactive protein is 18 mg/L. Direct antiglobulin test is negative.

Plain radiographs of both hands show soft tissue swelling around the PIP joints without joint space narrowing or erosive change. Musculoskeletal ultrasound confirms small joint synovitis with minimal effusion but no bone erosions.

When asked about contacts she says several children in her class had a recent outbreak of febrile illness followed by a bright facial erythema described by parents as a 'slapped cheek' appearance and a lacy truncal rash starting about three weeks ago.

explanation: The combination of acute symmetric non-erosive small-joint arthritis in an adult, a marked anaemia with reticulocytopenia, and recent exposure to children with a slapped-cheek exanthem points to infection with parvovirus B19 causing viral arthritis and transient red cell aplasia. The radiographs and negative direct antiglobulin test make autoimmune haemolysis or chronic erosive arthritis less likely.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man, ten days after emergency small-bowel resection for mesenteric ischemia, develops new fevers on postoperative day 14 while on the surgical ward. Temperature 38.3°C, heart rate 110/min, blood pressure 102/64 mmHg, he reports rigors, the right internal jugular central venous catheter appears intact with no surrounding erythema, and examination notes fine greasy scaling on the upper chest and back.

He has been nil by mouth and receiving total parenteral nutrition since surgery, including a soybean oil based intravenous lipid emulsion started on postoperative day 3. He received broad-spectrum antibiotics for suspected intra-abdominal contamination and has a longstanding history of seborrheic dermatitis treated with emollients.

Peripheral blood cultures flagged positive at 48 hours; Gram stain showed small, oval, faintly staining budding cells. White cell count 11.8 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 125 mg/L, and repeated subculture attempts on routine blood and chocolate agar produced no colonies.

Ultrasound of the right internal jugular catheter demonstrated a 2 cm non-compressible echogenic focus at the catheter tip consistent with thrombus. Chest radiograph and CT abdomen showed no pulmonary infiltrates or residual intra-abdominal collection to explain persistent fever.

Microbiology later reported that subcultures plated onto media overlaid with sterile olive oil produced small cream coloured colonies and that the isolate grew only with lipid supplementation. The patient had continued the intravenous lipid emulsion and had been applying coconut oil to his trunk; fevers abated after catheter removal and stopping the lipid emulsion.

explanation: A lipid-dependent yeast from the patient’s skin flora is the most likely cause of catheter related bloodstream infection. Positive blood culture Gram stain with failure to grow on routine media, growth only on oil-supplemented plates, ongoing intravenous lipid exposure and clinical resolution after stopping lipids and removing the catheter together support this diagnosis.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presented to the emergency department with three days of intermittent high fevers, rigors, frontal headache and diffuse myalgias. He reported a maximum temperature of 39.3°C, pulse 112 beats per minute, and on examination the spleen was palpable 4 cm below the left costal margin.

He had returned three weeks earlier from a six-month work assignment in rural eastern India where he slept in temporary housing beside irrigated rice paddies. He did not take chemoprophylaxis consistently and recalled frequent nocturnal mosquito bites; he has no chronic medical problems and takes no regular medications.

Blood tests showed haemoglobin 95 g/L, platelets 85 × 10^9/L and white cell count 3.6 × 10^9/L. Peripheral blood smear demonstrated low-level parasitaemia of approximately 0.6% with intraerythrocytic ring forms and infected red cells that were slightly larger than uninfected cells.
Abdominal ultrasound confirmed splenomegaly with a maximal longitudinal length of 16.5 cm and otherwise normal hepatic echotexture. Chest radiograph was unremarkable.

Eight weeks after apparent clinical clearance with a blood-stage antimalarial he returned with the same pattern of paroxysmal fevers. He again noted evenings working in irrigated lowlands with repeated mosquito exposure and received additional therapy aimed at eradicating presumed latent hepatic stages.

explanation: Travel to a South Asian rice-paddy region, splenomegaly with low-level parasitaemia, and infected red cells that are enlarged point to a parasite that prefers young erythrocytes. These features are most consistent with Plasmodium vivax infection.

hints.text: A 29-year-old man presented to the emergency department with three days of high fevers, drenching sweats, severe headache and progressive confusion. He became oliguric, and on examination was febrile 39.6 °C, pulse 120 beats per minute, blood pressure 95/60 mmHg, with mild scleral icterus and a palpable spleen 3 cm below the left costal margin.

He had returned 10 days earlier from a two-week volunteer placement in rural western Ghana. He did not take chemoprophylaxis, slept without a bed net, and reported numerous night-time mosquito bites. He has no chronic illnesses and takes no regular medications.

Initial bloods showed haemoglobin 78 g/L, platelet count 45 × 10^9/L, total bilirubin 85 µmol/L, creatinine 250 µmol/L and lactate 4.0 mmol/L. Thick and thin peripheral blood films demonstrated 12% of erythrocytes parasitized with predominantly early ring forms and multiple infections per red cell.
Non-contrast brain MRI demonstrated mild diffuse cerebral oedema with patchy T2 hyperintensities in the deep grey nuclei, without focal haemorrhage. Chest radiograph was unremarkable.

Three other volunteers from the same placement were hospitalised after return with high fevers, and regional public health notices from the districts visited warned of increased severe mosquito-borne febrile illness that season and poor response to older chloroquine regimens. The team had worked and slept in riverside villages with heavy night mosquito exposure.

explanation: Severe febrile illness after recent travel to sub-Saharan Africa with hyperparasitaemia, anaemia, thrombocytopenia, jaundice and cerebral oedema indicates severe malaria due to Plasmodium falciparum. The high percentage of parasitized erythrocytes and multiple infections per cell point to hyperparasitaemia with this species and explain the multiorgan dysfunction.

hints.text: A 36-year-old man presents to the outpatient clinic with 3 weeks of progressive exertional dyspnoea and a dry cough. He is now breathless at rest, afebrile, respiratory rate 24/min, oxygen saturation 88% on room air, and has fine inspiratory crackles at both bases.

He describes 5 kg weight loss and intermittent night sweats over the past 3 months but denies chronic lung disease, prior hospital admissions, recent travel, or smoking. He says he had been well previously and is not taking routine medications.

Full blood count shows white blood cells 5.6 × 10^9/L with lymphocytes 0.6 × 10^9/L. CRP 22 mg/L, lactate dehydrogenase 620 U/L, arterial PaO2 on room air 7.2 kPa. Serum 1,3-beta-D-glucan is markedly elevated at 600 pg/mL.

High-resolution CT of the chest demonstrates diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities with perihilar and upper lobe predominance and relative subpleural sparing. There is no focal lobar consolidation and only small apical cystic changes.

On further questioning he admits recent unprotected sexual contacts and reports a clinic HIV test done 4 days ago that returned positive. His same-day CD4 count was 82 × 10^6/L and he was not on antiretroviral therapy or on the daily prophylactic medication that reduces risk of this pneumonia.

explanation: Subacute progressive hypoxaemic pneumonitis with diffuse ground-glass opacities, high LDH, and markedly elevated beta-D-glucan in a patient with profound CD4 lymphopenia and no prophylaxis points to Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. The clinical picture fits an opportunistic fungal pneumonia causing disproportionate hypoxaemia and diffuse interstitial change.

hints.text: A 28-year-old male humanitarian aid worker presents with 48 hours of progressive weakness of his right leg. He reports a 3-day febrile illness with sore throat and myalgia before the weakness began; on examination he is afebrile, heart rate 88/min, power in the right lower limb 2/5 with flaccidity, absent right knee and ankle reflexes, intact pinprick and light touch, and normal strength on the left.

He is previously healthy with no chronic conditions. Ten days before presentation he returned from a two-week assignment in a region where routine childhood immunisation services had been disrupted; his childhood vaccination record is incomplete and he recalls frequent febrile gastroenteritis among children at the camp.

Lumbar puncture on day 2 of weakness showed CSF WBC 160 × 10^6/L with lymphocytic predominance, protein 0.8 g/L, glucose 3.3 mmol/L. Serum full blood count and electrolytes were unremarkable. Motor nerve conduction showed reduced compound muscle action potentials in the affected limb with preserved sensory responses, suggesting an anterior horn cell process rather than a primary demyelinating polyneuropathy.

MRI of the spine demonstrated T2 hyperintensity localized to the anterior horn grey matter of the lumbar cord on axial sequences. There was no extrinsic compression, no long-segment longitudinally extensive cord lesion, and no predominant posterior column involvement.

Local public health reported an outbreak of acute flaccid paralysis among underimmunised children during his deployment, with environmental sewage and stool isolates matching a vaccine-derived strain of a small non-enveloped enteric RNA virus known to cause anterior horn damage. Stool PCR from this patient later returned positive for the same strain.

explanation: The clinical course of febrile prodrome followed by acute asymmetric flaccid paralysis, CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis, MRI signal confined to anterior horn cells, and identical viral isolates in stool and sewage indicate infection with poliovirus. These findings point to viral anterior horn cell destruction rather than Guillain-Barré syndrome or compressive myelopathy. Stool PCR or culture from faeces provides the confirmatory diagnosis.

hints.text: A 29-year-old previously well man presented to the emergency department with three days of fever, increasing anxiety, and progressive numbness and burning pain in the right forearm. He reported new difficulty swallowing thin liquids and increased drooling. On arrival he was febrile to 38.3°C and tachycardic at 112/min. Neurological exam showed focal hyperesthesia over the right distal forearm and intermittent agitation with preserved limb strength.

He works as a field technician for a conservation group and had not received any occupational pre-exposure vaccination. He had no chronic medical conditions and takes no medications. On initial review he denied recent animal bites or scratches and reported a short hiking trip overseas two months ago.

Lumbar puncture on day 1 showed CSF white cell count 140 × 10^6/L with 90% lymphocytes, protein 1.1 g/L, glucose 3.7 mmol/L. CSF PCR was negative for herpes simplex and enterovirus. Routine blood counts and chemistry were within normal limits. Bacterial cultures of blood and CSF remained sterile.

Brain MRI obtained on hospital day 2 demonstrated T2/FLAIR hyperintensity involving the bilateral hippocampi and dorsal midbrain tegmentum. There was no focal mass lesion, restricted diffusion, or meningeal enhancement.

Targeted reinterview revealed that six weeks earlier he had awakened with a small painless puncture on the right forearm after finding a bat in his sleeping cabin, and he did not seek wound care or receive vaccine or immunoglobulin. Saliva RT-PCR returned positive for viral RNA. Nuchal skin biopsy immunofluorescence detected viral antigen in cutaneous nerve fibres.

explanation: The combination of progressive encephalitic signs with focal paresthesia at the site of a remote puncture, lymphocytic CSF, limbic and brainstem MRI signal abnormalities, and detection of viral RNA and antigen from saliva and nuchal skin supports infection with rabies virus. The six week interval from presumed exposure is compatible with the incubation period and the absence of postexposure prophylaxis explains disease progression.

hints.text: A 52-year-old man presented to the transplant clinic with five days of progressive cough, nasal congestion and increasing breathlessness. He was dyspnoeic at rest, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 88% on room air and had diffuse expiratory wheeze with scattered crackles on auscultation.

He underwent allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation six weeks ago for myelodysplastic syndrome and remains on tacrolimus and prednisone 15 mg daily for graft-versus-host disease prophylaxis. Two household contacts had recent uncomplicated upper respiratory symptoms and he had attended a crowded outpatient infusion centre three days before symptom onset.

Complete blood count showed WBC 2.1 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 1.2 × 10^9/L and lymphocytes 0.4 × 10^9/L. C reactive protein was 78 mg/L and procalcitonin 0.12 µg/L. Rapid influenza assay and routine bacterial blood cultures were negative; a multiplex respiratory PCR was sent but pending.

High-resolution CT chest demonstrated diffuse peribronchial wall thickening with multifocal ground-glass opacities and patchy centrilobular nodularity, most prominent in the perihilar and lower lobe zones. No focal lobar consolidation or pleural effusion was present.

Bronchoalveolar lavage PCR returned positive for a single-stranded negative-sense RNA paramyxoviral pathogen. After reduction of immunosuppression, initiation of supportive oxygen and a course of aerosolised antiviral therapy, his oxygen requirements fell and cough and wheeze improved over the following week.

explanation: An immunocompromised patient several weeks after stem cell transplant with upper respiratory prodrome progressing to lower respiratory tract disease, lymphopenia and a bronchiolitis-pattern CT strongly suggests a viral pneumonitis.

hints.text: A 34-year-old childcare worker presented to urgent care with four days of progressive hoarseness, daytime low-grade fever and a persistent harsh barking cough that worsened at night. She reports mild dyspnoea and intermittent inspiratory stridor on exertion; examination shows T 37.9°C, respiratory rate 20/min, O2 saturation 96% on room air, suprasternal and intercostal retractions and a muffled voice, chest auscultation without focal crackles.

She has mild intermittent asthma treated with salbutamol as needed, no inhaled corticosteroids and no other comorbidity. She works in an urban daycare where several toddlers developed sudden onset barking cough and hoarseness one week earlier, and she cares for an infant who required brief hospital observation for noisy breathing.

Blood tests show white cell count 8.4 × 10^9/L with lymphocytes 4.2 × 10^9/L, CRP 12 mg/L. Throat bacterial culture is negative and rapid influenza test is negative. A multiplex respiratory PCR panel was sent from a nasopharyngeal swab.

An expiratory anterior neck radiograph demonstrates symmetric narrowing of the subglottic tracheal air column consistent with upper airway inflammation. Frontal chest radiograph is clear without focal consolidation or diffuse bronchiolitis changes.

Multiplex PCR returned positive for a single non-influenza respiratory virus, and identical viral targets were detected in nasopharyngeal swabs from three symptomatic toddlers at the daycare the same week. Local public health recorded an outbreak of acute laryngotracheobronchitis among attendees in late autumn.

explanation: The combination of adult laryngotracheobronchitis with subglottic narrowing, a daycare cluster of croup-like illness in toddlers, and a single non-influenza respiratory virus detected by PCR is most consistent with parainfluenza virus. Normal to mildly elevated inflammatory markers and negative bacterial cultures support a viral upper airway process. The epidemiologic link to children with acute croup is the key discriminator.

hints.text: A 43-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 4 days of high fever, severe frontal headache, diffuse myalgias and a new skin eruption. He was febrile to 39.3°C and tachycardic at 110/min, and exam showed a maculopapular rash that began on the wrists and ankles and now involves the palms and soles.

He returned 7 days earlier from a weekend of camping in wooded foothills and recalled removing an engorged tick from his forearm about 6 days before symptom onset. He has no chronic medical conditions, takes no regular medications and denied recent antibiotic use.

Laboratory studies showed white blood cell count 4.3 × 10^9/L, platelet count 78 × 10^9/L, sodium 129 mmol/L, AST 180 U/L and ALT 95 U/L. C-reactive protein was elevated at 120 mg/L and renal function was within his baseline.

Chest radiograph was clear and non-contrast CT head showed no acute intracranial abnormality when performed because of persistent severe headache and photophobia. There were no focal neurological deficits on serial examinations.
Empiric doxycycline was started on admission and the patient defervesced within 36 hours. Over the next 72 hours his headache improved, the rash faded and platelet count rose to 120 × 10^9/L.

explanation: Acute febrile illness after a tick exposure with a rash that began on wrists and ankles and involved palms and soles, thrombocytopenia, hyponatraemia and transaminitis points to an acute tickborne rickettsial infection. Rapid clinical and laboratory improvement after doxycycline further supports infection by Rickettsia rickettsii.

hints.text: A 62-year-old man presented to the emergency department with four days of progressive dyspnea, dry cough, and wheeze. He reported low-grade fever and nasal congestion earlier in the illness; on arrival he was tachypneic with respiratory rate 26/min, temperature 38.0°C and oxygen saturation 90% on room air, and examination showed diffuse expiratory wheeze with scattered fine crackles.

His past medical history is notable for allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplant five months prior for myelodysplastic syndrome; current medications include low-dose prednisone 10 mg daily and tacrolimus. He lives with his adult daughter who had recent 'a bad cold' and a local outpatient clinic reported several concurrent cases of upper respiratory tract infection in the community.

Blood tests showed WBC 1.8 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 1.0 × 10^9/L and lymphocytes 0.4 × 10^9/L, CRP 28 mg/L. Blood cultures remained sterile, influenza and SARS-CoV-2 PCRs were negative, and a multiplex respiratory PCR on a nasopharyngeal swab detected an RNA virus signal commonly reported with community 'common cold' illnesses.

Chest CT performed for persistent hypoxaemia showed multifocal peribronchial ground-glass opacities and bronchiolar wall thickening, greatest in the perihilar regions, without lobar consolidation or focal abscess; the pattern was reported as most compatible with viral bronchiolitis or viral pneumonitis in an immunocompromised host.

Empirical antibacterial therapy produced no meaningful clinical improvement and bronchodilator therapy relieved wheeze but not hypoxaemia; bronchoalveolar lavage was obtained and viral culture displayed cytopathic effect only at lower incubation temperature near 33°C and not at 37°C. Sequence analysis of the cultured virus matched multiple distinct serotypes within a single common upper respiratory virus group known to replicate optimally in cooler nasal mucosa.

explanation: In an immunocompromised patient with upper respiratory prodrome followed by lower respiratory tract illness, negative bacterial studies, peribronchial viral-pattern imaging and a virus that grows only at cooler temperatures with many serotypes point to rhinovirus causing lower respiratory involvement. The combination of community exposure, positive respiratory PCR signal for a common cold agent, and temperature-dependent culture supports rhinovirus as the etiologic agent.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 3 days of severe left-sided facial pain, progressive swelling around the left eye, and blurred vision. He had fever 38.9°C and tachycardia 110 bpm. On examination there was marked left periorbital edema, proptosis, conjunctival chemosis, reduced visual acuity in the left eye to hand movements, and diminished sensation over the left maxillary distribution.

He has a 12-year history of type 2 diabetes with poor control, most recent HbA1c 11.2%. He was admitted one week earlier for hyperglycaemic ketoacidosis and discharged after insulin therapy. He also had a left upper molar tooth extraction five days before the onset of facial pain.

Blood tests showed WBC 16.9 × 10^9/L, serum glucose 23.4 mmol/L, CRP 210 mg/L and arterial blood gas pH 7.25 with an anion gap. Bedside nasal endoscopy revealed ulcerated mucosa with dark crusting and deep biopsies were sent. Histology reported extensive necrosis with fungal elements and clear angioinvasion on periodic acid Schiff stain. Routine bacterial cultures were sterile.

Contrast CT of the sinuses and orbits demonstrated opacification of the left maxillary, ethmoid and sphenoid sinuses with areas of non-enhancing mucosa consistent with devitalised tissue, erosion of the medial orbital wall, and inflammatory extension into the orbital apex. MRI venography raised concern for early cavernous sinus thrombosis.

The patient initially received empirical intravenous antibiotics and voriconazole but showed ongoing fever and progression of orbital signs over 48 hours. He had urgent surgical debridement and was switched to liposomal amphotericin B with rapid clinical stabilization over the next 72 hours. Culture of the debrided tissue produced a fast-growing woolly colony and microscopy later demonstrated broad, pauciseptate hyphae; in vitro testing showed lack of activity to voriconazole.

explanation: Poorly controlled diabetes with recent ketoacidosis, rapid necrotising sinusitis with angioinvasion and orbital extension, failure to.

hints.text: A 24-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with 10 days of high fevers, worsening headache, and diffuse abdominal discomfort. On examination she was febrile at 39.3°C, pulse 88 bpm, had tender hepatosplenomegaly and several faint maculopapular lesions on the anterior trunk.

She was previously healthy and not on regular medications. Her illness began with intermittent fevers that became sustained over the first week, she developed progressive constipation and malaise, and she did not take antibiotics before presentation.

Laboratory testing showed leukopenia with white blood cell count 3.6 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 110 g/L, platelets 120 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 150 mg/L and alanine aminotransferase 82 U/L. Blood cultures obtained on admission grew a motile, non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative bacillus after 48 hours.

Abdominal ultrasound confirmed splenomegaly measuring 14 cm. Contrast CT of the abdomen showed focal thickening of the terminal ileum with adjacent mesenteric lymphadenopathy, without free air or abscess.

She had returned three weeks earlier from a three-week visit to an urban area in South Asia where she frequently drank unbottled water and ate food from street vendors, and local public health later linked several similar febrile cases to contaminated municipal water.

explanation: Prolonged high fever with abdominal pain, hepatosplenomegaly, faint truncal macules, relative leukopenia and terminal ileal inflammation after recent travel with ingestion of contaminated water point to a systemic enteric infection acquired abroad. Growth of a motile non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative bacillus from blood cultures provides microbiological confirmation consistent with the likely imported food or waterborne pathogen.

hints.text: A 59-year-old man presented to the transplant ward 7 days after deceased-donor kidney transplantation with a 3-day history of profuse watery diarrhoea and repeated vomiting. He had marked oliguria and clinical dehydration, blood pressure 90/55 mmHg and heart rate 110 beats per minute on examination.

His immunosuppression included tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil. Two days before his illness onset his family visited and his 18-month-old grandchild had an episode of febrile diarrhoea. The family reported the toddler had not completed routine infant immunisations.

Serum creatinine rose from a baseline 95 µmol/L to 260 µmol/L. White cell count was 6.8 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 28 mg/L. Stool testing was negative for bacterial culture and for Clostridioides difficile toxin by PCR, and ova and parasite microscopy was negative.

Contrast CT abdomen showed diffuse small-bowel wall thickening and mucosal hyperenhancement without focal abscess or colonic involvement. There was no mechanical obstruction or intra-abdominal collection to account for the degree of volume loss.

Stool PCR from the patient and from the visiting toddler were both positive for a non-enveloped, segmented double-stranded RNA virus. The identical viral strain matched by sequencing is the agent most commonly implicated in severe dehydrating diarrhoea of infancy and is included in routine infant immunisation programmes.

explanation: An immunocompromised adult with profuse watery diarrhoea, marked dehydration and acute kidney injury after household exposure to an unvaccinated toddler points to a paediatric enteric virus transmitted by fecal-oral contact. Negative bacterial and C. difficile testing and CT evidence of small-bowel enteritis support a viral enteritis. The stool PCR identifying a non-enveloped, segmented double-stranded RNA virus that is a common cause of infantile severe gastroenteritis indicates infection with rotavirus.

hints.text: A 29-year-old neonatal nurse presents with 5 days of low-grade fever and a diffuse erythematous maculopapular rash that began on the face and spread to the trunk. She also reports migratory pain in her wrists and knees and tender right cervical lymph nodes; temperature is 37.8°C and she remains hemodynamically stable.

She is 11 weeks pregnant and unsure of her childhood vaccination history. Symptoms began 9 days after she cared for a term infant admitted to her unit. She has no recent travel, no known sick contacts outside work, and has not started any new medications.

Complete blood count shows white blood cells 3.6 × 10^9/L, lymphocytes 0.9 × 10^9/L, platelets 125 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein is 6 mg/L. Liver enzymes are mildly elevated with ALT 78 U/L and AST 65 U/L. Acute viral serology is pending.
Targeted fetal ultrasound at 14 weeks shows a perimembranous ventricular septal defect and decreased fetal growth for dates. The sonographer also notes increased echogenicity in both lenses.

Review of the unit chart revealed the infant she cared for was born to a mother who had a febrile rash in the first trimester; that newborn was documented to have bilateral cataracts, a patent ductus arteriosus, and severe sensorineural hearing loss.

explanation: Mild febrile maculopapular illness with lymphadenopathy and arthralgia in an early pregnant woman followed by fetal cardiac defect and lens abnormality, plus a neonate with cataracts, patent ductus arteriosus, and sensorineural deafness strongly indicate maternal infection with Rubella virus in the first trimester. The timeline and occupational contact with the affected neonate support a nosocomial exposure leading to maternal infection.

hints.text: A 78-year-old man resident in a long-term care facility presented with six weeks of progressive generalized pruritus, worst at night and interfering with sleep. He had multiple excoriations and scattered erythematous papules with focal thick scaling on the wrists, forearms, abdomen, and anterior thighs. On exam he was afebrile and he had fissuring and hyperkeratosis on the palmar surfaces of both hands.

His medical history is notable for chronic lymphocytic leukaemia treated with chemotherapy nine months ago and a recent two-week course of high-dose systemic corticosteroids for autoimmune cytopenia. Staff report progressive skin symptoms despite repeated courses of topical emollients and several courses of oral antibiotics for presumed secondary bacterial impetiginisation.

Blood tests showed lymphopenia 0.6 × 10^9/L and eosinophilia 0.9 × 10^9/L. CRP was 22 mg/L. Multiple bedside skin scrapings and potassium hydroxide preps were initially reported as negative, and wound swab from excoriated sites grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus.

Hand-held dermoscopy of several lesions demonstrated thin serpiginous linear tracks in the superficial epidermis overlying areas of scale. On slow, real-time inspection there was subtle movement within some of those tunnels and a small dark focus at the leading edge of a number of the tracks.

During investigation the infection control team documented that more than a dozen other residents and three care workers developed new nocturnal pruritus and a similar papular eruption over the same six-week period after shared laundering of bedding and close personal care tasks with this patient.

explanation: Nocturnal pruritus with serpiginous superficial epidermal tunnels on dermoscopy, an outbreak among close contacts in a care facility, eosinophilia, and an immunocompromised host point to infestation with a small epidermal mite. Repeated negative scrapings can occur, especially with heavy hyperkeratosis, so dermoscopic detection and the epidemiology are key to diagnosis of infestation by that mite.

hints.text: A 43-year-old man presented to the emergency department with six days of fever, profound fatigue and progressive dyspnoea. On arrival he was febrile to 38.7°C, tachypnoeic at 26 breaths/min, and required 3 L·min⁻¹ oxygen by nasal cannula to maintain saturation 94%.

He is a smoker with well controlled type 2 diabetes treated with metformin, and works loading luggage at an international airport. He had received two doses of an inactivated viral vaccine eight months earlier and reported no recent foreign travel, but said several co-workers had mild 'cold' symptoms the week before his illness began.

Blood tests showed leukocytes 4.1 × 10^9/L with lymphocytes 0.7 × 10^9/L, platelets 170 × 10^9/L. CRP 86 mg/L, D-dimer 1.8 mg/L FEU, ALT 78 U/L. Arterial blood gas on 3 L·min⁻¹ oxygen: PaO2 8.3 kPa, PaCO2 4.6 kPa.
Low-dose CT chest demonstrated bilateral, multilobar peripheral and posterior predominant ground-glass opacities with early subpleural organising changes and no lobar consolidation or effusion.

He was started empirically on supplemental oxygen and dexamethasone, and a nasopharyngeal nucleic-acid amplification test targeting the viral spike gene returned strongly positive with a low cycle threshold. Whole-genome sequencing matched the strain responsible for the 2019 global respiratory pandemic; within 48 hours of initiating antiviral therapy directed at the polymerase the patient’s oxygen requirement began to fall.

explanation: The combination of subacute fever and progressive hypoxaemic respiratory failure, lymphopenia and raised inflammatory markers, and peripheral ground-glass opacities suggest viral pneumonia. A strongly positive RT-PCR targeting the spike gene with sequencing that aligns to the pandemic 2019 strain confirms infection with SARS-CoV-2.

hints.text: A 24-year-old competitive swimmer presents with 3 days of severe right ear pain and progressive hearing reduction. He reports the pain worsens with tragal pressure, temperature 38.0°C, and otoscopy shows erythematous swollen external auditory canal with purulent green discharge obscuring the tympanic membrane.

He has no diabetes or known immunosuppression and is otherwise healthy. He trains daily in a municipal pool, cleans his ears with cotton buds, and began topical over-the-counter ear drops after symptom onset without improvement.
Peripheral blood count shows leucocytosis 12.6 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 48 mg/L. Microscopy of an ear swab reveals abundant neutrophils and gram-negative rods on Gram stain.

Non-contrast CT of the temporal bones performed to exclude deep extension shows soft tissue swelling confined to the external auditory canal with patent middle ear and no bony erosion of the temporal bone or mastoid air cell opacification.

He reports heavy recent exposure to the pool and showering at the facility. Culture of the ear swab after 48 hours grew a non-lactose-fermenting, oxidase-positive gram-negative rod that produced a blue-green diffusible pigment on agar and a characteristic fruity odour.

explanation: This is an acute external auditory canal infection after swimming with purulent green discharge, gram-negative rods on swab, and a culture that produces a blue-green pigment and is oxidase positive. Those features indicate the pathogen responsible for swimmer's otitis externa in this clinical context.

hints.text: A 28-year-old woman presents with a 9-month history of intermittent visible haematuria and lower urinary tract discomfort. She describes episodes of painless gross haematuria that tend to appear at the end of micturition, associated with fatigue; temperature 36.7°C, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, examination shows conjunctival pallor and mild suprapubic tenderness.

She emigrated from a rural region of West Africa to the city 12 years ago and has had no regular follow-up since. She has never smoked, has no known cancer history, reports childhood and adolescent swimming in local slow-moving rivers, and recalls several transient itchy rashes after freshwater immersion years ago.

Haemoglobin 102 g/L, white cell count 7.6 × 10^9/L with absolute eosinophils 0.9 × 10^9/L, creatinine 78 µmol/L. Urinalysis shows 3+ blood and sterile pyuria, urine culture remains negative after 48 hours, and urinary cytology did not demonstrate malignant cells.

Pelvic ultrasound demonstrates irregular focal thickening of the bladder wall with punctate intramural calcifications and mild bilateral hydronephrosis. CT urography confirms mucosal and submucosal calcific densities along the bladder base without an enhancing intraluminal mass.

On targeted re-questioning she emphasizes repeated childhood bathing and wading in the same freshwater lagoon. Concentrated mid-day urine microscopy identified ovoid ova with a conspicuous terminal spine.

explanation: Chronic terminal haematuria, eosinophilia, bladder wall calcifications and mild hydronephrosis after freshwater exposure point to a chronic urogenital trematode infection. The finding of ovoid eggs with a terminal spine in concentrated urine confirms the urinary blood-fluke etiology.

hints.text: A 31-year-old man presented to clinic with six months of progressive abdominal distension and early satiety. He also reports increasing fatigue and two episodes of non-painful rectal bleeding over that period. On examination he is afebrile, pulse 82/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, has a firm spleen palpable 15 cm below the left costal margin and moderate ascites, but no jaundice and no peripheral stigmata of chronic liver disease.

He was born and raised in a rural lakeside village in East Africa and emigrated at age 12, with a short visit back two years ago. He denies alcohol misuse and has no history of intravenous drug use. He has never been diagnosed with viral hepatitis and received routine childhood vaccinations.

Haemoglobin 95 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 74 fL, platelets 75 × 10^9/L. White cell count 6.2 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 0.9 × 10^9/L. ALT 48 U/L, albumin 38 g/L. Serology for hepatitis B surface antigen and anti-HCV antibody are negative. Faecal occult blood is positive.

Abdominal ultrasound shows marked splenomegaly and symmetric periportal echogenic thickening tracking along portal radicles, with a smooth hepatic capsule and preserved lobular contour. Doppler demonstrates portal vein enlargement without cirrhotic nodularity. Cross-sectional imaging confirms extensive presinusoidal periportal fibrosis and portosystemic collateral formation.

On further questioning he recalls frequent childhood bathing and playing in the nearby lake and irrigation channels. Three separate stool microscopy specimens revealed ovoid eggs approximately 140–180 μm long with a conspicuous lateral spine.

explanation: Chronic presinusoidal portal hypertension with periportal fibrosis, massive splenomegaly, eosinophilia, remote freshwater exposure in East Africa, and stool eggs with a lateral spine point to infection with Schistosoma mansoni. The pattern of preserved hepatic architecture and portosystemic collaterals supports chronic intestinal schistosomiasis as the cause of his portal hypertension and rectal bleeding.

hints.text: A 47-year-old male community gardener presents with a 3-week history of a slowly enlarging ulcerated papule on the dorsum of his right hand and new painful nodules ascending his forearm. He reports progressive stiffness of the right index finger limiting his ability to work; temperature 36.8°C, pulse 78/min, and examination shows a 1.2 cm shallow undermined ulcer with black crust on the hand and three tender, firm subcutaneous nodules in a linear distribution up the volar forearm.

He is otherwise well, takes no regular medications, and has no known immunosuppression or diabetes. He completed a 7-day course of oral cephalosporin prescribed by his primary clinician with no improvement; there are no respiratory or systemic symptoms and no household contacts with similar lesions.

Full blood count shows WBC 7.2 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 140 g/L, platelets 260 × 10^9/L; C-reactive protein 12 mg/L. Gram stain and routine bacterial culture of pus from the hand were negative; a tissue specimen sent for mycology produced scant growth of a slow-growing mould after 5 days.

Bedside ultrasound of the forearm reveals multiple well-defined hypoechoic subcutaneous nodules arranged linearly along the expected course of superficial lymphatic channels, without fluid collections, tendon sheath involvement, or deep fascial extension.

On targeted questioning he recalls a thorn puncture to the right hand while pruning rose bushes approximately 10 days before the initial papule. The mycology laboratory later reported that the isolate grew as a mould at 25°C with slender septate hyphae bearing conidia in rosette-like arrangements and converted to cigar-shaped budding yeast forms at 37°C.

explanation: Subcutaneous ulcer followed by proximal nodules along lymphatic channels after a thorn injury suggests cutaneous lymphangitic infection.

hints.text: A 24-year-old previously healthy graduate student presents with 48 hours of profuse crampy lower abdominal pain and frequent small-volume stools described as bloody and mucoid. He is febrile to 38.9°C, heart rate 102/min, appears mildly dehydrated, and reports marked tenesmus and urgency that limit his ability to work.

He cares for his 2-year-old nephew several days a week and reports changing nappies daily over the past week. There was no recent international travel, no consumption of undercooked meat or shellfish, and no antibiotic use prior to symptom onset.

Blood count shows leukocytosis 12.8 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 45 mg/L. Stool microscopy demonstrates numerous neutrophils and red cells, and preliminary culture yields a non-motile, gram-negative bacillus that ferments glucose but not lactose.

Contrast CT abdomen performed because of severe pain shows circumferential mucosal thickening and submucosal oedema localized to the rectosigmoid colon consistent with acute colitis. There is no free air or obstruction.

Local public-health follow-up found identical organisms in stool cultures from the patient and his nephew, and multiple daycare contacts reported small-volume bloody diarrhoea after the same time window. The outbreak pattern points to efficient person-to-person spread with a low infectious dose following close contact during nappy changing.

explanation: Small-volume bloody mucoid diarrhoea with tenesmus, fecal neutrophils, rectosigmoid-predominant colitis on imaging, and a non-motile, non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative bacillus transmitted in a household/daycare cluster is most consistent with Shigella species. The epidemiology of low infectious dose and direct contact transmission supports this diagnosis.

hints.text: A 29-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after two witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizures over 24 hours. She reports a three-week history of progressive, dull holocranial headache and intermittent vomiting; on arrival she is afebrile, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, heart rate 92/min, and has mild left-sided weakness, grade 4/5, with persistent postictal confusion.

She moved from a highland rural community to the city 18 months ago and has no chronic medical conditions. She denies recent travel outside the country, reports no diarrhoea, and says she cares for her elderly mother in the same household.

Complete blood count shows WBC 8.6 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 0.8 × 10^9/L. Lumbar puncture yields clear fluid with 32 × 10^6/L white cells (predominantly lymphocytes), protein 0.9 g/L, and normal glucose.

MRI brain with contrast demonstrates multiple parenchymal cystic lesions scattered in both cerebral hemispheres, some lesions with ring enhancement and surrounding vasogenic oedema; non-contrast CT shows a few small calcified nodules.

On further questioning the patient says her mother was diagnosed two months ago with an intestinal helminth infection after the family noticed long, mobile segments in her stool and the mother received a single oral dose of praziquantel.

explanation: New-onset seizures with multifocal cystic and calcified brain lesions plus mild peripheral eosinophilia and CSF pleocytosis suggest a parasitic intracerebral process. Household exposure to a person recently treated for an adult intestinal tapeworm supports acquisition of eggs from a human carrier leading to intracerebral cyst formation, which explains the imaging and clinical presentation.

hints.text: A 38-year-old man presents to the outpatient clinic with three months of intermittent crampy abdominal pain and loose stools and a 6 kg unintentional weight loss. Over the past two weeks he developed a nonproductive cough and a pruritic, rapidly migrating linear erythematous rash across the lower abdomen and buttocks. On examination he is afebrile, pulse 88/min, oxygen saturation 97% on room air, with scattered expiratory wheeze and a few erythematous linear tracks that blanch with pressure.

He emigrated from a rural area of Southeast Asia 12 years ago and worked intermittently in landscaping before changing to indoor employment. Six weeks ago he received a 10-day course of oral corticosteroids for presumed reactive airways disease. He has no known HIV, denies recent hospital admissions, and has had recurrent episodic gastrointestinal complaints for years that were never conclusively investigated.

Complete blood count shows leukocytes 11.8 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 2.1 × 10^9/L and haemoglobin 112 g/L. C-reactive protein 8 mg/L. Two routine stool ova and parasite examinations reported no ova or cysts.

Chest CT performed for persistent cough shows multiple small, ill-defined peripheral nodules and patchy ground-glass opacities in both lungs suggesting migrating inflammatory foci. Abdominal CT shows mild thickening of proximal small-bowel loops without obstruction.

Repeat testing with a specialised stool concentration and an agar plate culture produced motile, slender filiform larvae leaving characteristic tracks across the plate. The patient reports frequent barefoot walking in his childhood village and the corticosteroid course preceded worsening of cough and rash.

explanation: Eosinophilia with chronic GI symptoms, a rapidly migrating pruritic linear rash, and migrating pulmonary infiltrates point to a nematode with autoinfection. Negative routine stool exams followed by a positive specialised stool concentration and agar plate culture demonstrating motile filiform larvae in a patient with recent corticosteroid exposure confirms the diagnosis.

hints.text: A 72-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 36 hours of fever, productive cough and pleuritic right-sided chest pain. He has tachycardia to 110/min, temperature 39.0°C, respiratory rate 24/min and SpO2 91% on room air; examination shows dullness to percussion and bronchial breath sounds over the right mid-lung.

He is a retired factory worker with a 50 pack-year smoking history and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease managed with inhalers. He reports a brief viral upper respiratory illness one week earlier and says he has not received any adult polysaccharide or conjugate vaccination against common respiratory encapsulated bacteria.
Blood tests show WBC 18.6 × 10^9/L with 88% neutrophils and C-reactive protein 165 mg/L. Sputum Gram stain demonstrates many neutrophils and gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci in pairs.
Chest radiograph shows a dense, lobar consolidation confined to the right middle lobe with air bronchograms and no obvious pleural effusion.

No recent travel or animal exposures. A urine antigen test for the organism that commonly causes community-acquired lobar pneumonia in older adults returned positive. The sputum culture produced alpha-hemolytic colonies that were optochin-sensitive and bile-soluble.

explanation: Acute onset lobar pneumonia in an older smoker with rusty sputum, neutrophilic leukocytosis, and gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci points to Streptococcus pneumoniae. The optochin sensitivity, bile solubility and positive urine antigen confirm the diagnosis.

hints.text: A 55-year-old man presented to the emergency department with three weeks of progressive occipital headache, intermittent low-grade fever, and new right-hand clumsiness. He became intermittently disoriented at home this morning and was brought by family. On examination temperature 38.2°C, GCS 14, mild right pronator drift and 4/5 weakness of the right upper limb, no neck stiffness.

He received a deceased-donor renal transplant four months earlier. Current medications include tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone 10 mg daily. Pre-transplant screening recorded no detectable IgG to a common intracellular protozoan pathogen in the recipient. He has no known malignancy and no recent travel.

Peripheral blood leucocytes 5.6 × 10^9/L, CRP 24 mg/L, serum creatinine 120 µmol/L. Serum testing now shows positive IgG against a ubiquitous intracellular protozoan with negative IgM. Lumbar puncture opening pressure 160 mmH2O, CSF WBC 42 × 10^6/L with 85% lymphocytes, protein 1.0 g/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L.

Contrast MRI brain demonstrates three spherical ring-enhancing lesions measuring 1.5 to 3.0 cm, the largest in the left basal ganglia and others at the left frontal corticomedullary junction. Marked surrounding vasogenic oedema produces mild mass effect but no uncal herniation.
Two months before symptom onset he adopted a rescue kitten and performed daily litter box cleaning without gloves. He also ate undercooked lamb at a family meal three months earlier.

explanation: An immunosuppressed renal transplant recipient with multiple ring-enhancing basal ganglia lesions, CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis, and positive serum IgG with negative IgM is most consistent with reactivation of an intracellular protozoan infection. The recent close contact with a kitten and prior ingestion of undercooked meat provide the typical exposure history. These features together point to infection by Toxoplasma gondii causing cerebral toxoplasmosis.

hints.text: A 47-year-old previously healthy man presented with 10 days of fever, diffuse myalgias and progressive difficulty climbing stairs. He described a brief episode of abdominal cramps and watery diarrhoea one week before the myalgias began. On examination temperature was 38.3 °C, hip flexion was 4/5 bilaterally with marked tenderness of the thighs, and he had mild periorbital puffiness on the right.

He is an amateur hunter and helps process game for a local festival but has no chronic illness and takes no regular medications, including no statins. He reported no recent international travel, no new vaccinations, and no contact with sick animals other than handling carcasses and trimming meat for the community event three weeks earlier.

Full blood count showed WBC 14.2 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 2.8 × 10^9/L (20%). Serum creatine kinase was 1,200 U/L, alanine transaminase 72 U/L, and C-reactive protein 28 mg/L. Serology for common viral myositides was negative.

MRI of the pelvis and thighs demonstrated symmetric patchy T2 hyperintensity in the proximal limb muscles with prominent enhancement after contrast, most marked in the iliopsoas and vasti. Radiologist noted multiple small nodular intramuscular foci tracking along muscle fibres, interpreted as focal inflammatory or infiltrative lesions.

On targeted questioning he recalled eating undercooked wild boar sausages at the festival three weeks before symptom onset; several other attendees had short-lived gastroenteritis afterwards. The timeline of enteric symptoms followed by fever, marked eosinophilia and inflammatory myositis after a wild-game meal pointed to a parasitic infection from ingested meat.

explanation: The sequence of transient enteritis then delayed fever and proximal myositis with marked peripheral eosinophilia and elevated CK after consumption of undercooked wild game is most consistent with Trichinella spiralis. The MRI findings of inflammatory myositis with small intramuscular nodules and the exposure history support a muscle-invasive helminth acquired by eating contaminated meat.

hints.text: A 29-year-old man presents to a sexual health clinic with a solitary painless penile ulcer present for 3 weeks. On examination he is afebrile, the ulcer measures about 1.5 cm with a firm, slightly indurated base, and there is a single 2.5 cm firm, non-tender left inguinal lymph node.

He reports a single episode of unprotected vaginal intercourse with a new partner while travelling five weeks earlier. He has no previous sexually transmitted infections, last HIV test 6 months ago was negative, and he takes no regular medications or recreational injecting drugs.

Rapid plasma reagin (RPR) is reactive at a titre of 1:64. A confirmatory specific antibody assay is also reactive. Point-of-care HIV test is non-reactive and full blood count and C-reactive protein are within reference ranges.
Ultrasound of the left groin shows multiple enlarged solid lymph nodes, largest 3.2 cm in greatest dimension, without central liquefaction or features of abscess.

The patient says his partner developed a transient painless genital sore that healed on its own and later told him she had a reactive RPR when screened. She received a single intramuscular dose of long-acting benzathine penicillin.

explanation: A painless indurated genital ulcer with non-tender inguinal adenopathy, high-titre reactive RPR and confirmatory antibody, and a partner with the same clinical course and treatment point to infection with Treponema pallidum causing primary syphilis. The ultrasound finding of non-suppurative enlarged nodes supports a reactive rather than pyogenic process.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presents to a tropical medicine clinic with six weeks of intermittent fevers, frontal headache, and progressively worsening daytime sleepiness. He reports difficulty concentrating at work and two near-fainting episodes; on examination he is somnolent but arousable, febrile at 38.3°C, and has a 3 cm firm, tender posterior cervical lymph node.

He returned eight weeks ago from a three-month stay working on riverine farms in rural West Africa, where he frequently slept outdoors. He remembers a painful insect bite on his forearm that formed a small papule and did not improve after a five-day course of oral amoxicillin; he has no known immunodeficiency and tested HIV negative on screening.

Haemoglobin 105 g/L, white cell count 8.9 × 10^9/L, platelets 210 × 10^9/L, CRP 42 mg/L. Lumbar puncture: CSF white cell count 180 × 10^6/L with 85% lymphocytes, protein 1.1 g/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L with serum glucose 5.8 mmol/L. Blood cultures sterile after five days.

MRI brain shows diffuse T2 hyperintensity in periventricular and deep white matter and mild leptomeningeal enhancement on post-contrast sequences. Ultrasound of the neck confirms multiple enlarged posterior cervical lymph nodes without central necrosis.

Review of a fresh peripheral blood smear and a CSF wet preparation demonstrated live, actively motile, single-flagellated extracellular organisms. The patient reported multiple daytime bites from large biting flies while working in riverine grasslands during his stay in rural West Africa.

explanation: Subacute intermittent fever, prominent posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and progressive somnolence after riverine travel in sub-Saharan Africa with CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis and meningoencephalitic MRI changes point to a protozoal meningoencephalitis. Visualization of motile extracellular flagellated organisms in both blood and CSF confirms infection with Trypanosoma brucei involving the central nervous system.

hints.text: A 49-year-old Bolivian-born man presents to the cardiology clinic with nine months of progressive exertional dyspnea and two near-syncope episodes. He now tires when climbing a single flight of stairs, reports ankle swelling overnight, and on exam has blood pressure 100/64 mmHg, a displaced apical impulse, elevated jugular venous pressure and bibasilar crackles.

He emigrated to Spain 18 years ago and has no history of hypertension, diabetes, or coronary artery disease. He recalls growing up in a rural Andean village where his family lived in adobe walls and he frequently had insect bites at night; he denies heavy alcohol use and reports no illicit drug use.

NT-proBNP is 2 400 ng/L, high-sensitivity troponin I is 6 ng/L. Full blood count and renal function are within normal limits. Serology shows high-titre IgG with absent IgM against an intracellular protozoan known to be endemic in rural South America.

Transthoracic echocardiogram shows left ventricular dilation with LVEF 28% and a discrete thinned area at the cardiac apex with a small mural thrombus. Chest radiograph confirms cardiomegaly without pulmonary consolidation.

On targeted questioning he describes nocturnal household insects that bite the face and hide in cracks of adobe walls, recalled by locals as blood-feeding reduviid 'kissing' bugs, and he received a blood transfusion in Bolivia in 1999.

explanation: Chronic cardiomyopathy with apical wall thinning or aneurysm, positive specific IgG and a history of childhood exposure to nocturnal blood-feeding reduviid insects or historic transfusion from rural South America point to chronic infection by Trypanosoma cruzi as the unifying diagnosis. The conduction and ventricular remodeling pattern with mural thrombus and absence of ischemic risk factors further supports this etiology.

hints.text: A 72-year-old retired carpenter presented with 10 days of worsening headache, confusion, and new left-sided weakness. He was febrile at 38.3°C, blood pressure 150/85 mmHg, Glasgow Coma Scale 14, with left facial droop and 3/5 power in the left arm and leg, and mild nuchal rigidity on examination; no skin lesions were documented at initial assessment.

Medical history includes type 2 diabetes and hypertension. He began oral prednisolone 20 mg daily six weeks ago for polymyalgia rheumatica. Three weeks before admission he experienced severe unilateral scalp and ear pain with a small cluster of painful vesicles that healed over about ten days without systemic therapy.

Admission blood tests showed WBC 12.0 × 10^9/L and CRP 48 mg/L. Lumbar puncture produced clear CSF with white cells 210 × 10^6/L predominantly lymphocytes, protein 1.4 g/L, and glucose 3.4 mmol/L with concurrent serum glucose 7.6 mmol/L. Bacterial cultures were sterile.

MRI brain with diffusion weighting demonstrated multiple small acute infarcts in the right frontal cortex and adjacent deep white matter. MR angiography revealed segmental narrowing and beading of branches of the right middle cerebral artery consistent with focal intracranial arterial vasculopathy.
Empirical intravenous aciclovir was started on admission. Over five days the patient defervesced and his left-sided strength improved to 4/5 with marked reduction in confusion.

explanation: An older patient on corticosteroids who had a recent unilateral painful vesicular scalp eruption and then developed focal cerebral infarcts with segmental intracranial arterial narrowing fits reactivation-associated vasculopathy. CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis and clinical improvement with intravenous aciclovir support a reactivating neurotropic herpesvirus. The most likely pathogen is Varicella-zoster virus.

hints.text: A 24-year-old woman presents to the sexual health clinic with a 2-week history of increasing malodorous vaginal discharge and soreness with intercourse. She is afebrile and hemodynamically stable, pelvic examination shows copious yellow-green frothy discharge and mild cervical erythema without adnexal tenderness.

She reports a new male partner three weeks ago and inconsistent condom use. She takes combined oral contraception, has no recent antibiotic exposure, and has a remote treated chlamydial infection one year earlier; she is not pregnant.

Vaginal pH measures 5.5. Microscopy of a vaginal swab shows numerous polymorphonuclear leukocytes, no budding yeast and no clue cells. Nucleic acid amplification tests for two common bacterial sexually transmitted pathogens are negative.

A transvaginal ultrasound was obtained to exclude upper genital tract involvement. It shows a normal-appearing uterus and both ovaries, no adnexal masses and minimal free fluid in the pouch of Douglas.

She was given a single 2 g oral dose of a nitroimidazole and reported marked reduction in malodour and discharge within 48 hours. A repeat point-of-care wet mount demonstrated motile pear-shaped protozoa with jerky movement and targeted NAAT on the stored swab returned positive for that protozoan.

explanation: The combination of malodorous yellow-green discharge, vaginal pH above 4.5 and a heavy neutrophilic inflammatory response with negative tests for yeast and common bacterial STIs narrows the differential. Demonstration of motile pear-shaped protozoa on wet mount and rapid improvement after nitroimidazole treatment confirm infection with Trichomonas vaginalis.

hints.text: A 19-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with 48 hours of progressive right lower abdominal pain, fever to 38.7°C, and two loose stools. On examination she had localized tenderness in the right iliac fossa with voluntary guarding, a tender palpable 3 cm mass in the right lower quadrant, and heart rate 102 bpm; she was afebrile after paracetamol.

She is previously healthy, takes no regular medications, and is not pregnant. Symptoms began abruptly two days after a weekend onset, with one episode of red-tinged stool and no urinary symptoms; she had not taken antibiotics prior to presentation.
Blood tests showed WBC 11.8 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance, CRP 92 mg/L, and haemoglobin 132 g/L. Stool microscopy showed numerous polymorphonuclear cells and a stool culture was sent.

Right lower quadrant ultrasound demonstrated a thickened terminal ileum and several enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes up to 2.5 cm, with a normal calibre appendix visualised. Findings were reported as acute ileitis with mesenteric lymphadenitis rather than appendicitis.

On targeted history she recalled eating undercooked pork sausages at a family barbecue four days before illness and also drinking unpasteurised apple cider. The laboratory later reported stool culture growth of a small non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative bacillus that was ampicillin resistant and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole susceptible.

explanation: Young patient with acute terminal ileitis and mesenteric lymphadenitis presenting like appendicitis after undercooked pork exposure, plus a non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative isolate, points to Yersinia enterocolitica. The organism often produces pseudoappendicitis and is linked to pork and unpasteurised foods, and the reported.

hints.text: A 24-year-old previously healthy man presents to the emergency department six hours after the sudden onset of profuse watery diarrhoea and recurrent vomiting following travel to a coastal region. He reports passing voluminous pale, flecked stools without blood; on arrival he is light-headed, heart rate 122 beats/min, blood pressure 88/56 mmHg, capillary refill prolonged and mucous membranes dry.

He has no chronic medical problems and takes no regular medications. Symptoms began abruptly after a single evening of local food; he has had about 12 watery bowel movements in six hours, produced almost no urine, denies fever and describes only mild abdominal cramping.

Laboratory tests show haemoglobin 185 g/L, white cell count 9.8 × 10^9/L, sodium 148 mmol/L, potassium 2.8 mmol/L, creatinine 220 μmol/L, venous bicarbonate 16 mmol/L and lactate 4.1 mmol/L. Stool microscopy demonstrates no fecal leukocytes, and bacterial culture and molecular testing are pending.

Point-of-care ultrasound demonstrates a small inferior vena cava with greater than 50% respiratory collapsibility and normal left ventricular function. Upright abdominal radiograph shows a non-obstructive bowel gas pattern without dilated loops or free air.

Further questioning reveals he drank untreated village pump water and ate a street-vended seafood soup while in the coastal village; local public health later reported a cluster of other travellers and residents with abrupt profuse watery diarrhoea after using the same water source.

explanation: Profuse, non-bloody voluminous diarrhoea with rapid hypovolaemia, hypokalaemia and marked hemoconcentration after exposure to contaminated coastal water/food in a community cluster is most consistent with Vibrio cholerae. The absence of fecal leukocytes and the need for aggressive volume and electrolyte replacement further support a secretory diarrhoeal process caused by that organism.

hints.text: A 38-year-old man presented to the outpatient clinic with 3 weeks of a gradually enlarging right submandibular swelling. He complained of dull pain, progressive trismus with maximal mouth opening of about 2 cm, and intermittent low-grade fevers. On examination there was a 4 cm firm, indurated mass below the angle of the mandible with mild overlying erythema and skin tethering, but no obvious fluctuance and no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. Temperature 37.9°C, heart rate 88/min.

He was previously well and not immunosuppressed, with no diabetes and no recent respiratory illness. He had longstanding poor dentition on the right lower molars and had been given two short courses of oral amoxicillin by his general practitioner with only transient partial improvement.

Blood tests showed WBC 12.6 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 9.8 × 10^9/L and CRP 68 mg/L. Peripheral blood cultures remained negative. Percutaneous aspiration returned scant thick yellow material; initial aerobic cultures reported mixed oral flora without a single dominant aerobic pathogen.
