Contrast CT of the neck demonstrated an irregular infiltrative low-attenuation collection in the right submandibular and submental spaces measuring 3.8 × 2.5 cm with multiple small loculations, indistinct margins crossing the midline and extension through fascial planes. There was subtle cortical irregularity of the adjacent mandibular body but no discrete enlarged lymph nodes to suggest a primary nodal process.

On directed re-interview he recalled a difficult extraction of the right lower molar six weeks earlier with a prolonged nonhealing socket. During surgical drainage the team observed multiple small yellow 'sulfur' granules in the pus; prolonged anaerobic culture grew a slow-growing branching gram-positive filamentous organism that was not acid-fast.

explanation: A chronic indurated submandibular mass developing after dental manipulation, imaging showing infiltration across tissue planes with mandibular involvement, visible sulfur granules, and a slow-growing branching gram-positive filamentous organism on anaerobic culture that is not acid-fast support the diagnosis caused by the oral filamentous anaerobe.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man presents to clinic with a 3-week history of progressive bifrontal headache, intermittent low-grade fever, and new difficulty using his left hand. Family members report increasing confusion and unsteady gait over the past 10 days. On examination he is somnolent but arousable, febrile 37.8°C, disoriented to date, and has mild left-sided weakness with pronator drift.

He underwent a deceased-donor renal transplant 14 months ago and is maintained on tacrolimus and prednisone. Two months prior he had a painful right corneal ulcer that was culture-negative and treated with repeated topical corticosteroid courses. He denies recent travel outside the region or freshwater swimming.

Lumbar puncture: opening pressure 260 mmH2O, CSF WBC 120 × 10^6/L with 78% lymphocytes, protein 1.2 g/L, glucose 2.0 mmol/L (concurrent plasma glucose 5.0 mmol/L). CSF Gram stain and routine bacterial, mycobacterial and fungal cultures are negative; CSF PCR for herpesviruses and enterovirus is negative.

Contrast MRI brain shows multiple irregular T2 hyperintense lesions at the cortical–subcortical junction of both hemispheres with ring and nodular enhancement, surrounding vasogenic oedema, and a small focus of susceptibility within the right frontal lesion suggestive of petechial haemorrhage.

On targeted questioning he admits to nightly soft contact lens wear and routinely rinsing and storing lenses with tap water. Right corneal symptoms preceded the neurologic decline. Stereotactic brain biopsy revealed motile amoeboid trophozoites and double-walled cysts on silver stain, organisms that grew on non-nutrient agar overlaid with bacteria, and species-level PCR from tissue matched an environmental free-living amoeba linked epidemiologically to contact-lens and tap-water exposures.

explanation: Subacute focal encephalitis in an immunosuppressed solid-organ transplant recipient with lymphocytic CSF, multifocal enhancing parenchymal lesions and a preceding culture-negative contact-lens keratitis that involved tap-water exposure points to infection by Acanthamoeba species. Tissue demonstration of trophozoites and double-walled cysts with growth on non-nutrient agar and confirmatory PCR establishes the diagnosis.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presents with six months of progressive fatigue, exertional dyspnoea, intermittent crampy lower abdominal pain and loose stools. He works on small vegetable farms and reports reduced exercise tolerance; on examination he is pale with conjunctival pallor and a heart rate of 100 beats per minute, blood pressure 115/70 mmHg, and mild tenderness in the right lower quadrant without peritonism.

He emigrated from a tropical rural region eight years ago and recalls childhood episodes of persistent diarrhoea among classmates. He reports inconsistent access to clean water growing up, no known chronic disease, a single empiric antihelmintic dose administered in childhood, no recent travel, and no immunosuppressive medication use.

Full blood count shows haemoglobin 88 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 72 fL, white cell count 8.2 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 0.9 × 10^9/L, platelets 320 × 10^9/L. Iron studies show ferritin 12 µg/L and transferrin saturation 8%. Faecal occult blood is positive on two samples. A single routine stool microscopy reported no ova seen.

Colonoscopy demonstrates patchy erythema and multiple small mucosal nodules concentrated in the caecum and ascending colon, with several superficial erosions. Multiple biopsies were taken from nodular areas; histology shows chronic eosinophil-rich inflammation without granulomas.

Further questioning revealed he commonly ate raw leafy vegetables from fields fertilised with untreated human night soil in childhood. Concentration of a fresh stool sample using a faecal flotation technique identified ovoid barrel-shaped eggs about 50–55 µm long with prominent polar plugs at both ends.

explanation: Chronic microcytic anaemia with positive faecal occult blood, right-sided colonic inflammation and eosinophilia in a patient from an area with poor sanitation suggests a helminthic colonic infection. Identification of barrel-shaped eggs with bipolar plugs on concentrated stool microscopy is diagnostic of a whip-shaped nematode that embeds its thin anterior body in the colonic mucosa.

hints.text: A 27-year-old woman presents to clinic with a 3-week history of a progressively enlarging painful swelling in her left axilla and intermittent low-grade fevers. She notes increasing discomfort with shoulder movement, temperature in clinic 37.8°C, heart rate 92/min, and on examination a 4.0 cm tender, mobile left axillary lymph node and a 1 cm healing erythematous papule on the lateral aspect of the left forearm.

She is otherwise healthy, takes no regular medications, and has no known immunosuppression. There is no recent travel, no night sweats, no weight loss, and she has not responded to a 5-day course of oral phenoxymethylpenicillin prescribed by her primary care physician for presumed bacterial lymphadenitis.

Full blood count shows WBC 8.6 × 10^9/L with a normal differential, CRP 28 mg/L, ESR 36 mm/h. Two sets of blood cultures are sterile after 5 days, and a fine-needle aspirate of the node yielded serosanguinous fluid with no organisms seen on Gram stain and no growth on routine aerobic culture at 72 hours.

Ultrasound of the left axilla demonstrates a 38 mm lymph node with central hypoechogenicity consistent with focal necrosis and increased peripheral vascularity. The radiologist commented that findings favor suppurative regional lymphadenitis rather than malignancy.

On repeat history the patient recalls being scratched on the left forearm by a newly adopted kitten about 10 days before the forearm papule appeared, and the kitten had visible fleas. No other animal exposures were reported.

explanation: Regional tender axillary lymphadenitis following a recent kitten scratch, a resolving papule at the inoculation site, sterile routine cultures, and an ultrasound showing necrotic node point to infection with Bartonella henselae. This organism often causes subacute suppurative lymphadenitis in immunocompetent hosts and may require targeted testing such as serology or PCR and treatment with a macrolide or drainage if fluctuance develops.

hints.text: A 48-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with 7 days of progressive left lower quadrant pain and fever. She reported increasing pain that now limits walking; temperature 38.6 °C and pulse 102/minute. Examination showed focal tenderness and voluntary guarding over the left lower quadrant without diffuse peritonism. Bowel sounds were reduced and she appeared mildly dehydrated.

She has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. Five weeks earlier she had an episode of acute sigmoid diverticulitis treated as an outpatient with a short course of oral antibiotics and improved clinically. She has not had recent abdominal surgery or instrumentation and has no foreign travel.

White blood cell count 15.8 × 10^9/L with 85% neutrophils, haemoglobin 112 g/L, C-reactive protein 128 mg/L. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures obtained before antibiotics remained sterile at 48 hours. Basic metabolic panel and liver function tests were within reference ranges.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 5.8 cm multiloculated fluid collection with peripheral rim enhancement and internal gas locules abutting the sigmoid colon. The adjacent sigmoid wall was thickened with pericolic fat stranding, consistent with a contained perforation and abscess.

Percutaneous drainage produced foul-smelling purulent fluid. Anaerobic culture from the aspirate grew gram-negative rods that grew on bile-containing media and expressed beta-lactamase; isolates were resistant to penicillin and clindamycin and inhibited by metronidazole. The patient defervesced and symptoms improved within 48 hours of drainage plus intravenous metronidazole.

explanation: A post-colonic disease intra-abdominal abscess with foul anaerobic purulent fluid and anaerobic gram-negative bile-tolerant, beta-lactamase producing rods that. The clinical course, CT findings, and microbiology together support this diagnosis and the observed rapid improvement after drainage and metronidazole.

hints.text: A 56-year-old man presents to the emergency department in early June with 6 days of fever, diffuse myalgias, frontal headache and progressive lethargy. He has been unable to work because of fatigue; on arrival temperature 38.8°C, pulse 102/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, and examination shows mild confusion and palpable splenomegaly.

He is otherwise well, takes no regular medications and has no known immunosuppression. He lives in a temperate rural region and reports spending recent weekends repairing a family cabin in a wooded area; he did not seek medical attention until symptoms persisted and had taken two days of oral amoxicillin before presentation without improvement.

Complete blood count shows leukopenia 2.1 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 0.9 × 10^9/L and thrombocytopenia 78 × 10^9/L. Liver enzymes are elevated with ALT 165 U/L and AST 142 U/L. Blood cultures remain negative at 48 hours and CRP is 85 mg/L.
Abdominal ultrasound confirms splenomegaly with a craniocaudal length of 15.2 cm and no focal lesions. Chest radiograph is normal.

On focused re-questioning he remembers finding and removing an attached tick from his right thigh about 7 days before symptom onset after the weekend at the cabin. Polymerase chain reaction testing on whole blood returned positive for an obligate intracellular bacterium that localises to neutrophils.

explanation: The combination of an acute febrile illness after wooded exposure, leukopenia with neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, transaminitis and splenomegaly, together with whole-blood PCR positive for a neutrophil-tropic intracellular bacterium, indicates infection by Anaplasma phagocytophilum. These clinical and laboratory features distinguish it from other tickborne illnesses that more commonly cause lymphocytosis, marked haemolysis, or an expanding skin lesion.

hints.text: A 39-year-old man presents with six weeks of intermittent low-grade fevers, drenching night sweats, and progressive left buttock and groin pain that now limits his ability to climb stairs. He reports 5 kg weight loss over the same period. On examination temperature 37.9°C, focal tenderness over the left sacroiliac region and reduced internal rotation of the left hip, with a palpable liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin.

He is an otherwise well accountant with no known immunosuppression. Three weeks ago he completed a 7-day course of oral amoxicillin with transient symptom improvement. He spent two weeks visiting relatives in a rural Mediterranean region two months before symptom onset but initially denied any obvious animal bites or recent invasive procedures.

CBC shows Hb 108 g/L, leucocyte count 5.2 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 3.2 × 10^9/L, platelets 180 × 10^9/L. CRP 58 mg/L, ESR 64 mm/h, ALT 82 U/L, AST 65 U/L. Two sets of routine blood cultures were reported negative at 48 hours.

MRI pelvis demonstrates left sacroiliac joint marrow oedema with small cortical erosions and a 2 cm para-articular fluid collection tracking along the joint capsule. There is no large abscess and the adjacent hip joint is not effused.

On further questioning he acknowledges drinking unpasteurised goat's milk and homemade cheese daily while staying on his relatives' small farm in rural Anatolia six to eight weeks before symptoms began, and several neighbours reported recent livestock abortions.

explanation: A subacute febrile illness with night sweats, mild transaminitis, and focal sacroiliitis suggests a zoonotic osteoarticular infection. Negative routine cultures and a clear history of consuming unpasteurised goat dairy in an endemic rural setting point to Brucella species. Diagnosis is confirmed by targeted serology or prolonged culture of blood or joint fluid.

hints.text: A 72-year-old woman from a long-term care facility presented with 3 days of fever, progressive confusion and foul-smelling cloudy urine. She had an indwelling urinary catheter placed after a hip fracture two months earlier. Temperature was 38.4°C, heart rate 106/min, and suprapubic tenderness on examination.

Medical history included type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease stage 3. She had been hospitalised four weeks ago for community-acquired pneumonia and received a 7-day course of broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics. She was not on systemic immunosuppressants.

Blood tests showed WBC 15.8 × 10^9/L and serum creatinine 165 μmol/L (baseline ~130 μmol/L). Urinalysis demonstrated pyuria and many yeast forms on microscopy. A midstream sample from the catheter grew a pure heavy growth of a yeast at >10^5 CFU/mL; peripheral blood cultures remained sterile at 48 hours.

Renal and bladder ultrasound showed a non-obstructing right-sided moderate hydronephrosis and mobile echogenic debris layering in the bladder consistent with intraluminal material. No renal abscesses or calculi were identified.

The catheter was exchanged and oral fluconazole 200 mg once daily was started. After 72 hours the patient remained febrile and repeat urine culture still grew the same yeast. Therapy was changed to an echinocandin with defervescence within 48–72 hours and subsequent clearance of urine cultures.

explanation: An older patient with long-term urinary catheterisation and candiduria who fails fluconazole but improves on an echinocandin fits a non-albicans yeast with reduced azole susceptibility.

hints.text: A 57-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 36 hours of fever, progressive lethargy, and increasing pain in his left lower leg. He reported a rapidly spreading rash that began as small dusky spots; temperature 39.0°C, heart rate 118/min, blood pressure 98/58 mmHg, and examination showed extensive non-blanching purpura over both calves with a tender, swollen left calf.

He was previously independent, with no known immunodeficiency and no regular medications; he drank alcohol socially. Twenty-four hours before arrival he had been seen in primary care and started on oral flucloxacillin for presumed cellulitis after a nurse noted a small abrasion on the dorsum of his right hand.

Blood tests showed WBC 2.9 × 10^9/L, platelet count 24 × 10^9/L, creatinine 235 µmol/L, lactate 5.8 mmol/L, and INR 2.3, consistent with shock and coagulopathy. Two sets of blood cultures turned positive after 48 hours, yielding a slow-growing gram-negative bacillus on enriched media.
Contrast CT of the lower limbs demonstrated diffuse subcutaneous oedema of the left calf without gas or a discrete deep abscess. Transthoracic echocardiography showed no valvular vegetations.

On re-evaluation after culture growth the patient recalled a small puncture wound to his right hand from a friend's dog three days before symptom onset; he had only rinsed the wound with water. The laboratory later described the isolate as a fastidious, oxidase-negative, fusiform gram-negative bacillus that grows on blood and chocolate agar after prolonged incubation and is susceptible to beta-lactam antibiotics.

explanation: Severe sepsis with purpura, DIC, and a slow-growing fusiform gram-negative bacillus after a recent dog bite points to Capnocytophaga canimorsus.

hints.text: A 29-year-old woman presents to ambulatory care on day 4 of an acute illness with high fever and severe joint pain. She has temperature 39.1°C and appears uncomfortable; examination shows symmetric swelling and marked tenderness of both wrists and multiple metacarpophalangeal joints with reduced grip strength, limiting her ability to button clothing.

She was previously healthy with no history of rheumatologic disease and takes no regular medications. Symptoms began abruptly with fever and myalgia, then progressed to disabling peripheral joint pain over 48 hours; simple analgesics provided minimal relief. She is not pregnant and has no recent antibiotic use or hospital admissions.

Blood tests show WBC 3.2 × 10^9/L with lymphocytes 0.7 × 10^9/L, platelets 150 × 10^9/L. CRP is 118 mg/L and ALT 92 U/L. Point-of-care test for one other locally circulating mosquito-borne virus returned negative and thick film for malaria was negative.

Musculoskeletal ultrasound of the right wrist and second MCP joints demonstrates synovial thickening, small hypoechoic effusions and increased Doppler signal without erosive changes on plain radiographs.

She returned 7 days before symptom onset from a 10-day trip to a Caribbean island where she had multiple daytime mosquito bites despite using a bed net at night. Local public health notices reported a recent surge of a mosquito-transmitted febrile illness in tourists and residents characterized by abrupt high fever and incapacitating peripheral joint pain.

explanation: The combination of abrupt high fever, severe symmetric peripheral polyarthralgia with inflammatory synovitis, lymphopenia and mild transaminitis after recent travel to a Caribbean area with Aedes mosquito exposure points to infection with chikungunya virus. Confirmation is by PCR or virus-specific IgM/IgG serology in the appropriate time window.

hints.text: A 32-year-old primary school teacher presents with 10 days of progressively worsening dry cough, hoarseness, and early-morning wheeze. She has low-grade fevers and mild exertional dyspnoea, temperature 37.8°C, respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen saturation 95% on room air, and focal scattered wheeze with faint inspiratory crackles at the left base on auscultation.

She is generally well with no chronic lung disease and is a never-smoker. She received a 5-day course of oral amoxicillin prescribed in primary care with no symptomatic improvement and reports several pupils and two fellow teachers have had a similar prolonged cough over the past 3 weeks.

Full blood count shows white cell count 7.6 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 5.0 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein is 38 mg/L. Nasopharyngeal PCR panel for influenza and common respiratory viruses is negative, routine sputum culture after 48 hours shows no pathogenic growth, and cold agglutinin titre is negative.

Chest radiograph demonstrates patchy peribronchial and perihilar interstitial opacities greatest in the left lower zone without dense lobar consolidation or pleural effusion. A limited CT chest performed for persistent symptoms shows peribronchial cuffing and patchy subsegmental consolidation consistent with an atypical bronchopneumonia pattern.

Public-health follow-up identified a small cluster among school staff and children. A targeted PCR from a nasopharyngeal swab returned DNA consistent with an obligate intracellular Gram-negative organism that demonstrates a biphasic developmental cycle on electron microscopy; the patient improved rapidly after starting a macrolide antibiotic.

explanation: Subacute cough with hoarseness, cluster spread in a school, normal or modestly elevated inflammatory markers, interstitial peribronchial imaging, negative routine cultures and viral tests, PCR plus electron microscopy showing an obligate intracellular organism with a biphasic lifecycle, and prompt macrolide response point to infection by Chlamydophila pneumoniae.

hints.text: A 38-year-old woman presents to urgent care with 6 days of fever, dry cough and increasing fatigue that left her unable to work. On arrival temperature 38.8°C, respiratory rate 20/min and oxygen saturation 94% on room air; chest auscultation reveals diminished breath sounds and crackles at the right base and she reports a persistent frontal headache.

She is otherwise healthy, takes no regular medications and is immunocompetent. Her GP prescribed a 5-day course of oral amoxicillin for presumed bronchitis 3 days ago with no improvement in symptoms; she has no recent hospital admissions and no known tuberculosis contacts.

Blood tests show white cell count 8.6 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 6.5 × 10^9/L and lymphocytes 1.1 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein is 112 mg/L. Liver enzymes are elevated with ALT 162 U/L and AST 84 U/L. Two sets of blood cultures showed no growth at 48 hours.

Chest radiograph demonstrates a dense patchy consolidation of the right lower lobe with a small pleural effusion. A limited chest CT confirms focal lobar consolidation in the posterior segment of the right lower lobe without cavitation.

On directed questioning she recalls buying two young cockatiels one week before symptom onset and spending an afternoon cleaning heavily soiled cages and sweeping dried droppings; several birds at the shop had recent eye discharge and one died the prior week.

explanation: This patient has community-acquired pneumonia accompanied by headache, mild hypoxaemia, modest leukocytosis, marked transaminitis and failure to. The temporal link to inhalation of droppings and ill pet parrots points to Chlamydophila psittaci. The combination of bird exposure, systemic symptoms and elevated liver enzymes supports this diagnosis. confirmatory testing is by organism-specific PCR or serology.

hints.text: A 38-year-old woman presents to the hepatology clinic with a 3-month history of intermittent right upper quadrant discomfort, progressive pruritus, and two episodes of dark urine. She reports 4 kg weight loss and episodic low-grade fevers. On examination she is mildly icteric, temperature 37.8°C, and the liver edge is palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin without peritoneal signs.

Symptoms began insidiously after an episode of presumed 'gastroenteritis' abroad 7 months earlier. She has had several brief outpatient courses of antibiotics with only transient symptom improvement. She has no history of heavy alcohol use, blood transfusion, or intravenous drug use.

Serum tests show total bilirubin 42 μmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 680 U/L, gamma-glutamyltransferase 420 U/L, and ALT 98 U/L, indicating a cholestatic pattern. Full blood count shows leukocytes 9.8 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.4 × 10^9/L. CRP is 18 mg/L.

Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography demonstrates irregular, predominantly intrahepatic bile duct dilatation, most marked in the left hepatic lobe, with no obstructing stone or intraluminal mass in the common bile duct. Endoscopic ultrasound notes multiple small linear intraductal filling defects that move with irrigation.

On directed questioning she recalls frequent childhood and occasional adult consumption of lightly pickled raw freshwater fish while visiting family in her river-valley hometown. Three separate stool examinations identified small operculated trematode eggs consistent with a fish-borne liver fluke exposure.

explanation: Cholestatic liver tests with isolated intrahepatic duct dilatation, peripheral eosinophilia, intraductal linear defects on endoscopic imaging, and a history of eating raw freshwater fish together point to a fish-borne liver fluke infection. Identification of operculated trematode eggs on stool microscopy confirms the specific parasitic etiology in this clinical context.

hints.text: A 37-year-old veterinary student presented with 11 days of fever, marked fatigue and a dry cough. She reported daily temperatures to 38.6°C and progressive breathlessness on exertion, and on examination had oxygen saturation 94% on room air with reduced breath sounds and fine crackles at the right base.

She was previously well, takes no regular medications and has no known immunodeficiency. In the week before hospital presentation she had been seen in primary care and given a 5-day course of azithromycin for presumed community-acquired pneumonia with only modest symptomatic improvement.

Laboratory tests showed leucocytes 6.8 × 10^9/L, platelets 110 × 10^9/L, CRP 132 mg/L, ALT 240 U/L and AST 180 U/L. Three sets of blood cultures remained sterile after 5 days and rapid testing for common respiratory pathogens including urinary antigen and viral PCR were negative.

Chest radiograph demonstrated a dense consolidation in the right lower lobe with a small associated pleural effusion. Low-dose thoracic CT confirmed patchy right lower lobe air-space consolidation without cavitation and no significant lymphadenopathy.

On directed questioning she recalled assisting with the delivery of several goats and helping to dispose of placentas at a local farm about 10 days before symptom onset, and noted that several animals had recently aborted; two farm workers later reported similar febrile illnesses.

explanation: A subacute, culture-negative febrile pneumonia with disproportionate transaminitis and thrombocytopenia following aerosol exposure to ruminant birth products points to Coxiella burnetii. Diagnosis is confirmed by specific serology or PCR on blood or respiratory specimens.

hints.text: A 49-year-old man, 5 months after a deceased-donor kidney transplant, is seen for a 3-week history of progressive reduction in urine output and malaise. He has no dysuria, no flank pain, and reports only low-grade fatigue. On examination blood pressure is 150/92 mmHg and the graft in the right iliac fossa is non-tender on palpation.

Immunosuppression includes tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil and prednisone. Two months ago he received a 5-day course of lymphocyte-depleting antibody for biopsy-proven acute cellular rejection with subsequent steroid taper. He has no recent travel and no known sick contacts.

Serum creatinine has risen from a baseline 120 μmol/L to 260 μmol/L. White blood cell count is 5.8 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein is 12 mg/L. Urine dipstick shows trace blood and protein, microscopy shows numerous epithelial cells but urine culture is sterile.

Renal ultrasound demonstrates a mildly enlarged transplanted kidney with preserved corticomedullary differentiation and no hydronephrosis. Doppler study reports a resistive index of 0.80 in segmental arteries, suggesting parenchymal dysfunction rather than obstruction.

Urine cytology shows large epithelial cells with markedly enlarged nuclei and basophilic intranuclear inclusions. Quantitative nucleic acid testing reports urine viral DNA 1.2 × 10^8 copies/mL and plasma viral DNA 5.6 × 10^4 copies/mL.

explanation: A renal transplant recipient with recent intensified immunosuppression, rising creatinine and graft dysfunction on imaging who has characteristic decoy cells in urine and high-level viral DNA in urine and plasma most likely has BK virus nephropathy. These findings support viral-mediated tubular injury rather than obstruction or bacterial infection, and further assessment often includes graft biopsy and reduction of immunosuppression.

hints.text: A 29-year-old woman presents to the outpatient clinic with three weeks of profuse watery diarrhoea, crampy abdominal pain, bloating and a 7 kg weight loss. She reports up to six loose bowel movements daily, intermittent low-grade fevers and lightheadedness on standing. On exam temperature is 37.8 °C, pulse 102/min, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, mucous membranes are dry and abdominal palpation shows mild diffuse tenderness without peritonism.

She is previously healthy, takes no regular medications and is HIV negative by recent screening. Symptoms began about one week after a two-week trip to Central America where she ate at local markets and consumed salads and fresh herbs; she denied antibiotic use before symptom onset.

Blood tests show white blood cell count 9.8 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 22 mg/L. Stool bacterial cultures for enteric pathogens were negative and routine ova and parasite wet mount was non-diagnostic. Modified acid-fast stain of a concentrated stool specimen subsequently demonstrated variably acid-fast, spherical oocysts measuring about 8–10 μm.

Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen performed to assess for complications shows mild, diffuse thickening of the distal jejunum and proximal ileum with trace mesenteric adenopathy, changes judged compatible with enteritis but without abscess or obstruction.

After two days of empirical ciprofloxacin with no improvement she was started on high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole; diarrhoea frequency fell markedly within 48 hours and resolved over the subsequent week.

explanation: Prolonged watery diarrhoea after travel, detection of 8–10 μm variably acid-fast, autofluorescent oocysts in concentrated stool, and rapid clinical response to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole point to infection with Cyclospora cayetanensis. Negative routine cultures and the small oocyst size help distinguish this coccidian parasite from other enteric pathogens.

hints.text: A 19-year-old university student presented in mid-July with 48 hours of worsening frontal headache, photophobia, fever and progressive neck stiffness. On arrival temperature was 38.9°C and heart rate 96/min, he was alert and orientated but had marked nuchal rigidity and reported vomiting once.

He lives in a mixed-sex dormitory and returned from a week at the campus outdoor pool complex five days before onset. Three flatmates had self-limited diarrhoea and low-grade fevers a week earlier; he took no regular medications and has no relevant sexual exposures or recent travel outside the region.

Lumbar puncture yielded clear CSF with WBC 420 × 10^6/L, 85% lymphocytes, protein 0.9 g/L and glucose 3.6 mmol/L (concurrent serum glucose 5.9 mmol/L). Gram stain was negative, bacterial cultures pending, peripheral WBC 8.2 × 10^9/L and CRP 12 mg/L; HSV PCR on CSF was negative.
Non-contrast CT head was unremarkable. Contrast MRI brain showed mild, diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement over the cerebral convexities without focal parenchymal signal abnormality.

Local public health reported several similar aseptic meningitis cases among adolescents after use of the same outdoor pool and in the paediatric ward that week. Laboratory testing from multiple cases detected an RNA virus belonging to the picornavirus family in both CSF and stool, identified by neutralization as the same outbreak serotype long linked to community outbreaks of meningitis in summer months.

explanation: This is viral aseptic meningitis in a young adult with CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal CSF glucose, and MRI leptomeningeal enhancement. Detection of a non-polio picornavirus in CSF and stool during a summer pool-associated outbreak favors echovirus as the most likely cause.

hints.text: A 52-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 5 days of fever, progressive headache, and diffuse myalgia. He reported poor oral intake and light-headedness; temperature 39.2°C, heart rate 106/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, and he was mildly confused on examination.

He is an otherwise active carpenter with treated type 2 diabetes and no recent hospital admissions or antibiotic use. Three weeks earlier he spent a week clearing brush at his family's rural property in the central United States but initially denied any remembered insect bites.

Initial blood tests showed leukopenia with white cell count 2.4 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 1.4 × 10^9/L, thrombocytopenia with platelets 58 × 10^9/L, and haemoglobin 138 g/L. Transaminases were elevated with AST 210 U/L and ALT 177 U/L, sodium 131 mmol/L. Blood cultures were pending and a malaria smear was negative.
Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated mild splenomegaly with spleen length 14.5 cm and no focal lesions. Chest radiograph was clear with no consolidation or effusion.

On structured re-questioning he recalled removing an engorged tick from his right axilla about 10 days before symptom onset while clearing brush on the family property; his dog had a heavy tick burden that spring.

explanation: The combination of acute febrile illness with headache, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, elevated transaminases and splenomegaly after a recent tick attachment in the central United States is most consistent with infection by Ehrlichia chaffeensis. Diagnosis is supported by nucleic-acid testing or demonstration of intracellular bacterial inclusions in monocytes, and prompt treatment with doxycycline is indicated.

hints.text: A 68-year-old man on postoperative day 10 after emergency left hemicolectomy presents with 36 hours of fever, rigors and new confusion. Temperature 38.9°C, heart rate 110/min, blood pressure 95/60 mmHg; his midline abdominal wound is tender with scant serous drainage and an indwelling urinary catheter remains in place.

His hospital course included five days in the intensive care unit and two separate central venous catheters. He received 10 days of piperacillin–tazobactam and a 7-day course of vancomycin three weeks earlier for suspected catheter colonization.

White blood cell count 16.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 13.8 × 10^9/L, creatinine 190 μmol/L, C-reactive protein 220 mg/L. Two sets of blood cultures flagged positive and Gram stain showed Gram-positive cocci in short chains.

Contrast CT abdomen and pelvis demonstrates a 3.2 cm fluid collection adjacent to the colonic anastomosis with surrounding fat stranding, compatible with a contained leak and small pelvic fluid collection. No pulmonary consolidation or other visceral abscesses were identified.

Percutaneous drain fluid and both blood cultures grew catalase-negative Gram-positive cocci that hydrolysed esculin in bile and grew in 6.5% NaCl; susceptibility testing reported resistance to ampicillin and vancomycin with retained susceptibility to linezolid and tigecycline. The patient had prolonged inpatient exposure to broad-spectrum antibiotics and invasive vascular access prior to this presentation.

explanation: The combination of Gram-positive cocci in short chains with bile-esculin hydrolysis and growth in 6.5% NaCl, plus ampicillin and vancomycin resistance, is most consistent with Enterococcus faecium. The postoperative anastomotic leak provided an intra-abdominal source and the prior glycopeptide exposure and central access increased risk for this nosocomial bloodstream infection.

hints.text: A 34-year-old right-handed man presented to the emergency clinic with 72 hours of progressive pain and swelling over the dorsal aspect of his right hand. He reports difficulty extending the index finger and marked pain with movement. Temperature was 38.1°C and heart rate 96/min. Examination showed a tense 3 cm area of erythema and tenderness centered over the second metacarpophalangeal joint with limited active extension of the index finger and a small healing abrasion near the knuckle.

He works as a bartender, smokes 10 cigarettes daily, and has no history of diabetes or immune compromise. He recalls a minor skin break over the dorsum of the hand several days before symptom onset but did not seek care and thought it was trivial.

White blood cell count was 14.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance. C-reactive protein was 98 mg/L. Synovial aspirate Gram stain showed small gram-negative coccobacillary organisms. Blood cultures were negative at 48 hours.

MRI of the right hand obtained on day 3 demonstrated a second MCP joint effusion with synovial enhancement and early cortical irregularity of the second metacarpal head consistent with septic arthritis and early adjacent osteomyelitis. No retained foreign body was seen.

On targeted re-questioning the patient admitted he had struck another person's mouth with a closed fist in a bar altercation five days before onset. He now recalls teeth contacting his knuckle and that the other person bled and had poor dentition. Wound culture later grew small, slow-appearing colonies on blood agar after 48 to 72 hours that produced a faint bleach-like odour.

explanation: A clenched-fist injury with teeth contact supplies oral flora to the dorsum of the hand and MCP joint. The synovial aspirate contained small gram-negative coccobacilli and cultures were slow to grow with a characteristic faint bleach odour. These findings in the setting of septic arthritis after a human bite point to the implicated organism.

hints.text: A 38-year-old man presents to the emergency clinic with 5 days of fever, progressive malaise, and a painful swollen right groin. He reports a subjective fever to 38.9°C at home, appears tired but hemodynamically stable in clinic, and exam shows a 3 cm tender, fluctuant right inguinal lymph node with overlying erythema and a 5 mm crusted papule on the medial right calf.

He is previously well, an occasional smoker, and takes no regular medications. He notes onset of symptoms about five days after helping clear an overgrown rural property adjacent to his family farm two weeks earlier; he does not recall a definite tick bite, denies recent travel outside the region, and has no household pets or known sick contacts.

Full blood count shows leukocytosis 15.8 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance. CRP is 120 mg/L and alanine aminotransferase 58 U/L. Blood cultures remain sterile at 48 hours. Fine needle aspiration of the node yielded scant purulent fluid; Gram stain shows small, poorly staining pleomorphic coccobacilli. Routine media remained sterile for 48 hours but small grey colonies grew on a cysteine-enriched chocolate agar after 72 hours, oxidase negative.

Ultrasound of the groin demonstrates a 3.2 cm hypoechoic collection with internal echoes and peripheral hyperemia consistent with necrotic adenitis and early abscess formation. Chest radiograph is clear without focal consolidation.

On further questioning he admits he field-dressed several wild rabbits at the property two weeks before presentation and believes he had a small skin abrasion on the calf while handling carcasses; the crusted papule is at that same site.

explanation: The combination of a small skin lesion with tender regional necrotic lymphadenitis after field-dressing rabbits, a fastidious, small weakly staining gram-negative coccobacillus that grows only on cysteine-enriched media, and sterile routine blood cultures points to infection with Francisella tularensis. This history and laboratory pattern explain the ulcerated entry site and suppurative adenitis seen on imaging.

hints.text: A 29-year-old woman presents with 4 days of high fever, severe myalgia, headache and recurrent vomiting. She reports progressive lethargy and new mucosal bleeding from the gums. On arrival T 39.4°C, pulse 110/min, BP 95/60 mmHg, and scattered petechiae on her forearms; she is mildly confused.

Previously well with no chronic illnesses and no regular medications. She was seen at a rural clinic two days earlier and given antimalarial therapy and oral antibiotics without improvement. No recent transfusions or known needle exposures. Last menstrual period 3 weeks ago.

Admission bloods: WBC 2.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 1.0 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 130 g/L, platelets 38 × 10^9/L. Creatinine 210 μmol/L, potassium 5.8 mmol/L. AST 1 020 U/L, ALT 560 U/L, INR 2.0. Peripheral blood film negative for malaria parasites.

Focused abdominal ultrasound shows hepatomegaly with increased echogenicity and a small volume of free fluid in the pelvis. Chest radiograph is unremarkable. No focal abscesses or pneumonic consolidation to explain sepsis.

History reveals she returned 6 days before symptom onset from a two-week stay in a rural West African district where a cluster of febrile deaths occurred. She cared for an ill uncle who developed fever and bleeding and died; she participated in family body preparation rituals prior to the funeral.

explanation: Acute febrile illness with rapid progression to multisystem dysfunction, leukopenia, marked thrombocytopenia, very high transaminases, coagulopathy and recent high-risk contact at a funeral in an affected West African area points to a viral haemorrhagic fever. The exposure history and clinical-laboratory pattern are most consistent with infection by Ebola virus.

hints.text: A 28-year-old woman presented to a sexual health clinic with 7 days of increased vaginal discharge and intermittent malodour that she noticed after intercourse. She is otherwise well, afebrile with normal vital signs, and pelvic examination showed thin, non-bloody discharge coating the vaginal vault with minimal vulvovaginal erythema and no cervical motion tenderness.

She reports a new sexual partner three weeks ago and used a commercial intravaginal cleansing wash twice in the past fortnight. She had self-treated once with an over-the-counter topical antifungal without improvement and takes no regular medications; pregnancy test in clinic was negative.

Wet mount microscopy of vaginal fluid showed numerous epithelial cells with small bacteria adherent to their borders, obscuring cell margins. Gram stain revealed mixed polymicrobial flora with small Gram-variable coccobacillary forms predominant. Vaginal pH measured at 5.5 and a complete blood count was 6.2 × 10^9/L with normal differential.
Transvaginal ultrasound performed to exclude pelvic inflammatory disease and abscess was unremarkable with normal-appearing uterus and adnexa and no free fluid.

She confirms recent intravaginal douching and new sexual contact but no history of intrauterine device insertion, recent systemic antibiotics, or systemic symptoms. A clinic test using 10% potassium hydroxide produced a pronounced amine odour when mixed with her vaginal secretions.

explanation: The combination of thin homogenous vaginal discharge with minimal inflammation, epithelial cells coated with adherent bacteria on wet mount, elevated vaginal pH and a positive amine test in a patient who recently douched and had a new partner points to bacterial vaginosis caused by Gardnerella vaginalis. Normal pelvic imaging and lack of systemic inflammatory response make pelvic inflammatory disease or invasive infection unlikely.

hints.text: A 28-year-old previously well man presents to the emergency department with 4 days of fever, diffuse myalgia, and progressive shortness of breath. He was ambulatory until the past 24 hours, and on arrival he is febrile at 38.6°C, tachycardic at 112 beats/min, tachypnoeic at 26 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 89% on room air; examination shows bilateral fine crackles at the lung bases.

He has no chronic medical conditions and does not smoke. The illness began with high fever and severe muscle aches, followed on day 2 by nausea and two episodes of non-bloody vomiting; his GP started a short course of oral antibiotics for presumed bronchitis without improvement. He works as a field ecologist and spent several days on a remote mountain research trip three weeks before presentation.

Initial blood tests show leukocytosis 16.0 × 10^9/L, thrombocytopenia 65 × 10^9/L, and haemoconcentration with haematocrit 0.54 L/L. Serum creatinine is 140 µmol/L, C-reactive protein 140 mg/L. Arterial blood gas on room air shows PaO2 7.0 kPa with mild metabolic acidaemia and lactate 2.5 mmol/L.

Portable chest radiograph demonstrates bilateral, patchy interstitial and alveolar opacities most prominent in the mid and lower zones, with small bilateral pleural effusions and a normal cardiac silhouette. A repeat film six hours later shows interval progression of the airspace opacities.

On further questioning he recalls cleaning out an old field research cabin about 18 days before becoming ill, sweeping up a large amount of dry rodent faeces and nesting material without a mask. Several colleagues noted heavy mouse activity in the building around the same time.

explanation: The patient has a febrile prodrome with gastrointestinal symptoms followed by rapidly progressive hypoxaemic respiratory failure, haemoconcentration, thrombocytopenia, and bilateral non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema after recent exposure to aerosolised rodent excreta. These features are most consistent with hantavirus pulmonary syndrome. The temporal relation to cleaning a rodent-infested cabin and the laboratory pattern support that diagnosis.

hints.text: A 34-year-old woman presents to primary care with three months of progressive fatigue, exertional dyspnea, and intermittent loose stools. She has lost 4 kg, reports mild paresthesias in her fingertips, and on examination is pale with conjunctival pallor and a heart rate of 102/min; abdominal examination shows mild diffuse tenderness without organomegaly.

She is otherwise healthy, takes no regular medications, and is not pregnant. She moved 18 months ago to a lakeside town and works part time at a community kitchen. She denies overt bleeding, heavy menses, recent antibiotics, or travel outside the country. She tried an over-the-counter iron preparation for six weeks with little change in symptoms.

Complete blood count shows haemoglobin 85 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 110 fL, leukocytes 5.6 × 10^9/L, platelets 210 × 10^9/L. Peripheral smear demonstrates macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils. Serum cobalamin is 95 pmol/L (reference 140–652). Serum ferritin is 120 μg/L. Fecal occult blood test is negative.

Video capsule endoscopy was performed because symptoms persisted and showed a 15–20 cm glistening, ribbonlike structure adherent to the mucosa of the proximal jejunum with mild adjacent erythema. No obstructing lesion was seen and the remainder of the small bowel mucosa appeared grossly normal.

When asked specifically about diet she reports frequent meals of cold-smoked and lightly cured lake trout prepared by a local vendor over the past year. She also recalls passing a long flat white segment in her stool about two weeks ago.

explanation: The combination of progressive megaloblastic anemia with low serum cobalamin, visualization of a long ribbonlike intestinal worm on capsule endoscopy, and repeated consumption of undercooked or cured freshwater fish makes the diagnosis most consistent with infection by the fish tapeworm. Identification is supported by the reported passage of a flat segment in stool and the localization to the proximal small intestine.

hints.text: A 31-year-old previously well man presents to clinic with 10 days of progressive fatigue, anorexia, dark urine and yellowing of his eyes. He reports low-grade fevers and intermittent right upper quadrant discomfort, temperature 37.8°C on arrival, scleral icterus and mild tender hepatomegaly on abdominal palpation.

He has no prior liver disease, drinks alcohol only occasionally, denies injection drug use and reports monogamous sexual activity. His childhood immunisations included vaccines for two common vaccine-preventable hepatitides and he takes no regular medications.

Blood tests show ALT 1 240 U/L, AST 920 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 160 U/L, total bilirubin 88 μmol/L and INR 1.1. A laboratory panel for common hepatotropic viruses and routine blood-borne pathogens was negative, and platelet count was 210 × 10^9/L.
Abdominal ultrasound shows a mildly enlarged liver without focal lesions, normal biliary calibre and no gallstones or bile duct dilation to suggest obstructive cholestasis.

Three weeks before symptom onset he had spent two weeks working in rural South Asia, during which he drank untreated well water and ate several dishes prepared from undercooked pork and pig liver at local markets.

explanation: Acute symptomatic hepatitis with very high transaminases, nonobstructive imaging and a negative routine viral panel points to an enterically transmitted hepatotropic virus. The recent travel to an endemic rural area with ingestion of untreated water and undercooked pork is strongly suggestive of infection with the enteric hepatitis virus responsible for waterborne outbreaks and zoonotic foodborne cases.

hints.text: A 32-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 6 days of fever, severe myalgias and progressive malaise. He says the myalgias are worst in his calves and now limit his ability to walk. On arrival he was febrile at 38.9°C, pulse 112/min and blood pressure 102/64 mmHg; examination showed mild scleral icterus, diffuse calf tenderness without focal erythema, and no focal neurological deficit.

He is a municipal sanitation worker, previously healthy, with no chronic liver disease and no regular medications. Symptoms began about four days after a week of heavy seasonal rains in the city. He denies recent international travel, illicit drug use, or animal bites, and reports self-treatment with ibuprofen for the first three days.

Laboratory tests show white blood cells 14.2 × 10^9/L, platelets 85 × 10^9/L, creatinine 180 µmol/L, total bilirubin 85 µmol/L, ALT 110 U/L and AST 145 U/L. Urinalysis demonstrates protein 2+ and microscopic hematuria. Two sets of blood cultures remain sterile at 24 hours.

Chest radiograph shows bilateral, patchy alveolar opacities with small bilateral pleural effusions but no lobar consolidation. Abdominal ultrasound shows mild hepatomegaly without biliary dilatation or obstructing lesion.

On further questioning he reports wading through knee-deep floodwater in the city while clearing storm drains three days before symptom onset, and he recalls a recent rat infestation in the area. He also had a superficial abrasion on his shin at that time that he did not clean thoroughly.

explanation: Acute febrile illness with severe calf myalgia, conjunctival icterus, jaundice out of proportion to transaminases, acute kidney injury, thrombocytopenia and pulmonary involvement after exposure to floodwater contaminated by rodents is most consistent with leptospiral infection. The exposure history and combination of hepatic, renal and pulmonary manifestations point to Leptospira interrogans as the likely pathogen.

hints.text: A 49-year-old woman presented to neurology with three weeks of progressive right-sided clumsiness and difficulty reading that began insidiously. She described intermittent visual blurring and new falls. On examination she was afebrile, alert but slowed in speech, had a right homonymous hemianopia, 3/5 weakness of the right hand, and a broad-based ataxic gait.

She has relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis and started monthly monoclonal antibody therapy 11 months ago. She has not recently received high-dose corticosteroid pulses. She takes no other chronic immunosuppressants and has no history of HIV infection.

CSF obtained on day 5 showed WBC 3 × 10^6/L, protein 0.85 g/L, glucose 3.6 mmol/L. CSF bacterial Gram stain and fungal smear were negative and cultures remained sterile. Peripheral lymphocyte count was 0.9 × 10^9/L. Routine serum infection testing including HIV antibody was negative.

MRI brain with contrast demonstrated multifocal T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions in the subcortical white matter of the left parietal and occipital lobes and the splenium. Lesions were non-enhancing after gadolinium and produced minimal mass effect.

Her last monoclonal antibody infusion was three weeks before symptom onset and she had received 11 monthly doses in total. CSF nucleic acid amplification returned positive for viral DNA consistent with the agent responsible for subacute demyelinating lesions in patients treated with this therapy.

explanation: Subacute focal neurologic deficits in a patient receiving natalizumab, non-enhancing multifocal white matter lesions with little mass effect on MRI, and positive CSF viral DNA point to progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy due to JC virus. The clinical course and imaging distinguish this from inflammatory MS relapse or typical bacterial or fungal encephalitis.

hints.text: A 34-year-old woman presents to a clinic in the city with 3 weeks of jaundice, malaise and anorexia that began shortly after receiving a tattoo while traveling abroad. On exam she is afebrile, markedly jaundiced and tender in the right upper quadrant.

She reports no prior liver disease and had normal liver tests recorded two years earlier during antenatal care. She recalls the tattoo was performed with unregulated equipment and she had several unprotected sexual encounters during the same trip.

Laboratory testing shows ALT 1 900 U/L, AST 2 200 U/L, total bilirubin 150 µmol/L and INR 1.7. Newly positive hepatitis surface antigen is documented alongside negative results for other routine acute hepatitides.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the liver demonstrates diffuse hepatic enhancement without focal abscess or biliary obstruction, and no portal vein thrombosis. The overall appearance is consistent with acute hepatitis.

Acute serology showed IgM to a small circular RNA agent and PCR detected that agent's RNA in blood, in addition to the new surface antigen positivity. The pattern indicated simultaneous acquisition of the surface antigen and the dependent RNA agent.

explanation: New surface antigen seroconversion with concurrent IgM and RNA detection of a dependent small RNA virus after a percutaneous exposure points to acute coinfection with that satellite virus, explaining the severe acute hepatitis.

hints.text: A 48-year-old woman presented to neurology clinic with an 8-month history of progressive stiffness and weakness in both legs. She reports increasing difficulty climbing stairs and getting up from a chair, plus new urinary urgency and occasional urge incontinence. On examination she has marked lower limb spasticity with brisk knee and ankle reflexes and bilateral extensor plantar responses, gait is spastic and scissoring. Vital signs are normal.

Her past medical history is otherwise unremarkable and she takes no regular medications. She had an eczematous rash two years ago that resolved with topical steroids. She denies trauma, no family history of similar neurological disease, no diabetes, and no immunosuppressive therapy. She reports no intravenous drug use and has a long-term monogamous partner.

Routine bloods are within reference limits with white cell count 6.3 × 10^9/L and serum calcium normal. HIV serology is negative. Lumbar puncture shows opening pressure 15 cm H2O, CSF white cell count 38 × 10^6/L with 90% lymphocytes, CSF protein 1.2 g/L, and normal CSF glucose.

MRI thoracic spine demonstrates diffuse thinning of the thoracic cord and longitudinal T2 hyperintensity most prominent in the lateral columns spanning multiple segments. There is no focal compressive lesion. MRI brain is unremarkable.
She was born and raised in rural Jamaica and emigrated 15 years ago. She reports being breastfed in infancy and having received a blood transfusion after childbirth about 30 years ago.

explanation: Progressive spastic paraparesis with thoracic cord atrophy, lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis, and a history of residence in a Caribbean endemic area are most consistent with infection by Human T-lymphotropic virus 1. Confirmatory testing would include serology or PCR for the virus in serum and CSF. The imaging and age make multiple sclerosis or compressive myelopathy less likely in this clinical context.

hints.text: A 12-year-old boy presents to urgent care 48 hours after acute onset of fever, diffuse myalgias and dry cough. He reports bilateral calf pain that began this morning and makes walking downstairs difficult. Temperature 39.3°C, heart rate 110/min, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98% on room air. Pharynx is mildly erythematous without exudate, chest auscultation clear, and both calves are tender to palpation without swelling.

Previously healthy, no chronic respiratory disease or neuromuscular disorder, received the seasonal inactivated respiratory virus vaccine four months ago. His 8-year-old sister missed school yesterday with a febrile cough. No recent travel or animal exposures and no recent antibiotic use. He attends a local elementary school and was present in class through the day before presentation.

Complete blood count shows WBC 3.4 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 2.5 × 10^9/L and lymphocytes 0.5 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein 12 mg/L. Serum creatine kinase elevated at 820 U/L. Throat rapid streptococcal antigen negative and point-of-care antigen tests for respiratory syncytial virus and adenovirus were negative. A multiplex molecular respiratory panel was sent to the reference laboratory.

Frontal chest radiograph shows mild peribronchial cuffing and increased perihilar interstitial markings without focal lobar consolidation or pleural effusion. Ultrasound of the calves shows no deep venous thrombosis and no soft-tissue fluid collection.

The regional public health service contacted the family to report an outbreak in the boy's classroom. Reference-lab reverse-transcription PCR on samples from multiple classmates detected a segmented negative-sense RNA virus in the Orthomyxoviridae family, described as a human-restricted seasonal lineage that lacks the antigenic-shift features seen in animal-to-human pandemic strains. The patient's nasopharyngeal RT-PCR returned positive for the same lineage.

explanation: Acute febrile respiratory illness in a school-aged child with prominent myalgias and marked CK elevation suggests a viral myositis complicating a respiratory virus. Lymphopenia and peribronchial radiographic changes further point to a viral etiology. Reference-lab RT-PCR identifying a human-restricted orthomyxovirus lineage circulating in a school outbreak supports the seasonal B-lineage orthomyxovirus as the cause.

hints.text: A 42-year-old man presents to clinic with 10 days of progressive jaundice, dark urine, pale stools and severe fatigue. He has right upper-quadrant discomfort, a low-grade fever of 37.8°C, scleral icterus and a tender liver edge palpated 3 cm below the costal margin; he stopped working because of weakness.

He emigrated from West Africa 12 years ago and reports he was told he had chronic viral hepatitis about a decade ago but received no follow-up or treatment. He denies heavy alcohol use, takes no regular medications, and reports a new sexual partner over the past 2 months; remote recreational injection drug use was many years earlier.

Laboratory tests show AST 2 100 U/L, ALT 1 900 U/L, total bilirubin 210 µmol/L, INR 1.7 and platelets 130 × 10^9/L. Prior hospital records note persistent positivity for a marker of chronic infection with a DNA hepatotropic virus and current nucleic-acid testing demonstrates a high circulating viral load of that DNA virus.

Abdominal ultrasound shows hepatomegaly with coarse echotexture, no intrahepatic or extrahepatic bile duct dilatation and patent portal and hepatic veins on Doppler. Small volume ascites is present and there is no focal hepatic lesion to suggest obstruction or vascular thrombosis.

He reports his new partner recently returned from his country of origin. Serum testing now detects a small circular single-stranded RNA molecule that appears only in patients who carry the chronic DNA-virus marker described in his records and that is linked to abrupt severe hepatitis on the background of chronic infection.

explanation: The patient has acute severe hepatitis on a background of chronic infection with a DNA hepatotropic virus. Detection of a small circular single-stranded RNA that is found only with that chronic infection and that causes marked clinical worsening identifies a defective satellite RNA agent superinfecting his chronic disease. The pattern of abrupt transaminase rise, high bilirubin, prior chronic DNA-virus marker and detection of the small circular RNA supports this diagnosis.

hints.text: A 52-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 10 days of progressive jaundice, anorexia and new confusion. He has dark urine and daytime somnolence, temperature 38.2°C, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, examination shows scleral icterus, tender hepatomegaly and asterixis.

He was diagnosed with chronic blood-borne viral hepatitis 18 years ago and has had intermittent follow-up, with no history of harmful alcohol use. He reports no recent travel, no new medications, and no intravenous drug use.

Laboratory tests show AST 1 050 U/L, ALT 880 U/L, total bilirubin 220 μmol/L, INR 2.3, ammonia 120 μmol/L and platelets 85 × 10^9/L. Serologic testing for acute antibody markers of the common RNA hepatotropic pathogens is negative.

Abdominal ultrasound shows a nodular liver contour with splenomegaly and patent portal and hepatic veins, without biliary dilatation. The appearance is consistent with underlying chronic liver disease with acute hepatic injury.

Molecular testing of serum returns positive for a small circular negative-sense RNA detected only in the context of the patient's preexisting chronic envelope-producing hepatotropic infection, and prior records confirm persistent envelope protein on prior assays. The laboratory reports that the detected agent is a defective satellite RNA that requires the envelope proteins of the chronic virus for propagation.

explanation: This patient has acute-on-chronic hepatic decompensation on a background of long-standing viral hepatitis. Detection of a small circular negative-sense satellite RNA that depends on the chronic envelope-producing virus identifies the defective satellite infection responsible for the abrupt clinical worsening.

hints.text: A 34-year-old woman who injects drugs presents with 6 days of dark urine, severe nausea and marked fatigue. She is febrile to 38.6°C, has jaundice and right upper quadrant tenderness but no encephalopathy.

She reports a diagnosis of chronic viral hepatitis after a transfusion in childhood, with low-level abnormal liver tests but no cirrhosis on prior imaging. She stopped regular clinic follow-up three years ago and has not received antiviral therapy.

AST 1 800 U/L, ALT 2 100 U/L, total bilirubin 180 μmol/L, INR 1.6 and C-reactive protein 28 mg/L. Screening tests for acute primary infection with the usual hepatotropic RNA viruses are negative, while baseline markers of her chronic infection remain detectable.

Transient elastography performed in clinic two years earlier recorded values compatible with minimal fibrosis and an ultrasound at presentation shows hepatomegaly without nodularity and no biliary obstruction.

A targeted PCR assay performed on serum identifies a 1.7 kb circular negative-sense RNA molecule and the laboratory notes replicative intermediates consistent with an RNA satellite dependent on the patient’s existing envelope-producing chronic virus. The finding explains the sudden severe hepatitis superimposed on chronic infection.

explanation: A patient with longstanding chronic viral hepatitis and sudden marked transaminase elevation who tests positive for a small circular negative-sense RNA that requires the chronic envelope-producing virus has the defective satellite infection causing acute severe hepatitis.

hints.text: A 61-year-old man on maintenance haemodialysis presents with three weeks of progressive pruritus, jaundice and weight loss. He is lethargic, has marked scleral icterus and mild peripheral oedema, blood pressure 125/78 mmHg and no fever.

He received multiple blood transfusions 30 years ago and was told he had a chronic viral hepatitis infection decades ago. He has been clinically stable with mild routine transaminitis until the current decline.

AST 760 U/L, ALT 690 U/L, total bilirubin 150 μmol/L, INR 1.9, albumin 28 g/L and platelets 92 × 10^9/L. Serologies for acute seroconversion to other common hepatotropic agents are negative and HIV screening is negative.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen shows a shrunken, nodular liver with moderate ascites and collateral vessels, without focal hepatic lesions or biliary obstruction. Findings are consistent with established cirrhosis and portal hypertension.

Specialised molecular testing detects a small circular, single-stranded negative-sense RNA in serum and the clinical laboratory comments that this RNA is a defective satellite which requires the envelope proteins of the patient’s chronic hepatotropic infection for its lifecycle. This explains the recent acute-on-chronic deterioration.

explanation: The pattern of chronic liver disease with recent acute deterioration and identification of a small circular negative-sense satellite RNA dependent on the preexisting chronic envelope-producing infection indicates the defective satellite viral infection causing the acute decompensation.

hints.text: A 42-year-old woman treated with high-dose corticosteroids for a flare of autoimmune disease presents with 2 weeks of jaundice, profound fatigue and right upper quadrant discomfort. On examination she is icteric, afebrile and mildly tachycardic, with no stigmata of chronic liver disease externally.

She has a remote diagnosis of chronic viral hepatitis identified during pre-employment screening 10 years earlier, with irregular follow-up. She recently received a pulse of immunosuppression and reports no travel or new sexual partners.

AST 1 320 U/L, ALT 1 100 U/L, total bilirubin 210 μmol/L, INR 2.0 and eosinophils 0.2 × 10^9/L. Autoimmune liver serologies are negative and tests for acute primary infection by common RNA hepatotropic pathogens are negative.
Liver elastography from last year suggested moderate fibrosis and current ultrasound shows mild surface irregularity but no biliary obstruction and minimal ascites. No hepatic mass is identified.

Serum PCR identifies a compact circular negative-sense RNA molecule and paired testing documents presence of the patient’s long-standing envelope-producing hepatotropic infection. The laboratory describes the finding as a defective satellite RNA requiring the chronic virus envelope for assembly and release.

explanation: Immunosuppression precipitated acute worsening in a patient with prior chronic viral hepatitis. Detection of a small circular negative-sense satellite RNA that depends on the chronic envelope-producing infection confirms the defective satellite viral superinfection causing the presentation.

hints.text: A 38-year-old man 21 days after allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplant for acute myeloid leukaemia was brought from the ward with 48 hours of progressive confusion and new anterograde memory loss. He was febrile to 38.7°C, alert but disoriented to time, and family reported a witnessed brief focal seizure this morning.

Conditioning included fludarabine and busulphan and he remains on tacrolimus for graft-versus-host disease prophylaxis. He received aciclovir prophylaxis per protocol and has no prior central nervous system disease.

MRI brain performed urgently showed bilateral medial temporal lobe T2/FLAIR hyperintensity that was greater on the left, with minimal mass effect and no frank diffusion restriction or leptomeningeal enhancement.

Empirical intravenous aciclovir was started for presumed herpes encephalitis but there was no clinical improvement after 72 hours. After switching to intravenous foscarnet the patient had gradual recovery of orientation and memory over the next 7 days.

CSF PCR returned strongly positive with quantitative viral DNA >1.0 × 10^6 copies/mL. Peripheral blood PCR showed similar high levels, and hair‑follicle testing found no evidence of chromosomally integrated viral genome, indicating active reactivation rather than inherited integration.

explanation: Limbic-predominant encephalitis after allogeneic transplant with failure to respond to aciclovir but improvement on foscarnet, plus very high CSF viral DNA and absence of chromosomal integration, supports reactivation of a herpesvirus known to cause post‑transplant limbic encephalitis.

hints.text: A 52-year-old woman presented with 6 days of fever, a spreading pruritic morbilliform eruption and progressive jaundice. On exam she had facial oedema, tender cervical lymphadenopathy and scleral icterus; temperature was 38.9°C and she was somnolent but rousable.

She had started allopurinol four weeks earlier for gout. There was no recent travel and no new herbal supplements. She had been started on high‑dose systemic corticosteroids by a local team three days prior for presumed severe drug reaction.

Complete blood count showed leukocytosis 14.2 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.8 × 10^9/L and platelets 110 × 10^9/L. Liver tests were markedly abnormal with ALT 860 U/L and total bilirubin 155 μmol/L. Bacterial cultures were negative.
Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated hepatomegaly without biliary obstruction. CT neck and chest showed widespread small lymph nodes and no focal abscess.

Skin biopsy taken for the eruption and quantitative PCR on peripheral blood mononuclear cells both returned with very high viral DNA levels consistent with active replication; hair‑bulb testing was negative for chromosomal integration. Clinical course had worsened after corticosteroids were started.

explanation: A drug exposure followed by fever, rash, lymphadenopathy and severe hepatitis that worsened after immunosuppression, together with high viral DNA in blood and skin but no germline integration, points to reactivation of a herpesvirus implicated in drug‑reaction related systemic illness.

hints.text: A previously well 10-month-old infant was brought after 8 hours of febrile status epilepticus. Temperature on arrival was 40.1°C, the child was postictal and parents reported a faint pink macular rash that appeared as the fever fell.
The infant attends daycare and had a mild upper respiratory prodrome for two days before the seizure. There is no family history of epilepsy and the pregnancy and neonatal period were unremarkable.
Initial bloods showed WBC 9.4 × 10^9/L and CRP 7 mg/L. CSF cell count and chemistry were within reference intervals and HSV PCR was negative.
Head MRI performed after stabilization was unremarkable. EEG showed diffuse slowing without focal epileptiform discharges.

Quantitative PCR on whole blood reported persistently extremely high viral DNA >1.0 × 10^7 copies/mL. Identical high copy numbers were found in hair‑bulb and nail samples, consistent with an inherited chromosomally integrated viral genome rather than transient viraemia.

explanation: Prolonged febrile seizure in an infant with very high persistent viral DNA in blood and equivalent levels in hair and nail samples indicates inherited chromosomally integrated viral DNA, explaining persistent PCR positivity without necessarily indicating ongoing viraemic replication.

hints.text: A 60-year-old woman six weeks after orthotopic liver transplant presented with progressive dyspnoea, non‑productive cough and fever for five days. On exam she was tachypnoeic, oxygen saturation 92% on room air, and had scattered crackles on lung auscultation.
Her immunosuppression regimen includes tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil. Valganciclovir prophylaxis had been stopped two weeks earlier because of worsening neutropenia.
CBC showed neutrophils 0.4 × 10^9/L and platelets 48 × 10^9/L. Blood and sputum cultures were negative and serum galactomannan was not elevated.
CT thorax demonstrated bilateral perihilar ground glass opacities and small areas of consolidation without cavitation. There was no pleural effusion.

Bronchoalveolar lavage PCR and a bone marrow aspirate both returned strongly positive for viral DNA at high copy number. After initiation of intravenous ganciclovir the patient had gradual improvement in respiratory status and a slow rise in neutrophil count over two weeks.

explanation: An immunosuppressed solid‑organ transplant patient with interstitial pneumonitis, profound marrow suppression, and high viral DNA in both BAL and bone marrow that improves with anti‑herpesvirus.

hints.text: A 37-year-old man presented to an urban clinic with an 8-week history of progressive non-tender skin lesions on both lower legs and new swelling of the right ankle that limited his walking. He reports 5 kg weight loss over two months and intermittent oral bleeding; on examination there are multiple flat brown-red papules on the shins and a 1 cm erythematous plaque on the hard palate, temperature 37.4°C, right ankle pitting oedema 2+.

He has known HIV infection diagnosed 6 years earlier but stopped antiretroviral therapy three months ago after moving between cities and reports inconsistent clinic follow-up. He is an MSM, takes no immunosuppressants, and has no recent travel outside the country.
Laboratory tests show CD4 count 0.12 × 10^9/L and HIV RNA 1.2 × 10^5 copies/mL, haemoglobin 95 g/L, platelets 110 × 10^9/L and CRP 36 mg/L. A skin punch biopsy was obtained and sent to pathology.

Contrast CT of the chest shows multiple peribronchovascular nodules and small bilateral pleural effusions, without a dominant pulmonary mass; flexible nasopharyngoscopy notes mucosal erythema and a raised lesion on the posterior palate concordant with the oral plaque.

Histology of the skin lesion demonstrates a spindle-cell vascular proliferation with extravasated erythrocytes; immunohistochemistry stains positive for a viral latent nuclear antigen in lesional nuclei and quantitative PCR of plasma shows high copy number of the same viral DNA.

explanation: An HIV-positive patient with cutaneous and mucosal spindle-cell vascular lesions plus detection of viral DNA and latent antigen identifies infection with the virus known to drive Kaposi sarcoma. The combination of profound CD4 lymphopenia, characteristic biopsy features, and circulating viral DNA supports the diagnosis and implicates Human herpesvirus 8.

hints.text: A 78-year-old retired olive farmer presented with nine months of slowly progressive, non-painful nodules and thickening of the skin over the right lower leg, accompanied by chronic unilateral leg swelling that has increased his need for walking aids. He is afebrile, lesions are firm, dome-shaped nodules clustered over the anterior shin, and the leg shows chronic pitting oedema with skin hyperpigmentation.

He reports lifelong residence in a Mediterranean coastal region and no history of HIV risk behaviours or immunosuppressive medication. His past medical history includes well controlled hypertension and osteoarthritis; he denies systemic symptoms other than gradual mobility decline.

Routine bloodwork shows haemoglobin 120 g/L, white cell count 6.4 × 10^9/L, platelets 220 × 10^9/L and CRP 18 mg/L. An HIV test returned negative and a dermatology service obtained an excisional skin specimen.

Duplex ultrasound excludes deep venous thrombosis and CT of the pelvis and lower limbs demonstrates multiple subcutaneous nodular enhancing lesions and small ipsilateral inguinal lymph nodes but no deep soft tissue mass.

Excisional biopsy shows a vascular spindle-cell proliferation forming slit-like vascular channels; lesional cells stain positive for a viral latent nuclear antigen and tissue PCR demonstrates high copy number of the same viral DNA.

explanation: An elderly Mediterranean man with indolent nodular skin lesions, lymph node involvement, and biopsy-proven spindle-cell vascular proliferation with viral latent antigen and DNA indicates an infection that causes classic Kaposi sarcoma. The clinicopathologic picture is most consistent with Human herpesvirus 8 driven disease in the classic form.

hints.text: A 50-year-old woman presented to clinic nine months after a kidney transplant with a three-week history of fevers, night sweats and new diffuse small red-purple papules on the trunk, together with increasing fatigue and reduced appetite. On examination she had generalized non-tender lymphadenopathy, palpable splenomegaly and multiple 2–5 mm erythematous papules over the chest and back; temperature 38.2°C.

She is maintained on tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil following a deceased-donor renal transplant and received basiliximab induction. CMV prophylaxis was completed three months earlier and she has not had known HIV exposure; graft function has been stable.

Blood tests reveal haemoglobin 80 g/L, albumin 25 g/L, platelets 90 × 10^9/L and CRP 120 mg/L. Liver and renal function are otherwise at baseline and a peripheral blood PCR assay for a DNA virus was requested.
Contrast CT shows widespread hypermetabolic lymphadenopathy above and below the diaphragm and splenomegaly without focal hepatic lesions; an excisional lymph node biopsy is planned.

Reduction of immunosuppression and a single course of rituximab were followed by rapid defervescence and clinical improvement; concurrent testing showed a marked fall in plasma viral DNA copies and lymph node histology demonstrated plasmacytic proliferation with cells positive for a viral latent nuclear antigen.

explanation: A post-transplant patient with systemic inflammatory symptoms, generalized adenopathy, plasmacytic histology and a fall in viral DNA after reducing immunosuppression points to multicentric Castleman–type disease driven by the oncogenic virus detected in tissue. The clinical course and viral latent antigen detection indicate Human herpesvirus 8 involvement.

hints.text: A 62-year-old man presented with three weeks of progressive dyspnoea and pleuritic chest discomfort; he required therapeutic thoracentesis for a large right pleural effusion that recurred within days. He reports fatigue and night sweats, examination shows diminished breath sounds at the right base and oxygen saturation 94% on room air.

He was diagnosed with HIV infection several years ago and has had intermittent adherence to antiretroviral therapy; he denies intravenous drug use and has no known malignancy history. He had a recent community-acquired pneumonia treated with oral antibiotics two months earlier.

Pleural fluid is exudative and bloody with lactate dehydrogenase 580 IU/L, protein 48 g/L; cytology shows sheets of large plasmablastic cells that are negative for epithelial carcinoma markers and flow cytometry demonstrates a clonal plasma-cell phenotype. Peripheral blood CD4 count is 0.18 × 10^9/L.

Contrast-enhanced CT chest shows a large right pleural effusion without a discrete parenchymal or mediastinal mass and a small pericardial effusion; there is no significant lymphadenopathy to suggest systemic lymphoma.

PCR of the pleural fluid detected high copy numbers of viral DNA and immunohistochemical staining of the cell block was positive for a viral latent nuclear antigen within the atypical plasmablastic cells.

explanation: A recurrent bloody pleural effusion composed of clonal plasmablastic cells in an HIV-positive patient with detectable viral DNA and latent antigen in the tumour cells identifies the viral aetiology underlying primary effusion lymphoma. These findings point to Human herpesvirus 8 as the causative pathogen.

hints.text: A previously well 9-month-old boy was brought to the emergency department after a generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. He had had 36 hours of high fever to 39.8 °C and was postictal for 20 minutes; on arrival he was afebrile and had no focal neurologic deficits.

Parents report the fever began abruptly with poor feeding and irritability. He attends a small home-based playgroup and an older sibling returned from daycare one week earlier after a short febrile illness.
