hints.text: A 62-year-old man with longstanding rheumatoid arthritis presents with two months of low-grade fevers, three weeks of multiple tender subcutaneous nodules on his forearms and progressive right wrist pain and swelling limiting hand use. Temperature 37.8°C, right wrist tender with reduced range of motion.

He has been treated with a tumour necrosis factor blocker and methotrexate for three years. He gardens frequently and recalls several splinters from rose bushes over the past six months but reports no recent systemic antibiotic courses.

CRP 65 mg/L, white cell count 8.6 × 10^9/L. Blood cultures are sterile. Aspirate of a skin nodule and synovial fluid from the wrist both showed numerous acid-fast organisms on Ziehl-Neelsen stain while routine bacterial cultures remained negative.

MRI of the wrist demonstrates distal radial osteomyelitis with cortical destruction and adjacent soft tissue abscesses. Whole-body PET-CT shows multiple FDG-avid cutaneous nodules and corresponding marrow uptake at the right distal radius.

Cultures on specialized media required 2–3 weeks to form smooth, non-pigmented colonies. Molecular testing identified slow-growing environmental acid-fast organisms that have been reported to cause soft tissue and bone infections after skin breach in patients receiving TNF-blocking therapy. He was started on clarithromycin plus ethambutol with gradual clinical improvement.

explanation: An immunomodulated patient with gardening-related skin trauma, subcutaneous nodules, and osteomyelitis with acid-fast organisms on direct stain and slow-growing, non-pigmented colonies points to an environmental slow-growing acid-fast bacillus known to cause post-traumatic skin, bone and joint disease in patients on anti-TNF. Clinical improvement on macrolide plus ethambutol supports the diagnosis.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man presents to clinic with three weeks of productive cough, low-grade fevers, night sweats and 4 kg weight loss. He reports progressive dyspnoea and new intermittent headaches for five days. On exam temperature is 37.9°C, oxygen saturation 92% on room air, and there are scattered crackles over the right lung base.

He has sarcoidosis treated with oral prednisone 15 mg daily for two years and type 2 diabetes with recent HbA1c 8.1%. He is a retired carpenter who spends weekends gardening and has no recent travel or tuberculosis contact.

Blood work shows WBC 14.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance and C-reactive protein 86 mg/L. Two sets of routine blood cultures and sputum cultures after 48 hours are reported as no growth and routine AFB smear is negative.

Chest CT demonstrates multiple nodular consolidations in the right upper and middle lobes with central cavitation. Contrast MRI of the brain shows a 1.8 cm ring-enhancing lesion in the left parietal lobe with surrounding vasogenic oedema.

Bronchoalveolar lavage cultured slowly growing dry, chalky colonies after six days. Modified acid-fast staining of the colonies showed branching filamentous gram-positive organisms that were weakly acid-fast and the patient began high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole with clinical and radiographic improvement over the following weeks.

explanation: Subacute pulmonary nodules with cavitation and a concurrent brain abscess in a patient on chronic steroids suggests a disseminating environmental aerobic actinomycete. Growth of dry colonies and branching filamentous organisms that are weakly acid-fast with response to high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is diagnostic for Nocardia asteroides.

hints.text: A 62-year-old man presents to the emergency department with two weeks of fever, productive cough and worsening right-sided weakness. He reports malaise and one episode of confusion at home. On exam temperature is 38.3°C and he has reduced power 3/5 in the right arm and leg.
He underwent a renal transplant three years ago and is maintained on tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil and low-dose prednisone. He received a steroid bolus for rejection six weeks ago.

Chest CT shows multiple bilateral nodules, several with cavitation, predominantly in the upper lobes. Brain MRI demonstrates multiple rim-enhancing lesions in both cerebral hemispheres with surrounding oedema, the largest measuring 2.4 cm.

Bronchoscopic sampling and stereotactic aspirate of a brain lesion were sent for culture. After extended aerobic incubation, colonies appeared that were dry and chalky and microscopy of colony scrapings revealed branching filamentous gram-positive organisms that were partially acid-fast on modified staining.
The patient was started on high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and showed gradual neurological improvement with shrinkage of the brain lesions on follow-up imaging over six weeks.

explanation: An immunosuppressed transplant recipient with cavitating pulmonary nodules and multiple brain abscesses indicates a disseminated environmental aerobic filamentous bacillus. Culture morphology and partial acid-fastness with clinical response to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are consistent with Nocardia asteroides.

hints.text: A 67-year-old man presented to the emergency clinic with 36 hours of rapidly progressive swelling, pain, and erythema of the right hand. He was febrile at 38.2°C, heart rate 102 beats/min, and had tense swelling over the dorsum and painful limitation of active finger extension; there was no obvious puncture wound on initial inspection.

He has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and long-standing rheumatoid arthritis managed with methotrexate and prednisone 5 mg daily. He lives alone, performs routine gardening, and denied recent travel, intravenous drug use, or prior admissions. Symptoms evolved over less than two days from mild tenderness to marked swelling and systemic features.

Blood tests showed white cell count 14.2 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 210 mg/L. A swab from the wound site and the first set of blood cultures flagged positive within 18 hours, yielding small pleomorphic Gram-negative coccobacilli on Gram stain.
Ultrasound of the hand demonstrated hypoechoic fluid tracking along the flexor tendon sheaths without obvious cortical bone erosion on plain radiographs. No foreign body or gas was identified.
On directed questioning after culture results, he recalled being scratched on the dorsal right hand by his indoor cat while trying to separate it from a neighbour's cat 48 hours before symptom onset.

explanation: Rapid-onset hand cellulitis with early bacteremia following a cat scratch, plus growth of small Gram-negative coccobacilli, points to Pasteurella multocida.

hints.text: A 68-year-old man presented to the emergency department with four days of fever, increasing productive cough and dyspnoea. He was febrile at 38.7°C, tachypnoeic with respiratory rate 24/min, required 3 L/min oxygen to maintain saturation 93%, and had coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the right base on auscultation.

He has severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease treated with inhaled bronchodilators and was given a 10-day course of oral corticosteroids for a recent flare. He is retired, lives alone, and has longstanding alcohol use but no recent hospital admissions.

White blood cell count was 14.2 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 150 mg/L. Two sets of blood cultures flagged positive at 24 hours and showed small pleomorphic gram-negative coccobacilli on Gram stain.
Chest radiograph demonstrated dense consolidation in the right lower lobe with a small right pleural effusion. CT chest confirmed lobar consolidation and small loculated effusion without cavitation.
On directed questioning the patient recalled being bitten on his right index finger by a neighbour's cat six days before symptom onset, and he had allowed the animal to lick the uncleaned wound.

explanation: The timing, rapid blood culture growth and pulmonary focus support Pasteurella multocida as the most likely pathogen.

hints.text: A 38-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 3-week history of intense generalized itching and progressively excoriated papules on the trunk and proximal limbs. He reports disturbed sleep because of the pruritus, has had low-grade fevers up to 38.2 °C, and on examination is tachycardic at 104 min^-1 with multiple crusted erythematous papules concentrated on the abdomen and along the waistline under clothing.

He is unhoused and has been alternating between crowded shelters for the past four months, wearing the same unwashed coat most days; he denies recent travel outside the region. He uses communal bedding at shelters, has poor access to laundry facilities, and has no prior diagnosis of dermatologic disease.

Full blood count shows hemoglobin 92 g/L with mean corpuscular volume 73 fL, WBC 11.2 × 10^9/L, and C-reactive protein 28 mg/L. A bacterial swab of a secondary excoriated lesion grew Staphylococcus aureus sensitive to flucloxacillin.

A clinical photograph of the torso demonstrates densely grouped papules and excoriations in linear clusters aligned with the beltline and inner seams of the shirt, with relative sparing of the scalp and distal extremities.

Inspection of the patient's unwashed coat revealed numerous small wingless blood-stained arthropods and oval translucent eggs firmly attached to fabric fibers in the seams; laundering the coat at 65 °C and treating skin excoriations led to rapid reduction in pruritus and no further new lesions.

explanation: The leaflet distribution of pruritic papules along clothing contact points, discovery of wingless blood-feeding arthropods and eggs cemented to fabric seams, and improvement after high-temperature laundering are diagnostic of a human ectoparasite that lives in clothing rather than hair. Chronic feeding explains the microcytic anemia and secondary bacterial superinfection. The findings identify Pediculus humanus corporis as the cause.

hints.text: A 52-year-old woman presented to the ophthalmology clinic with one year of gradual blurring in the right eye and increasing glare in bright light. She noted intermittent redness and foreign body sensation but no acute pain. Visual acuity was 0.3 in the right eye and 0.8 in the left. On slit lamp there were multiple small anterior corneal opacities and mild conjunctival injection.

She emigrated from a rural region of West Africa twenty years ago after living by river rapids until age 35. In childhood she had frequent intensely itchy rashes and a small painless cheek nodule that was surgically removed. She has no diabetes and uses no topical medications currently.

Full blood count revealed eosinophils 1.1 × 10^9/L, leucocytes 6.9 × 10^9/L. Serologic testing for syphilis and onchocerciasis-directed antibody testing performed at regional lab were pending. Skin snips were not initially performed.

Ophthalmic examination revealed punctate corneal stromal opacities and early pannus formation. Funduscopy showed patchy chorioretinal scarring in the periphery of the right eye and vitreous opacities on B-scan ultrasonography.

She confirmed repeated painful bites from very small flies at the river while fetching water as a child. Ophthalmology obtained a small skin snip from the forearm which released motile microfilariae on immediate microscopy, correlating with her eye findings and past subcutaneous nodule history.

explanation: Progressive corneal involvement with peripheral chorioretinal scarring in a patient with lifelong riverine exposure and prior subcutaneous nodules suggests a filarial infection affecting skin and eye. The diagnostic skin snip showing motile microfilariae provides the confirmatory link to a parasite transmitted by small riverine flies.

hints.text: A 58-year-old woman presented to the emergency clinic 36 hours after developing progressive pain and swelling of her left hand. She reported fever and inability to fully flex the index finger, temperature 38.4 C, heart rate 102/min, a tense erythematous dorsal hand swelling with local tenderness and a small central puncture point.

She has type 2 diabetes mellitus, treated with metformin, recent glycated haemoglobin 7.8% and works as a veterinary technician. She initially denied significant trauma and had attempted oral analgesia at home without benefit.

Peripheral white blood cell count 14.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 11.0 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 120 mg/L. A wound swab showed numerous neutrophils and small Gram-negative coccobacilli on Gram stain.

Bedside ultrasound of the hand demonstrated a 12 mm subcutaneous fluid collection tracking toward the second metacarpophalangeal joint, no evidence of deep flexor sheath fluid or osteomyelitis on plain radiographs.

On further questioning she recalled a puncture from a client’s cat while restraining it 48 hours before symptom onset. Culture of the wound grew a rapidly growing organism typical of feline oral flora that was markedly susceptible to penicillin and amoxicillin.

explanation: Rapid-onset hand cellulitis after a cat puncture, presence of small Gram-negative coccobacilli on wound Gram stain and a culture profile showing susceptibility to penicillins point to Pasteurella multocida as the most likely pathogen.

hints.text: A 68-year-old woman presented with three weeks of progressive right knee pain and swelling, morning stiffness and difficulty weight-bearing. She was afebrile at presentation, had a warm effusion of the right knee, limited range of motion and marked pain on passive movement.

She underwent total knee replacement 11 months ago for osteoarthritis and takes methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis, prednisone 7.5 mg daily. She cares for neighbourhood stray cats and reported no obvious wound at the time of onset.

Arthrocentesis yielded turbid fluid with leukocyte count 58.0 × 10^9/L and 90% neutrophils. Gram stain showed a few small Gram-negative coccobacilli and synovial fluid culture grew small colonies within 24–48 hours.
Plain radiographs of the knee demonstrated new peri-prosthetic lucency consistent with loosening and a joint effusion on lateral view.

On reinterview she remembered being scratched on the lower leg by a kitten three weeks earlier while carrying it. Synovial fluid and wound cultures yielded the same organism which was highly susceptible to penicillin and tetracyclines.

explanation: Periprosthetic joint infection in an immunosuppressed patient, synovial fluid showing small Gram-negative coccobacilli, and a recent cat scratch with concordant cultures strongly support Pasteurella multocida infection of the prosthesis.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man from a riverside village presents with a 6-month history of intense pruritus and several slowly enlarging subcutaneous nodules. He reports progressive blurring of the right eye; on exam there are three firm, non-tender lumbar nodules and right visual acuity reduced to 6/12.

He has lived and worked as a farmer beside the same fast-flowing river for 12 years. He has no chronic medical conditions, has not received prior mass antiparasitic treatment, and an HIV rapid test performed in clinic was negative.

Full blood count shows eosinophils 1.3 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 130 g/L and CRP within reference range. Punch biopsy of a nodule shows granulomatous inflammation with numerous eosinophils; bacterial and mycobacterial stains are negative.
Ophthalmology slit-lamp and fundus exam reveal punctate corneal opacities and early optic disc pallor in the right eye consistent with chronic inflammatory damage.
He describes repeated day-biting insect exposure along riverbanks. Skin snips incubated in saline produced motile, slender microfilariae within 30 minutes.

explanation: The combination of long-term riverside exposure with intense pruritus, subcutaneous nodules, ocular inflammatory damage, eosinophilia, and motile microfilariae from skin snips supports infection with Onchocerca volvulus. Skin-snip detection of microfilariae provides the diagnostic confirmation and explains the ocular findings.

hints.text: A 28-year-old male subsistence farmer presents with 6 months of intense generalized pruritus and progressive blurring of vision in his left eye. He sleeps poorly because of itching; vitals are normal; examination shows multiple hyperpigmented papular lesions on the trunk and a 2 cm firm, mobile subcutaneous nodule over the right iliac crest, left visual acuity 6/24 with conjunctival injection.

He was born and remains in a rural West African river valley and fishes barefoot daily. He reports frequent daytime insect bites when working along the river and has used only topical emollients for the skin symptoms.

Full blood count shows eosinophils 1.6 × 10^9/L and total IgE 420 kU/L. Peripheral blood smear is negative for blood microfilariae. A punch biopsy of a papular lesion shows a dense inflammatory infiltrate with numerous eosinophils and granulomatous change, no organisms seen on routine stains.

Slit-lamp and dilated fundoscopy reveal punctate keratitis and focal chorioretinal scarring in the left eye. High-frequency ultrasound of the subcutaneous nodule demonstrates a linear tubular echogenic structure that shows slow movement within a fibrous capsule.

Skin snips incubated in saline produced numerous motile unsheathed microfilariae on microscopy. The patient reports decades of residence within 2 km of fast-flowing rivers with heavy exposure to small day-biting flies while working.

explanation: Chronic pruritic dermatitis with palpable subcutaneous nodules, ocular involvement and skin snips that release motile unsheathed microfilariae in a patient with long riverine exposure are diagnostic for infection by Onchocerca volvulus.

hints.text: A 13-year-old girl from a riverine village presents with 18 months of severe pruritus causing frequent school absence. On exam she has multiple hypopigmented macules and patches over the lower legs, two painless 1.5 cm subcutaneous nodules over the pelvis, normal vitals and visual acuity reduced to 6/12 bilaterally.

Her family farms beside a fast-flowing river and report regular exposure to many small biting flies while working fields. The household has received periodic mass treatment for intestinal helminths but not the drug used to clear skin-dwelling microfilariae.

Full blood count shows eosinophils 2.2 × 10^9/L and haemoglobin 115 g/L. A skin biopsy from a hypopigmented area shows granulomatous inflammation surrounding worm-like structures; routine special stains do not reveal bacteria or fungal elements.

Ultrasound of the pelvic nodules demonstrates two encapsulated lesions each containing a central tubular echogenic structure with slow motility, consistent with living helminths within subcutaneous nodules.

Two skin snip specimens incubated yielded numerous motile unsheathed microfilariae on light microscopy. The household describes heavy exposure to small biting flies at riverside farms over many years.

explanation: The combination of chronic pruritic skin changes with hypopigmentation, palpable nodules containing adult worms, skin snips showing motile unsheathed microfilariae, and prolonged riverine fly exposure is diagnostic of Onchocerca volvulus infection.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 10 days of intermittent fever, drenching sweats and severe headache. He reports rigors with each fever spike; on exam temperature 39.1 °C, heart rate 110/min, scleral icterus and a spleen palpable 2 cm below the left costal margin.

He is previously healthy, not on regular medication and has no known immunosuppression. He denies recent antibiotic use, blood transfusion or intravenous drug use and says his symptoms began gradually after returning to work from routine duties.

Laboratory tests show haemoglobin 98 g/L, white cell count 5.8 × 10^9/L, platelets 92 × 10^9/L, total bilirubin 34 µmol/L and elevated lactate dehydrogenase. Thick blood film demonstrates low-density parasitaemia with occasional ring forms; a rapid malaria antigen panel reported a low positive signal on the pan component.
Abdominal ultrasound shows homogeneous splenomegaly with maximal length 14 cm and no focal hepatic lesions or biliary obstruction.

On repeat questioning he describes multiple nights sleeping without a net during a two-week stay in a riverside village in western Kenya about four weeks before symptoms began, and he now reports that his fevers recur in a stereotyped pattern every 72 hours.

explanation: The combination of low-level persistent parasitaemia, thrombocytopenia, splenomegaly and a 72-hour (quartan) fever recurrence strongly points to infection with Plasmodium malariae. The travel history with nocturnal mosquito exposure supports vector-borne acquisition.

hints.text: A 52-year-old woman presents to clinic with six weeks of progressive peripheral oedema and frothy urine. Blood pressure 150/95 mmHg, marked pitting oedema to the knees and periorbital swelling are present; she reports increasing fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance.

She has no known diabetes or autoimmune disease. Eight months earlier she spent two weeks visiting family in a rural coastal region; she recalls a febrile illness there that resolved without medical care. She denies recent vaccinations, intravenous drug use or transfusion.

Urine protein excretion 12.0 g/24 h, serum albumin 18 g/L, creatinine 110 µmol/L. Haemoglobin 88 g/L and platelets 160 × 10^9/L. Repeat peripheral blood film at the nephrology clinic shows low-density parasitaemia on thick smear.
Renal ultrasound reveals normal-sized kidneys with mildly increased cortical echogenicity and no hydronephrosis.

Further history clarifies that during her visit she slept without a mosquito net on multiple nights in a mangrove village and had several brief febrile episodes after returning. Molecular testing of blood confirms a malaria species whose erythrocytic cycle produces fevers every 72 hours, and clinicians correlate the nephrotic syndrome with that infection.

explanation: New-onset nephrotic-range proteinuria after travel, together with persistent low-level parasitaemia and a 72-hour fever pattern, supports Plasmodium malariae as the cause of the renal presentation. This species is known to cause chronic low-density infection that can trigger glomerular disease.

hints.text: A 45-year-old man found by outreach workers in a city park presents with a 6-week history of worsening itch and multiple excoriated papules on his trunk and upper arms. He reports progressive weight loss and fatigue, temperature 37.8°C, and on exam there are numerous crusted excoriations concentrated along the waistband and axillary folds that limit his ability to sleep.

He has alcohol use disorder and reports sleeping rough for the past three months, wearing the same clothes for days to weeks and bathing rarely because he lacks access to facilities. He denies foreign travel, new sexual contacts, or exposure to farm animals.
Blood tests show haemoglobin 95 g/L, MCV 80 fL, WBC 8.6 × 10^9/L, CRP 18 mg/L. Bacterial culture from an excoriation grew Staphylococcus aureus. Skin scrapings for mites were negative.
Hand-lens photograph of the inner waistband of his trousers shows small elongated arthropods clinging to textile fibres and numerous oval pale eggs firmly attached to the cloth near the seam.

Public health inspection of his belongings found hundreds of live blood-feeding arthropods and eggs concentrated in clothing seams and undergarments, with the insects moving onto exposed skin only when garments were worn.

explanation: The rash concentrated where clothing contacts skin plus demonstration of live blood-feeding arthropods and eggs cemented to garments points to a clothing-borne ectoparasite. Chronic poor hygiene and anemia support ongoing blood feeding from the infestation. Negative skin scrapings argue against a burrowing mite as the cause.

hints.text: A previously well 8-year-old girl brought to a refugee clinic with a 2-week history of itchy papules and increasing low-grade fever. On examination she has numerous erythematous papules and excoriations over the torso and at sites covered by underwear and the belt line, weight 19 kg, temperature 37.6°C.

The family arrived from a conflict zone 10 days ago and have been living in a crowded tent with shared blankets and limited washing water for about one month. Several siblings have similar itch but the scalp appears unaffected.
Haemoglobin 100 g/L, eosinophils 0.6 × 10^9/L. Rapid malaria test was negative. Skin scrapings for burrowing mites were negative and no fungal elements were seen.
Photograph taken under a hand lens of the child’s underwear seam shows small elongated motile organisms clinging to fibres and oval translucent eggs attached to the textile near the seam area.

Inspection of the family’s clothing after communal laundering revealed dozens of live blood-feeding arthropods and eggs cemented to garments rather than to hair. After exchanging and hot-washing clothing and treating affected garments, the rash among family members improved.

explanation: The distribution of lesions under clothing and the finding of live blood-feeding arthropods and firmly attached eggs on garments indicate a parasite that lives in clothing and moves to skin to feed. Crowded temporary shelter and shared bedding create the exposure risk. Negative skin scrapings reduce the likelihood of a burrowing mite.

hints.text: A 38-year-old man is referred to nephrology with 3 months of progressive lower limb swelling and frothy urine, and several episodes of low-grade fever that his partner notes come and go over days. On examination he has pitting edema to the knees, blood pressure 150/95 mmHg, and no rash or lymphadenopathy.

He emigrated from West Africa at age 6 and has lived in northern Europe for the past 32 years. He reports no recent travel, takes no nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and has no history of hepatitis or diabetes. He recalls an unspecified febrile illness in early childhood for which there are no records.

Urine protein excretion is 6.2 g/24 h, serum albumin 18 g/L, total cholesterol 9.2 mmol/L, creatinine 98 µmol/L. Haemoglobin 98 g/L, platelets 110 × 10^9/L, direct Coombs test negative. Routine blood cultures and viral hepatitis serology are negative.

Renal ultrasound shows normal-sized kidneys with preserved corticomedullary differentiation. Abdominal ultrasound notes a spleen measuring 15 cm with preserved texture and no focal lesion. Chest radiograph is unremarkable.

On targeted questioning he describes an eight day camping trip in rural Ghana eight months earlier with frequent mosquito bites. A specialist parasitology review of a peripheral thin film shows low-density intraerythrocytic parasites with trophozoites forming a characteristic band across some erythrocytes and schizonts showing a rosette arrangement of merozoites. Nurses observed fever spikes approximately every third day while the patient was inpatient.

explanation: Nephrotic-range proteinuria with long-standing intermittent fevers, splenomegaly, and a low-density parasitemia with band-form trophozoites and rosette schizonts point to Plasmodium malariae. The organism can persist with low-level infection and is linked to nephrotic presentations. The documented fever spikes every third day support the diagnosis.

hints.text: A 67-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 2 days of high fevers, rigors, progressive confusion, and jaundice. He is febrile at 39.0°C, heart rate 110 min−1, blood pressure 110/65 mmHg, and has a palpable spleen 4 cm below the costal margin.

He sustained a hip fracture 8 weeks ago and received two units of packed red cells during surgical repair. He denies recent travel outside the country and has no known chronic liver disease. He is on warfarin for atrial fibrillation.

Haemoglobin has fallen to 82 g/L from 110 g/L postoperatively, bilirubin 55 µmol/L, lactate dehydrogenase 820 U/L, haptoglobin undetectable, platelets 70 × 10^9/L, creatinine 140 µmol/L. Two rapid diagnostic tests for a common haemoparasite were negative, blood cultures show no growth.
Contrast CT abdomen to exclude occult abscess shows marked splenomegaly with a spleen length of 18 cm and no focal hepatic lesion. Transthoracic echocardiography shows no valvular vegetations.

The transfusion service traced one donor to recent travel in a tropical region. Repeat expert microscopy of the recipient's thin film and a re-examined donor sample reveal low-density intraerythrocytic parasites with band-shaped trophozoites and schizonts containing a rosette of roughly 6 to 10 merozoites. Nurses charted recurrent fever peaks every third day while the patient was observed.

explanation: Delayed febrile hemolytic illness after transfusion, low parasitemia with band-form trophozoites and rosette-form schizonts, and documented fever peaks every third day indicate transfusion-transmitted Plasmodium malariae. The parasite's low-density carriage and potential to survive in donor blood explain the delayed presentation.

hints.text: A 68-year-old man found by outreach workers after several days outdoors, brought to the emergency department for fever and confusion. Over 72 hours he developed new scattered erythematous papules and excoriations on the trunk and shoulders, temperature 38.9°C, heart rate 112 min−1, blood pressure 100/62 mmHg, and he was somnolent but arousable on exam.

The patient is chronically homeless with alcohol dependence and mobility impairment. Outreach notes report irregular access to laundry or clean clothes for weeks and recent sleeping in a crowded drop-in shelter that had a reported heating outage.
Blood tests showed white cell count 15.8 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 114 g/L, C-reactive protein 132 mg/L, and mild hyponatraemia Na+ 128 mmol/L. Blood cultures were pending at 6 hours.
Head CT without contrast showed no acute intracranial abnormality. Chest radiograph was clear. There was no focal collection on focused bedside ultrasound of soft tissues.

When staff changed his clothing they noted multiple small, wingless blood-stained arthropods measuring about 2–3 mm clustered along the seams of his undershirt and numerous oval, pale eggs cemented to fabric fibres within the shirt's collar.

explanation: The combination of fever, altered mental status, papular excoriative lesions, crowded sleeping conditions and discovery of small blood-feeding arthropods and eggs attached to clothing points to heavy infestation by the human clothing-associated blood-feeding ectoparasite. The fabric-bound eggs and insects found in garment seams distinguish this from head or body hair infestations and explain the clinical syndrome through sustained blood feeding and potential secondary infection.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man presents to outpatient clinic with a 3-week history of intermittent fevers, drenching night sweats, and progressive fatigue. Fevers recur every few days with chills and occipital headache. On examination his temperature is 38.9°C, he is pale, and the spleen tip is palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin.

He returned 8 weeks ago from a 6-month work assignment in rural West Africa where he frequently slept without bed nets and reported heavy mosquito exposure. He did not take regular chemoprophylaxis and recalls a similar self-limited febrile illness three years earlier that was treated locally.

Full blood count shows haemoglobin 95 g/L, MCV 86 fL, leukocytes 5.9 × 10^9/L and platelets 120 × 10^9/L. Peripheral blood film demonstrates low parasitaemia at about 0.6%, with mature trophozoites occasionally forming a transverse band across erythrocytes and compact schizonts containing multiple merozoites.

Abdominal ultrasound done to evaluate the palpable spleen shows mild splenomegaly with a longitudinal span of 15 cm and no focal splenic collection. Both kidneys appear normal in size and echotexture.

On targeted review the patient emphasises that his febrile paroxysms follow a strict three-day rhythm with substantial improvement between episodes. A rapid diagnostic test aimed at a common high-virulence species was repeatedly negative while microscopy remained positive.

explanation: The combination of travel to endemic West Africa, splenomegaly with mild anaemia, low-level parasitaemia showing band-form trophozoites and compact schizonts, and a strict 72-hour fever cycle points to infection with Plasmodium malariae. The negative rapid test for the more virulent species together with characteristic morphology and quartan periodicity support this diagnosis.

hints.text: A 29-year-old male aid worker presents with 4 days of intermittent fevers, drenching sweats, rigors and progressive fatigue. He is febrile to 38.9°C, heart rate 110 bpm, and exam reveals a palpable spleen 3 cm below the left costal margin.

He returned three weeks ago from a six-month assignment in rural Sierra Leone. He reports inconsistent use of insect repellent and stopped his daily chemoprophylaxis after gastrointestinal side effects; he had one untreated febrile episode while abroad that resolved without medical care.
Full blood count shows haemoglobin 95 g/L, platelets 78 × 10^9/L and leukocytes 3.2 × 10^9/L. Hospital thick blood film demonstrates low-level parasitaemia with ring forms within erythrocytes.
Abdominal ultrasound confirms splenomegaly at 14 cm without focal hepatic lesions. Chest radiograph is normal.

Peripheral thin film review highlights enlarged oval erythrocytes with fimbriated margins and fine stippling of infected cells. He defervesced rapidly after oral chloroquine and was counselled to take an 8-aminoquinoline for radical cure to prevent relapse.

explanation: Travel to West Africa with a prior self-limited febrile episode, low parasitaemia, oval enlarged red cells with stippling, and the need for an 8-aminoquinoline to prevent relapse point to Plasmodium ovale.

hints.text: A 29-year-old male aid worker presents to an urban clinic with 5 days of fever, night sweats and increasing fatigue after returning from West Africa 10 weeks earlier. Temperature is 38.9°C, pulse 105/min, and examination shows a palpable spleen tip 3 cm below the costal margin and scleral icterus.

During a nine-month deployment he reported intermittent fevers that resolved after a short course of an unfamiliar oral medication obtained locally. He admits intermittent adherence to chemoprophylaxis and received no prolonged follow-up after repatriation.

Full blood count shows haemoglobin 95 g/L, white blood cells 3.6 × 10^9/L, platelets 78 × 10^9/L. Total bilirubin 38 µmol/L and lactate dehydrogenase 480 U/L. Thin blood film quantified parasitaemia at 0.3% by microscopy.
Abdominal ultrasound confirms splenomegaly with a longitudinal axis of 14 cm, no focal hepatic lesions and no abscess.

He received chloroquine with rapid defervescence and haemodynamic stability but redeveloped fevers at 10 weeks. Repeat smear at relapse demonstrated infected erythrocytes that were oval with fimbriated margins and Schuffner's stippling, low parasite density. G6PD was normal and a course of primaquine produced sustained clearance.

explanation: Travel to West Africa with delayed relapse after apparent treatment, low-density parasitaemia, oval fimbriated infected erythrocytes with Schuffner's stippling, and cure only after primaquine indicate infection with Plasmodium ovale. The clinical course reflects dormant hepatic forms causing relapse.

hints.text: A 48-year-old man presents with 6 days of high fevers, progressive jaundice and profound fatigue. He is febrile 39.2°C, markedly pale, and has scleral icterus; he has a history of splenectomy 12 years earlier after a motor vehicle collision.

He travelled to Nigeria for business three months before presentation and received intermittent antimalarial prophylaxis. He recalls a brief febrile illness while abroad that settled without formal medical follow-up.

Haemoglobin 62 g/L with reticulocytosis, white blood cells 5.2 × 10^9/L, platelets 55 × 10^9/L. Bilirubin 78 µmol/L and haptoglobin suppressed, consistent with haemolysis. Peripheral film shows low to moderate parasitaemia but not the high densities more typical of other severe erythrocytic infections.
Contrast CT abdomen shows expected postsplenectomy anatomy, mild hepatomegaly, and no intrahepatic abscess or biliary obstruction.

He received intravenous then oral chloroquine with symptomatic and parasitological improvement, but developed recurrent febrile episodes three months later. Repeat microscopy at relapse identified oval infected erythrocytes with Schuffner-type stippling at low parasite density, and administration of primaquine after confirming normal G6PD resulted in cure.

explanation: In a post-splenectomy traveller from West Africa with delayed relapse after blood-stage. Radical cure with primaquine eradicated the relapse source.

hints.text: A 38-year-old man presented with ten days of fever, progressive perineal pain and urinary hesitancy. He reported new difficulty voiding and systemic malaise; rectal exam revealed a tender, boggy prostate and low-grade fever of 38.2°C.

Two weeks earlier he underwent outpatient urethral dilation and cystoscopy for a recurrent bulbar urethral stricture. He received a single peri-procedural dose of antibiotic but no prolonged prophylaxis. He has no history of stones.

Pelvic MRI with endorectal coil showed three discrete 12–18 mm fluid collections within the peripheral zone of the prostate consistent with abscesses and marked surrounding inflammation tracking toward the bladder neck. The kidneys appeared normal on imaging.

Transrectal ultrasound-guided aspiration of the largest collection yielded turbid fluid that turned strongly alkaline on bedside testing and produced visible needle-shaped crystals after standing at room temperature.
Culture of the prostatic aspirate grew a swarming, urease-positive, indole-negative gram-negative bacillus that was responsive to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate. Blood cultures remained sterile.

explanation: Post-instrumentation prostatic abscess with alkaline aspirate and crystal formation indicates local urease activity creating an ammonia-rich environment. The culture phenotype of swarming growth with urease positivity and indole negativity is consistent with the organism most often responsible in this clinical setting.

hints.text: An 81-year-old woman from a residential care home presented with a three-week non-healing sacral pressure ulcer, increasing purulent drainage and new low-grade fevers. On exam she was afebrile in clinic but the ulcer base had foul-smelling grey exudate and surrounding erythema extending to subcutaneous tissue.

She has type 2 diabetes treated with oral agents and had intermittent urinary catheterisation over recent months for urinary retention. She received several short outpatient antibiotic courses for presumed cellulitis without durable improvement.

Contrast MRI of the pelvis demonstrated deep soft tissue inflammation tracking to the posterior sacral ala with focal marrow oedema suggestive of contiguous osteomyelitis. There was a small collection in the subcutaneous tissue adjacent to the ulcer.

During surgical debridement the team noted friable white film and punctate calcifications within sinus tracts and a distinct ammoniacal odour emanating from the wound bed. Deep tissue samples were taken for culture and histology.
Deep wound and paired blood cultures yielded a swarming, urease-positive, indole-negative gram-negative bacillus susceptible to piperacillin-tazobactam. Histology showed acute osteomyelitis.

explanation: A chronic catheterised resident with wound encrustation, ammoniacal odour, and calcified deposits suggests infection with a urease-producing bacillus. Isolation of a swarming, urease-positive, indole-negative gram-negative rod from deep tissue and blood identifies the most likely causative species in this scenario.

hints.text: A 54-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 36 hours of fever, rigors, progressive left flank pain and nausea. On arrival temperature 39.2 °C, heart rate 112 bpm, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg; examination showed marked left costovertebral angle tenderness and a palpable, tender bladder.

He reports a long history of recurrent nephrolithiasis and lower urinary tract symptoms attributed to benign prostatic enlargement. He is not diabetic, takes tamsulosin intermittently, and had no recent antibiotic courses before this illness.

Blood tests showed leukocytosis 15.8 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 120 mg/L. Urinalysis revealed pH 8.5, large leukocyte esterase, numerous white cells and bacteria on microscopy, and a positive nitrite test; preliminary urine culture flagged heavy growth of a Gram-negative bacillus.

Non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder demonstrated a 3.2 cm branching calculus filling much of the left renal pelvis consistent with a partial staghorn stone, upstream hydronephrosis and perinephric stranding.

Chart review showed he had an indwelling urethral catheter placed for urinary retention after an orthopaedic procedure two months earlier and required intermittent catheter care. Stone analysis after percutaneous removal was predominantly magnesium ammonium phosphate and the laboratory microbiology note described motile colonies with concentric swarming on nonselective agar and rapid alkalinization of culture media.

explanation: Obstructive staghorn calculus with alkaline urine, struvite stone composition and a motile, swarming Gram-negative bacillus point to a urease-producing, motile Gram-negative rod that commonly causes catheter-associated urinary tract infection and infection-related struvite stones. The clinical picture of pyelonephritis with these findings supports that diagnosis in this patient.

hints.text: A 28-year-old previously healthy man presents to a community clinic with 4 days of intermittent fevers, drenching night sweats and frontal headache. On arrival his temperature is 38.9°C, pulse 108 beats per minute and he reports marked fatigue that is limiting his ability to work.

He returned 10 weeks earlier from a two-week volunteer placement in rural western Africa where he slept in basic housing and recalls numerous mosquito bites. While abroad he had a brief febrile illness that resolved after a few days following empiric oral antibiotics; he did not take malaria chemoprophylaxis.

Full blood count shows haemoglobin 115 g/L, leukocytes 4.6 × 10^9/L and platelets 95 × 10^9/L. Liver tests show total bilirubin 38 μmol/L and ALT 42 U/L. A point-of-care malaria antigen test performed in clinic is negative.
Abdominal ultrasound performed to evaluate persistent symptoms demonstrates splenomegaly with a maximal splenic length of 14.5 cm and otherwise unremarkable hepatic appearance.

Further history confirms the prior short febrile episode during travel and multiple nocturnal mosquito exposures without nets. A reference laboratory thin blood film prepared from today shows low-level parasitaemia with infected erythrocytes that are oval with fimbriated cell borders and fine Schüffner's stippling.

explanation: Travel to western Africa with an initial febrile episode followed by a symptom-free interval and relapse supports a relapsing non-falciparum malaria. The thin film morphology of oval red cells with fimbriated edges and Schüffner's stippling with low parasitaemia is diagnostic of Plasmodium ovale. A negative rapid antigen test can occur with non-falciparum infections, so diagnosis rests on microscopy and the epidemiology.

hints.text: A 38-year-old man presented to a regional clinic on day 6 of illness with high fever, severe frontal headache, diffuse myalgia and progressive confusion. He was febrile at 39.8°C, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg and pulse 98 min−1. On examination he was somnolent but arousable, had marked photophobia, and a faint maculopapular rash over the trunk and proximal limbs. He was unable to ambulate without assistance because of weakness and malaise.

He had been staying for three weeks in an overcrowded temporary shelter after recent flooding in his region. Several other residents developed febrile illnesses during the same interval. He reported difficulty maintaining hygiene in the shelter. He had no recent travel abroad, no known tick exposure, and no chronic immunosuppressive therapy.

Full blood count showed leukocytes 3.6 × 10^9/L and platelets 72 × 10^9/L. Serum sodium 128 mmol/L, ALT 210 U/L and AST 175 U/L. C-reactive protein 155 mg/L. Malaria smear and two sets of blood cultures were negative.

Non-contrast CT brain showed no acute intracranial haemorrhage or mass effect. Chest radiograph demonstrated mild bilateral interstitial markings without focal consolidation. Lumbar puncture was performed and cerebrospinal fluid had 6 cells/μL, protein 0.55 g/L and normal glucose when compared with serum.

On re-interview he acknowledged intense pruritus for several weeks and that staff at the shelter had observed numerous lice and nits on clothing. Clinic colleagues reported a cluster of febrile rash illnesses in the shelter with several patients who became encephalopathic and two deaths before antibiotics were started.

explanation: A febrile febrile illness with headache, confusion and a truncal maculopapular rash in the setting of overcrowded shelter living and visible lice points to an outbreak of louse-borne febrile typhus. Laboratory features of thrombocytopenia, hyponatraemia and transaminitis support a systemic rickettsial process. The exposure history to body lice with clustered severe cases makes Rickettsia prowazekii the most likely pathogen.

hints.text: A 81-year-old woman resident of a long-term care facility developed 48 hours of fever, rigors and left flank pain. On arrival she was febrile to 38.9°C, heart rate 110/min, and had left costovertebral angle tenderness while an indwelling urinary catheter remained in place.

The Foley catheter was inserted two months earlier for chronic urinary retention after a hip fracture. She has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and was treated for a urinary infection with ciprofloxacin three weeks ago.
White cell count 15.3 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 92 mg/L, serum creatinine 160 μmol/L from a baseline of 90 μmol/L. Urinalysis showed marked pyuria and an alkaline pH of 8.7.
Non-contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a large branching calculus filling the left renal pelvis and calyces with hydronephrosis, consistent with a staghorn stone.

Cultures of urine and the removed Foley catheter tip grew a urease-producing, highly motile gram-negative bacillus that produced sheet-like colony expansion on nonselective agar and precipitated magnesium ammonium phosphate from the specimen.

explanation: A patient with a long-term catheter and diabetes who has alkaline urine and a branching renal calculus points to a urease-producing, motile gram-negative bacillus. The organism's urease activity explains the alkaline urine and struvite stone formation in this catheter-associated infection.

hints.text: A 29-year-old primigravida at 32 weeks' gestation presented with three days of dysuria, suprapubic discomfort and fever. She had right flank tenderness and was febrile to 38.5°C on examination.
She had a symptomatic urinary infection in the first trimester treated with nitrofurantoin and reports recurrent urinary symptoms this pregnancy. She denies catheter use and has had no recent travel.
White cell count 12.0 × 10^9/L, serum creatinine 78 μmol/L. Urine dipstick was positive for leukocyte esterase and showed an alkaline pH of 8.0, with numerous leukocytes on microscopy.
Point-of-care renal ultrasound identified a 1.8 cm echogenic, shadowing focus in the dependent bladder consistent with a bladder calculus.

A midstream urine culture grew a urease-positive, motile, non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative bacillus that produced alkaline colonies and precipitated magnesium ammonium phosphate crystals from the specimen.

explanation: Pregnancy with recurrent urinary symptoms, an alkaline urine, and a bladder calculus in the presence of a urease-positive motile gram-negative bacillus indicates an organism that produces ammonia and promotes magnesium ammonium phosphate precipitation. Those features point to the causative pathogen in this case.

hints.text: A 34-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with 6 days of high fever, frontal headache, and progressive malaise after several days of working at home. She developed a faint, nonpruritic erythematous rash on her trunk on day 4 and now reports increasing light sensitivity and mild confusion. On examination temperature was 39.1°C, heart rate 104/min, blood pressure 102/64 mmHg, and there were scattered macules over the chest and abdomen that spared the palms and soles.

She was previously healthy with no chronic medication use and no recent travel outside the metropolitan region. She had taken a 48-hour course of oral amoxicillin prescribed by her GP without improvement, denies known tick bites or recent sexual risk, and has two indoor-outdoor cats but no known sick contacts.

Laboratory tests showed WBC 3.8 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 2.4 × 10^9/L, platelets 92 × 10^9/L, sodium 129 mmol/L, ALT 146 U/L, AST 132 U/L, and CRP 84 mg/L. Blood cultures remained sterile at 48 hours and a rapid malaria screen was negative.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated mild hepatomegaly with a liver span of 16 cm and a spleen mildly enlarged to 13 cm, without biliary dilatation or focal hepatic lesions. Chest radiograph showed no focal consolidation or effusion.

On further questioning she recalled cleaning a neighbour's garage about 10 days before symptom onset, where she noted rodent droppings and sustained multiple small insect bites. Her household cats recently had visible fleas and local public health messaging had warned of sporadic flea-related febrile illness in the port neighbourhood over the past month.

explanation: Prolonged febrile illness with headache, a later-developing maculopapular rash, hyponatraemia, thrombocytopenia, transaminitis and mild hepatosplenomegaly suggests a zoonotic intracellular infection. The history of rodent droppings and recent flea bites in an endemic coastal neighbourhood points to a flea-transmitted bacterial pathogen. Clinical improvement after doxycycline would further support this diagnosis.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presented to the field clinic with 6 days of high fever, severe frontal headache and progressive confusion. He had diffuse myalgia and a new, faint maculopapular rash on his trunk, temperature 39.6°C, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, and Glasgow Coma Scale 13 on arrival.

He arrived from a nearby refugee settlement three weeks earlier after displacement by flood. He described crowded family tents, inability to wash clothes for prolonged periods, and sleeping in donated clothing, but denied recent travel outside the region or contact with sick animals.
Initial labs showed thrombocytopenia 58 × 10^9/L, hyponatraemia 127 mmol/L, AST 248 U/L and CRP 152 mg/L. Two sets of aerobic blood cultures remained sterile at 72 hours.
Chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral interstitial reticulonodular opacities without lobar consolidation. Non-contrast CT brain was unremarkable.

Inspection of his donated clothing revealed numerous live lice and nits attached to inner garments; convalescent serum showed a fourfold rise in antibody titre to the agent known from historical louse-borne epidemic fever outbreaks. He defervesced within 48 hours of starting doxycycline.

explanation: The combination of high fever, severe headache, encephalopathy, thrombocytopenia, elevated transaminases and documented body lice exposure with a rising specific antibody titre and rapid response to doxycycline indicates infection with Rickettsia prowazekii.

hints.text: A 72-year-old retired librarian presented with 3 days of fever, profound lethargy and a diffuse non-itchy blanching rash that began on his trunk. He complained of headache and lightheadedness, had temperature 38.9°C and blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, and family noted new cognitive slowing.

He was born in a rural area of Eastern Europe and emigrated in the 1950s. He recalled a severe community febrile illness during his childhood but reported no recent travel, no lice noted at home, and no known sick contacts.
Laboratory testing showed thrombocytopenia 85 × 10^9/L, hyponatraemia 131 mmol/L and AST 134 U/L. Acute serology revealed high IgG against a louse-associated epidemic agent with low IgM on admission.
Brain MRI with contrast showed no acute infarct or meningitic enhancement. Chest radiograph was unremarkable.

Empiric doxycycline was started because of the clinical picture and past exposure history, and his fever and mental status improved within 24 hours. Convalescent serology demonstrated a fourfold rise in IgG consistent with recrudescence of the same louse-borne agent he had likely acquired decades earlier.

explanation: An elderly patient with remote exposure during youth, acute febrile rash, laboratory pattern with transaminitis and thrombocytopenia, prompt clinical response to doxycycline and a rise in specific IgG is most consistent with recrudescent infection due to Rickettsia prowazekii.

hints.text: A 45-year-old man who sleeps in a city night shelter presented after 5 days of fever, cough and increasing breathlessness. He was hypotensive at 88/54 mmHg, febrile to 39.3°C, and had new diffuse dyspnoea with mild hypoxaemia on room air.

He has chronic alcohol use disorder and intermittent homelessness. He reported recent overcrowding in a temporary shelter after a local winter storm and difficulty changing clothing for many days, but denied known insect bites.
Blood tests showed creatinine 180 μmol/L, AST 198 U/L, platelets 62 × 10^9/L and CRP 220 mg/L. Multiple routine bacterial cultures remained negative and HIV test was negative.
Chest radiograph and subsequent CT chest showed bilateral patchy airspace and interstitial opacities with small bilateral pleural effusions, without focal lobar consolidation.

Public health inspection of the shelter identified heavy infestation of clothing lice among a cluster of residents. Molecular testing on whole-blood PCR from this patient detected nucleic acid matching the historical louse-borne epidemic fever agent, and he improved rapidly after doxycycline.

explanation: Severe febrile illness with pulmonary involvement, multiorgan laboratory abnormalities, documented clothing-lice exposure at a shelter, positive blood PCR for the louse-borne agent and quick doxycycline response indicate Rickettsia prowazekii infection.

hints.text: A 19-year-old volunteer returning from a humanitarian mission in a mountain refugee camp presented with 4 days of fever, severe retro-orbital headache and nausea. On exam she was febrile at 39.4°C, had tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and a faint non-vesicular rash on the trunk, heart rate 110 min−1.

She had spent three weeks distributing clothing and sleeping in crowded tents while laundering clothing infrequently. She had received routine childhood immunisations and took no prophylactic antibiotics during travel.
Complete blood count showed platelets 70 × 10^9/L and leukocyte count 3.8 × 10^9/L. Liver enzymes were abnormal with ALT 156 U/L and AST 172 U/L, and malaria smears were repeatedly negative.

Echocardiography performed for persistent tachycardia demonstrated mildly reduced left ventricular function with ejection fraction 45%, without focal wall motion abnormality. Chest radiograph was without consolidation.

On return public health review, several camp residents were found to have heavy clothing-lice infestation and two had similar febrile illnesses. Paired serum testing from the patient showed a fourfold rise in antibody to the classic louse-associated epidemic fever agent and PCR from her blood was positive.

explanation: A febrile traveller with headache, thrombocytopenia, transaminitis, myocardial involvement, clustered cases in a setting with clothing lice and positive PCR plus rising specific antibody titres supports infection with Rickettsia prowazekii.

hints.text: A 27-year-old woman presented to a makeshift clinic with 8 days of high fever, severe frontal headache and progressive confusion. She fled a conflict zone and has slept in crowded communal tents for the past three weeks. On examination temperature 39.4°C, pulse 100 beats per minute, she is drowsy and intermittently disoriented to time.

Her past health was unremarkable and she takes no regular medications. Over the past two weeks several people in her tent developed febrile illnesses. She reports washing clothes irregularly and noticing small crawling insects in the seams of undergarments.
Full blood count shows leucocytes 5.6 × 10^9/L and platelets 85 × 10^9/L. Sodium 128 mmol/L, ALT 78 IU/L, CRP 76 mg/L. Two sets of aerobic blood cultures remained sterile at 48 hours.
Non-contrast head CT is normal. Chest radiograph shows no focal consolidation. Fundoscopy shows no papilloedema.

Aid workers inspecting her belongings found numerous lice within the seams of clothing. Several tent mates developed similar high fevers with maculopapular rashes that began on the trunk and spread outward. Local clinicians began empiric doxycycline for affected patients with marked clinical improvement within 48 hours.

explanation: Clustered febrile illness in crowded shelter conditions with confirmed clothing lice, thrombocytopenia, hyponatraemia and transaminase elevation points to a louse-transmitted rickettsial infection.

hints.text: A previously independent 82-year-old man from a long term care facility arrived with five days of fever, progressive lethargy and new confusion. He developed a dry cough and complained of increased sleepiness. On exam temperature 38.9°C, pulse 86 beats per minute, he is disoriented and intermittently inattentive.

He has type 2 diabetes managed with metformin and had been given a three day course of oral amoxicillin by his primary care clinician without improvement. Staff report several new admissions and multiple visitors in the prior two weeks. One visiting family brought in clothing infested with lice noted by staff.

WBC 6.0 × 10^9/L, platelets 110 × 10^9/L, AST 130 IU/L, ALT 92 IU/L, sodium 130 mmol/L. CRP 120 mg/L. Lumbar puncture produced clear CSF with 2 × 10^6/L leucocytes, protein 0.48 g/L and glucose 3.6 mmol/L. Blood cultures negative.
Chest radiograph shows mild bibasal atelectasis but no lobar consolidation. CT brain without contrast reveals chronic small vessel ischaemic changes but no acute intracranial process.

Because of persistent fever, neurologic signs and concern for an atypical intracellular infection linked to lice exposure, doxycycline 100 mg twice daily was started. The patient became afebrile and mentation improved substantially within 48 hours after starting therapy while prior beta-lactam therapy had not helped.

explanation: The central nervous system involvement is consistent with severe disease in this host.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presents to the outpatient clinic with six days of fever, pounding frontal headache, diffuse myalgias and a new generalized maculopapular rash. He returned ten days ago from a 10-day stay in a crowded coastal city in Southeast Asia, is febrile to 39.2°C on arrival and reports multiple small insect bites on his lower legs; cardiopulmonary and neurological exams are otherwise normal.

He stayed in a low-cost waterfront guesthouse where he slept with windows open and noticed rats in the alley behind the building. He has no chronic medical conditions, did not take malaria prophylaxis, and denies known tick exposure or freshwater swimming.
Full blood count shows WBC 4.2 × 10^9/L and platelets 115 × 10^9/L. Serum sodium is 131 mmol/L, AST 156 U/L, ALT 98 U/L and CRP 48 mg/L.
Abdominal ultrasound performed for persistent abdominal discomfort shows mild hepatomegaly and a spleen at the upper limit of normal. Chest radiograph is clear.

Local public health notified the clinic of a recent cluster of typhus reported from the same waterfront quarter; the patient recalls several flea bites while sleeping and saw rodents near his lodging.

explanation: The combination of undifferentiated febrile illness with headache, a trunk-predominant rash, thrombocytopenia, mild transaminitis and recent exposure to rats and flea bites in an endemic port setting supports infection with Rickettsia typhi.

hints.text: A 66-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is brought in by family after five days of fever, progressive confusion and poor oral intake. On examination she is febrile to 38.9°C, disoriented to time, with a temperature–pulse discrepancy notable for a pulse of 82 bpm, and scattered petechial spots on the trunk.

She lives in a suburban house and recently rescued several stray cats that had heavy flea infestations. There is a marsh and open green space behind her property where opossums and rodents are often seen.
Laboratory studies show WBC 3.8 × 10^9/L, platelets 78 × 10^9/L, sodium 127 mmol/L, creatinine 130 µmol/L, AST 220 U/L and CRP 100 mg/L.
Non-contrast CT brain is performed because of altered mental status and shows no acute intracranial abnormality. Chest radiograph demonstrates no focal consolidation.

Empiric doxycycline was started because of concern for a flea-borne febrile illness, and fever resolved and mental status improved within 36 hours; later convalescent serology demonstrated a fourfold rise in antibody titre against typhus-group antigens.

explanation: An older patient with fever, confusion, thrombocytopenia, hyponatraemia and exposure to flea-infested animals who rapidly improves with doxycycline is most consistent with infection by Rickettsia typhi. The fourfold rise in typhus-group antibodies confirms the diagnosis in the clinical context.

hints.text: A 72-year-old man presented to acute care with five days of fever, progressive confusion and reduced oral intake. He had daily temperatures to 38.9°C; on exam he was somnolent but rousable, pulse 102/min, BP 98/60 mmHg, and no rash was evident.

He has well controlled type 2 diabetes and lives alone in an older flat. Three days before becoming unwell he had been clearing a damp storage room in his building; he denied recent travel or known tick exposures.

Laboratory tests showed platelets 92 × 10^9/L, sodium 126 mmol/L, creatinine 140 μmol/L, AST 260 U/L, ALT 150 U/L, CRP 145 mg/L. Lumbar puncture showed protein 0.7 g/L with a lymphocytic predominance and no organisms on Gram stain.
Non-contrast CT head showed chronic small vessel change without acute infarct. Chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral patchy perihilar interstitial markings.

His neighbours reported recent rodent activity and a pest-control notice for the block; he recalled a small bite on his forearm while clearing boxes and seeing tiny insects on his clothing. Several neighbours had brief febrile illnesses in the preceding week.

explanation: Encephalopathy with hyponatraemia, thrombocytopenia and marked transaminitis after exposure to rodents and biting insects is most consistent with infection by Rickettsia typhi. The combination of nonspecific CNS findings and the environmental exposure narrows the differential to a flea-borne rickettsial cause.

hints.text: A 29-year-old pregnant woman at 24 weeks' gestation presented with six days of fever, severe headache and nausea. Temperature was 38.8°C, pulse 96/min, BP 116/72 mmHg, fetal movements reported as normal, and there was a tender palpable liver edge on abdominal exam.

She works part-time at a veterinary grooming facility and recently adopted a stray cat. She denied travel outside the region and did not recall tick bites; her pregnancy has otherwise been uncomplicated.
Platelets 118 × 10^9/L, sodium 131 mmol/L, AST 190 U/L, ALT 170 U/L, CRP 98 mg/L. Serologic testing for common viral causes of febrile illness in pregnancy was negative.
Obstetric ultrasound showed a normally grown fetus with normal amniotic fluid and Dopplers. Maternal chest radiograph was normal.

Her workplace manager disclosed a rodent burrow behind the building and that the newly adopted cat had visible fleas. Several co-workers reported brief febrile illnesses over the past month after cleaning the kennel area.

explanation: Fever in pregnancy with thrombocytopenia, hyponatraemia and transaminitis plus occupational exposure to a flea-infested cat and nearby rodent burrows supports infection by Rickettsia typhi. The exposure history is the decisive clue that directs testing and treatment towards a flea-borne rickettsiosis.

hints.text: A 50-year-old man who is homeless presented with ten days of fever, progressive dyspnoea and a new non-productive cough. On arrival he was febrile 39.1°C, tachycardic 115/min, BP 100/60 mmHg, oxygen saturation 90% on room air, and mildly jaundiced on inspection.
He has known alcohol-related liver disease and sleeps in abandoned warehouses. He reports regular contact with stray cats and dogs and heavy alcohol use; he did not recall a tick bite.
Platelets 75 × 10^9/L, WBC 4.0 × 10^9/L, sodium 128 mmol/L, AST 340 U/L, ALT 210 U/L, bilirubin 48 μmol/L, CRP 180 mg/L. Blood cultures were sterile on prolonged incubation.
Chest radiograph showed bilateral patchy airspace opacities with small bilateral pleural effusions. Abdominal ultrasound confirmed cirrhosis with portal hypertension stigmata.

Outreach workers reported a recent rodent infestation at the warehouse where he sleeps and multiple occupants noted small biting insects on bedding; he identified several recent flea bites on his legs. Several other shelter users had short febrile illnesses.

explanation: Severe febrile illness with pulmonary findings, jaundice, thrombocytopenia, hyponatraemia and marked transaminitis in a person with rodent and flea exposure is most consistent with Rickettsia typhi infection. The exposure history combined with the laboratory pattern supports a flea-borne rickettsial diagnosis.

hints.text: A 31-year-old man presents with 4 months of progressive abdominal discomfort, early satiety and intermittent melaena. He reports a 6 kg weight loss and increasing fatigue. On examination he is afebrile with scleral icterus, a firm spleen palpated 7 cm below the left costal margin and visible abdominal wall collateral veins.

He was born and raised in a rural river valley in East Asia and relocated to the city six years ago. He denies heavy alcohol use, no history of viral hepatitis, no intravenous drug use and is not on immunosuppressive medication. Symptoms began insidiously months after a visit to his home region.

Full blood count shows haemoglobin 110 g/L, eosinophils 2.4 × 10^9/L and platelets 115 × 10^9/L. Liver tests show AST 92 U/L, ALT 74 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 210 U/L and total bilirubin 32 μmol/L. Single-sample stool microscopy performed early in the workup was negative for ova.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates hepatomegaly with symmetric periportal thickening and a patent but mildly dilated portal vein. Spleen measures 18 cm with collateral vessels consistent with portal hypertension. Contrast CT confirms periportal fibrotic-appearing bands with otherwise preserved hepatic parenchyma.

On repeat detailed history he describes repeated childhood and adolescent wading, bathing and working in rice paddies and slow-moving rivers in the Yangtze delta where freshwater snails are endemic. Concentration stool microscopy now yields numerous ova consistent with an East Asian blood-fluke and serology against that trematode group is positive.

explanation: Chronic portal hypertension with periportal fibrosis, marked eosinophilia, and positive stool concentration after a history of freshwater exposure in East Asia points to infection by an East Asian blood-fluke. Egg deposition in portal venules explains the periportal fibrosis, splenomegaly and cytopenias in this patient.

hints.text: A 29-year-old male research fellow presents with 6 weeks of intermittent fevers, night sweats, dry cough and progressive fatigue after returning from three months of fieldwork in rural central China. He is afebrile on arrival, pulse 96/min, and examination shows hepatomegaly 3 cm below the right costal margin with no peripheral stigmata of chronic liver disease.

During fieldwork he spent long days wading ankle to knee deep in irrigated rice paddies to collect water samples. He handled and restrained water buffalo for sampling and recalls a brief pruritic rash on his lower legs while in the field.

Full blood count shows eosinophilia 2.9 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 139 g/L and neutrophils 4.6 × 10^9/L. Liver enzymes are mildly elevated with ALT 92 U/L and AST 58 U/L. Three separate stool examinations reported trematode-type ova on microscopy but the local lab did not speciate the eggs.

High resolution chest CT demonstrates multiple small peripheral nodules and patchy ground glass opacities. Abdominal ultrasound notes mild diffuse hepatomegaly and subtle periportal thickening without focal hepatic lesion.

Public health follow-up identified persistent contamination of irrigation ditches and infection of local water buffalo and dogs with the same trematode eggs recovered from his stool. The combination of rice-paddy freshwater exposure in east Asia, zoonotic animal reservoirs, marked eosinophilia, pulmonary nodules and periportal hepatic change points to the regional zoonotic blood fluke.

explanation: Subacute febrile respiratory illness with marked eosinophilia, hepatomegaly, periportal changes and trematode ova on stool after rice-paddy exposure and infected bovines is most consistent with Schistosoma japonicum infection. The animal reservoir and pulmonary plus hepatic involvement support that species.

hints.text: A 9-year-old girl is brought for progressive abdominal swelling and poor growth over nine months. She is pale, height and weight are below the third centile for age, and examination shows firm hepatomegaly and marked splenomegaly extending to the left iliac fossa.

The family lives in an Indonesian riverside village and the children bathe and play daily in the shallow river used for household washing. The household keeps water buffalo and pigs that graze near the river banks.
Haemoglobin 82 g/L with microcytosis. Eosinophils 1.7 × 10^9/L. Repeated Kato-Katz stool examinations demonstrated numerous trematode eggs consistent with a schistosome-type trematode.

Abdominal ultrasound shows massive splenomegaly, a portal vein diameter increased above normal for age and periportal fibrotic bands producing a thickened echogenic appearance along portal tracts. No focal hepatic mass is identified.

Community screening revealed high prevalence of identical trematode eggs in both human and bovine stools along this river. The combination of paediatric growth failure, massive splenomegaly, periportal fibrosis and shared animal reservoirs in an Indonesian riverine setting is compatible with the Asian zoonotic schistosome.

explanation: The child has hepatosplenic disease with periportal fibrosis, anaemia and repeated trematode ova on stool in a riverine village with infected water buffalo. These features are most consistent with chronic Schistosoma japonicum infection.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man presents with 4 months of progressive fatigue, early satiety and increasing abdominal fullness. He reports two episodes of melaena in the last month; on examination he is mildly jaundiced and has a firm spleen palpable 8 cm below the left costal margin.

He emigrated from a rural river-delta province in eastern China three years ago and stopped agricultural work on arrival. He drinks little alcohol, has no known viral hepatitis, and denies prior blood transfusion.

Full blood count shows haemoglobin 105 g/L, platelets 85 × 10^9/L and eosinophils 1.5 × 10^9/L. Liver chemistry demonstrates albumin 32 g/L, ALT 78 U/L and AST 60 U/L. Faecal occult blood is positive.

Abdominal ultrasound reveals marked splenomegaly, dilated portal vein and concentric thickening of periportal tracts with preserved hepatic parenchymal echotexture, consistent with periportal fibrosis and portal hypertension.

On targeted testing stool microscopy demonstrates numerous small ovoid ova, mean diameter about 60 µm, and rectal biopsy shows multiple eggs embedded in submucosa. The patient describes frequent childhood bathing in freshwater irrigation canals in the Yangtze delta.

explanation: Chronic portal hypertension with periportal fibrosis, eosinophilia and numerous small ova on stool and rectal biopsy in a patient from the Yangtze delta points to a mesenteric vein helminth infection acquired by freshwater exposure. The constellation of imaging and egg burden best fits the parasite endemic to East Asian freshwater environments.

hints.text: A 47-year-old man presents with two months of progressive exertional dyspnoea, intermittent dry cough and three episodes of scant haemoptysis. On examination he is tachypnoeic with oxygen saturation 92% on room air and a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound.
He travels frequently for work between his home city and mainland China, most recently a week-long trip four months ago. He is a light smoker and has no known cardiac disease.

Blood tests show peripheral eosinophils 1.7 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 140 g/L and NT-proBNP within the reference range. Sputum microscopy and molecular tests are negative for mycobacteria and common respiratory pathogens.

Contrast CT of the chest shows numerous bilateral small nodules with surrounding ground-glass change and mild enlargement of the main pulmonary artery. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrates mild right ventricular hypertrophy and elevated estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure.

Further questioning reveals recreational swimming in several freshwater rivers and irrigation channels during work trips. Stool microscopy and serum antibody testing are positive, and ova consistent with a small mesenteric trematode are identified.

explanation: Subacute pulmonary nodules, pulmonary hypertension and eosinophilia in a patient with repeated freshwater exposure and positive stool ova/serology indicate embolization of mesenteric parasite eggs to the lungs. The travel and exposure history plus egg identification point to the East Asian freshwater trematode.

hints.text: A 52-year-old woman presents with three weeks of progressive bifrontal headache and two brief focal seizures affecting her right hand. On arrival she is alert but has mild left-sided weakness and a temperature of 37.8 °C.
She emigrated from a rural part of Taiwan 25 years ago and has not travelled back recently. She takes no immunosuppressive medication and has no prior history of malignancy.

Peripheral eosinophils are 2.3 × 10^9/L, CRP 18 mg/L and HIV test is negative. Cerebrospinal fluid shows white cell count 0.12 × 10^9/L with eosinophils comprising 35% of cells, protein mildly elevated and glucose normal.

MRI brain shows multiple small enhancing cortical and subcortical nodules with surrounding oedema at the grey–white junction and mild leptomeningeal enhancement, the largest in the left precentral gyrus correlating with her focal deficits.

On directed interview she recalls playing in rice paddy water and river streams as a child. Rectal biopsy performed to investigate chronic abdominal symptoms from adolescence demonstrates multiple ovoid eggs consistent with a freshwater mesenteric trematode.

explanation: Eosinophilic meningoencephalitis with multiple enhancing brain nodules and a history of childhood freshwater contact, together with rectal biopsy demonstrating ovoid eggs, indicate cerebral involvement by a mesenteric trematode. The combination of site of exposure, chronic intestinal findings and egg identification localises the diagnosis to the East Asian schistosomal species.

hints.text: A 72-year-old woman from a long-term care facility presented with 48 hours of fever, rigors, lower abdominal pain and new confusion. On arrival she was febrile to 39.1°C, heart rate 118/min, blood pressure 98/58 mmHg, with suprapubic tenderness and an indwelling urinary catheter that staff reported had been in place for six weeks.

Her past history includes a spinal cord injury with neurogenic bladder managed by a long-term indwelling catheter, recurrent catheter blockages, and two antibiotic courses in the prior month including a fluoroquinolone for a documented urinary tract infection. She had been transferred back from hospital after a fall three weeks earlier and remained largely dependent for transfers.

Full blood count showed WBC 18.6 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 16.2 × 10^9/L, CRP 220 mg/L and serum creatinine 150 μmol/L from a baseline of 80 μmol/L. Urinalysis demonstrated pyuria and leukocyte esterase positive but nitrite negative. Both urine and two sets of blood cultures signalled growth of Gram-negative bacilli within 18 hours; the organism was non-lactose-fermenting on MacConkey and showed resistance to ampicillin and cefazolin.

Contrast CT pelvis demonstrated marked diffuse bladder wall thickening with perivesical fat stranding and dense intraluminal debris adherent to the catheter tip, consistent with complicated catheter-associated infection without discrete renal or pelvic abscess.

Targeted environmental cultures from the ward found the same organism in the moist soap dispenser and the patient’s catheter drainage bag; colonies on culture plates incubated at room temperature developed a distinctive red pigment after 48 hours and molecular typing matched the clinical and environmental isolates.

explanation: A long-term indwelling urinary catheter, recent fluoroquinolone exposure, non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative bacilli resistant to ampicillin and cefazolin, and identical red-pigmented colonies from patient and ward sources indicate Serratia marcescens. Environmental contamination of moist hospital supplies explains catheter seeding and subsequent bacteraemia in this patient.

hints.text: A 28-year-old woman presents to the ophthalmology clinic with 48 hours of right-eye pain, photophobia and blurred vision after sleeping overnight in soft contact lenses. Visual acuity in the right eye is reduced to 6/18 and there is a central corneal epithelial defect with purulent discharge and intense ciliary injection.

She reports recent travel and admits to topping up and rinsing lenses with tap water and occasionally using homemade saline when commercial solution ran out. She has no systemic immunosuppression and no prior ocular disease.
Slit-lamp examination shows a 2.5 mm central stromal infiltrate with overlying epithelial loss and a 1 mm layered hypopyon. Corneal fluorescein staining highlights the epithelial defect.

The patient brings the lens storage case. She reports it sat in the bathroom cabinet near the shower and she refilled the case with homemade saline on trips. The case and solution were retained for culture.

Corneal scrapings and the contact lens case culture yielded an oxidase-negative gram-negative bacillus. After 48 hours colonies produced a characteristic deep red pigment on nutrient agar and the isolate was resistant to ampicillin and first-generation cephalosporins.

explanation: Contact-lens associated keratitis with matching growth from the lens case and corneal scrape of a red-pigmented, oxidase-negative gram-negative rod resistant to narrow-spectrum beta-lactams indicates Serratia marcescens as the most likely pathogen. The warm, aqueous lens storage exposure explains the inoculum source.

hints.text: A 78-year-old woman in a rehabilitation facility presented with 48 hours of fever, rigors and new suprapubic pain.
