She has an indwelling urinary catheter placed after a recent stroke, temperature 38.9°C, blood pressure 95/60 mmHg, heart rate 110 bpm, and markedly cloudy urine on catheter sampling.

Her medical history includes type 2 diabetes and a two-week stay in hospital prior to transfer. Nursing staff report intermittent catheter irrigation performed on the ward three days before symptom onset and a course of oral cephalexin for a skin infection one month earlier.

Blood tests show WBC 16.4 × 10^9/L and CRP 180 mg/L. Urine microscopy showed >100 leucocytes per high power field and many bacteria. Initial urine culture grew a motile gram-negative bacillus that did not ferment lactose on MacConkey agar.
Renal ultrasound demonstrated bladder wall thickening and no hydronephrosis or obstructing stone. No renal abscess was identified.

Environmental cultures from the rehabilitation unit sink drains and a liquid soap dispenser grew an oxidase-negative, motile gram-negative bacillus that produced conspicuous red colonies on nutrient agar. The antibiogram matched the organism recovered from the patient’s urine, showing resistance to ampicillin and cefazolin and susceptibility to ciprofloxacin and gentamicin.

explanation: Catheter-associated urinary infection in a diabetic, nosocomial source and matching environmental cultures with red-pigmented colonies and resistance to ampicillin/first-generation cephalosporins point to Serratia marcescens.

hints.text: A 74-year-old retired teacher presented with three weeks of progressive fatigue, night sweats and exertional breathlessness. He reported a 6 kg weight loss and intermittent dark stools. On examination temperature was 38.1 C, heart rate 92/min and there was a new 3/6 holosystolic murmur at the apex.

He has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and well controlled hypertension. He denied intravenous drug use and had a dental extraction three months earlier. He recalled a colonoscopy five years ago reported as normal but said he had felt more tired and had looser stools for several months.

Full blood count showed haemoglobin 88 g/L, MCV 72 fL, white cell count 11.8 × 10^9/L. CRP was 84 mg/L. Two sets of blood cultures flagged positive growing catalase negative Gram positive cocci in chains after about 32 hours.
Transthoracic echo was technically limited. Transoesophageal echocardiography demonstrated a 12 mm mobile vegetation on the posterior mitral leaflet with new mild regurgitation and no abscess cavity.

Colonoscopy performed for iron deficiency anaemia during admission showed an ulcerated mass in the ascending colon and biopsies were taken. The microbiology lab reported the blood isolate hydrolysed esculin in bile, was PYR negative and failed to grow in 6.5% NaCl.

explanation: Subacute mitral valve endocarditis with iron deficiency anaemia and an ascending colonic mass together with a bile-esculin positive, PYR-negative, non-NaCl-tolerant streptococcal isolate points to Streptococcus gallolyticus as the cause. The pathogen is known to present with indolent bacteremia and a strong association with colorectal neoplasia, explaining the concurrent findings.

hints.text: A 58-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with five days of fever, rigors and severe right upper quadrant pain radiating to the right shoulder. On arrival temperature was 38.9 C, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg and the abdomen was tender with a palpable liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin.

She has type 2 diabetes and cholelithiasis. She denied recent travel. Three months earlier she had a colonoscopy for change in bowel habit with removal of several large sessile polyps. She had no recent dental work.

White cell count was 15.4 × 10^9/L and CRP 220 mg/L. Liver enzymes showed alkaline phosphatase 310 U/L, bilirubin 28 µmol/L, AST 45 U/L, ALT 52 U/L. Two sets of blood cultures and aspirate from the liver collection yielded Gram positive cocci in chains.
Contrast CT abdomen demonstrated a solitary 6.0 cm rim-enhancing hypoattenuating lesion in segment VII consistent with a pyogenic liver abscess and no biliary obstruction.

Culture of abscess fluid and blood reported catalase negative streptococcal growth that hydrolysed esculin in bile, was PYR negative and did not grow in 6.5% NaCl. A repeat bowel evaluation identified a fungating lesion at the hepatic flexure.

explanation: The combination of pyogenic liver abscess with concordant blood and abscess cultures showing a bile-esculin positive, PYR-negative, non-NaCl-tolerant streptococcus and an occult colonic tumour is most consistent with Streptococcus gallolyticus bacteremia seeded to the liver. The colon lesion provides a plausible portal of entry.

hints.text: A 69-year-old woman with a mechanical aortic valve presented with ten days of malaise and low-grade fevers followed by sudden onset weakness of the right arm. On examination temperature was 37.8 C and there were new splinter haemorrhages on several fingernails and a subtle diastolic component at the left sternal edge.

She had valve replacement five years ago and takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation. She reported intermittent bright red rectal bleeding and change in bowel habit over the preceding six months. She denied intravenous drug use or recent dental procedures.

Haemoglobin was 95 g/L and white cell count 13.0 × 10^9/L. Multiple sets of blood cultures grew Gram positive cocci in short chains. The isolate was susceptible to penicillin on initial susceptibility testing.

Transoesophageal echocardiography showed a 9 mm vegetation attached to the sewing ring of the prosthetic aortic valve with mild periannular thickening. Brain MRI demonstrated multiple small cortical infarcts compatible with embolic events.

Gastroenterology performed colonoscopy which revealed an obstructing mass in the proximal sigmoid colon. Microbiology confirmed the blood isolate hydrolysed esculin in bile, was PYR negative and failed to grow in 6.5% NaCl.

explanation: Prosthetic valve endocarditis with embolic stroke, iron deficiency anaemia and a proximal colonic mass together with a bile-esculin positive, PYR-negative streptococcal isolate indicate Streptococcus gallolyticus. The organism frequently causes endocarditis that is linked to occult colorectal lesions.

hints.text: A 67-year-old male gardener presented with six weeks of progressive mid-thoracic back pain that was worse at night and unrelieved by simple analgesia. He also reported low grade fevers and an 8 kg unintentional weight loss. Temperature was 37.8 C and focal tenderness was present over the T10 vertebral level.

His medical history included hypertension and long-term tobacco use. He denied recent trauma or invasive spinal procedures. He had noticed intermittent dark stools and increasing fatigue over several months.
CRP was 148 mg/L, ESR 72 mm/h and white cell count 12.2 × 10^9/L. Blood cultures grew Gram positive cocci in chains after 36 hours. Haemoglobin was 92 g/L consistent with iron deficiency.
MRI spine showed T10–T11 endplate destruction with disc irregularity and a small paravertebral fluid collection consistent with vertebral osteomyelitis and a paravertebral abscess.

CT-guided aspiration of the paravertebral collection grew a catalase negative streptococcal isolate that hydrolysed esculin in bile, was PYR negative and did not grow in 6.5% NaCl. Colonoscopy performed for anaemia revealed an exophytic tumour in the ascending colon.

explanation: Vertebral osteomyelitis with concordant blood and abscess cultures showing a bile-esculin positive, PYR-negative, non-NaCl-tolerant streptococcus along with an ascending colonic tumour fits with Streptococcus gallolyticus bacteremia. The colonic lesion likely served as the source for haematogenous seeding of the spine.

hints.text: A 68-year-old man presents to the medical assessment unit with a 3-week history of intermittent fevers, progressive fatigue and exertional dyspnoea. He reports a 5 kg weight loss over two months, on examination temperature is 38.3°C and there is a new holosystolic murmur at the apex with mild pallor.

He has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and a remote repaired inguinal hernia. He denies recent dental procedures or intravenous drug use and reports long-standing constipation but no overt rectal bleeding.

Blood tests show haemoglobin 95 g/L, white cell count 12.4 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 86 mg/L. Two separate blood culture sets drawn on admission flagged positive after 24 hours for catalase-negative, Gram-positive cocci in chains.
Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrates a 12 mm mobile vegetation attached to the posterior leaflet of the mitral valve with moderate mitral regurgitation.

Given his anaemia and positive faecal occult testing, colonoscopy was performed and revealed an ulcerated 3 cm sigmoid mass; biopsy confirmed adenocarcinoma. The blood isolate hydrolysed esculin in bile and was pyrrolidonyl arylamidase negative.

explanation: The combination of streptococcal bacteraemia with mitral valve vegetation and new anaemia prompted colonoscopy that found colorectal adenocarcinoma. Bile-esculin positive, PYR-negative, catalase-negative cocci in chains match the typical microbiology of Streptococcus gallolyticus, which is strongly linked to colonic neoplasia and endocarditis.

hints.text: A 74-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after sudden onset left-sided weakness and slurred speech over the past 12 hours. He is febrile at 38.0°C and has left facial droop with dense weakness of the left arm and leg on examination.
He has a history of hypertension and a known systolic murmur but no prior diagnosis of cancer. He describes several months of altered bowel habit with occasional loose stools and a 6 kg weight loss.

Haemoglobin is 110 g/L and white cell count 13.2 × 10^9/L. Three sets of blood cultures returned positive for catalase-negative Gram-positive cocci in chains and preliminary susceptibility testing showed penicillin susceptibility.
Brain MRI demonstrates multiple acute cortical infarcts in the right hemisphere consistent with embolic strokes. Transoesophageal echocardiography identifies a 10 mm vegetation on the aortic valve.

Because of his new anaemia and weight loss, colonoscopy was performed and found a 4 cm mass in the ascending colon with adjacent adenomatous polyps; histology confirmed adenocarcinoma. The bloodstream isolate hydrolysed bile esculin.

explanation: Embolic strokes from valvular vegetations with concurrent Gram-positive coccal bacteraemia and occult colonic malignancy suggest Streptococcus gallolyticus endocarditis. The bile-esculin hydrolysis and penicillin susceptibility align with this organism and its known association with colorectal tumours.

hints.text: A 66-year-old woman presents to the clinic with five days of fever and malaise following an elective endoscopic polypectomy two weeks earlier. She is febrile at 38.5°C and mildly tachycardic, and examination reveals a new grade 2/6 systolic murmur and conjunctival pallor.
Her past history includes hypertension and a prior colonoscopy with removal of adenomatous polyps five years ago. She recalls no recent dental work and takes no immunosuppressive medications.

Full blood count shows haemoglobin 88 g/L and white cell count 10.8 × 10^9/L. Initial blood cultures grew catalase-negative Gram-positive cocci in chains and the isolate hydrolysed esculin in bile while testing PYR negative.
Transoesophageal echocardiography demonstrates a small vegetation on the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve with mild regurgitation and no abscess formation.

She was treated with intravenous ampicillin and monitored; fevers settled within 48 hours and repeat blood cultures were sterile. An interval diagnostic colonoscopy identified an obstructing sigmoid tumour which on resection proved to be adenocarcinoma.

explanation: Post-polypectomy bacteraemia with mitral valve vegetation, bile-esculin positive, PYR-negative streptococcal isolates, and an occult colonic adenocarcinoma support infection by Streptococcus gallolyticus.

hints.text: A 7-year-old previously well boy presented with three weeks of persistent dry cough, progressive fatigue, and intermittent central abdominal discomfort. Parents report reduced play and poor appetite; on examination temperature 37.8°C, pulse 110/min, scattered expiratory wheeze and a palpable liver edge 3 cm below the right costal margin.

He attends a local preschool and spends most afternoons playing in the family backyard sandbox. The family keeps a mixed-breed dog acquired from a rescue shelter 8 months ago, and the parents acknowledge occasional pica behaviour at home. No recent travel outside the region and no chronic medications.

Full blood count shows leukocytes 14.8 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 3.6 × 10^9/L. Total IgE 620 kU/L. C-reactive protein and alanine aminotransferase are within reference range. Three separate stool microscopy examinations are negative for ova and cysts.

Chest radiograph demonstrates fleeting patchy peripheral air-space opacities that vary between films. Abdominal ultrasound shows multiple small well defined hypoechoic lesions in the liver, the largest 1.3 cm, without biliary dilatation.

Local public-health inspection of the backyard and sandbox found fresh canine faeces and soil samples from the play area contained embryonated ascarid eggs consistent with canine origin; the household dog had no recent documented deworming.

explanation: Subacute pulmonary symptoms with hepatomegaly, marked peripheral eosinophilia, negative stool O&P, and imaging showing hepatic lesions and transient pulmonary infiltrates point to a tissue-migrating nematode. Detection of embryonated canine ascarid eggs in the child's play environment makes infection with Toxocara canis the most likely diagnosis in this clinical context.

hints.text: A 72-year-old retired schoolteacher presents with six weeks of low-grade fever, fatigue and progressive exertional breathlessness. She reports a 5 kg weight loss and intermittent loose stools; examination shows temperature 37.8°C, pulse 96/min and a new grade 3/6 early diastolic murmur at the left sternal border with mild pallor.

Her past history includes hypertension and a colon polypectomy performed more than a decade ago, no recent dental procedures and no intravenous drug use. She also notes several months of intermittent rectal bleeding and was investigated for iron-deficiency anaemia in the community but declined colonoscopy at that time.

Blood tests show haemoglobin 92 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 74 fL, white cell count 8.6 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 112 mg/L. Three sets of blood cultures flagged positive and Gram stain revealed Gram-positive cocci in chains.
Transoesophageal echocardiography demonstrated an 8 mm mobile vegetation attached to the aortic valve with moderate aortic regurgitation and no abscess cavity.

Colonoscopy, performed because of anaemia and bleeding, found an ulcerated sigmoid mass; biopsy confirmed adenocarcinoma. Final microbiology identified a bile-esculin positive, PYR-negative, non-enterococcal group D streptococcal isolate that was susceptible to penicillin.

explanation: This older patient has bacteremia and aortic-valve endocarditis with a group D streptococcal phenotype plus an occult colorectal adenocarcinoma. The combination of a bile-esculin positive, PYR-negative non-enterococcal group D streptococcus and concurrent colon cancer points to Streptococcus gallolyticus as the most likely pathogen.

hints.text: A previously well 4-year-old boy is brought with a 3-week history of persistent dry cough, intermittent low-grade fevers, and increasing abdominal discomfort that limits play. On examination he is afebrile with a respiratory rate 26/min, palpable liver edge 3 cm below the right costal margin, and scattered expiratory wheeze on auscultation.

Parents report gradual loss of appetite and 1.5 kg weight loss over the same interval. He attends day care, there has been no recent travel, he received a short course of oral antibiotics for presumed bronchitis two weeks before presentation, and growth milestones are otherwise normal.

Full blood count shows leukocytosis 18.4 × 10^9/L with marked eosinophilia 4.8 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein 20 mg/L, liver transaminases mildly elevated ALT 65 U/L, stool microscopy for ova and parasites reported as negative.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates multiple small, ill-defined hypoechoic lesions in both hepatic lobes without biliary dilatation. Chest radiograph shows patchy, peripheral air-space opacities in both lungs.

When asked about play, parents acknowledge the child spends daily time in a shaded neighbourhood sandpit where stray puppies are often seen defecating and the child sometimes eats sand. The combination of pulmonary symptoms, hepatomegaly with focal hepatic lesions and very high eosinophil count raised suspicion for a parasitic larval migration from canine sources.

explanation: This presentation of prolonged cough, hepatomegaly with focal hepatic lesions, and marked peripheral eosinophilia in a young child who ingests contaminated soil is most consistent with visceral larva migrans due to ingestion of embryonated ova from canine faeces. Negative stool microscopy does not exclude the diagnosis because larvae do not mature in the human gut. The exposure history of sandpit play with stray puppies completes the diagnostic picture.

hints.text: A 38-year-old woman presents with three weeks of progressive blurring and metamorphopsia in the right eye, associated with intermittent photopsia and new floaters. On ophthalmic exam right visual acuity is 6/24, there is vitreous haze and an elevated white lesion adjacent to the macula; the left eye is normal.

She has no recent travel, no contact lens use, and no history of systemic febrile illness. Her past medical history is notable only for seasonal allergic rhinitis and she is otherwise immunocompetent.

Full blood count shows mild leukocytosis 10.2 × 10^9/L with borderline eosinophilia 0.7 × 10^9/L. Serum IgE is elevated at 420 kU/L and toxoplasma serology is negative; routine infectious and inflammatory blood tests do not indicate systemic infection.

Optical coherence tomography demonstrates a subretinal hyperreflective mass beneath the macula with overlying vitreous opacities. B-scan ultrasound confirms a focal posterior pole intraocular mass without calcification and with adjacent vitreous inflammation.

On detailed questioning she reports regularly consuming thinly sliced raw liver at family gatherings and had eaten raw liver one week before symptom onset. The pattern of a unilateral intraocular inflammatory mass with elevated IgE and eosinophilia after ingesting animal liver pointed toward larval migration from a canine reservoir transmitted via a paratenic host.

explanation: A solitary inflammatory intraocular mass with vitreitis, mild peripheral eosinophilia and markedly raised IgE after recent ingestion of raw liver is most consistent with ocular larva migrans following consumption of infected paratenic tissue. The exposure to raw liver provides the route for larvae to reach the eye, making larval migration from canine sources the leading diagnosis.

hints.text: A 55-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes is admitted after two focal seizures involving his left arm and progressive headaches over 10 days. Neurological exam shows subtle left-sided weakness and slowed attention, temperature is normal and there is no neck stiffness.

He works part-time in a community garden and reports increasing fatigue for several weeks. He denies recent overseas travel, blood-borne exposures, or known immunosuppressive medications beyond his oral hypoglycaemic agents.

Peripheral blood shows leukocytosis 12.0 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.9 × 10^9/L. Lumbar puncture yields 250 × 10^6/L nucleated cells with 15% eosinophils, protein 0.8 g/L, and normal glucose; bacterial cultures are negative.

MRI brain demonstrates multiple small, enhancing subcortical nodules and a larger 1.5 cm enhancing lesion in the right frontal white matter with surrounding vasogenic oedema. No calcifications are seen and there is mild mass effect without midline shift.

Further questioning reveals he regularly feeds and handles stray dogs that visit the garden and sometimes cleans up faecal deposits with his bare hands. The combination of eosinophilic meningoencephalitis, multifocal enhancing brain lesions and direct contact with canine faecal material suggested larval neuroinvasion from a canine source.

explanation: Eosinophilic CSF pleocytosis together with multifocal enhancing white matter lesions and a history of handling stray dogs indicates central nervous system involvement by migrating helminth larvae from a canine reservoir. The exposure to dog faeces provides the likely route of infection, making canine-derived larval migration the most probable cause.

hints.text: A 6-year-old boy is brought to clinic with three weeks of intermittent low-grade fever, worsening cough, and diffuse abdominal pain. On examination temperature 38.1°C, respiratory rate 26/min with scattered wheeze, and the liver edge is palpable 4 cm below the costal margin.
Parents report the child often mouths objects and sometimes eats dirt from the garden. No recent travel, no chronic illnesses, and immunisations up to date.

Full blood count shows WBC 15.8 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 4.2 × 10^9/L. Alanine transaminase and bilirubin are within reference range. Stool microscopy for ova and parasites is negative on two samples.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates multiple ill defined hypoechoic lesions in the hepatic parenchyma, largest 1.4 cm, with mild hepatomegaly. Chest radiograph shows patchy ill defined peripheral nodular opacities.

The family recently adopted a stray puppy that had diarrhoea and had not received deworming treatment. The child often plays in the yard where dogs defecate and admitted to eating soil on several occasions.

explanation: Peripheral eosinophilia with hepatomegaly and multiple hepatic lesions plus transient pulmonary findings fit a migrating helminth. The history of pica and exposure to an untreated puppy supports visceral larva migrans from Toxocara canis. Negative stool ova is expected because larvae migrate rather than pass eggs in human stool.

hints.text: A 34-year-old male sous-chef presents with a 9-month history of pruritus and progressive scaling of both feet and thickening of several toenails. He reports worse symptoms after long shifts in closed shoes and now has pain when wearing footwear; on examination there is macerated erythema and white scaling in the third web space bilaterally and distal subungual hyperkeratosis with onycholysis of the left great toenail.

Symptoms began slowly and were treated intermittently with an over-the-counter corticosteroid cream after an initial diagnosis of 'eczema' by a primary clinician, with temporary modest clearing followed by recurrence. He has no diabetes, takes no systemic immunosuppressants, and has not travelled recently; he spends long shifts standing in occlusive shoes and has regular close contact with co-workers who complain of athlete's foot.
KOH preparation of skin scrapings and nail clippings shows abundant septate branching hyphae. A fungal culture was set up and growth was slow to appear over 10 days.
Nail dermoscopy shows longitudinal striae, proximal edge spikes, and subungual debris consistent with distal lateral subungual onychomycosis rather than psoriasis or traumatic dystrophy.

Colony morphology on Sabouraud medium becomes flat and velvety, initially white to cream, with a deep wine-red pigment visible on the agar reverse; microscopy of the colony shows numerous pyriform microconidia borne along the hyphae and occasional chlamydoconidia.

explanation: Chronic interdigital tinea and distal lateral onychomycosis in an adult with prolonged occlusive footwear and prior topical steroid use suggests a dermatophyte infection. KOH hyphae and dermoscopy support fungal onychomycosis. The culture morphology with red reverse and pyriform microconidia identifies Trichophyton rubrum as the most likely pathogen.

hints.text: A previously healthy 29-year-old male presents to the emergency department with four days of high fever to 39.5°C, severe headache and myalgia, and two days of a spreading skin eruption. On examination he is alert but ill appearing, heart rate 110/min, and dozens of firm papulovesicular lesions are clustered on the face and forearms; a few similar lesions are noted on the palms.

He works in a regional shipping warehouse and reports no international travel. He was born after routine childhood vaccination for the disease in question ceased and recalls no prior immunisation. Two colleagues on his shift developed fever and rash in the previous week.

Blood count shows leukopenia with total white cell count 2.1 × 10^9/L and lymphopenia. Bacterial cultures from lesions are sterile. Targeted PCR assays for varicella zoster virus and herpes simplex virus are negative. Electron microscopy was requested for lesion swabs.

High-resolution clinical photographs of the lesions show deep-seated, firm, rounded pustules with central indentation, all appearing to be at the same stage of evolution. Lesions are most numerous on the face and distal arms, and several well-formed pustules are present on the palms.

Public health investigators traced multiple secondary cases among unvaccinated warehouse staff after a sealed parcel from overseas was opened. Reference laboratory electron microscopy of crust material revealed large brick-shaped virions and nucleic acid testing matched sequences from the historical human-specific eradicated viral agent responsible for severe febrile syndromes with centrifugal, synchronous pustular eruptions.

explanation: A febrile prodrome followed by synchronous deep, firm pustules concentrated on the face and distal extremities including palms strongly indicates the historical smallpox syndrome. Negative varicella and HSV testing, brick-shaped virions on electron microscopy, and epidemiology with unvaccinated close contacts support infection by variola virus.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presented to an urban emergency clinic with 5 days of fever, severe myalgias and progressive sore throat followed by a papular rash. He was febrile to 38.9 °C, had tender cervical lymphadenopathy and reported difficulty swallowing because of painful oral lesions; there were scattered firm papules on his face and forearms at examination.

He was born in 1996 and reported never having received routine vaccination against historical pustular diseases. He works as a street-food vendor, lives with his partner and a recently ill neighbour who developed a febrile rash about 10 days before his own symptoms.

Full blood count showed leukocytes 2.3 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 0.9 × 10^9/L and platelets 85 × 10^9/L. Swabs from a pustule were negative by PCR for common herpetic and varicella pathogens and viral culture produced large cytoplasmic inclusions on epithelial monolayers.

Lateral neck inspection and oropharyngeal photography demonstrated multiple shallow mucosal ulcers and swollen tonsils with adjacent firm vesiculopustular lesions. Chest radiograph was clear without focal consolidation.

Within 48 hours his cutaneous lesions became deep-seated and firm, all lesions appearing in the same developmental stage with a centrifugal concentration on face and distal extremities including palms; his household contact had an almost identical illness after returning from a region with reports of an outbreak of an eradicated human poxvirus.

explanation: Prodrome of fever and sore throat followed by synchronous deep-seated pustules on the face and palms in an unvaccinated young adult with household transmission is most consistent with infection by an eradicated, human-specific poxvirus historically prevented by routine vaccination. The negative PCRs for herpes and varicella and viral culture showing cytoplasmic inclusions support this diagnosis.

hints.text: A previously healthy 6-year-old boy was brought from school with 6 days of fever and cough followed by a generalized vesiculopustular rash. On arrival he was irritable, febrile to 39.1 °C, had tender cervical nodes and dozens of firm pustules on the trunk and face, some causing difficulty with oral intake.

He lives in a rural village and his family reports no history of the routine childhood immunisation that once protected against severe pustular illnesses. An exchange student who recently boarded with another family at the school returned to their home country after developing a febrile rash about two weeks earlier.

Blood tests showed leukocytes 2.6 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 40 mg/L. A lesion swab was sent for broad viral testing; assays for varicella and herpes were negative and culture produced progressive cytopathic changes with large intracytoplasmic inclusions.
Oropharyngeal exam and photography demonstrated multiple mucosal erosions and pharyngeal pustules. A screening chest radiograph showed mild peribronchial cuffing without lobar consolidation.

Over the next 48 hours classmates and household contacts developed similar illness; clinicians noted all lesions on affected people were at the same developmental stage, deep-seated and prominent on distal extremities including palms, pointing to spread of an eradicated human poxvirus introduced by the visiting student.

explanation: A febrile prodrome followed by synchronous deep pustules with mucosal involvement in unvaccinated children and rapid household spread after an introduced case points to infection with the eradicated human poxvirus historically characterised by palm and sole involvement and uniform lesion stages.

hints.text: A 62-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 12 hours of severe left calf pain, swelling, and fever. He was febrile at 38.9 °C, blood pressure 88/52 mmHg, heart rate 112/min, and the calf had tense edema with several small haemorrhagic bullae and severe tenderness to palpation.

He has known alcohol-related cirrhosis with portal hypertension and a history of ascites. Two days earlier he had a small graze on the same leg while walking on a tidal flat but did not seek care at the time.

Blood tests showed WBC 22.4 × 10^9/L, lactate 4.8 mmol/L, creatinine 210 μmol/L and bilirubin 48 μmol/L. Gram stain of pus from a bulla showed gram-negative bacilli and blood cultures were drawn and reported as positive within 18 hours.

Contrast CT of the lower leg demonstrated marked subcutaneous oedema and fluid tracking along the fascial planes without clear gas formation, consistent with a rapidly progressive soft tissue infection extending into deep fascia.

Wound and blood cultures grew a motile, oxidase-positive curved gram-negative bacillus that failed to ferment sucrose and produced green colonies on thiosulfate-citrate-bile salts-sucrose agar. On further questioning he acknowledged eating raw oysters the previous day and exposure of the leg to seawater at low tide.

explanation: Rapidly progressive haemorrhagic bullous cellulitis in a patient with cirrhosis and recent seawater and raw oyster exposure points to a halophilic gram-negative bacillus. Early positive blood cultures and the described culture features identify the organism causing fulminant wound infection and sepsis in patients with liver disease.

hints.text: A 34-year-old woman presented with 24 hours of rapidly progressing swelling, pain, and violaceous blistering of her right hand. She was febrile at 38.5 °C and had markedly reduced range of motion of the wrist from pain.
She has poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, HbA1c 10.4%, and works at a fish market handling fresh seafood daily. She denied systemic symptoms until the sudden onset of hand pain the prior day.
WBC was 19.1 × 10^9/L, CRP 280 mg/L and glucose 22 mmol/L. Blood glucose was corrected and empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics were started, with samples sent for culture.
MRI of the right hand and forearm demonstrated extensive fascial enhancement with fluid layers tracking along the deep flexor compartments, findings concerning for necrotising soft tissue infection.

Deep tissue and blood cultures grew a motile, oxidase-positive curved gram-negative bacillus that required saline-enriched media and did not ferment sucrose. She reported a minor puncture from a fish bone while preparing raw shellfish and frequent handling of seawater-washed fish at work.

explanation: A rapidly progressive necrotising infection of the hand in a diabetic seafood handler with cultures showing a halophilic oxidase-positive curved gram-negative organism after a puncture from raw seafood supports the diagnosis. The culture requirements and clinical context identify the pathogen responsible for aggressive soft tissue disease.

hints.text: A 68-year-old man on chronic peritoneal dialysis presented with 48 hours of diffuse abdominal pain and cloudy dialysate. He was febrile at 38.2 °C and complained of nausea, and the peritoneal catheter exit site looked clean without purulence.

He has end-stage renal disease from diabetic nephropathy and performs nightly ambulatory peritoneal dialysis at home. Last week he vacationed on the coast but denied any recent gastrointestinal illness at presentation.
Peritoneal fluid cell count showed 2.1 × 10^9/L white cells with 92% neutrophils. Peripheral WBC was 14.6 × 10^9/L and CRP 180 mg/L.
Abdominal CT showed diffuse peritoneal enhancement without an obvious perforation or intra-abdominal abscess. The peritoneal catheter was in expected position.

Peritoneal fluid cultures yielded a motile, oxidase-positive curved gram-negative bacillus that grew on salt-supplemented media and failed to ferment sucrose. He admitted to rinsing his dialysis supplies with seawater while on holiday before returning home.

explanation: Peritonitis in a peritoneal dialysis patient following seawater exposure with cultures showing a halophilic oxidase-positive curved gram-negative organism indicates infection with the salt-loving marine bacterium. The exposure history and specific culture findings support the diagnosis in this clinical scenario.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man presented to the emergency department with an 18-hour history of rapidly spreading pain, swelling, and redness of his right lower leg. He was febrile at 38.9°C, blood pressure 90/55 mmHg, pulse 112/min, and unable to bear weight because of intense pain; examination showed tense erythema with several bullae and areas of ecchymosis tracking proximally from the ankle.

His medical history includes well compensated cirrhosis from alcohol use and type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. He reported a small abrasion on the right shin two days earlier but no recent hospital admissions or antibiotic courses.

Laboratory tests showed white blood cell count 20.2 × 10^9/L, lactate 4.3 mmol/L, creatinine 190 µmol/L, and C-reactive protein 320 mg/L. Blood cultures and a swab from a bulla were obtained, and preliminary Gram stain from the wound showed gram-negative bacilli.

Contrast CT of the right lower leg demonstrated marked subcutaneous oedema with fascial thickening and fluid tracking along fascial planes but minimal subcutaneous gas. Surgical teams proceeded to urgent debridement because of clinical and imaging concern for a rapidly progressive necrotizing soft tissue infection.

On directed questioning after surgery the patient said he had been wading in a warm coastal estuary and shucked and ate several raw oysters two nights before symptom onset; he recalled cutting his shin on a rock while wading.

explanation: Rapid hemorrhagic bullous cellulitis with fulminant sepsis in a patient with chronic liver disease after raw oyster exposure and a skin break points to infection by Vibrio vulnificus. Gram-negative bacilli from the wound and the need for urgent debridement support a disseminated, invasive gram-negative marine pathogen rather than routine skin flora.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 18 hours of severe right calf pain, progressive swelling and lightheadedness. He was febrile at 39.2°C, hypotensive at 90/50 mmHg and tachycardic. Examination showed tense erythema of the posterior calf with several rapidly enlarging dark bullae and marked tenderness out of proportion to touch.

He has known alcohol-related cirrhosis with ascites and a prior episode of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis treated one year ago. He is not on chronic antibiotics and reports only a minor graze to the leg a week earlier while gardening.

Blood tests showed white cell count 1.8 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 1.0 × 10^9/L, platelets 55 × 10^9/L, lactate 6.2 mmol/L, bilirubin 60 μmol/L and INR 2.1. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained on arrival.

Contrast CT of the lower limb demonstrated extensive subcutaneous and fascial plane edema without discrete gas collections. MRI confirmed diffuse fascial enhancement consistent with a rapidly progressive soft tissue infection.

On focused questioning he disclosed eating several raw oysters at a seaside market 48 hours before symptom onset and briefly wading while cleaning them. The combination of chronic liver disease, rapid fulminant cellulitis with bullae and recent raw oyster and seawater exposure points to a marine gram-negative pathogen.

explanation: Fulminant soft tissue infection with hemorrhagic bullae and early septic shock in a patient with cirrhosis after raw oyster and seawater exposure is most consistent with Vibrio vulnificus. The rapid progression, high lactate, coagulopathy and hepatic dysfunction fit this diagnosis.

hints.text: A 72-year-old woman arrived with 10 hours of sudden fever, rigors and profound weakness. She was hypotensive at 85/48 mmHg and had new tender erythematous patches on the dorsum of both hands and forearms that developed within hours of her systemic illness.

Her past history includes chronic viral hepatitis with compensated cirrhosis and type 2 diabetes managed with metformin. She had attended a family dinner the evening before and reports only mild nausea overnight.

Laboratory results showed white cell count 0.9 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 0.6 × 10^9/L, platelets 70 × 10^9/L, creatinine 210 μmol/L and lactate 5.8 mmol/L. Blood cultures became positive within 12 hours of incubation.

Punch biopsy of a forearm lesion revealed full thickness dermal necrosis with dense acute inflammation and thrombosed small vessels. CT abdomen showed small-volume ascites and features of chronic liver disease.

She subsequently remembered eating half a dozen raw oysters at that family meal less than 24 hours before becoming ill. The rapid onset of septicemia with cutaneous necrosis after raw shellfish ingestion in a cirrhotic patient is highly suggestive of a marine gram-negative bacterium.

explanation: Rapid primary septicemia with bullous and necrotic skin lesions following raw oyster ingestion in a patient with cirrhosis strongly indicates Vibrio vulnificus. The quick positive blood cultures and multi-organ dysfunction support this diagnosis.

hints.text: A 45-year-old man presented with 36 hours of severe pain and swelling of his right hand. He described a puncture injury a day before and on exam had tense dorsum swelling, rapidly enlarging bullae over the hand and early loss of finger flexion, with temperature 38.9°C and heart rate 115 bpm.
He has insulin dependent diabetes with poor glycaemic control and chronic kidney disease stage 3b. He works irregularly as a commercial fisherman and handles nets and rope daily.

White cell count was 18.0 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 280 mg/L and serum glucose 23 mmol/L. Wound swab cultured mixed skin organisms; blood cultures were pending and initial empiric antibiotics were started.

Despite prompt intravenous antibiotics aimed at typical skin pathogens and urgent surgical debridement, he developed persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors and expansion of necrotic skin into the forearm over the next 12 hours.

Further questioning revealed that the puncture occurred while he was removing barnacles from a rope in brackish harbour water and that his hands were exposed to shallow seawater that morning. The rapidly progressive wound sepsis following marine wound exposure is most compatible with a virulent halophilic gram-negative organism.

explanation: The occupational marine exposure and rapid necrosis with systemic compromise point to this pathogen.

hints.text: A 33-year-old man presented with 8 hours of high fever, myalgia and rapidly spreading tender erythematous lesions on both lower limbs. He was tachycardic but normotensive. The skin findings were violaceous plaques with evolving bullae and patchy skin sloughing.

He has a recent diagnosis of hereditary haemochromatosis managed with intermittent phlebotomy and otherwise is in good health. He returned 36 hours earlier from a coastal weekend trip and reports no chronic liver dysfunction.
White cell count was 3.2 × 10^9/L, platelets 95 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 220 mg/L and creatinine 140 μmol/L. Liver enzymes were near normal and blood cultures were obtained at presentation.

Serial clinical photographs and ultrasound documentation demonstrated rapid enlargement of bullae and progressive subcutaneous fluid without deep muscle involvement. Echocardiography showed no intracardiac source.

On further history he reported eating raw shellfish at a seaside barbecue the evening before symptom onset. The temporal link of raw shellfish ingestion with iron overload and fulminant septic skin disease makes a marine gram-negative pathogen most likely.

explanation: Fulminant skin and bloodstream infection soon after raw shellfish consumption in a patient with iron overload fits Vibrio vulnificus. The rapid cutaneous progression and systemic features in the setting of increased iron stores support this diagnosis.

hints.text: A 68-year-old retired schoolteacher presented in late July with four days of fever, progressive confusion and new difficulty walking. On arrival temperature was 38.9°C and heart rate 102/min, he was disoriented to time and place and had a flaccid right lower limb weakness with diminished knee and ankle reflexes.

Medical history included type 2 diabetes and atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation. He had required a packed red cell transfusion 12 days before symptom onset after a colonoscopic polypectomy, denied recent travel outside the region and reported no respiratory or gastrointestinal prodrome.

CSF: WBC 220 × 10^6/L with 82% lymphocytes, protein 1.2 g/L, glucose 3.4 mmol/L with concurrent serum glucose 6.9 mmol/L. Gram stain and bacterial culture from CSF were negative and HSV PCR returned negative. Peripheral blood leukocytes 11.8 × 10^9/L, sodium 128 mmol/L.

MRI brain with FLAIR sequences showed asymmetric high signal in the bilateral thalami and caudate heads, greater on the left. MRI of the cervical spinal cord showed focal T2 hyperintensity in the anterior horn regions corresponding to the clinically weak right leg.

Local public health reported clusters of human neuroinvasive illness and multiple dead corvids in the neighbourhood over the prior two weeks. The regional reference laboratory detected virus-specific IgM in the patient’s CSF and serum and reported confirmatory neutralization and RNA detection for the locally circulating mosquito-borne neurotropic virus.

explanation: An older adult with acute febrile encephalopathy, new flaccid limb weakness, CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis, thalamic and anterior horn MRI abnormalities, and CSF IgM plus neutralization confirming the locally circulating mosquito-borne neurotropic virus supports neuroinvasive infection with that virus.

hints.text: A 29-year-old man presents to the emergency department with five days of high fever, severe myalgias, and a progressive skin eruption. He reports the rash began as flat red spots on his face and forearms and evolved into dozens of firm, deep-seated vesiculopustular lesions by day five. On arrival he is febrile to 39.2 °C, tachycardic to 110 min−1, and mildly hypotensive. He feels too weak to work and notes that several lesions are painful rather than itchy.

He is previously healthy and takes no regular medications. He was born after routine immunisation against the disease was discontinued in his country and reports never having received that vaccine. He works as an archivist at a medical museum and last week handled a box of preserved human material and crusted scabs from early 20th century clinical collections while wearing only nitrile gloves; he recalls a small cut on his finger during handling.

Initial blood tests show white cell count 14.8 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 126 mg/L, alanine transaminase 48 U/L, and creatinine 82 µmol/L. Bacterial blood cultures remain negative at 48 hours. A swab of a fresh lesion yielded a high viral DNA load on broad-spectrum DNA PCR targeted to large DNA viruses.

Chest radiograph demonstrates patchy bilateral nodular opacities and small focal consolidations more prominent in the mid zones, consistent with viral pneumonitis and early secondary bacterial change. No cavitation is present. The pattern correlates with his worsening cough and increasing oxygen requirement over 24 hours.

Electron microscopy of lesion material shows large, brick-shaped enveloped virions. The same virions were recovered from the century-old scab material he handled and genomic sequencing demonstrated an identical viral genome in the archival specimen and the patient sample. Public health authorities report no recent community circulation of this pathogen and confirm he had not received the historical vaccine.

explanation: The combination of febrile systemic illness, deep-seated vesiculopustular lesions on the face and extremities, recent contact with preserved human scab material from the smallpox era, and electron microscopy showing brick-shaped enveloped virions with identical sequences from the archival material all point to infection with variola virus. Lack of prior vaccination and evidence of pulmonary involvement explain the patient's more severe course. Identification rests on the epidemiologic link and genomic confirmation between the archival specimen and the clinical isolate.

hints.text: A 52-year-old office worker presents with a 9-month history of slowly progressive thickening of the right great toenail. She reports minimal pain but increasing difficulty fitting shoes, and examination shows a yellowish, crumbly distal nail plate with subungual debris and mild onycholysis.

She has no diabetes and takes no systemic immunosuppressants. She recalls regular salon pedicures over the past two years and says topical antifungal lacquer used intermittently for several months produced no improvement.

Clinical photograph of the toe shows distal lateral subungual hyperkeratosis with onycholysis affecting the lateral half of the nail. A lateral foot radiograph shows no bony erosion or periosteal reaction.
She reports walking barefoot in a communal gym shower and describes that a household contact had similar chronic toenail changes that were never formally treated.

Nail clippings prepared with potassium hydroxide show septate branching hyphae. Culture on Sabouraud medium grows a white, cottony colony within 7–10 days with a deep red to wine-red pigment on the reverse. Microscopy of the colony reveals numerous small tear-drop shaped microconidia borne along the hyphae.

explanation: Chronic distal lateral subungual nail dystrophy with positive KOH and culture morphology including red reverse pigment and pyriform microconidia supports a dermatophyte infection caused by Trichophyton rubrum. The history of communal wet environments and failed topical lacquer are typical risk factors and explain the chronic course.

hints.text: A 42-year-old office worker presents with 9 months of intensely pruritic, expanding scaly plaques across the trunk and proximal arms that interfere with sleep. Lesions began as a single itchy papule after a coastal holiday and have gradually coalesced into multiple arcuate and annular plaques with active raised borders and central clearing. On examination there are numerous erythematous plaques with peripheral scale, several with fine surface excoriations; no fever.

She was treated intermittently with potent topical corticosteroid creams prescribed for presumed eczema, with temporary reduction of inflammation but subsequent spread of lesions. Two household contacts have had chronic toe nail changes. She is otherwise well, not diabetic, and takes no systemic immunosuppressive drugs.

Skin scrapings examined with KOH show short septate hyphae and abundant arthroconidia. Routine bacterial culture of skin scrapings is negative. A previously performed punch biopsy reported epidermal hyperplasia with perifollicular neutrophils.

Clinical photodocumentation shows multiple annular and arcuate plaques with sharply demarcated raised borders and central clearing. Dermoscopy of an active border demonstrates peripheral scaling and focal dotted vessels, with scale accentuated at the leading edge.

Fungal culture from skin scrapings on Sabouraud agar produced after 10 days a slow-growing white granular colony whose reverse developed a deep wine-red pigment. Microscopic mount from the colony showed numerous thin septate hyphae and many small, smooth-walled conidia borne singly along the hyphae; isolates with identical morphology were recovered from a symptomatic household member.

explanation: A chronic, steroid-modified expanding scaly eruption with KOH-positive septate hyphae indicates dermatophyte infection worsened by topical corticosteroid use. The culture pattern of a slow white colony with a red wine reverse and numerous small conidia, plus household transmission, points to the anthropophilic dermatophyte that commonly causes persistent human skin infections.

hints.text: A 29-year-old female nail technician presents with 14 months of progressive dystrophy of multiple fingernails and recurrent pruritic scaly plaques on both palms that interfere with her work. She notes nails separating from the bed, yellowish subungual debris and intermittent mild pain when filing acrylics. Examination shows distal onycholysis and subungual hyperkeratosis of several fingernails and well-demarcated erythematous scaly plaques on the palmar surfaces.

Her work involves prolonged wet work and exposure to nail filing dust and salon equipment. She wears gloves intermittently and had occasional minor trauma while filing. Two colleagues and one household member report toe nail changes. She has no diabetes and takes no systemic immunosuppressants.

KOH of nail clippings and palmar scrapings reveals abundant branching septate hyphae. Periodic acid–Schiff stain of nail clippings is positive for fungal elements. Full blood count and metabolic panel are within normal limits.

High-resolution clinical photographs show longitudinal nail plate dystrophy with distal subungual debris and palmar plaques with adherent scale; dermoscopy of affected nails reveals subungual hyperkeratosis and irregular distal edge separation.

Fungal cultures from both nail and palmar scrapings yielded after 9–11 days a slow-growing white granular colony with a distinctive wine-red pigment on the reverse. Microscopic examination showed numerous thin septate hyphae and abundant small smooth microconidia borne singly on the hyphae; identical isolates were recovered from two asymptomatic salon coworkers' toenails.

explanation: Occupational wet exposure and repeated minor trauma predispose to chronic dermatophyte infection of nails and palms. KOH and PAS confirm fungal invasion of keratin, and the culture pattern of a slow white colony with wine-red reverse pigment and single-borne microconidia, plus clustering among coworkers, points to the anthropophilic dermatophyte responsible for persistent nail and hand disease.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man presents to clinic with a 3-week history of profuse watery diarrhoea and crampy lower abdominal pain. He reports up to 8 liquid stools per day with nocturnal urgency, a 5 kg weight loss, and lightheadedness on standing. On examination he is afebrile, pulse 102 min−1, blood pressure 100/64 mmHg, with dry mucous membranes and hyperactive bowel sounds.

He has HIV diagnosed 6 years ago and admits poor adherence to antiretroviral therapy over the past 4 months. His most recent clinic record from 2 months ago lists a CD4 count of 80 × 10^6/L and a plasma viral load above the detection limit. He stopped prophylactic antibacterial medication several months ago because of supply interruptions.

Basic blood tests show Na 132 mmol/L and K 3.0 mmol/L consistent with ongoing losses, haemoglobin 110 g/L, white cell count 3.8 × 10^9/L. Routine bacterial stool culture and routine ova wet mount are negative. A modified acid-fast stain of a concentrated stool specimen demonstrates numerous oval acid-fast oocysts measuring approximately 20–30 µm.
Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen shows mild diffuse small-bowel wall thickening with mesenteric lymphadenopathy. The colon appears of normal caliber without wall thickening or pericolonic stranding.

He was started on high-dose oral trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole. Stool frequency fell to 1–2 formed stools per day within 48 hours and he regained 2 kg over two weeks. Follow-up stool concentration and modified acid-fast stain after treatment were negative.

explanation: An HIV-positive patient with low CD4 count and chronic profuse watery diarrhoea, oval acid-fast oocysts in stool, small-bowel predominant imaging, and rapid clinical response to trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole is most consistent with infection by Cystoisospora belli.

hints.text: A 43-year-old woman presents to clinic with three weeks of intermittent low-grade fevers, fatigue, and progressive exertional dyspnoea. She reports daily fevers up to 38.3°C and has become unable to walk the two flights of stairs she previously managed without breathlessness. On examination temperature 38.1°C, pulse 98/min, a new holosystolic murmur best heard at the apex radiating to the axilla, and a palpable spleen tip 2 cm below the costal margin.

She has known mitral valve prolapse with mild regurgitation diagnosed five years earlier and takes no regular medications. She had an infected lower molar extracted without antibiotic prophylaxis two weeks before symptom onset and reports poor dentition; she denies intravenous drug use or recent hospital admissions.

Two sets of blood cultures drawn prior to antibiotics grew organisms after 48 hours. Microscopy showed Gram-positive cocci arranged in chains, catalase-negative. Colonies on blood agar were small with alpha-haemolysis and were resistant to optochin. Laboratory markers: WBC 11.8 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 119 g/L, CRP 46 mg/L.

Transoesophageal echocardiography demonstrated a 7 mm mobile vegetation attached to the posterior leaflet of the mitral valve with new moderate mitral regurgitation and preserved left ventricular systolic function.

An oral swab from the extraction site and a dental plaque sample yielded organisms with colony morphology and biochemical profiles identical to the blood isolate. Molecular 16S sequencing matched the bloodstream isolate to common oral commensal bacteria. The isolate had a penicillin MIC of 0.06 mg/L.

explanation: The subacute febrile illness with a new mitral valve vegetation after dental extraction indicates native-valve infective endocarditis. Blood cultures grew catalase-negative, alpha-haemolytic, optochin-resistant Gram-positive cocci in chains that matched oral commensal isolates and showed low penicillin MIC. These findings point to an oral alpha-haemolytic coccus from the dental flora as the causative pathogen, explaining the clinical course and penicillin susceptibility.

hints.text: A 36-year-old man presents with 3 months of progressive exertional dyspnoea and fatigue, plus intermittent crampy lower abdominal pain and a 4 kg unintentional weight loss. He works seasonally on irrigated rice farms and on examination is pale with conjunctival pallor, heart rate 102 min-1, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, and several tender erythematous 3–5 mm papules between the toes of both feet.

He emigrated from a rural region of West Africa five years ago and returns annually to help at his family farm. He reports routinely walking barefoot in wet paddies and using pit latrines during visits. He has no chronic medical problems, is not taking regular medications, and has not received antiparasitic treatment in over a decade.

Complete blood count shows haemoglobin 78 g/L, MCV 68 fL, WBC 9.8 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.5 × 10^9/L (15%). Iron studies show serum ferritin 8 µg/L and transferrin saturation 6%. Two separate faecal occult blood tests are positive.

He describes a recent brief dry cough. Chest radiograph shows a small patchy ill-defined infiltrate in the right mid-lung field that was not present on a radiograph taken 6 months earlier. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates no focal masses and only mild small-bowel mucosal thickening.

After a single 400 mg dose of albendazole he noted passage of several thin white worms in stool. Direct inspection measured the expelled worms at about 10–12 mm; they were slender with a buccal capsule bearing crescentic cutting plates and lacked prominent paired teeth. Over two weeks his haemoglobin and symptoms began to improve after oral iron and a repeat anthelmintic course.

explanation: Chronic iron-deficiency anaemia with eosinophilia, faecal blood, barefoot exposure in irrigated soil, and transient pulmonary infiltrate point to a soil-transmitted helminth. Recovery of adult worms with buccal cutting plates after albendazole identifies Necator americanus rather than species that have prominent teeth.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man on postoperative day 8 after emergency small-bowel resection developed new fevers and confusion on the surgical ward. He was febrile to 38.9°C, heart rate 110/min, and noted to have a right internal jugular central venous catheter in place for nutrition and intravenous access.

He has type 2 diabetes with recent hyperglycaemia and has been receiving total parenteral nutrition through the central line for 6 days. He completed 7 days of broad-spectrum antibiotics for intra-abdominal sepsis and had no documented neutropenia prior to this febrile episode.

Two aerobic blood culture sets flagged positive after 48 hours. Gram stain of the positive bottles showed oval budding yeast; peripheral blood white cell count 13.8 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 156 mg/L.

Dilated fundus examination by ophthalmology demonstrated a 2 mm creamy, well-circumscribed intraretinal lesion in the right macula with surrounding vitreous haze. B-scan ultrasound confirmed particulate vitreous debris consistent with endogenous endophthalmitis.

The central line was removed and intravenous antifungal therapy was started, with defervescence and improved mentation within 48 hours. Microbiology later reported that the blood isolate produced germ tubes in serum and characteristic green colonies on chromogenic medium and was fluconazole-susceptible, findings concordant with the clinical response.

explanation: Blood cultures grew budding yeast and the isolate produced germ tubes and green colonies on chromogenic agar, which alongside prompt improvement after catheter removal and fluconazole indicates the organism most consistent with Candida albicans.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 4 days of high fever, severe myalgia, frontal headache and progressive nausea. He reported profound weakness and one episode of dark-coloured vomiting; temperature 39.1°C, pulse 108/min, and visible scleral icterus on examination.

He had returned five days earlier from a two-week humanitarian assignment in a West African country where he slept in village housing. He did not receive any pretravel immunization because of last-minute deployment and recalled numerous daytime and evening mosquito bites.

Initial bloods showed leukocytes 2.1 × 10^9/L and platelets 74 × 10^9/L. Liver enzymes were markedly elevated with aspartate aminotransferase 3 200 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 920 U/L, total bilirubin 86 μmol/L and INR 2.0.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a smooth, enlarged liver without biliary ductal dilatation or focal lesions. There was no sonographic evidence of portal vein thrombosis or obstructive biliary disease.

Local public health notified the hospital of an ongoing urban outbreak in the same region of a mosquito-borne febrile illness that presents with fever, jaundice and bleeding and is preventable by a single pretravel immunization. Several other travellers returning from that area have required admission with hepatic failure and haemorrhagic complications.

explanation: Recent travel to an endemic West African area with substantial mosquito exposure and no pretravel immunization, combined with marked hepatocellular injury with jaundice, coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia, points to a mosquito-transmitted viral hemorrhagic febrile hepatitis. The cluster of similar returning travellers and the single-dose vaccine recommendation make the diagnosis most likely in this context.

hints.text: A 78-year-old woman from a long-term care facility was brought to hospital with 48 hours of fever and progressive confusion. On arrival she was febrile at 39.2°C, hypotensive with blood pressure 85/52 mmHg and tachycardic at 112/min, and had an indwelling peripherally inserted central catheter in the right arm and a purulent sacral pressure ulcer.

Her medical history includes advanced dementia, insulin-treated diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease stage 4. Over the prior three weeks she had two separate courses of broad-spectrum antibiotics for suspected pneumonia and a urinary tract infection, and the central catheter had been placed seven days before this admission for intravenous fluids.

Blood cultures drawn on admission became positive at about 36 hours. Gram stain showed budding yeast forms, the routine automated biochemical system returned a low-confidence identification, and initial susceptibility testing reported a high minimal inhibitory concentration to fluconazole.

Contrast CT of the chest showed multiple small bilateral peripheral nodules, some with cavitation, interpreted as likely septic emboli. Transthoracic echocardiography showed no clear vegetations and the catheter tip imaging suggested a fibrin sleeve at the insertion site.

She was started on an echinocandin and the central catheter was removed, but repeat blood cultures remained positive after five days of therapy. A national reference laboratory using MALDI-TOF and sequencing returned identification of an emerging multidrug-resistant yeast notable for skin colonisation and transmission within healthcare facilities, prompting contact precautions and environmental screening at the sending care home.

explanation: Persistent candidemia in a patient from long-term care with recent broad-spectrum. The combination of fluconazole resistance on initial testing, failure to clear bloodstream infection after catheter removal and echinocandin.

hints.text: A 45-year-old male smallholder presented with 72 hours of fever, rigors and a rapidly painful swelling in his right axilla. He was febrile to 39.4°C, heart rate 112/min, and examination showed a 5 cm firm tender axillary lymph node with overlying erythema that limited shoulder abduction.

He has poorly controlled type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and smokes. He lives on a smallholding with chickens and a barn cat and reports frequent direct contact with animals and with soil while clearing brush, but had no recent hospital admissions or intravenous drug use.

Blood tests revealed WBC 16.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance and C-reactive protein 210 mg/L. Needle aspiration of the node was performed and the specimen grew small, non-lactose-fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar after 48 hours; isolates were oxidase-negative and initial blood cultures remained negative at 24 hours.

Ultrasound of the axilla showed a 5.5 cm complex hypoechoic collection with central necrosis and surrounding soft-tissue oedema, without clear fistula to skin. Chest radiograph was clear with no focal consolidation.

On targeted questioning the patient said that over the past month neighbours reported many sudden deaths of wild rodents around the village and his barn cat had recently returned with many insect bites after hunting. He also recalled handling a dead rat two weeks before symptom onset.

explanation: Fever with an acutely tender, necrotic regional lymphadenitis after animal contact, growth of a small non-lactose-fermenting, oxidase-negative Gram-negative bacillus, and recent die-off of wild rodents with insect bites point to infection by Yersinia pestis. The combination of bubonic-style lymphadenitis and epidemiologic link to rodent exposure supports this diagnosis and explains the necrotic suppurative node seen on imaging.

hints.text: A 29-year-old woman presents to the antenatal clinic with 4 days of a diffuse pruritic rash, low-grade fever and aching joints. She is 10 weeks pregnant by dates, afebrile in clinic, heart rate 88/min, and has non-purulent conjunctival injection and a blanching maculopapular rash over the trunk and limbs.

Her past medical history is unremarkable and she is taking no regular medication. Her partner returned from a three-week business trip abroad 3 weeks ago; they conceived shortly thereafter and both recall multiple mosquito bites while he was away.

Blood tests show WBC 3.4 × 10^9/L with lymphocytes 0.9 × 10^9/L, platelets 190 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 4 mg/L. Serum IgM by ELISA was indeterminate with cross-reactive signal, while nucleic-acid testing detected viral RNA in urine but not in concurrent serum.

Targeted fetal ultrasound at 18 weeks gestation demonstrates focal intracranial calcifications and cranial measurements about 2 SD below the expected mean for gestational age. No other structural anomalies were identified on standard survey.

Local public health later confirmed increased reports of a day-biting mosquito transmitted febrile rash illness in the region where her partner travelled, and he had an uncomplicated brief febrile illness with rash on return.

explanation: The combination of recent febrile maculopapular rash with conjunctivitis, mild lymphopenia, positive urine viral RNA with difficult serum serology, maternal early pregnancy exposure and fetal intracranial calcifications strongly point to congenital infection from Zika virus. The temporal link to a partner who travelled to an area with an outbreak of a mosquito-borne febrile rash illness supports this diagnosis.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 48 hours of worsening pain, swelling, and erythema of the left lower leg. He reports a shallow laceration over the shin three days earlier that he cleaned at home. On arrival temperature was 38.9°C, heart rate 110 min−1, and the left leg had tense oedema, scattered haemorrhagic bullae, and pain out of proportion to the area of erythema.

His past medical history includes alcohol-related cirrhosis with ascites and well established type 2 diabetes mellitus. He takes oral diuretics and metformin. He has not taken recent antibiotics and reports progressive deterioration in mobility of the leg since the injury.

Blood tests showed white cell count 18.6 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 16.2 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 220 mg/L. Two sets of blood cultures and a wound swab grew a pure culture of Gram-negative bacilli on aerobic media. The isolate was oxidase positive and produced beta-haemolytic colonies on blood agar.

Contrast CT of the lower leg demonstrated subcutaneous fat stranding with gas tracking along the superficial and deep fascial planes and a 3 cm fluid collection adjacent to the tibial periosteum. The appearance raised concern for a rapidly progressive necrotizing soft tissue infection requiring urgent surgical review.

On further questioning he recalled slipping and briefly submerging the injured leg in a shallow freshwater canal while clearing vegetation two days before presentation. Microbiology confirmed the same oxidase positive, motile Gram-negative rod from wound and blood cultures, resistant to ampicillin and first generation cephalosporins but susceptible to ciprofloxacin and ceftriaxone.

explanation: The combination of a freshwater wound exposure, rapidly progressive necrotizing soft tissue infection in a patient with cirrhosis and diabetes, and growth of an oxidase positive, beta-haemolytic Gram-negative rod with ampicillin resistance points to Aeromonas hydrophila.

hints.text: A 29-year-old man presents with 6 months of progressive left lower-limb swelling and 2 months of scrotal fullness. Symptoms are worse at the end of the day and limit his walking. Exam shows non-pitting oedema of the left leg with thickened skin and a 3 cm left-sided hydrocele, T 37.8°C.

He was raised in a rural, coastal community in a tropical country and moved to the city five years ago. Since adolescence he has had intermittent febrile episodes with painful groin swelling treated sporadically with antibiotics. No prior surgeries or known immunodeficiency.
Full blood count: WBC 10.8 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 2.6 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein 4 mg/L. HIV rapid test negative. Routine urine and renal function within reference range.
Scrotal ultrasound shows a 4 cm simple hydrocele and multiple thin, linear echogenic tubular structures within the scrotal sac that show continuous, twitching motion on real-time imaging.

A late-night peripheral blood film taken at 23:00 shows sheathed, motile larval forms. The nuclear column does not extend to the tip of the tail, and parasites are more numerous on night films; he reports frequent night-time mosquito exposure in childhood.

explanation: Chronic unilateral limb lymphoedema and hydrocele in a patient from a tropical, mosquito-exposed area with eosinophilia, a characteristic moving tubular appearance on scrotal ultrasound, and nocturnally periodic sheathed microfilariae lacking terminal nuclei indicate lymphatic filariasis due to Wuchereria bancrofti. The combination of imaging and nocturnal blood morphology is diagnostic in this clinical context.

hints.text: A 68-year-old man on day 12 of mechanical ventilation in the surgical intensive care unit developed a new fever to 38.9°C and a sudden increase in purulent tracheal secretions. Over 24 hours his oxygenation worsened, FiO2 requirement rose from 0.4 to 0.7, and nursing staff noted thick, greenish secretions at the endotracheal tube with coarse crackles over the right hemithorax.

He was admitted three weeks earlier after a motor vehicle collision and required exploratory laparotomy with temporary abdominal closure. His course has included a central venous catheter, urinary catheter, and two 7-day courses of broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, most recently piperacillin-tazobactam, stopped four days ago for presumed intra-abdominal source control.

White blood cell count is 16.8 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 210 mg/L. An endotracheal aspirate Gram stain showed small Gram-negative coccobacillary organisms; culture on MacConkey agar produced pale non-lactose-fermenting colonies and the isolate was oxidase negative.

Chest radiograph compared with the study 48 hours earlier shows a new dense consolidation in the right lower zone with air bronchograms and a small right pleural effusion. There is no focal abdominal collection on recent CT to suggest recurrent intra-abdominal sepsis.

Surveillance cultures from the ventilator circuit suction canister and the sink drain at the bedside grew the same oxidase-negative non-fermenting Gram-negative coccobacillus with an identical antibiogram. The organism was resistant to third-generation cephalosporins, aminoglycosides, and carbapenems and remained susceptible only to polymyxin-class agents and tigecycline; several nearby ICU beds showed colonization with the same strain.

explanation: The organism is a non-fermenting, oxidase-negative Gram-negative coccobacillus that survives in the ICU environment and demonstrates an extensively drug-resistant antibiogram, strongly pointing to Acinetobacter baumannii as the cause.

hints.text: A 26-year-old previously well woman presents to the emergency department with 7 days of progressively severe bifrontal headache, nausea and photophobia. She is febrile to 38.3°C, has marked neck stiffness on examination and reports intermittent paresthesia of the lips and fingertips, but no focal limb weakness.

Symptoms began a week after she returned from a three-week visit to relatives in rural Southeast Asia. She has no chronic medical conditions, takes no regular medications, and recalls frequent street-food meals and several swims in a slow-moving inland river while overseas.

Blood count shows leukocytes 9.1 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 0.8 × 10^9/L. Lumbar puncture opening pressure 26 cm H2O. CSF analysis: leukocytes 280 × 10^6/L with 40% eosinophils, protein 1.0 g/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L. Gram stain and routine bacterial culture are negative. PCR testing for common viral meningitides is negative.

Contrast MRI of the brain shows diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement greatest in the basal cisterns and mild enhancement of multiple cranial nerve roots including the trigeminal and facial nerves. There is no focal parenchymal abscess or space occupying lesion.

On further questioning the patient recalls eating a dish at a market that included small raw freshwater snails and raw freshwater shrimp about two weeks before symptom onset. A fresh wet mount of CSF performed in the laboratory demonstrated motile microscopic larvae consistent with a migrating nematode larva.

explanation: Eosinophilic meningitis with recent travel to an endemic region, ingestion of raw freshwater snails, and visualization of motile larvae in CSF point to Angiostrongylus cantonensis as the most likely cause in this patient. The MRI pattern of basal leptomeningeal and cranial nerve root enhancement supports meningeal inflammation rather than bacterial meningitis.

hints.text: A previously well 7-year-old boy presents with a 3-week history of progressive patchy hair loss and increasing tenderness at the back of his scalp. Parents report worsening pruritus and nightly rubbing; on examination there are two 3–5 cm scaly alopecic plaques with numerous broken hairs and a separate 4 cm erythematous, boggy, tender plaque over the occiput; temperature is 37.9 °C and posterior cervical nodes are palpable.

No chronic illnesses or recent systemic antibiotic use. The family first treated the areas with an over-the-counter topical corticosteroid for presumed eczema with transient reduction in erythema but progressive hair loss continued. He attends primary school and plays regularly with neighbourhood children.

Full blood count shows WBC 8.3 × 10^9/L and CRP 18 mg/L. KOH preparation of scalp scale and plucked hairs reveals branching septate fungal hyphae; routine bacterial cultures from the boggy plaque are sterile. A fungal culture has been submitted and is pending.

Scalp ultrasound of the occipital lesion demonstrates a 3.5 cm superficial heterogeneous fluid collection within the subcutaneous tissue with increased peripheral vascularity and no calvarial involvement. The pattern is consistent with an intense inflammatory scalp process rather than a simple pustule.

Parents report that a stray kitten was brought into the house 5 weeks before symptoms began and several neighbours subsequently developed scaly patches on their forearms. After 7–10 days of incubation the fungal culture produced a rapidly expanding white, woolly colony; microscopy of the colony preparation showed abundant thick-walled, spindle-shaped multicellular macroconidia and hair mounts demonstrated fungal elements on the external hair surface.

explanation: The child has an inflammatory scalp eruption with kerion formation and positive KOH for septate hyphae, pointing to a dermatophyte infection. Recent contact with a kitten plus ectothrix hair invasion and abundant spindle-shaped macroconidia on culture indicate a zoophilic dermatophyte transmitted from cats. These features together best fit a cat-associated dermatophyte causing tinea capitis with kerion.

hints.text: A 52-year-old man presented to an urban emergency department with a six-week history of low-grade fevers, drenching night sweats, progressive fatigue and exertional dyspnoea. He reports a 6 kg weight loss and now becomes breathless after climbing a single flight of stairs. On examination he is afebrile, pulse 98 min−1, blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, has a new grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur at the cardiac apex radiating to the axilla and a palpable spleen 3 cm below the costal margin.

The patient has a long history of alcohol use disorder and intermittent rough sleeping over the past two years, with four months in a crowded municipal shelter before presentation. He denies injecting drug use. Dental hygiene is poor and he reports multiple prior episodes of skin excoriation from itching, but he has not sought regular primary care.

Initial blood tests showed haemoglobin 92 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 86 fL, white cell count 7.4 × 10^9/L and platelets 210 × 10^9/L. C reactive protein was 72 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 58 mm/h. Three separate sets of blood cultures incubated for seven days remained sterile; serology and PCR testing for common culture-negative endocarditis agents were negative.

Transoesophageal echocardiography demonstrated a 12 mm highly mobile vegetation on the posterior mitral leaflet with moderate to severe mitral regurgitation. Contrast CT of the chest showed multiple small peripheral wedge-shaped infarcts consistent with embolic phenomena.

Shelter staff brought in discarded clothing and bedding that the patient had used, and public health inspection identified heavy infestation with body lice on the clothing. The patient described intense pruritus and repeated informal attempts to delouse while staying in the shelter.

explanation: A subacute, culture-negative mitral endocarditis with large mobile vegetations in a person with prolonged homelessness and documented body lice infestation points to a louse-borne bacterial cause. The combination of negative routine blood cultures and this exposure profile makes a louse-transmitted fastidious gram-negative bacillus the most likely pathogen in this clinical context.

hints.text: A 48-year-old man presents to the emergency department with three weeks of intermittent fevers, night sweats, progressive malaise and a painful lump in his left thigh. He reports a new productive cough and has lost 5 kg over three weeks. On arrival he is febrile 38.6°C, pulse 102/min, oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Examination shows a 5 cm tender, indurated subcutaneous mass with central softness on the left anterolateral thigh and decreased breath sounds at the right lung base.

Medical history notable for type 2 diabetes mellitus for 12 years, with recent HbA1c 9.2%. He drinks alcohol but denies tobacco or injected drugs. He says the thigh lump followed a small skin abrasion on the same leg several weeks earlier; he had no prior surgeries or known chronic lung disease.
