Blood tests show white cell count 16.8 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 210 mg/L. Two sets of blood cultures flagged positive at 48 hours for a Gram-negative bacillus that was oxidase positive on preliminary testing. Preliminary susceptibility from the laboratory reported resistance to gentamicin.

Contrast CT of chest and abdomen shows consolidation with small cavitary nodules in the right lower lobe and multiple discrete low-attenuation lesions in the liver and spleen, the largest measuring 2.5 cm in the spleen, consistent with multiple abscesses. Ultrasound-guided aspiration of the thigh mass returned purulent fluid.

On further questioning the patient reports return six weeks ago from a three-month work contract in rural northeastern Thailand where he spent long days planting rice in flooded paddies and sustained the shallow leg abrasion while working in wet soil.

explanation: The combination of poorly controlled diabetes, recent exposure to flooded rice paddies in an endemic region, multifocal visceral abscesses with concurrent pulmonary disease, and an oxidase-positive, gentamicin-resistant Gram-negative bacillus from blood cultures is most consistent with infection by Burkholderia pseudomallei.

hints.text: A 38-year-old man presented to a district hospital after four days of high fever, severe myalgia and frontal headache with progressive lethargy. During the prior 24 hours he developed gum bleeding and several new bruises, was febrile to 39.0°C, pulse 116/min, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, and had scattered petechiae on his trunk.

He is previously well and works as a shepherd in a nearby upland community, living in a household that cares for several goats and sheep. Family members report that a number of small ruminants had brief fevers earlier in the month, and he had no recent travel outside the district or known chronic medical conditions.

Initial blood tests showed WBC 1.9 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 1.2 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 124 g/L, and platelets 24 × 10^9/L. Transaminases were markedly elevated with AST 1,820 U/L and ALT 520 U/L, creatinine 180 µmol/L, INR 2.0, and aPTT prolonged. Malaria smear and routine blood cultures were negative.
Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated moderate hepatosplenomegaly and small-volume ascites. Chest radiograph showed small bilateral pleural effusions without focal airspace consolidation.

On targeted reinterview he said that two weeks before illness he assisted neighbours with slaughtering goats for a celebration, handled fresh carcass blood with bare forearms, and removed several embedded hard ticks from his lower legs by hand. Two people who helped with the slaughter became febrile within a week and a nurse who treated him at the local clinic has since developed febrile illness and mild bleeding.

explanation: Severe febrile illness with marked thrombocytopenia, extreme transaminitis with AST predominance, coagulopathy, and rapid onset mucocutaneous bleeding in a livestock handler who had direct contact with animal blood and tick exposure points to a tickborne viral haemorrhagic fever. The cluster of illness among slaughter participants and a subsequent febrile illness in a healthcare worker raise concern for a highly transmissible viral haemorrhagic pathogen best identified by specific nucleic acid testing, consistent with Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever virus in this epidemiologic setting.

hints.text: A 42-year-old woman presented with six weeks of dull right upper quadrant pain and intermittent low-grade fevers. She reported increasing fatigue and a 5 kg weight loss over that period. On examination temperature was 38.0 °C, there was mild tender hepatomegaly 3 cm below the costal margin, and no peripheral stigmata of chronic liver disease.

She had no prior liver disease, did not drink alcohol to excess, and was not taking hepatotoxic medications. Three months earlier she spent eight weeks volunteering in rural highland villages, helping at a school and assisting on small livestock holdings. She denied blood transfusion, intravenous drug use, or immunosuppressive therapy.

Full blood count showed leukocytosis 15.2 × 10^9/L with marked eosinophilia 4.2 × 10^9/L. Liver tests had a cholestatic pattern with alkaline phosphatase 560 U/L, gamma glutamyl transferase 290 U/L, alanine transaminase 68 U/L, and total bilirubin 28 µmol/L. Viral hepatitis serology was negative and blood cultures showed no growth.

Abdominal ultrasound showed heterogeneous, subcapsular hypoechoic tracts in the right hepatic lobe and moderate intrahepatic biliary dilatation. MR cholangiopancreatography demonstrated serpiginous, nonenhancing filling defects within the right hepatic ducts that appeared mobile on real-time sequences.

On repeat history she recalled eating raw watercress and other aquatic plants at village meals along mountain streams during the volunteer stay. Stool microscopy subsequently revealed operculated ovoid eggs measuring approximately 140 × 80 µm, consistent with a large hepatic trematode.

explanation: Prolonged RUQ pain with cholestatic LFTs and marked peripheral eosinophilia raises a parasitic biliary process. Imaging showing mobile serpiginous intraductal defects and subcapsular hepatic tracts localises the problem to migrating and biliary-dwelling trematodes. The history of raw aquatic plant ingestion plus large operculated eggs on stool microscopy confirms infection with the liver fluke Fasciola hepatica.

hints.text: A 34-year-old woman presents to the outpatient clinic with three weeks of progressive right calf pain and difficulty walking. She reports the lesion began as an itchy papule that formed a blister which ruptured ten days ago; exam shows a 5 cm tender indurated area over the distal calf with a shallow serous-draining ulcer and a palpable firm linear cord beneath the skin, temperature 37.9 °C and able to bear only partial weight on the affected leg.

She returned two months ago from a six-month stay in a riverside village where she helped collect water and worked barefoot in shallow standing pools during the dry season. She has no chronic medical conditions, is not taking immunosuppressive drugs, had no recent injections or puncture wounds to the leg, and reports no obvious insect bite prior to onset.

Blood tests show WBC 12.4 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 0.9 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 110 g/L and CRP 42 mg/L. Blood cultures remain negative and routine bacterial culture of the wound yields no pathogenic growth after 48 hours.

Soft-tissue ultrasound of the calf demonstrates a long tubular anechoic structure in the subcutaneous plane measuring at least 30 cm in visible length, with surrounding oedema and a tract extending towards the skin ulcer. Venous duplex study shows no deep venous thrombosis.

During a bedside procedure gentle traction on material emerging from the ulcer delivered an intact, slender, white cylindrical organism approximately 60 cm long that was photographed and sent to parasitology; the wound was irrigated and the patient reported progressive pain relief over the following week with resolution of serous drainage and restored ability to weight-bear.

explanation: A long, subcutaneous adult female nematode emerging from a skin ulcer in a patient who waded in stagnant fresh water fits infection with Dracunculus medinensis. The sterile wound cultures, peripheral eosinophilia, imaging showing a long tubular subcutaneous structure, and clinical improvement after extraction support this diagnosis.

hints.text: A 19-year-old university student presents to the emergency department with five days of worsening sore throat, progressive left-sided neck pain and swelling, and two days of pleuritic chest pain with blood-tinged sputum. He is febrile to 39.2°C, heart rate 116/min, respiratory rate 24/min and SpO2 91% on room air. On exam he has tender, firm swelling along the left lateral neck beneath the angle of the mandible and reduced neck extension.

He was previously well. The illness began as a sore throat and malaise nine days ago; he briefly took a three-day course of oral amoxicillin prescribed in primary care for presumed bacterial pharyngitis with initial improvement followed by recrudescence of fever and new chest symptoms. He denies recent dental procedures, intravenous drug use, foreign travel, or immunosuppression.

Admission bloods show white blood cell count 22.3 × 10^9/L with 88% neutrophils and C-reactive protein 246 mg/L. Two sets of blood cultures flagged positive in the anaerobic bottles at 48 hours; Gram stain from the anaerobic bottle demonstrated pleomorphic gram-negative rods.

Contrast CT of neck and chest demonstrates a non-opacified segment of the left internal jugular vein consistent with thrombosis and multiple bilateral peripheral nodular cavitary lesions in both lungs, findings felt most consistent with septic emboli.

The patient remained febrile on empiric ceftriaxone and vancomycin. Metronidazole was added to cover anaerobes and within 48 hours fevers settled and oxygenation improved. Final anaerobic culture at the reference laboratory identified an obligate anaerobic, non-spore-forming gram-negative bacillus originating from oropharyngeal flora that was metronidazole-susceptible.

explanation: The clinical sequence and microbiology strongly support the identified obligate anaerobic gram-negative bacillus as the cause.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man presented to a regional hospital with 10 days of fever, diffuse myalgia, and a progressively painful sore throat that impaired swallowing. He complained of lightheadedness when standing and increasing fatigue. On arrival he was febrile to 38.8 °C, heart rate 112/min, blood pressure 94/62 mmHg, and appeared dehydrated. The oropharynx was erythematous with scattered petechial spots on the soft palate.

He was previously well and had taken a short course of oral amoxicillin prescribed at a primary clinic without improvement. He works in hospital environmental services and reported that two coworkers had recent febrile illnesses, one requiring brief admission. He had no known chronic illnesses and was not on regular medications.

Initial blood tests showed leucopenia with a white cell count 2.4 × 10^9/L and thrombocytopenia with platelets 65 × 10^9/L. Alanine aminotransferase 240 U/L and aspartate aminotransferase 680 U/L. Creatinine 150 μmol/L. Urinalysis showed proteinuria and microscopic haematuria. Malaria rapid test and two sets of aerobic blood cultures were negative.

Chest radiograph showed mild bilateral interstitial markings and a small bilateral pleural effusion. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated mild hepatomegaly without focal lesions and a spleen at the upper limit of normal size. Non-contrast CT brain was normal.

Further history revealed he had returned three weeks earlier from a six-week stay in rural eastern Sierra Leone helping on a relative's farm. He had slept in a mud-walled dwelling where household rodents were frequently seen and food stores were noted to be contaminated with droppings. Local public health identified a small household cluster of febrile illnesses during his visit, including a pregnant family member who died.

explanation: The combination of prolonged febrile pharyngitis, progressive systemic illness with leucopenia and thrombocytopenia, markedly elevated AST, and a history of recent rural travel to West Africa with peridomestic rodent exposure and a household cluster points to infection with Lassa virus. The clinical picture and exposures explain the mucosal petechiae, renal involvement, and risk to close contacts and pregnant patients.

hints.text: A 38-year-old previously well male research assistant presented to the emergency department on day 6 of illness with high fever, severe myalgia, diffuse abdominal pain and profuse watery diarrhoea. He was hypotensive at 86/52 mmHg, tachycardic 118/min, febrile to 39.7°C and noted to have injected conjunctivae and scattered petechiae on his palate. Urine output was markedly reduced since the previous day and he was lethargic but arousable.

He had returned 10 days before symptom onset from a 12-day field study in rural southern Uganda where the team sampled water and surveyed abandoned mine workings. He reported spending several nights inside an old limestone shaft while carrying equipment and walking through accumulations of bat guano. He took intermittent antimalarial prophylaxis and had no chronic medical conditions or immunosuppression.

Initial labs showed white blood cell count 2.1 × 10^9/L, platelet count 28 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 135 g/L, creatinine 220 μmol/L. Liver enzymes were markedly elevated with AST 1 250 U/L and ALT 680 U/L. Coagulation studies revealed INR 2.6, activated partial thromboplastin time prolonged, fibrinogen 0.9 g/L and lactate 6.8 mmol/L. Blood cultures and malaria thick films were negative.

Contrast CT abdomen performed because of worsening pain showed diffuse small-bowel and colonic wall thickening with mucosal hyperenhancement, moderate ascites and no localized intra-abdominal collection. Chest radiograph showed developing bilateral patchy air-space opacities.

A high-containment reference laboratory examined the patient’s serum. Electron microscopy demonstrated long filamentous viral particles, and a specialised molecular assay detected a high load of a single-stranded negative-sense RNA virus that matched sequences previously recovered from haemorrhagic fever outbreaks linked to caves and mines in that region.

explanation: Severe febrile illness after time spent in an African mine with bat guano exposure, early leukopenia and profound thrombocytopenia, marked transaminase elevation and consumptive coagulopathy indicate a viral haemorrhagic fever. Identification of long filamentous virions and negative-sense RNA in a reference laboratory together with the exposure history support a diagnosis of Marburg virus infection.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man presented to a regional hospital with an eight-week history of a productive cough and three episodes of frank haemoptysis. He reported gradually worsening left-sided pleuritic chest pain and exertional breathlessness, and had lost 4 kg over two months. On examination temperature was 37.9°C, respiratory rate 20/min, oxygen saturation 95% on air, and chest auscultation revealed reduced breath sounds and coarse crackles at the left base.

He was previously well, HIV negative, and a non-smoker. Two months before cough onset he had travelled for two weeks to rural river valleys in Southeast Asia where he attended several communal meals; he received a week of oral amoxicillin from a local clinic without improvement. He denied known tuberculosis contact and had no recent hospital admissions or intravenous procedures.

Full blood count showed WBC 11.8 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 2.8 × 10^9/L (24%). C-reactive protein was 48 mg/L. Three sputum specimens were negative for acid fast bacilli by smear and mycobacterial culture remained sterile at two weeks. Thoracentesis yielded a serous exudative effusion with pleural fluid WBC 1.2 × 10^9/L composed of 67% eosinophils, protein 42 g/L, LDH 360 U/L, and pH 7.36.

Chest CT demonstrated a 3.5 cm thick-walled cavitary lesion in the posterior segment of the left lower lobe with adjacent patchy consolidation and several small subpleural nodules. A moderate left pleural effusion was present with subtle linear bandlike opacities extending from the cavity toward the pleura. No mediastinal lymphadenopathy was seen.

On further questioning he recalled eating a local dish containing undercooked freshwater crab during the river festival. Direct microscopy of a fresh sputum wet mount and of centrifuged pleural fluid identified ovoid, operculated eggs measuring about 80–100 μm by 45–70 μm, consistent with a trematode that infects the lung.

explanation: The combination of subacute haemoptysis, peripheral and marked pleural eosinophilia, cavitary and subpleural nodular lung lesions, travel to a freshwater river area with ingestion of undercooked crab, and demonstration of operculated eggs in sputum/pleural fluid indicates infection with Paragonimus westermani. These clues separate it from bacterial pneumonia and pulmonary tuberculosis and point to a trematode pulmonary infestation confirmed by egg detection.

hints.text: A 52-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 5 days of progressive frontal headache, malaise and new confusion. On examination he was febrile at 38.4 °C, had photophobia and nuchal rigidity, and was somnolent but intermittently oriented to person and place.

He received a deceased-donor kidney transplant 18 days before presentation and is maintained on tacrolimus, mycophenolate and prednisone. The operation and early recovery were uncomplicated, the donor had an unexpected intracranial bleed, and two other organ recipients from the same donor have developed febrile illnesses in the same interval.

Lumbar puncture showed opening pressure 260 mmH2O, CSF white cell count 160 × 10^6/L with 90% lymphocytes, protein 1.2 g/L and glucose 3.3 mmol/L (serum glucose 6.6 mmol/L). Blood tests revealed leukopenia 1.8 × 10^9/L, thrombocytopenia 85 × 10^9/L and transaminitis with AST 220 U/L and ALT 140 U/L. CSF Gram stain and bacterial cultures were negative and PCRs for herpes simplex virus, varicella zoster virus and enterovirus were negative.

Brain MRI showed diffuse leptomeningeal contrast enhancement and patchy T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the medial temporal lobes and periventricular white matter. Susceptibility-weighted sequences disclosed a few tiny foci of microhaemorrhage not accounted for by infarct.

Public health investigation found the donor worked in a rodent breeding facility and kept pet hamsters at home. PCR testing of archived donor organ tissue and specimens from the donor's mouse colony yielded an identical sequence to the virus detected in this patient's CSF.

explanation: Post-transplant meningoencephalitis with lymphocytic CSF, negative routine viral PCRs, concurrent illness in other recipients and identical viral sequences recovered from donor tissues and the donor's rodent colony indicate transmission from an infected rodent to the organ donor and then to recipients. These findings are most consistent with lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus as the cause of this patient's meningoencephalitis.

hints.text: A 48-year-old man presented to the regional hospital with a 2-week history of diarrhoea that progressed from watery to bloody stools. He reported 8–12 bowel movements per day, crampy lower abdominal pain, fatigue with a 4 kg weight loss, and on arrival had temperature 38.5°C and marked right lower quadrant tenderness on palpation.

He lives in a rural village and performs general outdoor work; he has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and no known immunosuppressive therapy. Two weeks before symptom onset he drank untreated well water intermittently while helping with heavy chores for neighbours; he denied recent international travel or antibiotic use.

Laboratory tests showed white blood cell count 14.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance, haemoglobin 98 g/L and C-reactive protein 120 mg/L. Stool testing returned positive for fecal leukocytes and occult blood, bacterial culture and Clostridioides difficile toxin were negative; routine stool ova and parasite screening had been requested and was pending.

Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen demonstrated segmental wall thickening of the cecum and ascending colon with pericolonic fat stranding, without discrete abscess. Colonoscopy showed multiple deep, discrete ulcers in the cecum and proximal colon with friable surrounding mucosa; endoscopic biopsies revealed acute mucosal necrosis and heavy neutrophilic inflammation but no organisms identified on initial H&E.

On further questioning he admitted daily assistance with his neighbour's small-scale pig herd and frequent handling of fresh manure. A stool wet mount performed because of the exposure showed large, actively motile trophozoites about 50–150 μm in size with uniform surface ciliation and a single large, kidney-shaped macronucleus; thick-walled cyst forms were also seen.

explanation: The patient has an inflammatory colitis with fever, right-sided colonic ulcers, neutrophilic peripheral leukocytosis and negative routine bacterial studies. The history of close contact with swine plus identification of very large motile trophozoites bearing surface cilia and a kidney-shaped macronucleus on stool wet mount is diagnostic for the ciliated protozoan causing zoonotic colitis in people exposed to pig faeces.

hints.text: A 52-year-old man presents with a 5-month history of productive cough, night sweats, progressive weight loss of 10 kg and a painful ulcer on the hard palate. On examination he is afebrile at 37.4°C, has a 2.5 cm indurated ulcer with a friable granular base on the right posterior hard palate and several firm, nonfluctuant cervical lymph nodes measuring 2–3 cm.

He is a current smoker with a 20 pack-year history and drinks alcohol socially. He emigrated from a rural region of South America 12 years ago and has had multiple outpatient courses of amoxicillin and doxycycline without improvement; he is not known to be immunosuppressed and is HIV antibody negative.

Haemoglobin 105 g/L, white blood cell count 11.8 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 0.9 × 10^9/L, CRP 46 mg/L and ESR 62 mm/h. Sputum acid fast smear and nucleic acid amplification for Mycobacterium tuberculosis are negative.
Chest CT shows bilateral, predominantly upper-lobe reticulonodular opacities with several thin-walled cavities and mild mediastinal lymphadenopathy, without focal lobar consolidation.

He reports childhood and young-adult work as a farm labourer disturbing soil and plant material. Biopsy of the palatal ulcer sent for mycology grew a dimorphic fungus: at 25°C it produced mould colonies and at 37°C yeast colonies; microscopy from the yeast phase showed large mother cells with multiple narrow-based buds radiating from a single cell.

explanation: Chronic pulmonary disease with mucosal ulceration and cervical lymphadenopathy in a middle-aged man from rural South America, together with culture showing a thermally dimorphic fungus and characteristic multiple-budding yeast morphology, supports infection with Paracoccidioides brasiliensis.

hints.text: A 62-year-old man in the surgical intensive care unit on day 12 after emergency sigmoid resection developed new fever and worsening oxygenation. Over 48 hours he became febrile to 38.9°C, heart rate 110/min, his ventilator FiO2 requirement rose from 40% to 70%, and staff noted copious purulent tracheal secretions with new right-sided crackles on auscultation.

His background includes type 2 diabetes and COPD. He required endotracheal intubation on admission with tracheostomy on day 5, has a right internal jugular central line, and received 10 days of broad-spectrum therapy including meropenem and vancomycin for intra-abdominal sepsis; he underwent bronchoscopy with saline lavage on day 10.

Blood tests show WBC 15.8 × 10^9/L and CRP 220 mg/L. A tracheal aspirate Gram stain shows Gram-negative rods and preliminary culture yielded a non-fermenting Gram-negative bacillus with an antibiogram resistant to meropenem and gentamicin and susceptible to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and levofloxacin.

Chest radiograph and subsequent CT show a new dense consolidation in the right lower lobe with surrounding patchy air-space opacities and small bilateral peribronchial infiltrates, no cavitation, and no large pleural effusion.

Environmental cultures from the ICU found the same non-fermenting Gram-negative organism with an identical antibiogram in a sink aerator and on the reusable bronchoscope washing tray; the isolates matched the patient’s tracheal aspirate by laboratory typing.

explanation: Hospital-acquired ventilator-associated pneumonia after prolonged carbapenem exposure, isolation of a non-fermenting Gram-negative bacillus resistant to carbapenems but susceptible to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and identical environmental isolates from water and bronchoscopic equipment point to Stenotrophomonas maltophilia. The outbreak-linked environmental source and antibiogram are characteristic and explain the clinical course.

hints.text: A 35-year-old man presented to the regional hospital with four weeks of fever, night sweats, nonproductive cough and 8 kg weight loss. He was febrile to 38.6°C, respiratory rate 22/min, had multiple non-tender cervical and inguinal lymph nodes and new hepatosplenomegaly on palpation.

He was diagnosed with HIV three months earlier and had not yet started antiretroviral therapy or opportunistic infection prophylaxis. Recent laboratory testing showed a CD4 count of 45 × 10^6/L and an HIV viral load of 1.2 × 10^6 copies/mL.

Blood tests showed haemoglobin 85 g/L, leucocyte count 2.2 × 10^9/L with neutropenia, platelets 90 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 72 mg/L. Bone marrow aspirate with Giemsa stain demonstrated numerous small oval yeastlike organisms inside macrophages, and peripheral blood cultures later became positive for yeast forms.

Contrast chest CT demonstrated bilateral diffuse reticulonodular and peribronchial nodules with mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Abdominal ultrasound confirmed splenomegaly to 15 cm without discrete focal hepatic lesions.

He emigrated from northern Thailand nine months earlier after years working on river valley rice farms. After seven days incubation a blood culture isolate grew a mould at 25°C that produced a diffusible red pigment and the same isolate converted to a yeast phase when incubated at 37°C.

explanation: Advanced untreated HIV with disseminated febrile illness, marrow intracellular yeast, and a dimorphic blood culture that produces a red diffusible pigment at lower temperature and converts to yeast at 37°C fits Talaromyces marneffei. The culture phenotype together with the Southeast Asia exposure clinches the diagnosis.

hints.text: A 62-year-old man presented to the respiratory clinic with 10 days of worsening productive cough, pleuritic left-sided chest pain and low-grade fevers. He had tachypnoea of 22 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 91% on room air and purulent sputum, and was limited to walking 50 metres before dyspnoea worsened.

He has known non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis diagnosed eight years ago after recurrent pneumonias, and type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. Five days before presentation he finished a 10-day outpatient course of oral levofloxacin for a presumed exacerbation with only modest symptomatic improvement.

Blood tests showed WBC 15.8 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 96 mg/L. Sputum culture incubated on routine media produced a non-lactose fermenting gram-negative rod after 48 hours; the isolate had an unusual antibiogram with resistance to gentamicin and colistin but retained susceptibility to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and ceftazidime. Blood cultures were negative.

High-resolution CT thorax demonstrated cylindrical bronchiectasis most pronounced in the right middle lobe and lingula, a new left lower lobe consolidation with small central cavitation, and small adjacent pleural fluid.

Environmental cultures from the patient’s home jet nebulizer and a multi-dose saline bottle used at his outpatient respiratory clinic grew the same non-fermenting gram-negative bacillus with an identical antibiogram and matching molecular fingerprint; the organism also grew in solutions containing benzalkonium chloride.

explanation: A patient with chronic non-CF bronchiectasis and progressive purulent sputum developed infection with a multidrug-resistant non-fermenting gram-negative bacillus. Recovery of the same organism from contaminated aqueous respiratory equipment and its ability to persist in antiseptic-containing solutions strongly points to an opportunistic environmental non-fermenter known to cause respiratory colonization and outbreaks in patients with chronic lung disease.

hints.text: A 34-year-old previously well man presented to a district hospital with five days of high fevers, rigors, severe headache and progressive lethargy. On arrival he was febrile to 39.8°C, pulse 116/min, blood pressure 105/65 mmHg, noted to be jaundiced with dark urine and complained of reduced urine output over 24 hours.

He had returned eight days earlier from a two-week field survey in northern Borneo where he slept in makeshift forest camps and worked at dawn and dusk. He did not take any chemoprophylaxis, recalled numerous mosquito bites, had no chronic illnesses and no previous history of blood-borne infections.

Initial blood tests showed haemoglobin 88 g/L, platelet count 48 × 10^9/L, total bilirubin 65 µmol/L, lactate dehydrogenase 780 U/L, creatinine 120 µmol/L and C-reactive protein 38 mg/L. Thick and thin blood films demonstrated parasitaemia estimated at 2.4% of erythrocytes with mixed parasite stages; two rapid antigen tests for common human erythrocytic parasites were non-diagnostic and a pan-target PCR was sent to reference laboratory.

Abdominal ultrasound showed a spleen length of 16.5 cm without focal lesions. On hospital day 3 the patient developed worsening oxygenation and chest radiograph demonstrated new bilateral interstitial opacities consistent with evolving lung injury.

While working in the camps he repeatedly observed long-tailed macaques close to sleeping shelters and a number of co-workers reported brief febrile illnesses after the trip. Real-time PCR from the reference laboratory returned positive for an erythrocytic parasite that completes its asexual erythrocytic cycle every 24 hours and is known to circulate in macaque reservoirs in forested areas of Southeast Asia, confirming a simian-origin infection.

explanation: The combination of recent forest exposure in northern Borneo with nocturnal mosquito bites, marked thrombocytopenia and haemolytic features, mixed-stage parasitaemia and a PCR result indicating a 24-hour erythrocytic cycle points to Plasmodium knowlesi. Splenomegaly and progressive lung involvement reflect known potential for severe disease with this simian-origin parasite.

hints.text: A 68-year-old retired schoolteacher presented in late August with 3 days of fever, progressive confusion, and a new unsteady gait. On arrival temperature 38.6°C, pulse 98/min, blood pressure 142/78 mmHg, Glasgow Coma Scale 13 for disorientation; exam notable for mild bilateral pronator drift and a coarse intention tremor on finger-to-nose testing.

She lives in a midwestern river-valley city and had no recent travel or hospital admissions. Past medical history includes hypertension and well controlled type 2 diabetes on metformin; she had a 48-hour prodrome of headache and myalgias before cognitive decline and takes no immunosuppressive drugs.

Lumbar puncture on hospital day 2: opening pressure 18 cm H2O, CSF WBC 140 × 10^6/L with 80% lymphocytes, protein 1.1 g/L, glucose 3.5 mmol/L with serum glucose 6.8 mmol/L. CSF bacterial culture and PCR for herpes simplex and enteroviruses were negative. Peripheral white cell count 9.8 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 6 mg/L.

MRI brain on day 2 showed bilateral T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in the thalami and caudate nuclei with mild surrounding oedema and no diffusion restriction. Routine EEG demonstrated diffuse background slowing without epileptiform discharges.

Local public-health alerts reported increased mosquito activity and multiple dead corvids in her neighbourhood that week. Paired serum and CSF testing returned positive IgM directed at a mosquito-borne arbovirus; plaque reduction neutralization testing produced a fourfold higher neutralizing titre to the urban midwestern North American arbovirus than to other regional mosquito-borne viruses.

explanation: An older adult with late-summer onset of fever, rapid cognitive decline, CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis, and basal ganglia/thalami MRI changes suggests a mosquito-borne neuroinvasive viral infection. Detection of specific IgM in CSF and serum with neutralization favouring the urban midwestern arbovirus confirms infection by St. Louis encephalitis virus.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presents to a sexual health clinic with 3 weeks of intense nocturnal groin itching and disturbed sleep. He reports multiple excoriations and erythematous papules across the pubic region and proximal inner thighs, temperature 36.9°C, and no urethral discharge.

He reports a new sexual partner six weeks ago and inconsistent condom use. He denies recent travel but says both he and his partner have been sharing towels and slept in the same bed the week before symptoms began.

Sexually transmitted infection screening was negative. Full blood count shows white cell count 7.4 × 10^9/L and eosinophils 0.30 × 10^9/L. Bacterial swab from an excoriated papule grew normal skin flora.

Dermatoscopy of the pubic hair-bearing skin reveals numerous small, oval, translucent eggs firmly cemented to the shafts of coarse hairs and occasional tiny, wingless insects clasping individual hairs with stout forelegs.

On return visit the patient brings a video from his partner showing several minute, broad-bodied insects clinging to pubic hair and a few similar organisms visible on the partner's eyelashes. Both partners report itching and visible 'specks' on hair.

explanation: Nocturnal groin pruritus with excoriations and eggs cemented to coarse hair shafts points to an obligate ectoparasite that lays nits on terminal hair. The dermatoscopy morphology and involvement of eyelashes in the partner narrow the diagnosis to the broad-bodied, grasping-legged hair-clinging parasite seen here.

hints.text: A 29-year-old man presented to outpatient clinic with a 3-month history of intermittent crampy abdominal pain, postprandial bloating, and a 5 kg unintentional weight loss. He also noted episodic perianal pruritus and occasional loose stools. On examination he was afebrile, pulse 78/min, blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, and had mild conjunctival pallor without abdominal tenderness or organomegaly.

He was born and raised in a river-valley rural district and moved to the regional city 9 months ago for work. He has no chronic illnesses and takes no immunosuppressive medications. He reports regularly attending family gatherings where home slaughter of livestock occurred and often ate meat prepared at those events, but he denies foreign travel outside the region.

Full blood count showed haemoglobin 110 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 76 fL, neutrophils 4.0 × 10^9/L and eosinophils 1.4 × 10^9/L. Routine stool bacterial culture and assays for common protozoa were negative. Faecal occult blood was intermittently positive and concentrated stool parasitology was requested.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a slender, curvilinear echogenic structure about 2–3 mm in width within the lumen of the proximal colon that changed position with patient manoeuvres. CT enterography showed no mural thickening or obstruction and no extraintestinal lesions.

Two days later the patient brought a pale segmented ribbon expelled in stool. Macroscopic length measured about 3.6 m and width approximately 3 mm. Microscopy of gravid proglottids showed more than 20 lateral uterine branches per side and the scolex lacked hooklets. He confirmed frequent consumption of lightly cooked strips of local meat at family events.

explanation: The patient expelled an intact long strobila and microscopy demonstrated numerous lateral uterine branches with a scolex without hooklets, findings diagnostic for the beef tapeworm, Taenia saginata. The chronic intermittent abdominal symptoms, mild eosinophilia and iron deficiency reflect prolonged intestinal colonisation by this cestode.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presents to a sexual health clinic with three weeks of intense itching localized to the groin and suprapubic region, worst at night. On examination he has multiple excoriated papules on the scrotum and over the pubic hair, temperature 36.8°C, and sleep disturbed by the pruritus.

He reports a new sexual partner one month ago and intermittent condom use. He denies recent travel, systemic symptoms, or previous dermatologic disease. He bathes daily and uses shared towels at the gym occasionally.

Complete blood count shows leukocytes 6.2 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 0.2 × 10^9/L. Nucleic acid amplification tests for common urethral sexually transmitted pathogens are negative. Bacterial swab of an excoriation grows mixed skin flora only.
Dermatoscopic inspection of pubic hair at 10× magnification shows small dark specks adherent at hair bases and tiny translucent ovoid structures attached along individual hair shafts.

On targeted microscopy of removed material a 1.5 to 2 mm wingless arthropod was seen clasping a pubic hair with stout grasping legs and several elongate eggs cemented to hair shafts. The patient reports his partner had similar symptoms.

explanation: Localized nocturnal pruritus in the pubic region with papular excoriations and dermatoscopic identification of eggs attached to terminal hairs point to an infestation by a small, clawed, hair-clinging arthropod acquired by close sexual contact. Negative STI tests and normal blood counts make other infectious dermatoses less likely.

hints.text: A 24-year-old woman presents to the university health clinic with a 3-week history of intense pruritus localized to the groin and both axillae. She reports worse itching at night with sleep disruption, and examination shows multiple excoriated erythematous papules in the inguinal folds and scattered follicular papules in the axillae, temperature 36.8°C and otherwise well.

She is sexually active and began a relationship with a new partner about 6 weeks ago. She tried over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream and oral antihistamines without relief, denies recent travel, has no chronic immunosuppressive conditions, and the partner noted onset of similar itching around the same time.

Complete blood count shows WBC 7.2 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 0.2 × 10^9/L. Bacterial culture from excoriated lesions grew mixed skin flora. Skin scraping for mites was negative and potassium hydroxide preparation showed no fungal elements.

Dermoscopy of inguinal hair demonstrates multiple small, oval translucent adherent structures firmly attached along hair shafts, each approximately 0.5 mm, and a few dark brown particulate fragments at hair bases.

She produces a photograph from her partner taken at home showing tiny slow-moving insects clinging to groin hair, with prominent grasping forelegs visible and small whitish eggs glued to hair shafts after recent intimate skin-to-skin contact and occasional shared bedding.

explanation: Localized severe pruritus of groin and axillae with nocturnal worsening, negative scabies scraping, dermoscopic adherent oval eggs on hair shafts, and a partner photo showing slow-moving insects with grasping forelegs after intimate contact point to an infestation by a hair-clinging ectoparasite transmitted by close sexual or skin-to-skin exposure. These features distinguish it from scabies and fungal or allergic dermatitis and explain the clustered distribution on coarse body hair.

hints.text: A 29-year-old male with a lower-leg blast injury presents three weeks after field debridement with increasing malodorous wound drainage, low-grade fever to 38.1 °C and progressive pain that limits weight bearing. On examination the wound margin is erythematous with purulent drainage and exposed cortical bone at the distal tibia.

He underwent multiple debridements and external fixation at a forward field surgical unit, received short courses of ceftriaxone and metronidazole there, and was evacuated to a tertiary hospital two weeks ago for repeat washouts. He is otherwise healthy and not immunosuppressed.
Leukocyte count 12.2 × 10^9/L and CRP 154 mg/L. Blood cultures remain negative. Serial wound swabs were sent and poor clinical response followed initial empiric therapy with vancomycin and cefepime.

Plain radiographs show cortical irregularity and a developing sequestrum of the distal tibia. MRI demonstrates a contiguous sinus tract to a 2 cm intramedullary abscess with marrow edema consistent with chronic osteomyelitis.

Repeated wound cultures grew a monomicrobial oxidase-negative, non-fermenting Gram-negative coccobacillus that grew on MacConkey agar. The isolate was resistant to ceftazidime, cefepime, gentamicin and levofloxacin and remained susceptible to ampicillin-sulbactam and colistin. Environmental swabs from the field operating tent and a contaminated saline bag yielded genetically indistinguishable isolates.

explanation: A delayed post-traumatic wound and osteomyelitis after forward-field surgery with persistent isolates that are oxidase-negative non-fermenters and demonstrate multi-drug resistance and environmental contamination is characteristic of Acinetobacter baumannii causing device- or environment-associated wound infections.

hints.text: A 19-year-old college student presents to the student health clinic with 48 hours of fever, sore throat, and rapidly developing red eyes. Temperature 39.0°C, bilateral conjunctival injection with watery discharge, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and diffuse pharyngeal erythema without heavy exudate; he reports no cough or shortness of breath.

He lives in a crowded dormitory and swam in the campus recreational pool four days before symptom onset. Two roommates had 'cold' symptoms earlier in the week and several classmates reported eye redness the same day he became ill.

Rapid streptococcal antigen test from a throat swab is negative. Complete blood count shows WBC 10.2 × 10^9/L with 58% lymphocytes and 1.2 × 10^9/L atypical lymphocytes on peripheral smear. A multiplex respiratory PCR on a nasopharyngeal swab detected a DNA respiratory virus, negative for influenza and RSV.
A frontal chest radiograph shows no focal consolidation or infiltrate. No orbital imaging was performed as ocular exam excluded proptosis and visual acuity remained intact.

Several other swimmers and lifeguards at the same pool developed concurrent pharyngitis with conjunctivitis. Conjunctival swab PCR and viral culture identified a non-enveloped, double-stranded DNA respiratory virus known to cause community outbreaks after pool exposure.

explanation: The combination of acute fever, pharyngitis, bilateral watery conjunctivitis, dormitory and swimming-pool exposures, lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes, and detection of a non-enveloped double-stranded DNA respiratory virus points to infection with adenovirus. Negative rapid strep and absence of lower respiratory findings support a mucosal pharyngoconjunctival syndrome rather than bacterial pharyngitis or influenza.

hints.text: A previously well 6-year-old boy presents with 48 hours of high fever to 39.5°C, sore throat and watery then purulent discharge from both eyes. He is eating poorly and has tender anterior cervical lymph nodes about 2 cm; pharynx is erythematous without discrete exudates.

Symptoms began two days after a week at a supervised community swimming programme where staff reported several children with conjunctivitis. He has no chronic medical conditions and his childhood immunisations are up to date.
Rapid streptococcal test on throat swab negative. CBC 10.8 × 10^9/L with relative lymphocytosis. Conjunctival swab sent for multiplex PCR and bacterial culture.

Topical antibiotic drops were given empirically. After six days of supportive care and topical therapy fever and conjunctival injection persisted and a follicular conjunctival response developed in both eyes.

Local public-health follow-up confirmed an outbreak of pharyngoconjunctival illness linked to the swimming programme. Conjunctival PCR identified a non-enveloped, linear double-stranded DNA virus notable for environmental stability and resistance to standard chlorination levels.

explanation: The sudden onset of fever, sore throat and bilateral conjunctivitis in a child with a swimming-pool outbreak is most consistent with an environmentally stable respiratory virus that causes pharyngoconjunctival illness.

hints.text: A 9-year-old boy presents on day 18 after allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplant with sudden gross haematuria, suprapubic pain and urinary frequency. He is febrile 38.2°C and voiding produces visibly bloody urine with clots.

Transplant conditioning included cyclophosphamide. Neutrophil engraftment occurred on day 12. He receives aciclovir prophylaxis and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. He had increasing bladder irritation at home and intermittent bladder irrigation was performed two days before the haematuria.

Urinalysis shows numerous erythrocytes and sterile pyuria. Bacterial urine cultures are negative. Serum creatinine is 48 µmol/L and haemoglobin 96 g/L. A urine PCR panel for viral pathogens was requested.
Pelvic ultrasound shows a bladder filled with clot material and no upper tract dilatation. There is no evidence of urinary tract obstruction or calculi.

Conservative measures and cessation of bladder irrigation failed to control bleeding. Urine PCR returned strongly positive for a non-enveloped, linear double-stranded DNA virus known to cause late-onset haemorrhagic cystitis after stem cell transplant.

explanation: Late-onset haemorrhagic cystitis after stem cell transplant with sterile pyuria, clotting and failure of conservative measures suggests a viral aetiology. A strongly positive urine PCR for a non-enveloped dsDNA virus known to cause post-transplant cystitis confirms the likely cause.

hints.text: A 19-year-old male recruit presents to the barracks clinic after five days of fever, severe cough and progressive dyspnoea. He is tachypnoeic and hypoxaemic with SpO2 90% on room air and auscultation reveals bilateral coarse inspiratory crackles.

He is in basic training where several trainees have developed febrile respiratory illnesses over the past two weeks. He was given two days of oral amoxicillin by the unit medic without improvement. He has no chronic lung disease.
CBC demonstrates WBC 12.5 × 10^9/L with relative lymphocytosis. CRP 120 mg/L. Sputum Gram stain shows no predominant bacteria. Nasopharyngeal PCR respiratory panel was sent.
Chest radiograph shows bilateral patchy perihilar and peribronchial air-space opacities without lobar consolidation or pleural effusion.

The field clinic identified a cluster of similar severe respiratory illnesses among recruits sleeping in close quarters. Nasopharyngeal PCR returned positive for a non-enveloped, linear double-stranded DNA virus historically linked to outbreaks of febrile respiratory disease in training camps.

explanation: A cluster of febrile respiratory illness among recruits with bilateral perihilar infiltrates and lymphocyte-predominant leukocytosis suggests a viral outbreak. A positive nasopharyngeal PCR for a non-enveloped double-stranded DNA virus associated with training camp outbreaks identifies the responsible pathogen.

hints.text: A 21-year-old man, three weeks after allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for acute myeloid leukaemia, presents with 48 hours of painful gross haematuria and dysuria. He is febrile to 38.2°C, tachycardic 105/min, and has suprapubic tenderness on palpation without flank pain.

His transplant course included myeloablative conditioning with cyclophosphamide and total body irradiation. He achieved neutrophil engraftment on day +14 but remains lymphopenic and is on tacrolimus and low-dose corticosteroids for mild graft versus host disease.
Bladder ultrasound shows diffuse bladder wall thickening and mobile echogenic material consistent with clot. No hydronephrosis or renal stones are visualised.
Continuous bladder irrigation and empirical intravenous ciprofloxacin produced no clinical improvement over 48 hours and haematuria persisted requiring transfusion support.
Urine PCR returns strongly positive with high copy number for a non-enveloped double-stranded DNA virus; simultaneous plasma PCR detects the same viral DNA at lower but measurable levels.

explanation: Post-transplant haemorrhagic cystitis with concurrent viraemia in a lymphopenic patient points to a viral aetiology. High-copy urine and detectable plasma DNA of a non-enveloped double-stranded DNA virus in this clinical context is most consistent with adenovirus infection causing urinary tract disease after stem cell transplant.

hints.text: A previously well 10-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department with 12 hours of severe intermittent abdominal pain, non-bilious vomiting, and several small bloody mucoid stools. He is febrile 38.4°C and on abdominal exam has a palpable right-sided 'sausage' mass and knees drawn to chest between pain episodes.

Parents report a five-day history of rhinorrhoea and low-grade fever with conjunctival injection that began a week before the abdominal pain. He attends a local daycare and had normal growth and vaccination history.
Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates a classic target sign in the right lower quadrant consistent with ileocolic intussusception, and moderate small-bowel dilatation proximal to the lesion.

Air contrast enema reduces the intussusception but the child redevelops similar symptoms eight hours later requiring repeat enema. Recurrence suggests a persistent lead point rather than a single mechanical event.
Stool PCR is positive for a non-enveloped double-stranded DNA virus at high copy number; no bacterial pathogens are identified by stool culture or multiplex PCR panel.

explanation: Recent upper respiratory and conjunctival symptoms followed by recurrent ileocolic intussusception in an infant suggest a viral trigger causing Peyer patch hyperplasia. Detection of high-copy non-enveloped double-stranded DNA viral DNA in stool supports adenovirus as the precipitant of the intussusception.

hints.text: A 56-year-old man presents with five days of progressive cough, high fever, and increasing dyspnoea that has worsened over 48 hours. On arrival he is tachypnoeic with oxygen saturation 88% on room air and requires supplemental oxygen, and he reports several episodes of watery diarrhoea over the preceding three days.
He is otherwise well and recently spent a weekend caring for his two young grandchildren who had viral upper respiratory illness. He is a non-smoker and has no chronic lung disease.

Chest radiograph shows bilateral patchy air-space consolidation, more pronounced in the perihilar regions. CT thorax demonstrates multifocal peribronchovascular consolidation with small areas of ground-glass change.

Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics and oseltamivir were started, but the patient deteriorated over 48 hours with escalating oxygen needs and rising serum transaminases despite negative bacterial cultures.

Respiratory multiplex PCR and plasma viral PCR are positive for a non-enveloped double-stranded DNA virus with a high respiratory viral load and detectable viraemia; bacterial and influenza testing remain negative.

explanation: Severe community-onset pneumonia with concurrent diarrhoea, elevated transaminases, and recent exposure to children with URTI points to a viral cause. High respiratory and plasma PCR for a non-enveloped double-stranded DNA virus in the absence of other pathogens supports adenovirus as the cause of fulminant respiratory and systemic disease.

hints.text: A 21-year-old male military recruit presents with five days of high fever, dry cough and progressive shortness of breath. On exam he is tachypnoeic with respiratory rate 28/min, heart rate 110/min and SpO2 89% on room air.
He moved into crowded barracks three weeks ago. Several bunkmates have had influenza-like illnesses since arrival. He is a current smoker and otherwise healthy.
Chest radiograph shows bilateral patchy air-space consolidations and peribronchial cuffing, worse in the right middle and lower zones. No focal lobar consolidation is identified.

He was started on empirical antibiotics for community-acquired pneumonia but has not improved after 72 hours. Blood and sputum bacterial cultures are sterile and inflammatory markers are only modestly elevated.
Respiratory viral PCR from a nasopharyngeal swab detected a nonenveloped double-stranded DNA virus that has caused outbreaks of febrile respiratory illness in barracks settings.

explanation: The epidemiology and sterile bacterial cultures argue against typical bacterial causes.

hints.text: A previously healthy 6-year-old boy is brought with a 6-month history of poor weight gain, pallor, and intermittent abdominal pain. On exam he is thin, has koilonychia, and heart rate 120 beats per minute.
Parents note he often eats dirt and plays without shoes in the compound near the household latrine. There is no history of overt gastrointestinal bleeding or chronic diarrhoea.
Haemoglobin 65 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 59 fL, serum iron low and transferrin saturation reduced. Absolute eosinophil count 2.1 × 10^9/L.
Chest radiograph obtained for a cough during clinic visit shows fleeting, patchy peripheral airspace opacities that were not present on a film taken 2 weeks earlier.
Family confirms the child routinely runs barefoot in contaminated soil around the latrine and occasionally eats mouthfuls of soil when playing.

explanation: Chronic iron-deficiency anaemia with marked eosinophilia in a toddler who practises geophagia and habitual barefoot play in contaminated soil, together with transient pulmonary infiltrates, strongly indicates infection by a soil-transmitted larval nematode that migrates through the lungs and later feeds on intestinal blood.

hints.text: A 33-year-old woman at 28 weeks' gestation presents with worsening fatigue and dizziness over 2 months. She is pale on exam and her blood pressure is 100/60 mmHg with a pulse of 105 beats per minute.
She emigrated from a rural region 6 months ago and reports no prior antenatal deworming. Her diet is limited and she denies overt gastrointestinal bleeding.
Haemoglobin 72 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 62 fL, ferritin 5 µg/L. Absolute eosinophil count 1.6 × 10^9/L.
Urgent upper endoscopy performed because of severe anaemia shows multiple slender organisms attached to the duodenal folds and mild adjacent petechial mucosal haemorrhage.
She reports frequent barefoot work in household vegetable gardens fertilised with untreated human waste before emigrating.

explanation: Pregnant woman with marked iron-deficiency anaemia and eosinophilia plus endoscopic identification of attached slender intestinal nematodes and a history of barefoot exposure to soil fertilised with human waste supports infection by a blood-feeding soil-transmitted intestinal nematode acquired through the skin.

hints.text: A 28-year-old woman at 28 weeks' gestation presented to the antenatal clinic with progressive fatigue and lightheadedness over two months. She had tachycardia to 110 bpm on examination and conjunctival pallor; fetal movements were reported as normal.

Her pregnancy had been uncomplicated until this presentation. She reported intermittent adherence to prescribed oral iron. She had no prior gastrointestinal bleeding, no recent transfusions, and no known chronic disease.

Obstetric ultrasound showed a single viable fetus with estimated gestational age consistent with dates and normal placental location. There were no sonographic signs of intraabdominal mass or acute pathology to explain blood loss.
She lives in a farming community and continues to work in irrigated rice paddies several times per week, often barefoot. Community practice includes use of untreated organic fertilizer.

Blood tests showed haemoglobin 68 g/L, MCV 68 fL, ferritin 6 µg/L and eosinophil count 1.6 × 10^9/L. Night-soil use was confirmed and stool microscopy on concentrated specimen plus duodenal aspirate yielded slender adult worms; inspection of the anterior end showed two pairs of prominent ventral buccal teeth.

explanation: Severe iron deficiency anemia with peripheral eosinophilia in a barefoot agricultural worker raises helminthic blood loss as a cause. Identification of adult worms with multiple buccal teeth on duodenal aspirate explains chronic intestinal blood loss and is diagnostic for the species implicated in this clinical setting.

hints.text: A 55-year-old man presented to the clinic with months of exertional dyspnoea and several episodes of melaena. He described syncope on standing last week and was orthostatic on examination with blood pressure 100/60 mmHg while supine and 80/50 mmHg on standing.

He works in an underground phosphate mine and reports barefoot walking in damp tunnel areas to retrieve tools. He takes no regular medications and has no history of peptic ulcer disease. He has a 30 pack-year smoking history.

Upper and lower endoscopies performed as part of initial bleeding evaluation were unremarkable apart from a small amount of fresh blood in the proximal small bowel that could not be localized to an ulcer. Abdominal ultrasound was normal.

Colleagues described informal sanitation in tunnel work areas with occasional human faecal contamination of walkways. He denies travel outside the region but reports regularly standing and working barefoot on moist soil surfaces.

Laboratory studies showed haemoglobin 72 g/L and eosinophils 2.0 × 10^9/L. Concentrated stool examination recovered an adult anterior worm fragment; microscopic inspection showed a buccal capsule bearing two pairs of robust ventral teeth.

explanation: Chronic iron loss with occult proximal small-bowel bleeding and prominent eosinophilia in a patient with barefoot exposure to contaminated soil suggests a blood-feeding intestinal helminth. Visualization of an adult anterior end with two pairs of buccal teeth confirms the diagnosis in this clinical context.

hints.text: A 72-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presented with a two-week history of dry cough, intermittent scant haemoptysis and increasing fatigue. He was afebrile and had bibasal crackles on chest auscultation with resting oxygen saturation 95% on room air.

He returned three weeks earlier from a month-long visit to relatives in a Mediterranean coastal town where he often walked on the beach at dusk. His diabetes is well controlled on metformin and he has no known pulmonary disease.
Chest radiograph showed a small patchy right middle lobe infiltrate. Repeat radiography three days later demonstrated migratory patchy opacities that resolved partially without antibiotic therapy.
He recalled walking barefoot on damp sand and reported occasional pruritic papules on his feet during the trip that resolved spontaneously. There were domestic dogs and cats at his relatives' home.

Full blood count showed haemoglobin 90 g/L and eosinophils 1.9 × 10^9/L. Sputum and stool concentrated examinations were performed; stool did not show diagnostic eggs but upper gastrointestinal endoscopy retrieved a live slender worm whose anterior buccal capsule displayed two pairs of prominent ventral teeth on microscopic inspection.

explanation: Transient pulmonary infiltrates with eosinophilia, anaemia, and a history of barefoot exposure on contaminated sand suggest a helminth with tissue migration. Endoscopic recovery of an adult with two pairs of ventral buccal teeth explains both the pulmonary symptoms from larval migration and intestinal blood loss, confirming the diagnosis.

hints.text: A 24-year-old woman presents to the clinic with three months of progressive fatigue, exertional dyspnoea and lightheadedness. She is pale on exam and heart rate is 112 beats/min, blood pressure 100/64 mmHg.

She returned three months ago from a six-month stay in a rural district of northern India where she had an uncomplicated vaginal delivery 10 weeks before presentation. She breastfeeds and reports poor appetite, intermittent abdominal discomfort and that iron tablets were stopped after the delivery.

Complete blood count shows haemoglobin 72 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 64 fL, white blood cells 8.9 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.3 × 10^9/L. Ferritin is 8 µg/L and a faecal occult blood test is positive; a routine stool microscopy shows oval eggs consistent with a small intestinal nematode.

Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy performed for ongoing bleeding shows several slender, motile worms attached to the duodenal mucosa, some with small amounts of adjacent fresh blood but no discrete ulcer.
After a single dose of an oral benzimidazole she passed a 12 mm reddish cylindrical adult. Light microscopy of the anterior end of the worm revealed two pairs of small teeth in the buccal cavity.

explanation: Severe microcytic anaemia with eosinophilia and live small intestinal worms explain chronic blood loss. The adult worm's buccal teeth on microscopy identify Ancylostoma duodenale as the cause in this patient who had recent exposure in an endemic rural area.

hints.text: A 29-year-old pregnant woman at 32 weeks gestation presents with worsening fatigue and exertional breathlessness over six weeks. She has marked conjunctival pallor and exertional tachycardia on examination.

She spent the first trimester visiting relatives in a rural community in southern Italy. She ate home-grown salads and reports an episode of itchy, erythematous lesions on the soles of her feet early in the trip that resolved spontaneously.

Haemoglobin is 68 g/L with MCV 62 fL, ferritin 6 µg/L and eosinophils 1.9 × 10^9/L. Faecal occult blood is positive and stool microscopy demonstrates eggs compatible with a blood-feeding small intestinal nematode.
Obstetric ultrasound shows mild fetal growth restriction but otherwise normal anatomy for gestational age. Maternal chest imaging is unremarkable.

She describes frequent consumption of raw vegetables fertilised with untreated human waste while visiting relatives in the rural region, an exposure known to allow this species to infect by oral ingestion as well as by skin penetration.

explanation: Severe iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy with eosinophilia, positive stool eggs and early 'ground itch' after travel combined with a history of consuming vegetables fertilised with untreated human waste supports Ancylostoma duodenale. Oral transmission in addition to percutaneous exposure helps explain heavy maternal blood loss.

hints.text: A 24-year-old woman at 28 weeks' gestation presents to a community clinic with three months of progressive fatigue and exertional dyspnoea. Pulse 110/min, blood pressure 98/60 mmHg, marked conjunctival pallor on exam and mild pedal oedema when standing.

She works barefoot in irrigated rice paddies near her village and has not received antenatal iron supplementation or deworming. She reports intermittent vague abdominal discomfort but no overt haematemesis or recent travel outside the region.
Haemoglobin 65 g/L, MCV 68 fL, ferritin 8 µg/L. White cell count 9.2 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.8 × 10^9/L. Stool occult blood positive on two samples.
Chest radiograph performed for pre‑anaesthetic assessment shows a small patchy right lower zone air‑space opacity that was not present on a chest film taken three weeks earlier.

She has worked barefoot in fields in northern India for the past two years and reports using night soil as fertiliser on some plots. Local public health records note persistent transmission of a soil‑transmitted nematode that commonly causes heavy iron‑deficiency anaemia in pregnant women.

explanation: Severe microcytic anaemia with eosinophilia, transient pulmonary infiltrate, positive faecal occult blood and barefoot agricultural exposure in an endemic region indicate hookworm infection. The epidemiology and heavy iron loss during pregnancy point to Ancylostoma duodenale as the most likely species.

hints.text: A 32-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 72 hours of progressive colicky abdominal pain, bilious vomiting, and abdominal distension. He was afebrile, pulse 110/min, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, abdomen distended with high-pitched bowel sounds and marked tympany on percussion.

He returned three weeks earlier from a community sanitation project in a rural region where he reported frequent barefoot work in vegetable beds and eating unwashed produce. He had no prior abdominal operations and no chronic gastrointestinal disease.
Blood tests showed WBC 14.2 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 2.4 × 10^9/L, sodium 132 mmol/L and mild metabolic alkalosis consistent with vomiting. C-reactive protein 36 mg/L.

Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen showed multiple long, tubular intraluminal filling defects within dilated jejunal loops with a clear transition point and proximal small-bowel dilation consistent with mechanical obstruction; there was no pneumatosis or free intraperitoneal air.

After nasogastric decompression and a single-dose oral anthelmintic, the patient passed several long, white cylindrical organisms in stool, up to 25 cm in length, and his bowel function returned over 48 hours.

explanation: These features explain the mechanical obstruction and clinical improvement after deworming.

hints.text: A 29-year-old woman at 18 weeks' gestation presented with sudden severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and repeated vomiting for 12 hours. Temperature 37.6°C, pulse 102/min, abdominal exam showed epigastric tenderness without peritonism.

She recently moved from an area with limited sanitation infrastructure and had intermittent biliary-type pain over the past year. She had no alcohol use and no prior gallstone history on earlier antenatal ultrasound.
Serum lipase 580 U/L, alanine transaminase 95 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 220 U/L. WBC 15.0 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 0.9 × 10^9/L.

Right upper quadrant ultrasound showed a dilated common bile duct to 9 mm containing a non-shadowing tubular echogenic structure that moved slightly with patient repositioning. Gallbladder had no bulky calculi and intrahepatic ducts were mildly dilated.

During endoscopic retrieval of the ductal contents several long, motile pale tubular organisms were removed from the common bile duct and the patient’s abdominal pain and enzyme elevations fell rapidly after the procedure.

explanation: Acute pancreatitis with imaging showing a movable tubular intraductal structure and subsequent endoscopic retrieval of motile tubular organisms indicates biliary invasion by a large intestinal nematode. The ductal obstruction explains the cholestatic enzymes and elevated lipase, and removal produced clinical improvement.

hints.text: A 14-year-old girl presented with 36 hours of right lower quadrant pain, anorexia and low-grade fever. On examination temperature 38.2°C, heart rate 96/min, there was focal tenderness and guarding at McBurney point with localized rebound.

She is from a semi-urban area with intermittent municipal water outages and had mild intermittent abdominal discomfort and poor weight gain for the past year. She had not received routine deworming at school.
WBC 12.5 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance and eosinophils 1.1 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein 48 mg/L, haemoglobin 110 g/L.

Right lower quadrant ultrasound showed a distended non-compressible tubular structure 9 mm diameter consistent with appendicitis; a faint internal central linear echogenicity was noted within the lumen but there was no calcification.

During appendicectomy a 12 cm smooth, white cylindrical organism was removed intact from the appendiceal lumen. Postoperative recovery was uncomplicated after the specimen was sent for parasitologic examination.

explanation: Appendicitis with ultrasound evidence of a linear intraluminal structure and intraoperative extraction of a long white worm indicates appendiceal obstruction by a large intestinal nematode. The perioperative eosinophilia and chronic exposure history support heavy intestinal helminth infection as the underlying cause.

hints.text: A 6-year-old boy is brought to a rural district hospital with 48 hours of worsening colicky abdominal pain, bilious vomiting, and progressive abdominal distension. He is febrile to 38.1°C, pulse 120/min, abdomen markedly distended with visible peristalsis and a palpable sausage-shaped mass in the right lower quadrant.

Parents report a two-week history of intermittent vague abdominal discomfort and poor appetite. The family subsists on small-scale farming, the child practices pica, and there has been no routine deworming.
CBC shows WBC 12.8 × 10^9/L, eosinophils 1.8 × 10^9/L and Hb 96 g/L. C-reactive protein 18 mg/L.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates multiple long, parallel tubular echogenic structures within the small-bowel lumen forming a clustered mass that shows spontaneous movement on repeat scanning. Plain abdominal radiograph demonstrates small-bowel dilatation consistent with obstruction.
On hospital day 1 the parents report passage of three pale cylindrical worms in the stool, each measuring approximately 10–18 cm; specimens were photographed and submitted to the laboratory.

explanation: Obstructive small-bowel symptoms with a palpable sausage mass and ultrasound showing multiple long tubular intraluminal structures point to an adult helminth bolus. Eosinophilia, pica, lack of deworming and passage of long pale cylindrical worms after presentation make the diagnosis most consistent with Ascaris lumbricoides.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presents with 10 days of nonproductive cough, intermittent wheeze and night sweats. He returned two weeks ago from voluntary work in a rural agricultural region and on exam has scattered wheeze and oxygen saturation 95% on room air.

While abroad he worked excavating irrigation channels and frequently ate unwashed raw vegetables. He experienced a brief episode of loose stools two weeks into his trip that resolved without treatment.
CBC shows WBC 14.0 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 2.3 × 10^9/L. CRP 6 mg/L and routine bacterial sputum studies were unrevealing.

Chest radiograph shows transient patchy air‑space opacities in the perihilar and lower-zone regions that were not present on a radiograph obtained five days earlier. CT chest shows small peripheral nodular opacities without cavitation.

Stool ova and parasite microscopy returns with numerous thick-shelled oval eggs with a coarse, rough outer coat and the laboratory forwards photomicrographs demonstrating the characteristic mammillated surface.

explanation: Fleeting pulmonary infiltrates with eosinophilia after agricultural soil exposure suggest a helminth with pulmonary migration. The presence of characteristic thick-shelled mammillated eggs in stool ties the clinical syndrome to Ascaris lumbricoides.

hints.text: A 32-year-old primigravida at 26 weeks presents with 12 hours of sudden severe right upper quadrant pain, high fever and new-onset jaundice. She is tachycardic to 110/min, appears ill and has a tender hepatomegaly on examination.

She relocated from a rural village two months ago where household wells are used for irrigation. She reports intermittent mid‑abdominal discomfort over the past year and has not received routine anthelmintic treatment during pregnancy.
Serum bilirubin 70 μmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 420 U/L and ALT 86 U/L. CBC shows WBC 16.5 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.4 × 10^9/L.

Right upper-quadrant ultrasound demonstrates a dilated common bile duct containing a linear tubular echogenic structure. Gentle transducer pressure elicits longitudinal motion of the structure within the duct.
During endoscopic retrograde cholangiography an approximately 20 cm pale, cylindrical, motile worm was seen emerging from the ampulla and was removed intact with forceps.

explanation: Acute cholangitis in a pregnant woman with ultrasound evidence of an intraductal motile tubular structure and extraction of a long motile cylindrical worm from the ampulla indicates biliary migration of a large intestinal nematode. This combination is most consistent with Ascaris lumbricoides causing biliary obstruction.

hints.text: A 24-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with three days of crampy, colicky periumbilical pain, progressive abdominal distension and intermittent bilious vomiting. On arrival she was afebrile, heart rate 108 beats/min, blood pressure 115/72 mmHg, abdomen distended with diffuse tenderness and visible high-pitched bowel sounds, and she had not opened her bowels for 24 hours.

She was otherwise healthy and had no prior abdominal surgery. Two weeks earlier she returned from a six-week field placement living with a host family in a rural region of South Asia where she helped in vegetable harvesting and sometimes drank unboiled well water.

Blood tests showed white blood cell count 13.6 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.9 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 24 mg/L, serum sodium 136 mmol/L and potassium 3.2 mmol/L. Routine stool bacterial culture and faecal occult blood were negative; a formal parasitology report was pending.

Abdominal radiograph demonstrated dilated small-bowel loops with multiple air-fluid levels consistent with small-bowel obstruction. Point-of-care ultrasound showed several long, curvilinear echogenic structures within the small-bowel lumen each with a central anechoic tube and limited independent peristalsis, some showing gentle movement on real-time imaging.

While receiving nasogastric decompression on hospital day 2 the patient noted passage of a single pale, cylindrical worm about 25 cm long in the stool; parasitology described an adult intestinal nematode with a thick cuticle and three prominent oral lips, and subsequent stool microscopy showed large oval fertilized eggs with a rough mammillated outer layer. Her hosts in the village reported common open defecation and use of untreated nightsoil as fertiliser.

explanation: The combination of subacute small-bowel obstruction, peripheral eosinophilia, ultrasound evidence of long intraluminal tubular organisms, and passage of a large adult nematode with three oral lips and mammillated eggs points to Ascaris lumbricoides infection causing mechanical intestinal obstruction after exposure to faecally contaminated soil and produce.

hints.text: A 28-year-old woman in her second trimester of pregnancy presents with 48 hours of severe right upper quadrant colicky pain, associated nausea and a single episode of vomiting. She is febrile at 38.3°C, icteric on exam, and tender in the right upper quadrant without guarding.

She travelled to visit relatives in a rural region overseas two weeks before presentation and ate home-prepared raw salads. She has not received recent anthelmintic treatment and reports occasional transient abdominal discomfort in the preceding months.
WBC 14.2 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.2 × 10^9/L. Total bilirubin 48 μmol/L and alkaline phosphatase 360 IU/L.
Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates a dilated common bile duct with a tubular, linear, non-shadowing echogenic structure within the lumen that shows intermittent motion on repeat scan.
Endoscopic extraction retrieved an 18 cm pale, motile cylindrical worm from the common bile duct, after which her pain and bilirubin rapidly improved.

explanation: RUQ pain, obstructive LFT pattern, a mobile tubular structure in the common bile duct on ultrasound, and removal of a long pale worm during endoscopy indicate migration of a large intestinal nematode into the biliary tree. Rapid clinical improvement after extraction supports a mechanical obstruction by a luminal parasite.

hints.text: A 35-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 48 hours of worsening colicky abdominal pain, bilious vomiting and failure to pass flatus or stool. He appears dehydrated, pulse 110/min, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, abdomen distended with generalized tenderness and hyperactive bowel sounds.

He recently emigrated from a region with limited sanitation and reports chronic intermittent abdominal discomfort for months. He has not had prior abdominal surgery and has not taken recent antiparasitic medication.
WBC 16.0 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 2.1 × 10^9/L. Serum electrolytes show mild hypokalaemia, potassium 3.2 mmol/L.

Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen shows small-bowel dilatation with an intraluminal conglomerate of tubular, rounded filling defects forming a central mass in the mid-ileum and a transition point consistent with a bolus obstruction.
At laparotomy the surgeon removed a tangle of numerous pale cylindrical worms occupying a metre of small intestine; the obstruction resolved after enterotomy and removal.

explanation: The clinical picture of small-bowel obstruction in a patient from an endemic area, marked eosinophilia, CT evidence of an intraluminal bolus, and surgical recovery of many long pale worms indicate heavy intestinal infection with a large luminal nematode. Removal of the worm bolus explains resolution of obstruction and symptoms.

hints.text: A previously healthy 8-year-old girl is brought with a 10-day history of dry cough, intermittent wheeze and low-grade fever. On arrival she has expiratory wheeze and scattered crackles over the right lower chest, oxygen saturation 97% on room air.
The family lives in a peri-urban area and the child has frequent pica, including eating soil and clay. No recent travel outside the region and vaccinations are current.

Chest radiograph shows a patchy right lower lobe air-space opacity that is subtle compared with symptoms; prior radiograph from eight days earlier showed a small left midzone patch that has since cleared.
Full blood count demonstrates WBC 9.4 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 3.0 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein 18 mg/L.
The mother produced a tissue in which the child had coughed up an 8 cm cream-coloured mobile worm the previous evening.

explanation: Recurrent transient pulmonary infiltrates, prominent eosinophilia, pica with soil ingestion, and expectoration of an 8 cm pale worm indicate larval migration through the lungs and the presence of a large intestinal nematode in the airway or gut. The expelled adult worm clinches the diagnosis in this clinical context.

hints.text: A 7-year-old boy from a rural village presents to the emergency department with 48 hours of colicky periumbilical abdominal pain, progressive abdominal distension, and repeated non-bloody vomiting. He has not passed stool for 24 hours. On examination temperature 37.8°C and pulse 110/min. The abdomen is diffusely distended with visible peristaltic waves and a palpable elongated, mobile mass in the right upper quadrant. Bowel sounds are high-pitched and the child appears mildly dehydrated.

He is previously well and helps his family in a backyard vegetable garden. His mother reports habitual soil eating when younger and frequent consumption of unwashed raw greens from the garden. The child has never received routine deworming and the household uses untreated human manure to fertilize crops.
Complete blood count shows white cell count 14.2 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.8 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein is 28 mg/L. A stool sample has been submitted for microscopy.

Supine abdominal radiograph shows multiple dilated small-bowel loops with prominent air-fluid levels consistent with small-bowel obstruction. Point-of-care abdominal ultrasound demonstrates clustered tubular echogenic structures with a central anechoic lumen occupying the proximal jejunum and moderate proximal dilatation.

The mother produces a smartphone photograph taken earlier that morning after an episode of severe retching, showing a pale, mobile cylindrical worm roughly 15 cm long that the child vomited. Several neighbours reported recent mass deworming campaigns because of widespread soil-transmitted helminth exposure in the community.
